title: Donald Trump tells Mobile rally to ‘pretend I’m on the ballot’

Mobile was the president’s second stop in a month-long campaign for Republican congressional candidates across […]
text:
President Donald Trump dances at the Mitchell Center at the University of South Alabama in Mobile, Alabama, on Oct. 2, 2026.  The president is visiting several red states in support of GOP nominees about a month ahead of midterm elections in November. (Dan Anderson for Alabama Reflector)MOBILE — President Donald Trump told a crowd of roughly 8,000 supporters Friday night to vote like he is on the ballot in November.
“Can everybody just close your eyes and pretend I’m on the ballot?” Trump asked the crowd.
Mobile was the president’s second stop in a month-long campaign for Republican congressional candidates across the country. Supporters lined up at the Mitchell Center on the University of South Alabama’s campus hours before doors opened. The building was roughly 75 percent full by the time Trump took the stage.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
Alabama is a Republican state, and Alabama’s 1st Congressional District – which Mobile falls in under a new map – is rated solidly Republican by Cook Political Report. The neighboring 2nd Congressional District, where incumbent U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Mobile faces state Rep. Rhett Marques, R-Enterprise, the GOP nominee, is considered more competitive. 
Trump said Friday he came to Alabama, and plans to go to other Republican states, to pay his respects to the people who love him. 
“Oklahoma and Alabama, I’m here to say hello,” he said. “I’m here because sometimes even though you don’t have to come here, you’ve got to pay respect to the people that have loved me every year.”
Trump’s approval rating has fallen across the country – and in Alabama – since the beginning of the Iran war in February and the subsequent increase in gas prices. He told attendees the war will end sometime after the midterms. 
“They’re never going to have a nuclear weapon,” he said. “As soon as it does end, oil prices will come tumbling down.” 
Trump-endorsed Alabama Republican nominees opened for Trump, including gubernatorial nominee and U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville, who walked on stage to Lynyrd Skynyrd’s “Sweet Home Alabama.” 
U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville, R-Alabama (left), the Republican nominee for governor of Alabama, shakes hands with President Donald Trump at the Mitchell Center at the University of South Alabama in Mobile, Alabama on October 2, 2026. The president is visiting several red states in support of GOP nominees about a month ahead of midterm elections in November. (Dan Anderson for Alabama Reflector)
Tuberville pledged to invest in workforce development as governor. 
“We’re going to use our hands. We’re going to teach people and our kids. We’re going to teach them education, and we’re going to teach them how to live a life, to do things with their hands and make decisions,” Tuberville said. 
Trump touted the Senate’s bipartisan passage of the Protect College Sports Act, and urged Alabamians to elect Tuberville as governor. The senator coached football at Auburn University from 1999 to 2008. 
“We’re going to pass something that brings sanity to college football. The Senate passed it, and we had a lot of help, bipartisan help. Can you believe it? Shocking,” Trump said. 
The president also reiterated his endorsements of U.S. Rep. Barry Moore, R-Enterprise, the nominee to replace Tuberville; Jerry Carl, the nominee for the 1st Congressional District; state Rep. Rhett Marques, R-Enterprise, the nominee for the 2nd Congressional District; John Wahl, the nominee for lieutenant governor and Florida gubernatorial nominee Byron Donalds. 
He also endorsed Katherine Robertson, the party’s nominee for Alabama Attorney General. He mentioned Republican U.S. Reps. Robert Aderholt of Haleyville, Dale Strong of Madison and Gary Palmer of Hoover, but said he did not need to “waste time” on them because they are “so far ahead.” He did not mention Republican nominee for the 7th Congressional District Ammie Akin, who is challenging U.S. Rep. Terri Sewell, D-Selma, or U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers, R-Saks. 
At the party’s midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, last month, Trump promised to give every U.S. adult citizen $5,000 if Republicans held the House and Senate. He doubled down Friday evening with a caveat: the money must be spent in the U.S.
“The Trump dividend is approximately $1 trillion, but we have a record-setting $21 trillion that’s being invested in our country in just 15 months,” he said. “When you spend it and recirculate it in our country, it costs us far less than it sounds.”
The nonpartisan Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget warned last month that Trump’s plan would cost about $1.2 trillion, and “explode” the nation’s deficit.
He criticized Democrats throughout his 90-minute speech, often referring to them as “dumocrats.” He also touted policies on economic development, immigration and lowering taxes.
Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones, who held a counter-event in Mobile Friday evening, accused Trump of coming to Mobile to soothe his ego.
“We were going to Mobile anyway, but then all of a sudden Trump started trolling me,” Jones said at a town hall. “I don’t think it’s about Tommy Tuberville. I think he is campaigning, not for a candidate, I think he’s campaigning to get the Mobile Bay bridge named after him.” 
Attendees were not allowed to bring their own signs, but signs were provided to them in the lower level of the area echoing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Signs read “No Tax on Overtime,” “No Tax On Tips,” “No Tax on Social Security” and “Lower Prices.” 
President Donald Trump speaks at the Mitchell Center at the University of South Alabama in Mobile, Alabama on October 2, 2026. The president is visiting several red states in support of GOP nominees about a month ahead of midterm elections in November. (Dan Anderson for Alabama Reflector)
Trump also criticized the “fake news media” which led to boos from the crowd directed at the press pool. 
“Our nation is doing better now than ever before. But the fake news media right back there … refuses to talk about our ranks and the numbers, so I have to do it myself,” Trump said. 
Each opening speaker urged attendees to vote Republican in November, and to spread the word. 
“We need each and everybody in this room to go out and vote, and get their neighbors, their family, and their friends to go vote,” Marques said. “We win if everybody in this state votes because we are a Republican state.”
Trump is expected to travel to Ohio over the weekend and Nebraska on Monday. He said he will attend the football game between the University of Alabama and the University of Georgia in Tuscaloosa on Oct. 10.

title: Candidates for Utah’s 3rd Congressional District clash on national monuments, nuclear energy
description: Candidates vying for Utah’s 3rd Congressional District made their pitches for what will be the largest district in the state, clashing over environmental issues, nuclear energy, forest management and the boundaries of Utah’s recently reduced national monuments.  Republican Rep. Celeste Maloy, going into her second general election candidacy, now for an updat[...]
text:
Celeste Maloy, left, listens as Kent Udell answers a question during a 3rd Congressional District debate at Utah Tech University in St. George, Friday, Oct. 2, 2026. (Pool photo by Jud Burkett special to The Tribune)Candidates vying for Utah’s 3rd Congressional District made their pitches for what will be the largest district in the state, clashing over environmental issues, nuclear energy, forest management and the boundaries of Utah’s recently reduced national monuments. 
Republican Rep. Celeste Maloy, going into her second general election candidacy, now for an updated district, faced Democratic nominee Kent Udell, a mechanical engineer in a debate held Friday at Utah Tech University in St George, moderated by Bob Evans from FOX 13 and broadcast by PBS Utah.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Maloy has represented Utah’s District 2 since late 2023. After the state’s congressional maps changed this year, she’s competing for the 3rd Congressional District’s seat, the home of Utah’s five national parks as well as posh ski resort cities, miles and miles of rural lands eyed by eager energy developers, and national monuments with controversial borders.
“I was standing in the Oval Office when the announcement was made about reducing the monument boundaries. So obviously, I support that decision. It was made by listening to elected officials from Utah,” Maloy said during the debate.
Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante are probably two of the most controversial monuments in the nation, Maloy said, because of the way they were created — by the executive branch.
Celeste Maloy answers a question during a 3rd Congressional District debate at Utah Tech University in St. George, Friday, Oct. 2, 2026. (Pool photo by Jud Burkett special to The Tribune)
“Congress should be making those decisions, and when Congress declares a national monument like Cedar Breaks, they tend to be uncontroversial.”
But, for Udell, the previous, larger boundaries, established by Democratic administrations “worked out great,” he said.
“To throw that out the window to disrupt our tourist industry, to disrupt our system, for what? A handful of sagebrush rebels and mining companies? No, that’s public land, and that needs to be protected for everybody,” Udell said, adding that if elected, he would work to get the former boundaries established by law.
Kent Udell answers a question during a 3rd Congressional District debate at Utah Tech University in St. George, Friday, Oct. 2, 2026. (Pool photo by Jud Burkett special to The Tribune)
Another point of contention between the candidates was on the country’s energy strategy. When Maloy thinks about the oil and gas industry in Utah, she thinks about substantial jobs for rural Utahns. When she thinks about other energy sources, she sees big potential for nuclear power.
Udell criticized that nuclear power is one of the most expensive energy resources in the country.  
“We have better options. We have wind and we have solar,” he said. “So who is pushing this? Well, it seems like it is a bunch of entrepreneurs that are keeping the prices of their stocks up.”
For Maloy, the interest of entrepreneurs in a technology is a good hint to determine whether investing in it will pay off, she said. The resource would also be reliable and capable of being turned on and off on demand.
“It’s going to be the energy source of the future that doesn’t disappear. That isn’t controversial,” she said. “It’s going to power the AI future that we are going to have. AI is here. We’re going to be using it. We have to have the power to power it.”
Apart from that, Maloy said, a lot of jobs in rural Utah are in mining, oil, gas and in the future, in nuclear energy — “things that my opponent just said he doesn’t care about,” she said.
“I want to do regulatory reform and make sure that we are removing federal barriers to bringing those jobs to rural Utah. I’ve talked to people in the basin who have the training, they have the know-how,” Maloy said. “They just need the federal red tape out of the way so that they can be out producing the energy we need in this country.”
But Udell contested the notion that he doesn’t care about nuclear energy.
“I think it’s got a place. Carbon-free power. That’s great, but we don’t jump into that without having proven that it is going to work and it is going to be safe and it is going to be decreasing our energy costs,” he said. “And until that is proven, I am not in favor of it. Just hold back and make sure that we’re not being forced into buying a timeshare that we don’t want.”
Celeste Maloy, left, and Kent Udell shake hands at the conclusion of a 3rd Congressional District debate at Utah Tech University in St. George, Friday, Oct. 2, 2026. (Pool photo by Jud Burkett special to The Tribune)

title: Gov. Kay Ivey dismisses five members of Alabama Public Television governing board
description: Gov. Kay Ivey dismissed five of the Alabama Educational Television Commission’s seven members Friday evening. Commissioners Pete Conroy, Ferris Stephens, Les Barnett, Bebe Williams and William Green were removed from the AETC. Commissioners Tijuanna Adetunji and Logan Glass remain on the board. A message seeking comment was left with Ivey’s office Friday nig[...]
text:
Members of the Alabama Educational Television Commission listen to a speaker during a meeting on July 21, 2026 in Birmingham. Gov. Kay Ivey removed five members of the AETC Friday night. (Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)Gov. Kay Ivey dismissed five of the Alabama Educational Television Commission’s seven members Friday evening.
Commissioners Pete Conroy, Ferris Stephens, Les Barnett, Bebe Williams and William Green were removed from the AETC. Commissioners Tijuanna Adetunji and Logan Glass remain on the board.
A message seeking comment was left with Ivey’s office Friday night.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The story was first reported by Al.com. The move to dismiss the members came days after a survey conducted by the board showed support for Alabama Public Television continuing its relationship with the Public Broadcasting Service. 
Last October, Stephens and Barnett, two conservative members of the board, brought the idea of disaffiliating from PBS. Barnett accused PBS of being “anathema” to President Donald Trump, and said they had “made themselves the enemy of what I stand with, and so I do not like them, and I don’t follow the philosophy of feeding the beast.” 
The moves prompted public backlash from donors. The following month, the board voted to maintain PBS programming.
Conroy, who served on the board since 2018, said in an interview Friday night he received a letter announcing his dismissal earlier in the day. The new board was the “ultimate goal” for the station, and Conroy said he’s “looking forward to serving APT in whatever way I can.”
A message seeking comment was left with Green Friday night. 
APT Executive Director Wayne Reid said in a text message Friday night the station would have a full statement on the removals Monday and “Alabama Public Television looks forward to welcoming the new commissioners and working together with the Commission to build on APT’s longstanding service to the state.”
The dismissed commissioners also served on the Alabama Educational Television Foundation Authority. Reid said the new commissioners will replace the ones on the foundation board as well.
Under HB 220, sponsored by Rep. Chris Pringle, R-Mobile, Ivey has the authority to remove members of boards she has appointing authority over. Ivey signed the bill into law in April. It went into effect Oct. 1.
The governor last November urged the governing board of APT to pause before voting for disaffiliation and suggested surveying public attitudes before taking that step.
New appointments have been made available on the APT website and include:

Wallace Gilberry for the 1st Congressional District, replacing Les Barnett
Ric Smith for the 3rd Congressional District, replacing Pete Conroy
Neil Lamb for the 5th Congressional District, replacing Bebe Williams
Sally Smith for the 6th Congressional District, replacing Ferris Stephens
Samory Pruitt for the 7th Congressional District, replacing William Green

Conroy said he was optimistic for the future of APT’s governing board.
“There’s a really good new appointee up from the Huntsville area, and he’s a scientist, and he’s well respected, so I’m optimistic about at least one of these appointees,” Conroy said.
In April, the AETC voted to survey Alabamians on their attitude towards APT’s programming. The survey was originally to be conducted by McLaughlin & Associates, a national survey company that has worked with several Republican candidates, including former Attorney General Jeff Sessions and U.S. Rep. Robert Aderholt, R-Haleyville.
The contract with McLaughlin fell through in late August and in a specially called September meeting for the AETFA, members voted to conduct the survey with Cygna, a polling firm that mainly works with Republican candidates, including U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville’s gubernatorial campaign.
Conroy condemned the actions taken by the board in the interview.
“I think we always need to listen to the people,” Conroy said. “And ultimately, it was the weird survey that ended up pointing us in the right direction. But when you listen to people, they’ll remind you what path you need to stay on.”

The governor signed House[...]
text:
Gov. Kim Reynolds signed into law a measure that would allow the state of Iowa more tax incentives for a steel mill project being considered in southeast Iowa after lawmakers passed the bill in a special session Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Gov. Kim Reynolds signed into law Friday a measure changing a state’s economic development program that could provide nearly $1.4 billion in tax incentives for a $15 billion steel mill project planned in southeast Iowa.
“Today, we advance the most consequential economic development project ever to come to our state,” Reynolds said.
The governor signed House File 2801 just hours after lawmakers approved the proposal during a special session Friday, convened for the sole purpose of considering the legislation. The Iowa House approved the bill in a 75-17 vote, and the Senate approved the bill in a 28-19 vote. The proposal would modify the state’s Major Economic Growth Attraction (MEGA) program to include further incentives for businesses within rural areas, a targeted change to benefit the Mesabi Metallics project planned in Lee County.
At a news conference Monday, President Donald Trump announced the steel plant was a $15 billion project. When operational — with a goal of 2030 — the steel mill is estimated to create 1,750 permanent jobs paying an average of $48 per hour, alongside 6,000 temporary construction jobs as the facility is built, state and business officials said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Rep. Matt Rinker, R-Burlington, said the project would be a major victory for southeast Iowa and was the culmination of years of work from local, state and federal officials alongside Mesabi Metallics.
During his time at the Burlington City Council and as a state legislator, Rinker said he has thousands of conversations with members of his community about what was needed to bring success to the area. He told the House, “I’m proud to say that what everyone has been asking for has finally arrived.”
“Our vote today isn’t just about a change to something that already exists, or just about incentives for a steel plant, or just about bringing a new industry to Iowa,” Rinker said. “It’s about mortgage payments, grocery bills, dance lessons. It’s about infrastructure and public safety. It’s about opportunities for Iowans and growing our communities while also supporting them at the same time. It’s about thousands of new homes. It’s about the revitalization of a region of our state that has experienced its fair share of tough times.”
Iowa Rep. Matt Rinker, R-Burlington, spoke in support of legislation making changes to the state’s Major Economic Growth Attraction program to allow the Iowa Economic Development Authority to provide tax incentives to a proposed $15 billion steel mill project in Iowa during a special session Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
As she signed the measure into law, Reynolds thanked “everybody who helped pave the way for this moment,” including local southeast Iowa leaders, companies and workers who advocated for the business to locate in Iowa.
“We don’t do this without you, so thanks for being bold and believing in this state and believing that in America we build things, and we are really going to build things right here in Iowa,” Reynolds said. “And then again, I just want to thank Mesabi Metallics for this opportunity. And we really truly look forward to a very long partnership with them and what this means for our state.”
Sen. Dan Dawson, R-Council Bluffs, who voted against the bill, called it the “largest corporate giveaway in the state of Iowa’s history.”
He also warned the change to the tax incentive program for Mesabi Metallics would influence any future negotiations between the state and companies considering bringing their facilities to Iowa, “because the ceiling now becomes the floor.”
“Incentives are supposed to make a good deal better, not a bad deal good,” Dawson said. “So to all my colleagues, I know you’ve been put in a difficult position. And you’ve been put into position by people and entities who, frankly, do not care. If they did, you wouldn’t be jammed with this bill in front of you today.”
The bill would allow the Iowa Economic Development Authority to authorize a tax credit for a business up to 10% of the business’ qualifying investment in a rural county — an increase from the 5% tax credit currently allowed under the MEGA program for projects representing $1 billion or more in capital investment.
According to analysis from the nonpartisan Legislative Services Agency, the net impact of changes to the MEGA program’s Investment Tax Credit made by the bill would result in estimated revenue decreases to the state’s general fund of $575 million from fiscal year 2029 through 2041 — on top of the $575 million that would come under the current MEGA program structure. The MEGA program’s sales and use tax refunds and withholding tax credits are not changed by the legislation, but under the current program, Mesabi Metallics would be eligible to claim $215 million in tax incentives from FY 2028 through 2041.
IEDA Director Debi Durham said this investment will provide greater benefits for Iowa through later revenue to the state, as well as an expansion of jobs and economic value to the region.
“The state’s portion on the deal that is before you today (is) a 1 to 5.6% return,” Durham said. “So that means for every dollar that we invest as a state, that we get that return back. And when you think of manufacturing, it is the largest part of our gross state product — there is a multiplier of jobs attached to manufacturing, anywhere from three to five jobs will follow. When you happen to talk about a (project) as complicated as this, and as many investments, the investment being made, it is a 5-to-1 job ratio as well, meaning, for every job that they hire, there’s a follow-on job that will occur in our economy.”
Rep. Carter Nordman, R-Adel, floor manager for the bill in the House, said the change is not an increased tax incentive for the MEGA program — created with wide bipartisan support in 2024 — but a way to combine the two 5% MEGA program investment tax credits that IEDA can currently offer. The IEDA has not previously awarded any MEGA program tax incentives.
“The reality is we are not reinventing the wheel here,” Nordman said. “All we are doing is modernizing and combining two existing incentive programs into one, so Iowa is not on the sidelines, but actively competing on the national and global level for large projects. When creating those incentives of packages a couple years ago … this body could never have imagined the possibility of a $15 billion investment landing here.”
Iowa Sen. Dan Dawson, R-Council Bluffs, spoke in opposition to legislation passed by the Iowa Legislature in a special session Oct. 2, 2026 making changes to a state economic development program to provide more tax incentive for a steel mill project in southeast Iowa. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Dawson said this was a fundamental misunderstanding of the original intent of MEGA program — a measure Dawson said he helped negotiate when it was approved in 2024.
“To be clear, the intent was never 5% plus 5% equals 10%,” Dawson said. “And that the intent was never that we throw the entire farm into one basket, and it could be a ‘one and done’ proposition. We wanted to see this spread throughout Iowa.”
Durham told lawmakers increasing the tax credit to 10% was necessary for Iowa to bring the steel plant to Iowa.
“We basically do have to be competitive in the marketplace,” Durham said. “So, we look at deals all across the country with this type of industry, and I will say 10% is is a national average of what these businesses are getting.”
Supporters say MEGA program change needed to compete against other states for steel mill
The IEDA director said the states of Arkansas and Kentucky were also competing for the steel mill project, with Arkansas being “our biggest competitor.”
Dawson said Senate Republicans were told Arkansas lawmakers were expected to call their own special session to create an offer providing “cash up front” to the company by modify their state’s recycling tax credit and funding the tax credit change by borrowing against the Arkansas teacher pension fund. He said officials who knew about the Arkansas proposal told him Arkansas officials walked away from these negotiations, “because the companies seemed to lack equity and could never locate where the equity would come from and the paperwork that they provided to the state.”
“While I respect Governor Reynolds’ deep desire to bring a MEGA site to the state of Iowa before her term ends, because she wasn’t willing to walk away from this deal, it’s my belief she negotiated against herself,” Dawson said. “Because Arkansas, I do not believe, was ever actually at the table seriously. And by negotiating against herself, she negotiated against the Iowa taxpayer.”
Durham also emphasized the bill is written to ensure the state will not provide tax incentives to the Mesabi Metallics if the project is not completed. The measures states the tax credit will not be issued to a business until the business begins operations, or until “a designated portion of the project” has been placed in service, and until at least half of created jobs — which must meet a qualifying wage threshold — associated with the project or a designated portion have been added to the payroll. The legislation also states the 10% tax credit will be remitted over the course of a decade.
Some Democrats had questions about portions of the bill which allow the tax credit to be transferred to another person or entity. During the House subcommittee meeting on the bill, Jacoby shared concerns from a constituent that the state would not be able to claw back tax credits “against the buyer if the project goes wrong” — a statement Durham said was incorrect.
“We will have not only oversight into the transferability, we will have approvals over the transferability, and so that is not correct,” Durham said. “We will be fully protected even with the transferability.”
Opponents express concerns about Mesabi Metallics past
Iowa GOP leaders have praised the planned steel mill, with Reynolds saying, “this opportunity will fundamentally change the economic trajectory of our state and the entire region for decades to come.” But others are cautious about the project, saying there are concerns about Mesabi Metallics’ commitment to finishing and opening the plant given the company’s history as it also seeks to open an iron ore mine in Nashwauk, a city in the Minnesota Iron Range.
The mine has not yet officially started operation. The project began in 2008, under the India-based Essar Group’s company Essar Steel Minnesota, the Des Moines Register reported. The Essar Group was founded by brothers Sashi and Ravi Ruia, and expanded to include the Minnesota company as well as a Essar Steel Algoma in Canada.
Essar Steel Minnesota filed for bankruptcy protection in 2016, blocking the Minnesota governor’s attempt to revoke its mineral lease. Investors took control of the company and rebranded it as Mesabi Metallics in 2017 and came out from bankruptcy protection, before Essar Group took over the project again in 2019 under its new name.
Marshall Singer, a local activist from Des Moines, shared these details about Essar Group during subcommittee meetings on the proposal. Singer also highlighted Essar Group and associated companies had received loans from a VTB, a Russian state owned-bank, according to the Guardian. VTB has been sanctioned by the European Union and other countries following the start of the Russia-Ukraine war in 2022.
“Iowa’s economic incentive law bars the state with providing tax credits and refunds to a business tied to a foreign adversary,” Singer said. He also added, “This will cost every taxpayer $866, and this is irresponsible when we are running a $1.4 billion dollar deficit.”
Joe Broking, president and chief executive officer of Mesabi Metallics, the company seeking to build a $15 billion steel mill in Lee County Iowa, spoke to lawmakers about the project at a subcommittee meeting Oct. 2, 2026 as lawmakers considered a bill making changes to a state economic development program to allow the state to offer a more substantial tax incentive package than currently allowed. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Joe Broking, president and chief executive officer of Mesabi Metallics, addressed some of the comments by Singer about the Minnesota project and Essar Group. He said “there was a global commodity price collapse that happened in 2015, and there were hundreds of companies globally that went through restructurings,” not just Essar Steel Minnesota.
He also said the delays of the mine construction were in part due to “certain activities by a competitor to try and stop development on the Iron Range.” Broking’s comments referenced allegations that fellow steel company Cleveland-Cliffs committed antitrust violations. Mesabi Metallics sued the company for in 2025 in a pending case.
Additionally, Broking said Mesabi Metallics has “completely rebuilt all of those relationships” with Minnesota public officials, including Gov. Tim Walz, state legislators and the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources. He also added Mesabi Metallics has “invested close to $3 billion to complete this project, and we’re about to start it now.”
“And Essar Group and the Ruia family have been a fantastic partner, an absolutely wonderful partner,” Broking said. “They’ve met that commitment the entire time. They’ve invested $2 billion of their family money to complete this project, and like I said earlier, we are on the precipice of doing this.”
Answering questions from Sen. Tony Bisignano, D-Des Moines, Durham said she believed the company would be able to complete the Iowa project. Durham said based on the company’s “capital stack,” financing from the Export–Import Bank of the United States and what it has been able to accomplish in Minnesota after “missteps,” she felt confident supporting the project.
“When you see where they are today, and when you see what their business plan is, and when you see the people that are coming in and supporting them, I absolutely have no hesitation to say that they will (do) what they say,” Durham said. “And if they don’t, then we’re going to hold them accountable. But I believe that this project is a good project for the state of Iowa, and I do believe that they have the ability to pull it off.”
But several lawmakers said they were not as confident as Durham in the project’s viability. Bisignano criticized how Republican leaders and the company brought about the legislation, saying it was concerning that many state legislators did not know about the proposal — or the steel mill project in general — a week before the special session. As Trump and many state leaders have touted the project as the “biggest thing to come to state of Iowa,” Bisignano said there should be more time for legislators and the public to review the project and MEGA program changes.
“This should be one of those occasions where — if this is the biggest thing to come to the state of Iowa — that we as a group ought rejoice, with no suspicions, with full knowledge, with defendability when we go back home and we’re asked, ‘why are you giving away a billion and a half of my tax earnings,” Bisignano said. “… I would love to embrace a job creation, of 1,700 jobs with good wages and good benefits that’s going to help a small community that’s been struggling. Who wouldn’t? … Again, we failed. We failed to be transparent with the public, and so they also could rejoice in something like this coming to the state of Iowa.”
Timing of special session, budget impacts questioned
Bisignano also questioned the timing of the special session, which came just shy of a month before the Nov. 3, 2026 general election. Iowa is situated to play a key role in deciding control of Congress with several competitive U.S. House races, in addition to contentious elections for U.S. Senate and Iowa governor. This is a major change from previous recent elections where Republicans saw decisive victories. Heading into the midterms, all members of Iowa’s federal delegation are Republicans, and there are GOP majorities in both chambers of the Iowa Legislature.
There were also questions about the Trump administration’s presentation of the steel mill plan. At the White House announcement, U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick said, “I think this deal is done” when a reporter asked if the project was contingent on approval of state or local tax breaks.
Sen. Janet Petersen, D-Des Moines asked Durham “why are we here and putting more of their taxpayer dollars on the line” if the deal was finalized.
“Senator, I was surprised by that comment as well, because this is not a done deal,” Durham said. “As we said, you have to pass legislation. It still has to go through the final negotiation. So, I don’t know why that that was stated. I can’t speak to that.”
Nordman said he believed the comments made in the Oval Office were “more about the Minnesota mine rather than the plant itself.”
While the measure was approved by both the House and Senate Ways and Means committees, the two chambers had differing views of the bill. The House committee approved the measure with bipartisan support — a 20-5 vote — while the Senate committee only narrowly passed the measure with a 10-8 vote as all Democrats, alongside Dawson and Sen. Jason Schultz, R-Schleswig, voted against the measure.
The majority approval from Senate Ways and Means only came after two Senate Republicans — Sens. Jeff Taylor and Dawn Driscoll — were replaced on the committee by Sens. Tim Kraayenbrink and Dan Zumbach, who voted in favor of the bill. Taylor voted against the the measure on the Senate floor.
When the Iowa Senate debated the measure, Senate Democrats introduced two amendments calling for certain protections for labor unions and organizations to be codified in the legislation. Both proposals failed.
Schultz said during debate he was voting against the legislation, saying, “I’m worried about paying for it, I’m worried about our budget, I am worried about the the situation we’ll find ourselves in in January.” He said the Republican trifecta at the Iowa Legislature chose to the state income tax in previous sessions with the understanding “that the key to tax cuts is controlling spending.” 
“As we go through, and I look back on my years in the legislature, for all of this time, tax credits have been counted against revenue as an expenditure,” Schultz said. “As we authorized additional tax credits, they were against the tax plan, as I see it, and puts us in a difficult situation where we are spending — in advance — revenue.”
Iowa Rep. Dave Jacoby, D-Coralville, said the package amounts to a cost of roughly $3,000 per household.
“What I do want Iowans to know is this: Today is not a ribbon cutting,” Jacoby said. “… We do not have men and women in hard hats and carrying lunch buckets, ready to go to work. This truly is a concept plan right now, a concept plan with many questions. … But sadly, this is a concept that is sorely needed in our great state of Iowa.”
Jacoby said he was voting in support of the bill with the hope that “this plan is real.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Navy warship named for Alaska statesman Ted Stevens
description: Before he was known to Alaskans as “Uncle Ted,” Ted Stevens was a decorated war hero, making dangerous missions behind enemy lines as part of the Flying Tigers, a group of American pilots who fought the Japanese in the China-Burma-India theater of World War II. Stevens represented Alaska as one of the longest-serving U.S. senators […]
text:
Visitors on the deck of the USS Ted Stevens brave blustery weather in Whittier to learn about the new Navy warship's features during a media tour on Thursday. The ship is named for the late U.S. senator, who was decorated World War II aviator before he came to Alaska. The USS Ted Stevens is set to be commissioned in Whittier on Saturday. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon) 

Captain Mary Katey Hays, commanding officer of the USS Ted Stevens, speaks to reporters in Whittier during an Oct. 1, 2026, media tour. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	Before he was known to Alaskans as “Uncle Ted,” Ted Stevens was a decorated war hero, making dangerous missions behind enemy lines as part of the Flying Tigers, a group of American pilots who fought the Japanese in the China-Burma-India theater of World War II.
Stevens represented Alaska as one of the longest-serving U.S. senators in history, and is now being honored by the U.S. Navy with a namesake warship.
The USS Ted Stevens is a brand-new, state-of-the-art guided-missile destroyer, a missile-equipped ship that can conduct warfare at levels ranging from the air to the depths of the sea.
The ship is set to be commissioned in Whittier on Saturday, an event that is expected to draw 3,000 people to the tiny and quirky Prince William Sound town that is home to about 250 people.
 

A visitor takes a photo of USS Ted Stevens’ banner during an Oct. 1, 2026, media tour of the new Navy warship. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	The event is filled to capacity, according to the host committee. Those with tickets will travel by train or bus; regular traffic in the single-lane tunnel that connects Whittier to the road system will be halted for the duration of the ceremony. Those without tickets can watch events on a livestream link.
Even though modern Whittier is a military legacy, established to support the World War II effort and defense of Alaska, the USS Ted Stevens is the first Navy warship to visit the town in 80 years, according to military officials.
But it is an appropriate spot for Saturday’s ceremony, said Captain Mary Katey Hays, the ship’s commanding officer.
Doing the commissioning in Alaska was considered a must, Hayes said at a media briefing on Thursday. And Whittier, a deepwater port and transportation hub, was chosen for its proximity to Anchorage and its abundant support facilities, she said.
 

A Whittier resident waves an American flag to welcome the USS Ted Stevens to town on Sept. 27, 2026. The ship is the Navy’s newest Flight III Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer. (U.S. Navy Photo by Mass Communication Specialist 1st Class Chelsea D. Daily/U.S. Navy)
 

	Before the ship arrived in Whittier on Sept. 27, she and the other senior officials had to prepare the Norfolk, Virginia-based crew of 380 for Alaska conditions, which on Thursday featured a blustery rain-snow mix.
“We had a lot of talks with the crew about bringing all of their gloves, their hats, their winter clothing,” she said.
Despite the weather, the reception in Whittier has been warm, Hayes said.
“Everyone’s so friendly, everyone’s so kind and welcoming, the community has been wonderful,” she said.
During the tour, officers proudly described the attributes of the ship, which measures over 500 feet in length. Those attributes include its 100,000-horsepower engine system, its efficient equipment for hooking up to shoreside electrical power, its accommodations for air crews, its systems for receiving supplies and fuel at sea and its battery gun that can fire off 20 rounds in a minute.
 

A welcome mat on USS Ted Stevens, seen on Oct. 1, 2026, when the new warship was docked on Whittier, features the ship’s motto “Lead With Courage.” (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	There was plenty of evidence of the ship’s Alaska connection on board.
Alaska flags were draped or displayed at strategic spots. The two small shipboard boats on the USS Ted Stevens are named Denali and Kodiak.
And, most prominently, Stevens’ widow Catherine and two daughters, Susan Stevens Covich and Lily Stevens Becker, are “sponsors” of the ship. That means “they’re kind of like the godmothers of the ship,” Hayes said. “They help bring the ship to life.”
Commander Stephen Roman, the ship’s executive officer, lauded the Steven women’s work.
 

The battery gun on the deck of the USS Ted Stevens, seen Oct. 1, 2026, in the Prince WIlliam Sound town of Whittier, is decorated with an Alaska flag. The new Navy destroyer is named for the late U.S. Sen. Ted Stevens, a Navy veteran. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	“The Stevens family has been just phenomenal sponsors,” Roman said. “I couldn’t have asked for a better set of sponsors for the ship. The love and care they’ve shown the crew has been amazing.”
The younger daughter, Lily Stevens Becker, who leads a foundation named after her father, came aboard the ship when it was stopping in San Diego on the way to Alaska, he said.
Stevens, who died in a 2010 plane crash, left a big legacy in Alaska.
He played key roles in the statehood battle, approval of the Trans Alaska Pipeline System, passage of the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act and other milestones. He was known for securing federal funds for important infrastructure projects and programs, such as the University of Alaska’s Geophysical Institute, the Denali Commission and transportation facilities throughout the state — a record that earned him the affectionate “Uncle Ted” nickname. The main federal law governing fisheries, the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act, bears his name, as does the international airport in Anchorage.
 

Commander Stephen Roman, chief executive of the USS Ted Stevens, describes some of the features of the new warship during a media tour on Oct. 1, 2026, Behind him, mist hangs over Prince William Sound waters in Whittier. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	He was also instrumental in major legislation with significance beyond Alaska, such as the Title IX antidiscrimination law, the Ted Stevens Olympic and Amateur Sports Act and the Americans With Disabilities Act.
Roman, as he concluded the tour, admitted that he did not know much about Stevens before being assigned to the ship. Now he is reading about and hearing about the legacy, he said.
“It has been an absolute pleasure and honor to learn more about the man and the things that he did,” said Roman, who grew up in Colorado and found Alaska to be a bit “like home for me.”
 

A statue of the late Sen. Ted Stevens is seen on Feb. 25, 2024, at the airport that is named for him, the Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport. One of the longest-serving U.S. senators in history, Stevens left a legacy that shaped Alaska. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	Following the Whittier ceremony, the USS Ted Stevens will sail to Juneau for a stop in the capital city, then return through the Panama Canal to its homeport of Norfolk.
The journey after that is yet to be determined.
“We’re just like every other ship in the Navy. We’re able to be deployed globally,” Hayes told reporters. And that will depend on world events, she said.
“Wherever the mission takes us, we’ll be there. Whether it’s here in the snowy part of Alaska or way down south. We can go anywhere and get the job done,” she said.
The bow of the USS Ted Stevens provides a view on Oct. 1, 2026, of the area of Whittier known as the “Head of the Bay.” Beyond the shore is the Whittier entrance to the Anton Anderson Memorial Tunnel, the single-lane auto-rail tunnel that connects Whittier to the state road system. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
The USS Ted Stevens, a new U.S. Navy warship, towers over boats in Whittier’s small harbor on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)

name: Washington State Standard
title: WA governor ‘disappointed’ Canada is fast-tracking new oil pipeline to B.C.
description: A proposed Canadian oil pipeline to a supertanker terminal at the Port of Vancouver in British Columbia is raising hackles among Washington state’s political leaders.  Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday designated the West Coast Oil Pipeline, now known as the Pacific Link, as a project of national interest. That enables a speedier regulatory […]
text:
Increased tanker traffic through the shared border waters of Washington and British Columbia could rise further if Alberta succeeds in building a new crude export pipeline to the West Coast. Here, an oil/chemical tanker steers through Boundary Pass on the way to the Port of Vancouver in late June. (Photo credit by Tom Banse)A proposed Canadian oil pipeline to a supertanker terminal at the Port of Vancouver in British Columbia is raising hackles among Washington state’s political leaders. 
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday designated the West Coast Oil Pipeline, now known as the Pacific Link, as a project of national interest. That enables a speedier regulatory review that could see pipeline design and construction under way by next fall.
In response, Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson on Friday sounded alarms about increased oil spill risk to the Salish Sea in his first public comments on the massive project.
The Carney announcement wasn’t a surprise. In July, the prime minister and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith talked of fast-tracking the proposed 775-mile pipeline capable of carrying one million barrels of crude oil a day. 
It would run from the Edmonton region to a new export terminal capable of handling supertankers proposed for Port of Vancouver’s Roberts Bank in British Columbia just north of the U.S. border. Oil could flow through by the early 2030s.
Once operating, many more oil-filled vessels traveling from the port would pass by the San Juan Islands and Olympic Peninsula on their way to Asia. Project critics fear a spill could easily reach north Puget Sound, the Strait of Juan de Fuca and Washington’s outer coast, threatening sensitive ecosystems and killer whale habitat. 
Ferguson said Friday that he was “disappointed” at the decision because resources needed to respond to a major spill are insufficient today.
“If a project of this scale is going to proceed, it needs to come with a corresponding commitment to also increase our region’s capacity to prevent and respond to a catastrophic spill,” he said in a joint statement with Casey Sixkiller, director of the state Department of Ecology.
Ferguson said the size of the oil supertankers envisioned for the route are unprecedented, and have been barred from Washington ports since the 1970s. Their capacity of 92 million gallons of oil is eight times the volume of oil spilled by the Exxon Valdez, he noted.
“If this project proceeds, it is critical that the Canadian government make detailed commitments to safeguard our shared marine waters and fill these gaps in our response capabilities,” he and Sixkiller said in the statement.
San Juan County council members, northern Washington tribal representatives and others have been pushing Ferguson since July to speak out and engage with the Canadian provincial and federal governments about the crude pipeline and tanker traffic.
On Tuesday, Ferguson met with Mark Wiseman, Canada’s ambassador to the U.S. in Seattle. It is not known if the two discussed the pipeline and Ferguson’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the meeting.
Sixkiller dispatched a lengthy letter to Canadian Intergovernmental Affairs Minister Dominic LeBlanc in mid-September in a vain bid to forestall the fast-tracking of the Alberta pipeline permitting.
U.S. Rep. Rick Larsen of Everett, whose 2nd Congressional District includes the state waters through which the supertankers would travel, was equally vexed. Many questions about the project and oil spill response need answers, he said.
“This project is not ready for prime time, and speeding up the review process will only make that worse,” he said in an email. “Canada’s plan to fast track this new oil pipeline project puts sensitive marine habitats at risk and raises the chance of a devastating spill occurring before the U.S. and Canada can put updated plans in place.”
The project comes as Canada looks to strengthen its economic ties beyond the U.S. and as Carney has said the nation is seeking to become an “energy superpower.”
Smith has said the province chose a southern pipeline route that ends on the shores of the Salish Sea because it can take advantage of the existing Trans Mountain Pipeline corridor as well as established relationships with First Nations.
Northern Washington tribes, including the Lummi, Samish, Swinomish and Makah, strongly opposed a previous Canadian pipeline expansion. The tribes argue that the large increase in vessel traffic endangers their treaty rights and threatens vital fisheries.
Maithili Devadas of the Georgia Strait Alliance, an environmental group in British Columbia fighting the export terminal proposed at Roberts Bank, panned Carney’s announcement.
“It would be reasonable to expect that a project with the potential to shape the environmental, economic, and social future of a region for decades to come would face an especially rigorous level of scrutiny. Instead, this project is being fast-tracked without any concern for its long-term impacts on ecosystems, communities and the people who depend on them,” she wrote in an update to supporters Friday.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Families of Arkansans with disabilities urge lawmakers for faster work on clearing waitlist
description: Arkansans whose loved ones are seeking supportive services for complex disabilities continued Friday to urge lawmakers to clear a waiting list of nearly 2,500, saying the promise of relief in 2027 is not enough. Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders and the Department of Human Services announced in September that they will work to provide affordable in-home […]
text:
Jonesboro Republican Rep. Jack Ladyman asks Arkansas Department of Human Services administrators questions about supportive services for people with disabilities during a meeting of the House and Senate Public Health, Welfare and Labor committees on Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)Arkansans whose loved ones are seeking supportive services for complex disabilities continued Friday to urge lawmakers to clear a waiting list of nearly 2,500, saying the promise of relief in 2027 is not enough.
Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders and the Department of Human Services announced in September that they will work to provide affordable in-home care for those waiting for the Community and Employment Services Medicaid waiver. Sanders said it should cost about $17 million for the state’s managed-care Medicaid program to start serving these families’ non-medical needs by January.
Arkansas spent about $460.6 million on supportive living services in 2025 and expects to spend $745.7 million in 2027, accounting for services to the waitlist population and an upcoming increase in provider reimbursement rates, Division of Developmental Disabilities Services Director Jennifer Brezée told the House and Senate Public Health, Welfare and Labor committees.
Supportive living is one of four services the managed-care Medicaid program does not offer to families on the waiver waitlist, but it is the most requested, Brezée said.
These non-medical support systems are not necessarily life-saving, DHS Director of Specialty Medicaid Services Melissa Weatherton said.
Jonesboro Republican Rep. Jack Ladyman disagreed.
“If you have a three- or four-year-old in a wheelchair or a walker, if they’re not monitored most of the time, that can be life-threatening,” said Ladyman, whose adult son lives in a state-run group home for people with disabilities.

Paige McCammon, whose 2-year-old son has complex health needs, advocates for more supportive services for people with disabilities during a meeting of the Arkansas House and Senate Public Health, Welfare and Labor committees on Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)

Paige McCammon expressed similar frustrations during the meeting’s public comment period.
“There is a whole lot that can happen to a profoundly disabled child between being perfectly fine and being dead,” said McCammon, whose 2-year-old son has multiple disabilities, including epilepsy, which she said gives him about 50 seizures per day.
Many Arkansas parents, including McCammon, have been sharing stories on social media about their children’s health needs. She and others said in a Sept. 16 news conference that they appreciated the state’s moves to help them but needed more assistance caring for their children.
McCammon was one of six relatives of disabled Arkansans to ask lawmakers for more help Friday. Some said they have reduced their work hours or quit their jobs entirely to care for their loved ones.
Caretakers can be paid employees of the managed-care insurance companies that cover this population, but they pay $11 per hour, a recent decrease from $14 per hour.
The Department of Human Services has to prove to the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services that providing home and community-based support for people with disabilities saves money compared to institutionalization, Brezée said.
In June, the U.S. Department of Justice alarmed disability advocates by announcing that states are no longer required to provide home- or community-based care for people with disabilities.
Waitlist, policy changes stir worries among families of Arkansans with disabilities

McCammon said she has learned from conversations with other caretakers of children with disabilities that many are told “that institutional placement, foster care, hospitalization, or a crisis situation could help speed up access to services.” She said this is unacceptable.
“My child is not a budget line item, and I’m done accepting that his quality of life can depend on whether Arkansas decided there was enough room for him in this year’s budget,” McCammon said.
In 2021, then-Gov. Asa Hutchinson directed $37.6 million toward disability support services in an effort to clear the waitlist, which had more than 3,000 people on it. All of those people received waiver services by 2025, but the waitlist refilled.
Lawmakers on Friday questioned how and why the backlog continues to grow. Weatherton said the state receives between 400 and 500 waiver applications per year. 
This was a manageable workload in the early years of the managed care system, which started in 2018, but the Department of Human Services’ information technology is now overwhelmed by applications, she said.
The agency will ask the Arkansas Legislative Council later this month to approve a contract with a customer service vendor to create a “one-stop shop” for Medicaid beneficiaries seeking help from the agency, Weatherton said.
This will help people “stop being bounced across our department,” whether they’re applying for disability support services or addressing upcoming Medicaid work requirements, she said.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Lawsuit alleges Miramar ICE facility is acting as a de facto civil detention center
description: A federal class action was filed in Miami Friday against the Department of Homeland Security, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and top executives at the agencies, alleging they’re using a Miramar field office as a de facto civil detention center. The lawsuit says the agencies are holding people illegally for days, denying them medicine and medical […]
text:
The 42-page challenge was filed in federal court in Miami (Getty images)A federal class action was filed in Miami Friday against the Department of Homeland Security, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and top executives at the agencies, alleging they’re using a Miramar field office as a de facto civil detention center.
The lawsuit says the agencies are holding people illegally for days, denying them medicine and medical care, coercing them into signing documents, and restricting access to legal counsel.
Attorneys for the Southern Poverty Law Center (SPLC) and Americans for Immigrant Justice (AI Justice) filed the 42-page challenge on behalf of two noncitizens being detained at the facility as the suit was filed: Orlando Rosales Salmeron and another detainee under the pseudonym John Doe.
The suit alleges Salmeron and Doe are being detained in the Miramar facility with as many as 150 people even though the maximum occupancy is 56. 
“Mr. Salmeron has not been provided with a bed, cot, mattress, or adequate bedding. He has attempted to sleep on the floor in the same crowded space where people spend their waking hours. These conditions interfere with his ability to sleep and cause physical discomfort and fatigue,” the suit notes. 
“Mr. Salmeron receives inadequate food and drinking water. He also lacks access to showers, clean clothing, and basic hygiene supplies. The crowded and unsanitary conditions make it difficult to maintain personal hygiene.”
Salmeron is represented by an immigration attorney but the suit alleges the agencies “restrict his ability to communicate with that attorney, confidentially or otherwise. “



Quotation







He cannot make or receive confidential attorney calls, meet with his attorney in person, or review or sign legal documents provided by his attorneys while confined at the Miramar Facility.


– From a 42-page complaint filed by the Southern Poverty Law Center and Americans for Immigrant Justice


The allegations also stem from observations by U.S. Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz, who made an unannounced visit to the facility July 2 as well as accounts from families, advocates, and the Sept. 21 release of a whistleblower report, which prompted the U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform to launch an investigation.
“Whistleblowers also reported prolonged shackling, including shackling elderly people with serious health issues and limited mobility for 16 hours a day. Whistleblowers also detailed an abject lack of proper medical care at the Miramar facility and provided examples of individuals who did not receive needed medical treatment, including a woman who was seven months pregnant detained for three weeks without medical care, a person with hypertension detained for 17 days, and a person in their 60s with HIV/AIDS detained for more than 14 days,” the suit alleges.
“The application of due process does not depend on convenience. Due process is an obligation the U.S. Constitution has with every single human being,” said Sui Chung, executive director of AI Justice. 
“Holding someone in the inhuman conditions detailed in this complaint means what people are facing inside Miramar is not a matter of limited resources. It is about being. Whether fundamental human decency is followed should not depend on which building a person happens to be held in.”  
Demands
The attorneys are asking the judge to declare that the facility is an ICE sub-office or field office and as such must be “emptied at the conclusion of daily operations,” meaning it cannot hold people overnight.
Attorneys also are asking the judge to enjoin the government from using “threat, coercion, abuse, deprivation or threatened deprivation of necessities, material misrepresentation, or other pressure” to obtain signatures from detainees for any forms.
Moreover, they are asking the judge to require the government to:

Provide people in holding rooms access to potable water at all times and a meal at least every six hours.
Permit detained people to retain personal inhaled medication and access other prescribed medication as necessary. 
Allow detained people to perform bodily functions and change clothing without being viewed by staff of another gender except in the limited circumstances.
Permit confidential in-person legal visitation seven days per week, for at least eight hours per day on regular business days and four hours per day on weekends and holidays. 
Provide a reasonable opportunity for a confidential legal call during each subsequent twelve-hour period of confinement.

“While due process is supposed to extend to every person in this country, ICE has chosen to ignore the Fifth Amendment and instead detain people for days on end in degrading and dangerous conditions at the Miramar field office,” SPLC legal director for Immigrant Justice A.J. Hernandez Anderson said in a prepared statement. “We’re asking the court to force ICE to stop using Miramar as the detention facility it was never built to be.”

name: VTDigger
title: Stepping inside Vermont’s creative spaces during Open Studio Weekend
description:
The twice-yearly event allows visitors to learn about the art process at the source.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Stepping inside Vermont’s creative spaces during Open Studio Weekend.
text:
Frank Saliani handles freshly thrown plates in his Montpelier studio, Green House Pottery. Photo by Emma Rosenthal

This story by Emma Rosenthal was first published Oct. 1, 2026.
Via Community News Service, a University of Vermont journalism internship, for the Bridge. 
Twice a year, the doors to Vermont’s creative spaces swing open, giving visitors a peek into pottery studios, galleries and artists’ workspaces across the state. 
Organized by the Vermont Crafts Council, Vermont Open Studio Weekend returns Oct. 3 and 4, bringing together artists and makers for two days of studio visits and demonstrations. The event offers visitors a chance to explore Vermont’s diverse craft community at the source.  
The event is free and self-guided, allowing visitors to choose from over 100 independent studios and build their own route through the state. 
For artists, the weekend offers an opportunity to share their work and creative process directly with the public. For visitors, it is a chance to see artists’ workspaces and perhaps leave with not only something handmade, but with a better understanding of what went into making it. 
For Martha Fitch, executive director of the Vermont Crafts Council, a nonprofit organization supporting the state’s craft community, Open Studio Weekend is part of a decades-long effort to connect Vermont artists with the public. 
“We hope some visitors feel like they’ve had a transformative experience where they’ve understood more about what it takes to be an artist,” Fitch said. 
Fitch has been involved with the Vermont Crafts Council since its founding in 1990. The first Open Studio Weekend took place in 1993, and since then, the event has changed significantly. 
“The first Open Studio, we didn’t have a map,” Fitch said. “You just had a list of addresses, and if you wanted to find out what studios were taking part, we directed you to the local hub and hoped you could figure it out.” 
Now, navigating the event is much easier. The free Vermont Studio Tour booklet, which contains maps and directions, can be found at Vermont welcome centers or the craft council’s website. Bright yellow road signs direct visitors toward the studios. There is also a new tour app where art hounds can “plan your tour and share it with your traveling companions,” according to the craft council’s website. 
Still, “Open Studio isn’t an easy event for the people to access. They have to get in their cars and drive around,” Fitch said. “It attracts people that are up for the adventure.”
Despite the shifting logistics, the premise of Open Studio Weekend has remained that same: to connect the public directly to the people who make art. 
This connection is something that Frank Saliani, owner of Green House Pottery in Montpelier and a craft council board member, knows firsthand. 
“Especially in this day and age where we’re so removed from the way things are produced, it’s important for people like me to open our studios so that people that are interested can come and see how someone like me makes what I make,” Saliani said. “And that also helps to support a larger bridge to the community.” 
At Saliani’s studio, visitors will be able to tour his workspace and learn about the process that turns materials such as stoneware and porcelain into functional pieces of art.
“Every time I do open studios, I tend to be at a different point in my production process. In the spring, I was in the middle of throwing a lot of pots,” Saliani said. 
For visitors, seeing the process of clay being transformed can change the way they think about an object, Saliani said. They learn that a mug isn’t simply a mug; it is the result of hours of work and a series of meticulous decisions. 
“How things in our lives are made and come into our lives is just as important as the object,” Saliani said. “The means are as important as the end.”
For Saliani, the value of opening his studio extends beyond showing how pottery is made. It’s an opportunity to share what’s meaningful to him, he said. 
“Inviting people into your studio is kind of like inviting them into your world,” Saliani said. “And selling your pots to people is then taking a little piece of your world into theirs.”

title: Amanda Janoo bests Phil Scott in September campaign fundraising blitz
description:
The fundraising numbers are another indicator that this year’s governor’s race could be the closest in a decade.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Amanda Janoo bests Phil Scott in September campaign fundraising blitz.
text:
Democratic nominee for governor Amanda Janoo, left, and Republican Gov. Phil Scott. Photos by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Vermont’s Democratic candidate for governor, Amanda Janoo, raised more money than Republican Gov. Phil Scott in September, according to newly filed campaign finance reports, putting her nearly level with the governor in cash on hand heading into the final month of the campaign.
The fundraising numbers are another data point indicating this year’s race for governor is the closest the state has seen in years. 
Two recent polls from the University of New Hampshire and Vermont Public showed Scott’s support slipping among likely voters while Janoo’s has increased, though Scott maintained a 10-point advantage according to the Vermont Public poll. 
“Vermonters want a new direction,” Janoo said in a press release Friday. “I’m humbled by the support.”
Janoo, an economist from Strafford, had never run for office before this year. She beat out childcare advocate Aly Richards in August’s Democratic primary. Scott is seeking his sixth term.
Over the past month, Janoo raised $291,000, according to an Oct. 1 report. She spent $70,000, leaving her with about $280,000 on hand. 
Scott raised $223,240, his report shows. The governor started the month with far more cash than Janoo, however: $307,000. He spent about $234,330 of that, leaving him with $295,845. It was the largest single month of spending Scott has reported so far in the 2026 election cycle.
Janoo brought in large hauls last month from some of the state’s most recognizable names in left-leaning politics. Treasurer Mike Pieciak’s campaign contributed $5,180, the maximum amount allowed by campaign finance law. Democratic U.S. Sen. Peter Welch’s campaign donated $4,700. Ben Cohen and Jerry Greenfield, co-founders of Ben & Jerry’s, contributed more than $7,000 between the two of them.
Janoo also received a $5,180 contribution from the state’s largest union, the Vermont NEA. The Vermont Public Interest Research Group, a prominent advocacy and lobbying organization, gave her $4,000.
Still, Janoo has brought in more than twice as much money from individual donors as Scott over the course of the campaign so far. Janoo raised about $689,180 from individuals as of Oct. 1, according to the Vermont Secretary of State’s campaign finance database, while Scott brought in about $323,570 from individual donors. 
Scott garnered the maximum contribution of $5,180 from Barre Mayor Thom Lauzon and others who appear to be members of Lauzon’s family. Scott grew up in Barre. He brought in the same amount from Richard Tarrant, the founder of healthcare technology company IDX and a former Republican nominee for U.S. Senate, as well as others who appear to be members of Tarrant’s family. The Vermont Association of Realtors contributed the $5,180 maximum.
The governor also raised money from a number of companies, including $1,000 from Meta, which owns Facebook. AT&T gave him $500, as did Casella Waste Systems, the state’s largest trash hauler, which contributed $500.
Janoo has said repeatedly that she will not accept donations from corporations, though to be sure, Cohen and Greenfield started one of the state’s best-known businesses. Scott, for his part, told reporters in August that “I’ll take money from anyone,” including corporations, saying such donations did not influence his decision-making in office.
Since the start of the election cycle, Janoo has raised $706,080 in total. That’s more than any Democrat who’s challenged Scott in a reelection campaign at this stage in the race. When Scott was first elected governor in 2016, he had raised about $1.1 million by this point, past filings show.
Most of Scott’s spending over the past month was on TV ads, according to media filings. Of the $160,000 he spent on media, though, about $34,000 was for online advertising mentioning both himself as well as a slew of candidates for the state House and Senate, reports show.
The governor has voiced his support this year for incumbent Lt. Gov. John Rodgers, a Republican. The two have appeared in a TV ad together in recent weeks. 
Unlike Scott, Rodgers outraised his Democratic challenger, Molly Gray, over the past month, according to new filings. Rodgers brought in $150,220, the Oct. 1 reports show, while Gray raised $95,380. Rodgers also spent more, leaving Gray with the financial edge heading into the final month of the campaign.
Gray has $141,540 heading toward the Nov. 3 election, while Rodgers has $84,160. Recent polling also suggested Gray has a substantial lead with likely voters.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Amanda Janoo bests Phil Scott in September campaign fundraising blitz.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas to receive at least $32M through settlement with Monsanto in contamination case
description: Arkansas is set to receive between $32 million and $80 million to resolve claims that now-banned industrial chemicals known as PCBs manufactured by Monsanto Company caused environmental contamination, state Attorney General Tim Griffin announced Friday. Griffin said the state reached the settlement with Monsanto and affiliates Pharmacia LLC and Solutia, Inc.[...]
text:
(Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)Arkansas is set to receive between $32 million and $80 million to resolve claims that now-banned industrial chemicals known as PCBs manufactured by Monsanto Company caused environmental contamination, state Attorney General Tim Griffin announced Friday.
Griffin said the state reached the settlement with Monsanto and affiliates Pharmacia LLC and Solutia, Inc. Griffin said the state could receive up to $80 million total depending on the outcome of separate litigation.
“I am pleased that this case is resolved and that Monsanto is doing right by Arkansans,” Griffin said in a news release. “Although the company stopped manufacturing PCBs in the late 1970s, before the federal government banned them in 1979, Monsanto’s PCBs had been in circulation for nearly half a century.”
PCBs, or polychlorinated biphenyls, are mixtures of compounds manufactured by Monsanto Co. that were used as coolants and lubricants in electrical equipment. They were banned in 1979 and have been associated with adverse effects to aquatic life and humans when found in waterways.
Monsanto was the sole manufacturer of PCBs in the U.S. from the 1930s through the 1970s. A message left with Bayer, Monsanto’s parent company, was not immediately returned Friday afternoon.
The settlement with Arkansas was one of four announced this week by Baron & Budd, a Dallas law firm. The firm also announced settlements between Monsanto and Arizona, Hawaii and Mississippi. Settlements have been announced in several other states in recent months.
Arkansas’ settlement funds are restricted in nature and will be spent in furtherance of water quality, Griffin said in the news release.

title: Hackers demand ransom from Slate Valley school district after compromising teachers’ personal data
description:
Teachers’ personal information was compromised after hackers infiltrated the district’s online systems last month. Hackers are demanding hundreds of thousands of dollars from the district, which has sought help from the FBI.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Hackers demand ransom from Slate Valley school district after compromising teachers’ personal data.
text:
Fair Haven Grade School. Photo Courtesy of Slate Valley Unified Union School District Communications Coordinator Lisa Cacciatore

Hackers are demanding hundreds of thousands of dollars in ransom from the Slate Valley Unified School District after hacking a district server last month and compromising teachers’ personal information, according to Superintendent Brooke Olsen-Farrell. 
The incident continues to wreak havoc on the district after hackers breached the district’s internet system in early September and obtained teachers’ records, she said Friday. 
Many questions remain unanswered according to district leadership: Who is behind the attack? Where are they based? Why was the district targeted? 
“It’s absolutely, you know, a challenge to navigate,” she said. 
The district first learned it had been attacked by a ransomware group on Sept. 3 when teachers came in to school and couldn’t log in to Microsoft Windows. The district was without internet and internal platforms, like the grading system Powerschool, for a week before it was able to restore connection with the help of its cyber security contractors, Olsen-Farrell said. 
The district is seeking information from the FBI, which is investigating the incident, and from cyber security firms, who the district is paying hundreds of thousands of dollars to pinpoint which teachers had their information compromised, Olsen-Farrell said.
The district has been able to restore its internet and the school board denied making any ransom payments earlier this week. 
Meanwhile, the purported hackers, who call themselves Kairos ransomware group, wrote in an email addressed to members of the media that they possess personal information from Slate Valley staff. 
“The personal info of more than 1,500 employees — including SSNs and home addresses and other highly confidential information is about to be leaked,” they wrote. 
Olsen-Farrell said the email was “an extortion attempt.” 
Cyber security websites recognize Kairos as a group that has gained traction since emerging in 2024. The group has been paid ransom by a county in Ohio in the past, according to The Hacker News, a cyber security publication. 
Similar emails written under the name “Kairos Support Group” have been sent out to staff and community members in the district, said Lindsey Hedges, policy and communications specialist for the Vermont Agency of Education, in an email. 
“We are urging members of the Slate Valley community who receive suspicious communications not to respond or engage with the sender, click links, open attachments, call phone numbers provided in the message, or provide personal or financial information,” Hedges said. 
“Suspicious emails should be preserved and forwarded to the district,” she wrote. 
Sarah Ruane, a spokesperson for the FBI’s office in Albany, confirmed in an email that the bureau is investigating and assisting with the incident. The bureau itself was recently hacked by a group eager to solicit the press in an incident that compromised the data of thousands of its employees. 
“As this is an ongoing investigation, DOJ policy prevents me from providing any additional information,” Ruane wrote. 
Olsen-Farrell said the FBI cautioned them against paying the ransom, advising that paying the hackers incentivizes them and can lead to future attempts. She declined to disclose the dollar amount the  hackers demanded while the investigation is  ongoing but said they were asking for hundreds of thousands of dollars. 
“This is, you know, kind of new territory for me. I think these types of things are increasing with AI,” she said. 
The district reached out to the education agency to alert them to the issue, she said, but the agency wasn’t equipped to respond to the issue.
Hedges said the education agency is working to support Slate Valley and ensure that families and staff in the district have clear information about how to recognize suspicious outreach. 
So far, the district believes that the personal information of current and former teachers has been compromised, according to Olsen-Farrell, so the district has notified staff about the breach. 
“We’re working with a third-party outside consultant to assess every person’s name that was impacted and to make the proper individual notification. So that takes quite a bit of time,” she said. 
The district expects to be reimbursed by its cybersecurity insurer for the costs of hiring outside cybersecurity firms and legal experts, Olsen-Farrell said. 
“Certainly, I hope that this doesn’t happen to others and other school districts,” she said.
