name: Minnesota Reformer
title: At AG debate, Republican Ron Schutz commits to putting stocks in blind trust
description: Republican Ron Schutz said if he’s elected Minnesota attorney general, he will give up control of his vast stock portfolio and divest from any companies that are currently in litigation with the state. Schutz made the commitment on Friday during an MPR News debate with Democratic Attorney General Keith Ellison, days after the Reformer reported […]
text:
Democratic Attorney General Keith Ellison and Republican challenger Ron Schutz debate at MPR News in St. Paul on Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo by Max Nesterak/Minnesota Reformer)Republican Ron Schutz said if he’s elected Minnesota attorney general, he will give up control of his vast stock portfolio and divest from any companies that are currently in litigation with the state.
Schutz made the commitment on Friday during an MPR News debate with Democratic Attorney General Keith Ellison, days after the Reformer reported on the potential conflicts of interest presented by his 174 individual stock holdings.
“I will divest from any stocks that I currently own from companies that are in litigation with the state. I will put the rest of it in a vehicle that I won’t have any insight into,” Schutz said, noting that his portfolio is already professionally managed by RBC Wealth Management.
During Friday’s debate, the first in what’s one of the most competitive statewide races, Ellison and Schutz also answered questions from MPR’s Brian Bakst on fraud, the Trump administration, pardons and prediction markets.
Schutz said he would approach the job as a trial attorney — not a politician — leaning on his experience as a partner at a large national law firm. Schutz is not new to politics, though, having spent years as a Republican Party donor and conservative activist. He’s a member of the Federalist Society and serves as a board member of the think tank Center of the American Experiment.
He criticized Ellison for not doing more to stop the fraud scandal that has enveloped Minnesota government and politics since 2022 and accused Ellison of following the lead of California and other Democratic attorneys general.
“I’ve got three grandchildren that live in this state, and I prefer that they grow up in a state that looks a lot more like the one I grew up in and was known as the ‘Land of 10,000 Lakes’ and not the state, as it’s currently known, as the land of 10,000 frauds,” Schutz said.
Ellison, who is seeking a third term, focused his message on affordability, pointing to his track record of going after Big Pharma for price gouging insulin users, employers for wage theft and predatory lenders for deceptive business practices. He also defended his record going after fraudsters, boasting he’s convicted more than 350 people for Medicaid fraud.
“Vote for the person who’s going to fight for your family and help you afford your life,” said Ellison, who’s been using the phrase “afford your life” since his time in Congress.
Trump and Operation Metro Surge
The Attorney General’s Office can serve as a powerful check on the presidential administration and a bulwark against executive actions that affect the state.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Ellison’s office has acted aggressively to push back against President Trump with 75 lawsuits challenging his administration’s use of tariffs, Operation Metro Surge, cuts to safety-net programs and more.
Schutz has mostly avoided criticizing the Trump administration, but he also would not say if he opposes any of the lawsuits Ellison’s office has filed.
“I’m one guy running for attorney general,” Schutz said. “I haven’t had a chance to look at all these cases.”
He did say he issued a press release following the January killing of Alex Pretti by Border Patrol agents in Minneapolis, calling for transparency and a joint investigation by federal and state authorities. Federal agents blocked state investigators from the scene, and Ellison has sued for access to evidence in Pretti’s killing, as well as that of Renee Good.
Schutz said he would “absolutely” continue pursuing possible prosecutions of the federal officers involved in Good’s and Pretti’s killings.
Pardons
Ellison defended his vote to pardon Tou Lue Vang, a Hmong immigrant convicted in 2006 of sexually abusing a 10-year-old girl, because the victim supported it. The decision garnered national attention after the Trump administration highlighted the case and deported the man to Laos.
The case underscored the significant power the attorney general has in granting mercy to people with convictions as a member of the Board of Pardons with the governor and state Supreme Court chief justice, both of whom also voted to pardon Vang.
“I thought it’s important to listen to victims,” Ellison said, noting he has voted against pardoning many others who didn’t have victim support.
Schutz said he wouldn’t have voted to pardon Vang. He said he thinks pardons should only be granted to people who were wrongfully convicted, though it’s unclear how he would determine who was wrongfully convicted.
(Trump, meanwhile, has been particularly profligate with his pardon power, granting clemency to fraudsters, major drug traffickers and the people who stormed the Capitol and beat police officers during the Jan. 6 insurrection attempt.)
Schutz also noted the pardon of Vang was opposed by the local prosecutor’s office and that Democratic gubernatorial candidate Sen. Amy Klobuchar said she wouldn’t have supported it.
Stocks
Schutz previously declined to answer questions from the Reformer about how he would manage the potential conflicts of interest from his large stock portfolio.
Ethics experts say continuing to hold individual stocks while serving as attorney general would be untenable because the public wouldn’t know whose interests he was representing.
Minnesota AG candidate’s stock portfolio presents 174 potential conflicts of interest

If elected, Schutz would have to sell his stock in at least six corporations to uphold his commitment to divest from companies in litigation with the state: Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Exxon Mobil, Pfizer and Uber.
Ellison says he doesn’t own any individual stocks.
Schutz said he’s gone up against big corporations such as Apple and General Electric during his career as a patent attorney, winning tens of millions of dollars for his clients.
“I will take that track record, that aggressiveness, and I will use it to make sure that nobody — and I mean nobody — takes advantage of Minnesotans,” Schutz said.
It’s unclear how much his portfolio is worth or how much divesting could cost him because state law only requires candidates to list companies in which they own more than $10,000 of stock. Schutz did not make himself available for questions from reporters after the debate.
Agreements
The two appeared to be broadly in agreement on abortion, prediction markets and banning mining near the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness — but would likely diverge in practice.
Schutz said he views the right to abortion as “settled law” in Minnesota, noting the state Legislature codified that right in 2023. Ellison said he will continue to fight “tooth and nail” to protect patients’ access to abortion and doctors who provide it.
Both described prediction markets as a scourge. Minnesota passed a first-of-its-kind ban on prediction markets, which a federal judge blocked from taking effect pending litigation.
Asked about defending Gov. Tim Walz’s executive order banning mining near the Boundary Waters, Schutz said it’s the job of the attorney general to defend executive orders unless they are unconstitutional.

title: Polk County lawyer sanctioned for practicing law with a suspended license
description: A former Polk County lawyer is facing additional sanctions after admitting he practiced law for years while his license was under suspension. State records indicate Warren J. Polson was first licensed to practice law in Iowa in April 2016. In April 2022, his license was suspended for failing to cooperate with the Iowa Supreme Court’s […]
text:
The Iowa Supreme Court's Attorney Disciplinary Board and the Grievance Commission of the Iowa Supreme Court handle ethics complaints filed against Iowa lawyers. (Photo via Canva; seal courtesy of the Iowa Supreme Court) A former Polk County lawyer is facing additional sanctions after admitting he practiced law for years while his license was under suspension.
State records indicate Warren J. Polson was first licensed to practice law in Iowa in April 2016. In April 2022, his license was suspended for failing to cooperate with the Iowa Supreme Court’s Client Security Commission in conducting an audit of his trust account.
In recent court filings, Polson acknowledged that in 2023, with his license still under suspension, he was hired by Iowa Defenders in Clive to perform legal work, including drafting legal motions and responses, as a paralegal and failed to report his employment to the state’s Attorney Disciplinary Board.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In February 2026, Polson acknowledged, the board learned of his employment at Iowa Defenders, where the organization’s website identified him as a “senior legal analyst with a wealth of experience and a commitment to excellence.” Polson admitted that visitors to the website were encouraged to contact him “to benefit from his knowledge and insights in navigating your legal challenges,”
In addition, Polson acknowledged, his LinkedIn profile, which he said was years out of date, stated in 2026, “I am an attorney. If you need help with a legal issue, give my office a call.”
Polson recently consented to a 60-day suspension of his law license but asked that it run concurrent to his still-active 2022 suspension. The Attorney Disciplinary Board then recommended that the Iowa Supreme Court suspend Polson’s license for 30 days, concurrent with his ongoing 2022 suspension.
“Polson’s misconduct, while quite extensive in duration, does not appear to have involved any mal intent, and upon receiving notice of the disciplinary complaint he and his employer took prompt remedial action,” the board noted in its recommendation.
On Sept. 25, 2026, the court issued an order suspending Polson’s license for 30 days, concurrent with his still-active suspension from 2022.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Polson at Iowa Defenders, but in an affidavit recently filed with the Iowa Supreme Court, he stated, “I have accepted responsibility for my misconduct.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Local code and utility tariffs are tools Alaska can use to fix the housing shortage
description: Alaska has roughly the population it had in 2013. What little growth the state has seen in the past three years came from residents over 65, while the working-age population shrank. A state that is not growing should not have a housing shortage. It has one anyway. Rental vacancy in March was 4.9% in Anchorage, […]
text:
Cars travel at midday on 7th Avenue in downtown Anchorage  on June 17, 2026. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)Alaska has roughly the population it had in 2013. What little growth the state has seen in the past three years came from residents over 65, while the working-age population shrank. A state that is not growing should not have a housing shortage.
It has one anyway.
Rental vacancy in March was 4.9% in Anchorage, 3.5% in Mat-Su and 4.1% in Juneau, according to the Department of Labor’s spring survey. Affordable housing from the Alaska Housing Finance Corporation had a statewide median rent that reached $1,450 a month, up about 30% over the past 7 years, and a two-bedroom in Anchorage, utilities included, now runs $1,720. It took 1.37 average Alaska wage earners to afford a median-value home last year, close to the record high. If population is not driving the squeeze, something else is, and at a Commonwealth North forum on August 27, six practitioners spent an afternoon exploring the causes.
Four explanations came through clearly.
The first is interest rates. Anyone who bought or refinanced in 2020 or 2021 locked in a mortgage near 3%. Moving today means trading that for 6.25%, last year’s median, or closer to 6.7%, where national rates stood in July. So the retiree who might downsize and the family that might trade up stay put. The house exists. It just never comes to market. The state’s figures show the freeze: a typical new mortgage payment in Alaska is $2,044 a month, 84% higher than in 2019, and new mortgages have fallen 21% statewide and 25% in Anchorage. Daniel Delfino, Director of Planning and Program Development at the Alaska Housing Finance Corporation, called it an open question whether the thin inventory is a real estate problem or a rate-lock problem.
Slide courtesy Commonwealth North
The second is what it costs to build. Utility economist Mark Foster put construction at roughly $300 to $450 per square foot in urban Alaska and as high as $2,500 in rural multi-unit projects. A 2×4 costs about $13 by the time it reaches a village. The ground itself charges a premium: Anchorage water lines sit ten feet down to stay below frost, which means digging twelve.
The third is how we live. Thirty-nine percent of Alaska renters now live alone, up from about 34% in the 2010s. The same number of people needs more doors. Nobody at the forum raised this one. The Department of Labor did, in its September report.
The fourth is newer, and Delfino was careful to present it as arithmetic rather than accusation. Short-term rentals in the surveyed markets swing from about 1,500 occupied units in slow months to more than 5,000 at peak tourism, earning anywhere from $1,200 to $5,100 a month. Against a $1,450 long-term rent, a unit can earn three times as much housing a tourist in July as it earns housing a neighbor all year. The revenue is volatile and dips below a lease in winter. But for some owners the spreadsheet decides, and thousands of units now sit on that fence. “The numbers are pointing them in certain directions,” Delfino observed.
Slide courtesy of Commonwealth North
Add the costs no one in Alaska sets. Congress has not reauthorized the federal law governing tribal housing since 2008, and the Indian Housing Block Grant has lost more than 30% of its purchasing power since 2000. Rate-regulated utilities cannot bank reserves to extend water and sewer, and Alaska never inherited the infrastructure older states got for free. Heating oil costs more than 30% more than it did a year ago, and Tyler Robinson of Cook Inlet Housing Authority, which sponsored the forum and also sat on the panel, told the room he is not sure his affordable portfolio can absorb the natural gas prices ahead: “I don’t know that we’re going to be in this business.”
That is the inherited column. It is long. What follows is more encouraging than most Alaskans probably expect.
What has been done
There are things outside our control, but in Anchorage we’ve seen how municipal code and utility tariffs can spur an increase to housing. Bob Doehl, who runs Anchorage’s Office of Community and Economic Development, brought a ledger. Anchorage’s land use, development and zoning laws, known collectively as Title 21, are shrinking for the first time. A multifamily tax incentive, expanded in 2025 to run longer and reach more of the city, lets projects pencil out that otherwise would not. A design mandate that applied to apartments but not hotels is paused, with a possible return in 2028. Builder Shaun Debenham of Debenham LLC estimates it added about 15% to construction cost. A rebuilt Title 23 allows single-stair buildings up to six stories.
The list runs past city hall. Enstar now credits new customers half the cost of a typical service line, and the Interior Gas Utility credits 90%. Rural housing authorities went after logistics instead: a 2024 military training airlift moved 39 tons of building material to the North Slope and saved roughly a million dollars.
The effect
Permitted dwellings in Anchorage grew 33% from 2024 to 2025, and 2026 passed last year’s total by August. The state’s count agrees. Anchorage permitted 234 multifamily units last year, the most in eight years, and Alaska as a whole recorded 2,261 new homes, the most since 2016. Doehl credits the multifamily incentive with 386 units in two years. Robinson said two Cook Inlet Housing Association developments are underway a year early because of the design-mandate pause. Block 96 became the first market-rate apartment building downtown in more than 15 years.
One detail worth pausing on. A city official, a nonprofit and a private builder each independently named tax abatement as the tool that made their projects feasible. Abatement was the one response all three said is working.
Two caveats. Mat-Su built 949 homes last year to Anchorage’s 404, and it is Mat-Su and the Kenai Peninsula, the two boroughs still gaining people, where rents jumped 13% and 11% this spring while Anchorage rose 2%. Statewide the picture is flat. The pressure is moving to wherever Alaskans are moving. And inventory has not caught up anywhere. Spokane, a regional hub Anchorage used to outpace in listings, now has 1,375 more homes on the market than we do. The pipeline improved. The shortage has not yet.
What presenters said could be done
Debenham asked for a setback analysis of Title 21 and a fire code review benchmarked against cities that do not require 38- and 44-foot fire lanes. On his 58-unit South Anchorage project, the fire lane alone consumed 7,520 square feet of asphalt. By his count, that is 15 homes.
Foster proposed extending a pricing rule Alaska already allows for industrial customers to houses: credit a new home, up front, for the fixed costs it will pay the utility over its first seven years. His preliminary math puts the combined water, sewer, electric and gas credit near $13,800 per home, roughly the effect of cutting a mortgage rate by three points. None of it needs the Legislature. Enstar did it with a tariff filing to the Regulatory Commission of Alaska in 2025; water, sewer and electric could follow the same route.
Debenham, whose last permit took nine months, wants the review outsourced to local professionals. Doehl’s answer is a new municipal permit system arriving in the first quarter of next year, plus a proposal to let the planning director resolve trivial variances without a hearing.
Each carries a tradeoff. Narrower fire lanes are a fire safety question. Hookup credits shift initial costs to existing ratepayers or the utility. The forum resolved none of them, and Commonwealth North does not endorse a specific policy.
What it established is a map. Rates, freight, frost and Congress will stay where they are. Local code and utility tariffs are ours, and the last two years show that rewriting them produces buildings.
Debenham, who has built in Anchorage for twenty years, told the room what changed for him. For most of that time, when a project hit a wall at the municipality, there was no one to call. Now there is. He called it revolutionary, which is a big word for a returned phone call, and a fair measure of where the bar had been.

title: Mental health professionals sanctioned for improper client relationships
description: Several Iowa mental health professionals have been charged recently with violating regulations concerning their relationships with clients. Among the most recent cases is that of Cheryl Schromen, who has been an Iowa-licensed mental health counselor since June 2024. The Iowa Board of Behavioral Health Professionals recently charged Schromen with failing to c[...]
text:
(Stock photo by Getty Images)Several Iowa mental health professionals have been charged recently with violating regulations concerning their relationships with clients.
Among the most recent cases is that of Cheryl Schromen, who has been an Iowa-licensed mental health counselor since June 2024. The Iowa Board of Behavioral Health Professionals recently charged Schromen with failing to comply with the American Counseling Association’s code of ethics, engaging in physical contact with a client when there is a possibility of psychological harm to the client and engaging in a sexually oriented, personal relationship with a client.
The board has disclosed none of the factual circumstances that led to the filing of the charges other than to say Schromen “engaged in a sexually oriented, personal relationship with a client” at some unspecified time in the past. The available board documents give no indication as to where Schromen was practicing when the alleged conduct occurred.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In response to the charges being filed, Schromen has agreed to surrender her license with the understanding that she can seek reinstatement in one year.
Other licensed professionals recently sanctioned by the board include:
— Ben Mineck, who has been an Iowa-licensed mental health counselor since October 2021. The board recently charged Mineck with engaging in a personal, virtual relationship, through social and other media, with individuals with whom they have a current counseling relationship.
According to the board, Mineck, while working for the Abbe Center for Community Mental Health in Cedar Rapids, provided two sessions to a female client and then added her to his SnapChat account and “engaged in flirtatious conversation” with her until the individual removed Mineck as a “friend” on the account.
The board has issued Mineck a warning and ordered him to complete 12 hours of educational training on boundaries and professionalism.
— Charity Dangelser, who has been an Iowa-licensed independent social worker since August 2025. The board recently charged Dangelser with engaging in a “dual relationship” of some kind with a client.
According to the board, Dangelser provided therapy services to a client on eight occasions, and over the course of time their relationship “became increasingly social and personal in nature.” The board has not disclosed any information as to when or where the alleged conduct occurred.
As a result of the charges, Dangelser recently agreed to surrender her license.
— Tyler Gray, who has been an Iowa-licensed mental health counselor since September 2025. The board recently charged Gray with entering into a nonprofessional relationship with a former client when the interaction was potentially harmful to the client.
According to the board, from April to July 2025, when Gray was practicing in Iowa under a “temporary license,” he provided counseling services to an individual and, throughout the course of their professional relationship, “ethics and dual relationships were addressed” due to the two of them residing in the same community – although the board has not disclosed where Gray was working at the time.
The professional relationship was terminated by the client in July 2025, according to the board, but there is no documentation as to the client’s continuity of care. After the professional relationship ended, “a personal relationship began,” the board alleges.
The board recently issued Gray a warning in the matter and ordered him to complete a course on ethics and professionalism. In addition, Gray’s license is being placed on probationary status for two years.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach any of the above four licensed professionals for comment.

name: WyoFile
title: Judge denies qualified immunity to Wyoming Boys’ School staff in abuse lawsuit
description:
In the first of multiple cases against the state-run facility for delinquent boys, some but not all claims of civil rights violations have been cleared for trial. 
The post Judge denies qualified immunity to Wyoming Boys’ School staff in abuse lawsuit appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The first of six lawsuits alleging Wyoming Boys’ School residents suffered abuse and civil rights violations will move forward after a federal judge denied the state-run facility’s request for qualified immunity.
In 2024, six former residents — Blaise Chivers-King, Dylan Tolar, Charles “Rees” Karn, D.H., Haiden Willis and Koby Cranford — joined the lawsuit alleging abuse at the Wyoming Boys’ School, including extended periods of solitary confinement and physical harm. The school, which detains delinquent boys ages 12 to 21, is a 38-acre residential facility near Worland that’s overseen by the Wyoming Department of Family Services.
The defendants, which include the Wyoming Department of Family Services, the Wyoming Boys’ School and school employees, requested separate trials for each of the six plaintiffs. The court granted that request on Sept. 10 to avoid confusion for the jury, given that “the case is deeply complex and full of fact-intensive claims involving multiple plaintiffs and defendants over a four-year time span.” 
In May, before the lawsuit was split into six cases, the defendants filed a motion for summary judgment, asking a judge to dismiss the plaintiffs’ claims. Friday’s ruling from U.S. District Court Judge Scott Skavdahl concerns only Chivers-King’s case, which is scheduled to go to trial first, on Nov. 9, in the U.S. District Court in Casper. Responses to the motion for summary judgment on the other five cases are expected on a staggered basis. 
A surveillance camera feed shows a solitary confinement room at the Wyoming Boys’ School in Worland. The room has a small black box over the toilet seat to protect student privacy. (Lauren Miller/Casper Star-Tribune)
Chivers-King alleged the Wyoming Boys’ School staff violated his 14th Amendment rights by placing him in isolation, using excessive force and infringing on due process. Friday’s ruling allows some, but not all of his claims to go to trial. 
Chivers-King, who served two stints at the Boys’ School between the ages of 15 and 17 for roughly 11 months, “was kept in isolation conditions for more than 42 days total during his first placement at WBS; and for more than 32 days total during his second placement,” the ruling states. 
Defendants argue “every instance of claimed ‘isolation’ served a legitimate purpose and was not excessive in relation to that purpose.” 
Skavdahl disagreed, pointing to evidence that some uses of isolation “were, or became, simply punishment or unrelated to management of a safety threat.”  
Skavdahl’s ruling doesn’t guarantee Chivers-King’s case will win before a jury, but suggests the court has concerns with the constitutionality of how Boys’ School staff used isolation. 
While “some of these isolations may have been legitimate and nonpunitive,” Skavdahl drew attention to how staff placed Chivers-King “in isolation for predetermined amounts of time, which is at least arguably unrelated to the legitimate purpose of managing a child who is physically violent or attempting suicide.”
He pointed to one instance on Nov. 18, 2021, when Chivers-King kicked and attempted to push through a locked door and then broke a sprinkler head. In response, Wyoming Boys’ School Superintendent Dale Weber and staffer Mike Nelson signed a memorandum placing Chivers-King in isolation “at least until November 22, 2021,” the motion describes. “This fixed isolation period was imposed despite notes that Mr. Chivers-King ‘began to calm down’ the evening of November 18 and was deemed safe enough to shower and eat dinner.” 
Dale Weber, superintendent of the Wyoming Boys’ School, sits for a portrait on April 19, 2022 in Worland. He took over in January. Prior to that, he’d been the school’s clinical director for several years. (Victoria Eavis/Casper Star-Tribune)
Mentioning several other examples, Skavdahl wrote that release dates “being fixed and noncontingent on behavior, were divorced from the safety risks that may have initially justified Mr. Chivers-King being placed in isolation.” 
The idea that Chivers-King remained in isolation even after he changed his behavior, Skavdahl wrote, would raise questions for a jury about its use for a legitimate purpose. 
He referenced two 10th Circuit Court of Appeals decisions — Milonas v. Williams and Blackmon v. Sutton, that “clearly establish such use of isolation to punish juveniles not convicted of a crime is unconstitutional.”
Boys’ School residents are adjudicated delinquents, which is a distinct legal category from convicted criminals. 
Chivers-King also made several constitutional claims concerning due process and excessive force, but not all of them are cleared for trial.   
The due process claims overlap with the claims that isolation was used for punitive reasons. An unconstitutional procedural due process claim against Del Olson was denied, but one will proceed against Weber.  
An unconstitutional use of force claim against Mike Nelson was denied, whereas claims against Mark Nelson, Tad Shaffer and Del Olson will proceed. 
Chivers-King conceded his deliberate indifference to medical needs claim, which will not go to trial. Skavdahl denied a disability discrimination claim. 
After Chivers-King’s trial, Dylan Toler’s trial will begin Nov. 30, 2026, and DH’s is set for December 14, 2026. 
Following the first two trials, the court will schedule the remaining three for Karn, Willis and Cranford.
All six plaintiffs asserted claims relating to isolation, resulting in deprivation of their basic human needs, in violation of their Eight and 14th amendment rights.

name: VTDigger
title: Anti-ICE activists plan week of community engagement, learning and protest
description:
The events aim to focus attention on the role that facilities in Vermont play in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations nationwide.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Anti-ICE activists plan week of community engagement, learning and protest.
text:
Musicians from across the state play at a protest against ICE and CBP in St. Albans in May 2026. File photo by Emma Green/VTDigger

In the eyes of Julie Macuga, the time is ripe for “mass civil disobedience.”
She’s one of the main organizers for Shut Down ICE VT, which is hosting a week of community action against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations in Vermont. This is a small state, Macuga said, and activists need more “people power” to have a sustained impact.
“We called for this week of action not only to get more people in the region and hopefully across the country involved in what’s going on here,” Macuga said, “but also just to generally be aware of what’s happening here in Vermont.” 
Shut Down ICE VT, a collaboration of local individuals and groups, will join together Oct. 4-9 to attempt to halt the operations of ICE’s national surveillance centers in Vermont. The week will include a variety of events, with the goal of educating people about the role Vermont facilities play in ICE’s national efforts.
There are two ICE facilities in Williston. The Law Enforcement Support Center is home to ICE’s national tip line, and the National Criminal Analysis and Targeting Center, located in White Cap Business Park, acts as a hub for social media surveillance on the East Coast. 
“It’s not typically known that, you know, two-thirds of the surveillance infrastructure for ICE nationally is just in this one town of 10,000 people,” Macuga said. 
The week of action centers on community engagement as well as civil disobedience, with events ranging from skills trainings to art activities and community meals, Macuga said.
“There’s roles for everyone,” Macuga said. “… You don’t have to, you know, go face a line of police if that’s not something that you’re ready to do.”
The biggest public event will be a rally at the Law Enforcement Support Center from 10 to 11:30 a.m. on Oct. 8, Macuga said.
The Williston facilities have been the site of earlier protests in February, May and July. Sarah George, the Chittenden County state’s attorney, has repeatedly declined to press charges against ICE protesters in her county, but Vermont Attorney General Charity Clark recently stepped in to charge 13 protesters arrested at the White Cap facility in July. Clark’s move sparked outcry among some Democrats, including Chittenden County Sen. Kesha Ram Hinsdale and gubernatorial nominee Amanda Janoo.
Federal prosecutors have also recently charged past protesters in Chittenden County.
Gov. Phil Scott praised Clark’s decision to press charges.
“We talk a lot about accountability,” Scott said at a press conference Sept. 24. “I know it’s not easy for the attorney general to make this decision to prosecute, and that doesn’t mean that they’re all going to be thrown in jail, but they’re going to be held accountable for violating the law.”
Vermonters are carrying on with their protesting despite those recent actions, Macuga said.
“People are more committed than ever to stopping the atrocities,” Macuga said. 
Macuga sees Vermonters across the state devoting their time to “standing on the side of the road holding a political sign” but feeling discouraged by the lack of change that their efforts are producing. Recent polling by Vermont Public suggests that a majority of Vermonters disapprove of ICE’s actions.
“We’re trying to create this opportunity for people to do something that will actually impact ICE operations,” Macuga said.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Teacher who sued Iowa school district for students’ ‘racist’ acts wins $425,000
description: A school teacher who alleged the Ottumwa public schools encouraged students’ racist behavior by failing to impose sufficient discipline has won a $425,000 judgment against the district. In June 2023, Robert Bender sued the Ottumwa Community School District in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa, seeking damages related to alleged harassment[...]
text:
A Black schoolteacher at Ottumwa High School sued the district for allegedly failing to discipline students for racist behavior. (Photo courtesy of Ottumwa Community School District)A school teacher who alleged the Ottumwa public schools encouraged students’ racist behavior by failing to impose sufficient discipline has won a $425,000 judgment against the district.
In June 2023, Robert Bender sued the Ottumwa Community School District in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa, seeking damages related to alleged harassment, discrimination, retaliation and violations of the federal Civil Rights Act. Also named as defendants were Jerry Miller, a school principal, and Dana Warnecke, an assistant school principal.
Bender, who is Black, began working for the district in July 2021 as a behavior instructor teacher and the high school’s junior varsity boys’ basketball coach. He later held the position of junior high school girls’ track coach and a high school special education teacher.
In his lawsuit, Bender alleged that from the time he first began working for the district in 2021, he was the target of racially motivated abuse and harassment by students. In early September 2021, he alleges, a student referred to him using the n-word. While several of co-workers witnessed the incident, they did not challenge the student’s behavior, the lawsuit alleges.
According to the lawsuit, two more incidents of a similar nature occurred in the weeks that followed, and after the matter was reported to Miller and Warnecke, the student who was involved was suspended for either a half day or a full day.
Over the next three months, the lawsuit claims, Bender was routinely called the same racial epithet by different students in front of other district employees, administrators and students.
During that time, Bender also received sticky notes with racist messages written on them, according to the lawsuit. Bender reported the conduct to Miller and Warnecke. The matter was referred to the district’s executive director of human resources, who assured Bender such behavior would not be tolerated, according to the lawsuit.
“Unfortunately, the lack of discipline emboldened the students, and they continued to refer to Mr. Bender as a “n—–” in front of staff and administration,” the lawsuit alleges. “One student in particular has repeatedly used the racist term in reference to Mr. Bender. The student was eventually sent to ‘timeout’ for his use of the term, but Mr. Bender was the adult in charge of supervising the student. Throughout the duration of the timeout, the student continued to use the term directed toward Mr. Bender.”
In March 2022, Miller allegedly reassigned Bender from a “behavioral teacher” to an “inclusion teacher” for the 2022-23 school year. The reassignment was reportedly because Bender had allowed a student to walk out of his class – a common occurrence in the district, the lawsuit claims.
That same month, a student at a bus stop allegedly directed the n-word at Bender in front of staff and parents and, a few weeks later, used the word again in front of Miller. The student was not removed from class and, to Bender’s knowledge, was not disciplined, the lawsuit states.
Around the same time, other students were being suspended for three days — one for slamming a door in the face of an assistant principal and one for calling a teacher “fat man.” According to the lawsuit, Miller later told Bender that while he took no offense to the n-word, he understood why Bender would.
The lawsuit alleged the defendants enabled students to harass and humiliate Bender through the students’ “severe and pervasive” daily use of racial slurs and racially charged language.
In court filings, the district denied any wrongdoing. After four days of testimony last month, a jury deliberated for five and a half hours, at one point asking the judge whether the district, if it had to pay damages for emotional distress, could recover that money from Miller and Warnecke. The judge advised the jurors that “you should not concern yourself with who ultimately would pay any award of damages that you decide to make.”
The jury then returned its verdict, finding that Bender, with regard to all three defendants, had proved his case and awarded $425,000 in actual, compensatory damages. With regard to punitive damages against Miller and Warnecke specifically, the jury assessed $100 in damages against each of the two individuals.
Earlier this week, U.S. District Judge Stephen H. Locher, citing a lack of evidence that Miller and Warnecke had acted with malice or reckless indifference, vacated the two $100 verdicts, leaving the $425,000 judgment intact.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Data privacy lawsuit, subsidies for childcare staff: CT politics news
description: Plus: Schools get funding toward special ed and addressing attendance, while CT outpaces rest of New England in second quarter GDP growth.
text:
These news briefs are part of The Connecticut Mirror’s 2026 political coverage. For more Connecticut political news, sign up here for The Issue, the CT Mirror’s weekly politics newsletter.
CT data privacy law sparks lawsuit
A new crop of data privacy laws just went into effect in Connecticut, even as part of the law faces a new legal challenge.
A coalition of data brokers have filed a lawsuit against parts of Public Act No. 26-64, which outlines resident rights and consumer protections. The lawsuit, which was filed in September, specifically challenges the law’s requirement that data brokers delete consumer information from their websites if a deletion request is made by a Connecticut resident.
The plaintiffs, which include broker sites like Spokeo and PeopleConnect, argue that the deletion mechanism will violate decades of First Amendment precedent. A judge has not yet weighed in on the suit, but the case will likely serve as a notable sign of how courts will handle state data privacy regulations moving forward.
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter
Healthcare subsidies for childcare workers
Connecticut is launching a new program to help early childcare workers pay for plans purchased through Access Health CT, the state’s health insurance marketplace. 
Early childhood educators purchasing 2027 coverage through Access Health CT can apply for subsidies of anywhere from $1,000 to $2,000 annually. The initiative is funded through $10 million from the state’s Early Childhood Education Endowment. 
Earlier this year, Gov. Ned Lamont said the subsidies are meant to reflect “Connecticut’s continued commitment to recruiting and retaining qualified educators.”
Open enrollment for 2027 plans runs from Oct. 23, 2026 to Jan. 15, 2027.
— Katy Golvala, Health Reporter
CT receives federal grant for special ed
The U.S. Department of Education has awarded Connecticut over $4.7 million to boost its special education workforce.
The money will expand Connecticut’s existing Teacher Registered Apprenticeship Program, or T-RAP, statewide, with an emphasis on training new special education and early intervention teachers. The program pays student teachers to work in the classroom, which advocates say is an important step to make becoming a teacher more affordable.
T-RAP also has $2 million in funding from the state, not limited to special education. It currently has 28 apprentices in eight districts across the state.
— Theo Peck-Suzuki, Education Reporter
Business owners, politicians highlight trade concerns
Ongoing concerns over tariffs and trade policy were top of mind for attendees at this week’s Manufacturing Summit, an annual event hosted by the Connecticut Business and Industry Association.
Small manufacturers and business owners described continued uncertainty around the issue, saying that the trade war with Canada has put further strain on their work.
Those issues are further explored in CBIA’s new manufacturing report, which highlights that the manufacturing industry is growing, but continues to face issues with workforce shortages, high energy costs and rising expenses.
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter
CT announces LEAP grant winners
The Connecticut State Department of Education has announced awardees for $6.2 million in grant funds for 29 school districts to expand its touted Learner Engagement and Attendance Program, or LEAP.
The largest grants went to Waterbury, which is receiving $525,000, and Bridgeport, which is getting $475,000. 
LEAP began as an effort to draw students back to school following the pandemic. Local volunteers visit families at home to build trust and connect them to resources. State officials say those efforts have played a major role in reducing chronic absenteeism in Connecticut.
— Theo Peck-Suzuki, Education Reporter
CT outpaces rest of New England in 2nd quarter GDP growth
While the state economy in Connecticut continues to face a muddled picture on unemployment and labor force shortages, it is also seeing strong GDP growth, according to new data released this week.
The state’s economy grew 3% in the second quarter of 2026. That places its growth at seventh in the nation, with Connecticut’s second quarter GDP growth outpacing every other New England state. The growth was largely fueled by the financial services industry and  Connecticut’s manufacturing industry, which grew 10.6%.
Still, business groups warn that even with the economic growth, the state needs to address a range of issues, including high costs of living, more than 86,000 job openings and affordability issues.
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter

title: New Mexico joins coalition in car fuel efficiency lawsuit against Trump administration
description: New Mexico, in a coalition of 26 states, counties and cities, sued the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration on Friday over a rollback of fuel economy standards for passenger cars and trucks manufactured in the United States. The lawsuit argues the rollback will increase gasoline consumption by billions of gallons and cost drivers nearly $220 billio[...]
text:
New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez joined California Attorney General Rob Bonta for a news conference Oct. 2, 2026, announcing a lawsuit against the Trump administration over revised fuel economy rules the AGs say will cause Americans to pay more at the pump. (Amanda Watford/Stateline)New Mexico, in a coalition of 26 states, counties and cities, sued the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration on Friday over a rollback of fuel economy standards for passenger cars and trucks manufactured in the United States.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Corporate Average Fuel Economy standards set average fuel economy levels for car manufacturers. The Trump administration announced revised rules Monday that now require carmakers to make new passenger cars and trucks up to 1% more fuel efficient each year — lowering the previous rule set by former President Joe Biden, which required an annual 2% increase. 
In the lawsuit, filed in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, the coalition alleges that the revised rule is illegal and that NHTSA violated its mandate from Congress to set fuel-economy standards.
“Working families should not have to pay more at the pump because the federal government has chosen to weaken commonsense fuel-efficiency standards,” New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said in a statement. 
In announcing the revised rules, Trump administration officials said the cost of vehicles has increased due to the manufacturing cost of fuel efficiency technology. The revised rules, they added, would reduce the average cost of a new vehicle by $1,300.
“While Joe Biden and Pete Buttigieg pushed a green agenda that made our roads less safe and drove up costs for hardworking Americans, this administration is delivering relief to families and reviving the beating heart of American manufacturing,” U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy said in a statement.
Torrez joined California Attorney General Rob Bonta in a virtual news conference on Friday to announce the litigation.
Bonta said the rollback will increase gasoline consumption by billions of gallons and cost drivers nearly $220 billion at the pump by 2050. 
“More gasoline burned means more gasoline sold. This rule lines the pockets of Trump’s oil executive buddies and donors,” Bonta said. 
Torrez highlighted that the standards set by NHTSA impact the environment as more fuel efficiency in cars lowers the amount of fossil fuel emission.
“These standards help reduce fuel consumption, lower costs for consumers and protect New Mexicans from the economic consequences of volatile global oil markets,” Torrez said in a statement. “The Trump Administration should be working to make life more affordable for families, not making decisions that will drive up costs and put our economy and environment at greater risk.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Center for Intellectual Freedom advisory council advances director candidates
description: Members of the advisory council for the Center for Intellectual Freedom at the University of Iowa met Friday to discuss next steps in the search for a permanent director and their hopes for the center’s future. The field of applicants for the director job — currently held on an interim basis by Luciano de Castro […]
text:
Panelists speaking Dec. 6, 2025, at the Center for Intellectual Freedom at the University of Iowa, from left, are center Interim Director Luciano de Castro, U.S. Assistant Secretary for Postsecondary Education David Barker, state Rep. Taylor Collins, state Sen. Kerry Gruenhagen and Regent Christine Hensley. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Members of the advisory council for the Center for Intellectual Freedom at the University of Iowa met Friday to discuss next steps in the search for a permanent director and their hopes for the center’s future.
The field of applicants for the director job — currently held on an interim basis by Luciano de Castro — has been narrowed from 62 to four candidates by the advisory council, which itself has seen a reduction in numbers after 11 members resigned.
Mark Bauerlein, an English professor at Emory University and faculty member on the advisory council, was named at the council’s Sept. 25 meeting as chair of the executive committee. He told advisory council members Friday they’ve pared down director candidates from 11 to six and now to four, with “several very strong candidates” in the larger pool not making the cut.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“The candidates all provided a letter outlining how they saw the future of the center, what their thoughts were moving forward, and there were some that had actually made reference to the media coverage that the center has had,” said Regent Christine Hensley,  chair of the Iowa Board of Regents committee overseeing the center. “So, I thought that all of them, the ones that we ended up with, really are looking at the center with their eyes wide open.”
Each of the candidates will remain anonymous for now, having signed confidentiality agreements, and Hensley said executive committee members involved with the search have signed nondisclosure agreements. The council’s plan is to bring the candidates to the UI campus for visits before a director is selected.
Bauerlein said he had four criteria for center director candidates, which other advisory council members said they agreed with — research in the areas of U.S. history, government and civics, administrative experience, experiences with universities similar to the UI and practice engaging with people outside of academic peers and circles, such as with members of the board of regents, donors and reporters.
Norman Johnson, former CEO of filtration system company Clarcor and new advisory council member, said something for the advisory council and board of regents members involved in the search to keep in mind is whether each candidate is flexible and a “good salesperson,” and whether they can keep all of the parties involved with the center happy.
With the finalists selected, the advisory council approved sending them to the board of regents to launch the next steps in the selection process. Hensley said a special meeting for the board has been set for Oct. 20, but adjustments are still possible.
Advisory board member and former lawmaker Liz Mathis told the advisory committee that while she didn’t approve of every candidate moving ahead in the search, she does support the process advancing. She added that the referral to the center as a “vehicle for conservative thought on what some call a liberal campus” as Hensley and others have previously said, doesn’t serve the students who will be required to interact with the center.
Students have largely been left out of conversations about the center, Mathis said, and as a UI alum and liberal arts fellow, she cares “about whether this curriculum is built around a student’s discovery and curiosity and their growth, or around an agenda decided for them before they ever walk into the classroom.”
Iowa Board of Regents President Robert Cramer agreed with Mathis’s point, saying he wants to see a shift toward ensuring the center is student-focused and instilling in them the ability to listen to both sides of an argument, disagree and debate.
“Intellectual freedom isn’t about swapping one orthodoxy for another,” Mathis said. “It’s really about teaching students to listen carefully, and to understand a position before they agree or disagree with it, as I think our advisory board has done well in this last meeting, and to disagree, when they do, civilly and on the merits, and that has to include both sides of our hardest arguments, not one.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Bipartisan group of Maryland legislators call for menhaden harvest reductions
description: A bipartisan group of Maryland legislators is pushing for fishery managers to institute further restrictions on the harvest of Atlantic menhaden, a small fish that sits at the base of the Chesapeake Bay food chain.
text:
A menhaden pulled from the Chesapeake Bay in the area of Jordan Point Marina. (Photo by Charlie Paullin/Virginia Mercury)A bipartisan group of Maryland legislators is pushing for fishery managers to institute further restrictions on the harvest of Atlantic menhaden, a small fish that sits at the base of the Chesapeake Bay food chain.
In their letter, the 29 Maryland senators and delegates endorsed a suite of policies that would set new rules for harvesting the silvery forage fish, a key food group for species including striped bass and osprey.
The policies would limit the Chesapeake Bay harvest of menhaden to 13.6% of the total coastwide cap. They would also establish three even-length fishing periods to spread out the catch, and require that fishery managers at the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission reevaluate the menhaden regulations every three years.
In their letter, the lawmakers cited worrying signs about the bay’s menhaden population, and possible impacts to other species that call the estuary home.
“Maryland’s menhaden harvest has fallen by more than 80 percent since 2020 and now sits below ten percent of the quota the State is allowed to take. Crabbers are struggling to find affordable bait and harvesters are unable to participate in the fishery,” reads the Sept. 25 letter.
Maryland has a small commercial and recreational bait fishery for menhaden. The state has prohibited purse seine netting of menhaden in Maryland waters “since before the 1950s,” according to Maryland’s Department of Natural Resources.
Osprey nesting woes in the Chesapeake Bay worsen, survey finds

But in the Virginia portion of the bay, including at the mouth of the Chesapeake, there is a commercial fishery that harvest the small fish in purse seine nets for oil and fish meal. A single company, Ocean Harvesters, conducts the fishing, contracting it out to a company called Omega Protein. The company is able to harvest up to 51,000 metric tons of menhaden per year, a cap that was last reduced in 2018, when it fell from 87,216.
The Maryland lawmakers’ letter also cited recent research from the Center for Conservation Biology at William & Mary, which pointed to concerning breeding numbers for osprey in the Chesapeake Bay.
The scientists determined that osprey pairs nesting in tidal fresh waters were reproducing at an adequate rate to keep the population stable. But 81% of osprey pairs nesting in saltier waters failed to fledge any chicks. And when they did, scientists frequently observed chicks starving in nests.
Scientists at the center cited food stress as the cause for low breeding numbers, writing that the problem “appears to be caused by changes in the availability of Atlantic menhaden to nesting ospreys in the Chesapeake Bay.”
The Maryland lawmakers wrote that, “Taken together with what our watermen are seeing, there is considerable evidence that menhaden availability in the Chesapeake Bay is in serious decline – much to the detriment of Marylanders and the Bay’s frontline species.”
The Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission, the regional compact that manages the fishery, is holding a public comment period about the possible menhaden regulations through Oct. 9. In November, the group’s menhaden board, with representatives from each of the Atlantic coastal states, will vote on a final decision.
One of Maryland’s three representatives is state fisheries Director Mike Luisi, who said he is still “digesting” all of the public comment coming from Marylanders in order to arrive at a final decision.
“We believe that there is an availability issue in the bay, and it’s likely that some action is going to be needed in order to see whether or not this reduction fleet is part of that equation,” Luisi said.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
There may not be one “silver bullet,” Luisi added. It’s possible that other factors, including changing ocean temperatures, could be influencing menhaden migratory patterns, causing fewer to travel up into the Chesapeake. By adjusting the bay fishery, managers might be able to get a sense of how much the reduction fleet is playing a role.
“I see the board taking some action,” Luisi said. “It’s going to be determining how extreme that action is.”
The Maryland lawmakers on the letter are an “interesting coalition,” said Del. Dylan Behler (D-Anne Arundel). It includes 22 Democrats and seven Republicans, spanning a group that spans various Maryland counties.
“There’s wide, bipartisan consensus on the importance of the Chesapeake Bay to our state’s culture, history and economy,” Behler said in an interview. “We all see the importance of menhaden in that ecosystem.”
And “every corner of the state” is seeing effects that lawmakers believe to be related to a possible overharvesting of menhaden, Behler added.
Ocean Harvesters has long denied charges that the fishery could be contributing to the lack of menhaden in the bay or problems further up the food chain. The company has pushed against new restrictions on the fishery, citing potential job losses.
Representatives from the company suggested that detractors haven’t fully considered how the environment and other factors contribute to the situation. More data is needed, the company insisted, to make informed decisions on any potential restrictions.
In a comment to the Virginia Mercury, the company highlighted the lack of definite data “to comprehensively characterize menhaden abundance and distribution in the Bay or the influence of fishing pressure.”
The Chesapeake Bay Program, which is also pushing for additional menhaden restrictions, agrees that there isn’t much data specific to the menhaden stock in the estuary. But it says the existing evidence is worrisome enough.
“Without really good, effective science that exclusively is looking at Chesapeake Bay menhaden, we have to look and take some of these other data points seriously — and that’s exactly what CBF is doing,” said Will Poston, the Bay Foundation’s forage campaign manager.
Instead of calling for a reduction of the 51,000 metric ton cap, the Bay Foundation and the Maryland legislators are calling for it to be tied to a percentage of the coastwide total allowable catch. If the menhaden harvest were 13.6% of the total allowable harvest, the current harvest level would be reduced about 50%, Poston said.
As a result, the number can change from year to year based on the overall health of the menhaden stock, Poston said.
That way, Poston says, “We’re not going to end up in a similar situation as this year, where maybe we’re concentrating too much menhaden harvest pressures in this estuary when looking at the coastwide ecosystem.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas education leaders celebrate groundbreaking of STEM-focused university at former Walmart HQ
description: A new STEM-focused university being built on the site of Walmart’s former headquarters in Bentonville aims to create a new model of higher education, officials announced during a groundbreaking ceremony Friday.  Steuart and Tom Walton, grandsons of Walmart founder Sam Walton, announced plans for the university focused on science, technology, engineering and[...]
text:
Philanthropist Alice Walton and her nephew Tom share a laugh with David Mazyck, inaugural president of the Bentonville Institute of Technology, during a groundbreaking ceremony on Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)https://arkansasadvocate.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/20261002_BentonvilleInstituteofTechnologyGroundbreaking_ArkansasAdvocate.mp3
 Click above to listen to guests speak at the groundbreaking ceremony for the Bentonville Institute of Technology on Oct. 2, 2026.
A new STEM-focused university being built on the site of Walmart’s former headquarters in Bentonville aims to create a new model of higher education, officials announced during a groundbreaking ceremony Friday. 
Steuart and Tom Walton, grandsons of Walmart founder Sam Walton, announced plans for the university focused on science, technology, engineering and mathematics last year. 
The Bentonville Institute of Technology will feature “a modern, flexible, and accessible model that combines STEM education with business, artificial intelligence, and real-world application,” according to a press release. 
David Mazyck, a former professor and head of Penn State’s school of engineering design and innovation, will serve as Bentonville Institute of Technology’s inaugural president. Mazyck said the new school is needed to fill a gap in STEM education. 
“Universities can produce technically capable graduates, but technical capability alone is no longer enough,” he said. “The people who create meaningful impact must also know how to identify the right problems, understand human needs, work across disciplines, exercise judgment, communicate complex ideas, understand how value is created and turn ideas into solutions that actually work in the world.”
(From left)Tom Walton; Ann Bordelon, vice president of finance; Jim Walton; David Mazyck, president, Alice Walton, Steuart WaltonMembers of the Walton family  and Bentonville Institute of Technology staff pose for a photo during a groundbreaking ceremony on Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)Guests gather at the future site of the Bentonville Institute of Technology during a groundbreaking ceremony on Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)Members of the Walton family  applaud a speaker during a groundbreaking ceremony for the Bentonville Institute of Technology on Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)David Mazyck, inaugural president of the Bentonville Institute of Technology, addresses the crowd of a groundbreaking ceremony on Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)Philanthropist Alice Walton shares a high-five with her nephew Tom after posing for a photo during a groundbreaking ceremony for  the Bentonville Institute of Technology on Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)Jim Walton, son of Walmart founder Sam Walton, smiles after posing for a photo at a groundbreaking celebration for the Bentonville Institute of Technology on Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)Ken Warden, Arkansas Division of Higher Education commissioner, speaks with Republican state Reps. Hope Hendren Duke (left) and Mindy McAlindon at the Bentonville Institute of Technology groundbreaking ceremony on Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)University of Arkansas System Board of Trustees President Randy Lawson (far left) and University of Arkansas Chancellor Charles Robinson (second from right) chat with guests prior to the start of a groundbreaking ceremony for the Bentonville Institute of Technology on Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)Ed Fryar, a member of the University of Arkansas System Board of Trustees, shares a laugh with guests at the Bentonville Institute of Technology groundbreaking ceremony on Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)Sharmila Makhija, founding dean of the Alice L. Walton School of Medicine, speaks with state Rep. Bart Hester prior to a groundbreaking ceremony for the Bentonville Institute of Technology on Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)Guests gather at the future site of the Bentonville Institute of Technology during a groundbreaking ceremony on Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)Crossland Construction employees monitor the site of the future Bentonville Institute of Technology during a groundbreaking celebration on Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)
The nonprofit, “business-infused institute,” will embed artificial intelligence throughout its programs to help prepare students for a world full of rapid technological changes, according to the release. 
The school is expected to welcome its first undergraduate class of approximately 300 students in 2029, and eventually grow to around 1,500 undergrads and 500 working professionals. Tuition is expected to be fully covered during the institute’s initial years, according to the release.  
The project is backed by multiple members of the Walton family, including Alice Walton through her foundation. Alice, the daughter of Sam and Helen Walton, has supported the creation of multiple projects in Bentonville over the last 15 years, including an art museum, medical school and healthcare campus. 
The first phase of Bentonville Institute of Technology’s campus will include more than 400,000 square feet across three facilities — an academic building, student residences and a makerspace, according to the release. 
The institute will be part of a mixed-use development planned for the former Walmart Home Office site. The global retailer’s new headquarters, located just over a mile east of its former home, began opening buildings on its new campus last year.
(Rendering courtesy of Bjarke Ingels Group)(Rendering courtesy of Bjarke Ingels Group)(Rendering courtesy of Bjarke Ingels Group)(Rendering courtesy of Bjarke Ingels Group)(Rendering courtesy of Bjarke Ingels Group)(Rendering courtesy of Bjarke Ingels Group)
Tom Walton said the university’s 64-acre site is located near downtown so students can seamlessly integrate with the community. The hope is to build a new neighborhood over time that will include office buildings, a variety of housing, a new hotel and another town square, he said. 
“What we’re going to do to change the way the model could be for higher education is going to be outstanding,” he said. 
Though it will be a few years before the university opens, the institute’s leaders will help educate Bentonville students in the coming months. Debbie Jones, Bentonville School District superintendent, said teachers and leaders have worked with Mazyck’s team to develop a university-level curriculum that will be taught in the district next semester. 
“Together our teams have dreamed big, creating rare and transformative STEM opportunities for both high school and college-level students,” Jones said.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota Supreme Court hears arguments over oil royalty deductions
description: The North Dakota Supreme Court is poised to make a key decision in a case where one of the state’s largest oil companies is accused of withholding excessive amounts of money from the royalty checks it pays to mineral owners.  The mineral owners, led by Diana Skarphol, are appealing a district court’s decision to dismiss […]
text:
Plaintiff attorney Bruce Bowman makes oral arguments to the North Dakota Supreme Court on Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)The North Dakota Supreme Court is poised to make a key decision in a case where one of the state’s largest oil companies is accused of withholding excessive amounts of money from the royalty checks it pays to mineral owners. 
The mineral owners, led by Diana Skarphol, are appealing a district court’s decision to dismiss the case against Hess, the oil company that pays them royalties, before a jury trial could take place. They allege the oil company is withholding unreasonably large sums of money from the royalties paid on oil and gas production in North Dakota.
The Supreme Court’s ruling will decide whether the case moves forward or not. 
North Dakota mineral owners say oil companies unfairly keep millions from checks without oversight

Justices expressed skepticism of the legal arguments made by the mineral owners’ lawyers, led by Texas attorney Bruce Bowman, during Friday’s oral arguments. Bowman argued Hess has the responsibility to prove they are in compliance with North Dakota law and failed to do so. But Justice Jon Jensen said putting that obligation on the defendant would overturn existing contract law. 
“Why are we switching the obligation?” Jensen asked. “It’s your client’s burden to demonstrate that.”
North Dakota law often allows oil companies to pass on a share of their expenses to royalty owners by deducting postproduction costs like transportation and processing from the monthly royalty payments. 
The mineral owners in this case allege the deductions taken by Hess are much higher than those imposed by other companies and are therefore commercially unreasonable. 
Attorney Bruce Bowman makes oral arguments to the North Dakota Supreme Court on Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
In court documents, Bowman has argued royalty statements going back to 2014 showed deductions from royalty checks surged from under 2% to over 30% and that Hess uses subsidiaries and affiliated companies to artificially increase the costs royalty owners pay. He noted they have reports from experts stating the deductions are excessive.
Bowman argued they have presented sufficient evidence to show Hess’ deductions are excessive under North Dakota law and that a jury should have an opportunity to determine the amount of damages his clients are owed by the company. 
“The jury is going to be the expert in this case,” Bowman said. 
Ragan Naresh, a Washington, D.C., attorney representing Hess, said evidence has not been presented in this case to show that Hess is passing on significantly higher costs than other oil companies. He argued the mineral owners have failed to show Hess’ deductions are excessive. 
“The evidence of damages is completely missing,” Naresh said. 
Attorney Ragan Naresh makes oral arguments to the North Dakota Supreme Court on Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
The court took the case under advisement.
The North Dakota Monitor and ProPublica published a joint investigation in 2025 showing some oil companies frequently deduct more than 20% of a royalty check for postproduction costs. More than a dozen mineral owners shared royalty statements that showed postproduction costs would subtract more than half of a royalty check in some months. 
The North Dakota Petroleum Council said at the time it would be impossible to calculate an average of how much was being deducted but suggested it couldn’t be more than 7% to 10% based on the cost of transporting oil to markets out of state. 
There is no official accounting of how much money is deducted by companies.
Postproduction deductions potentially affect as many as 300,000 people, the industry’s estimate for the number of people who own oil and gas mineral rights in North Dakota. 
Not all states take North Dakota’s approach to what postproduction costs can be shared among royalty owners and the oil companies. Courts in states like Colorado, Oklahoma and Kansas require a company to make the commodities “marketable” and limit what costs can be shared with royalty owners. West Virginia doesn’t allow deductions unless a lease explicitly allows a company to take them. 
Lawmakers in Wyoming, Nevada, Michigan and West Virginia have taken action to limit postproduction deductions in various forms. 
North Dakota lawmakers have rejected legislative proposals to address royalty owners’ concerns. Legislators have argued that these disputes should be settled in the courts.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Jacob Orledge can be reached at jorledge@northdakotamonitor.com.
