name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Money begins to flow in fight over threshold for South Dakota constitutional changes
description: The backers of a South Dakota ballot measure that would make it harder to change the state constitution accused their opponents this week of misleading voters with campaign ads tying the measure to “out-of-state billionaires.”  The spokesperson for the opposition called the allegations “comical.” The ads are a nod to how much more expensive campaigns […]
text:
Mailed campaign materials from L-No, a South Dakota ballot question committee formed to opposed a measure that would require 60% voter approval to change the state constitution. (John Hult/South Dakota Searchlight)The backers of a South Dakota ballot measure that would make it harder to change the state constitution accused their opponents this week of misleading voters with campaign ads tying the measure to “out-of-state billionaires.” 
The spokesperson for the opposition called the allegations “comical.” The ads are a nod to how much more expensive campaigns for ballot measures would become if it took more votes to pass them, he said.
The dust-up highlights the role out-of-state funders and interest groups have had in recent debates about direct democracy in South Dakota, which was the first state in the U.S. to allow citizens to change laws through initiatives and referendums.
If a majority of voters support it during the general election, Amendment L would change the constitution to require 60% of voters to back any future attempt to change it at the ballot box. The amendment would not change the threshold for passage of citizen-initiated measures or referendums, which deal with laws rather than the constitution.[Voter Guide: 2026 general election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.] This is the third attempt to increase the threshold for ballot question passage in South Dakota. Similar measures failed in the 2018 general election and the 2022 primary. 
This year’s election is Nov. 3, advance voting is underway, and the voter registration deadline is Oct. 19.
Backers: Grassroots effort to protect constitution 
Things like the expansion of Medicaid or the legalization of recreational marijuana — both of which have appeared as constitutional amendments on general election ballots in South Dakota — don’t belong in the state constitution, said state Rep. John Hughes, R-Sioux Falls, who sponsored the 2025 resolution that lawmakers passed to put Amendment L on the 2026 ballot. He argues changing the state’s foundational document ought to be more difficult than changing its laws.
Hughes, a Sioux Falls attorney, is a member of a ballot question committee called Save Our South Dakota Constitution that was launched to support Amendment L. On Tuesday, he sent a cease-and-desist letter to four media organizations that had been airing an advertisement opposing Amendment L.
“Out-of-state billionaires and their lobbyists are coming to South Dakota, pushing Amendment L,” the ads say. “They’re trying to change the South Dakota Constitution again.”
The letter asks station managers to pull the ads for being misleading. 
The ads “contain multiple false and materially misleading statements that are defamatory” to the ballot question committee and “associated individuals,” Hughes’ letter said.
Hughes told South Dakota Searchlight his committee doesn’t get its money from out-of-state donors but is supported by a “grassroots coalition” that includes the groups Protecting South Dakota Kids, South Dakota Family Voice, the South Dakota Retailers Association and South Dakota Right to Life.
Hughes said he’s upset about the ads in part because he believes out-of-state money is backing the ads calling out his side for having the support of wealthy out-of-staters.
“We hardly have two nickels to rub together,” Hughes said.
T.J. Nelson, a Sioux Falls lawyer, testified on behalf of the 2025 resolution to put the amendment on the ballot. 
Podcast: Pros and cons on a ballot question to raise the bar for changing the state constitution

He did so as a lobbyist for the Foundation for Government Accountability, a think tank whose website says it supports work requirements for the beneficiaries of social welfare programs, annual recertification for unions and the securing or elimination of ballot drop boxes to protect what it calls election integrity, among other issues. It opposes “far-left” efforts to promote diversity, equity and inclusion.
As a 501(c)(3) organization, the Foundation for Government Accountability is not required to disclose its donors by name, but The Washington Post reported that its largest donors in 2022 included a foundation led by billionaire Richard Uihlein.
Nelson sent a press release about the cease-and-desist letter from Save Our South Dakota Constitution on Wednesday. 
Campaign finance disclosures for ballot question committees are not due until Oct. 19, but Nelson told South Dakota Searchlight that Foundation for Government Accountability has contributed nothing financially to the Amendment L campaign.
“They have not made any financial commitments,” said Nelson, who said the Foundation for Government Accountability is “one of many clients” served by the Redstone law firm in Sioux Falls, where he works. 
All the funding for Save Our South Dakota Constitution comes from within the state, Nelson and Hughes said.
L-No: Ads make a broader point 
Zach Nistler is a spokesperson for L-No, the ballot question committee formed to oppose Amendment L.
The ads, which Nistler said had already been scheduled for replacement with newer materials by the time the cease-and-desist letter was delivered, were not meant to call out Save Our South Dakota Constitution as a group supported financially by out-of-state billionaires, Nistler said. 
They couldn’t have been, he said. The ad contracts were signed and initial broadcasts aired before the pro-Amendment L group had filed its statement of organization with the South Dakota Secretary of State’s Office. 
“We find it comical,” Nistler said, that the committee members or Hughes would believe the ads were about them specifically.

Mailed campaign materials from L-No, a South Dakota ballot question committee formed to opposed a measure that would require 60% voter approval to change the state constitution. (John Hult/South Dakota Searchlight)
 

“I don’t mean to be rude, but we weren’t even thinking about them,” he said.
The idea behind the broadcast ads and mailed opposition materials that reference “out-of-state billionaires,” Nistler said, is that making it more difficult to pass a constitutional amendment would inevitably push up the price of campaigns to do so. 
The costlier the campaign, Nistler said, the more likely campaigners are to need backing from wealthy non-South Dakotans. 
The reference to billionaires is meant to highlight “how much further out of reach it is for regular South Dakotans to make changes to their constitution” at a 60% vote threshold, Nistler said, “and how it doesn’t make a dent for the people who have unlimited resources.”
Nistler also pointed out that a group called Americans for Prosperity supported the campaign for Amendment C, the 2022 measure to raise the threshold for passing ballot questions. 
Americans for Prosperity, founded by billionaire businessman David Koch, bills itself as a group whose political operations support limited government and personal freedom.
Outside funding for L-No
The news release on the cease-and-desist letters says that Amendment L’s opponents have spent “at least $400,000” on advertising. Nelson said he calculated the figures based on invoices for the L-No broadcast ads filed with the Federal Communications Commission.
When asked if the $400,000 figure was roughly representative of L-No’s spending thus far, Nistler did not address the figure. He sent a statement via text that read, in part, “the L-No campaign will continue to highlight that South Dakotans have overwhelmingly voted no twice” on amendments similar to Amendment L, “and will do so again.” 
Lawmakers consider higher bar for constitutional amendments and a trigger to end Medicaid expansion

Meanwhile, the secretary of state’s website lists $260,000 in campaigning against Amendment L paid for by the nonprofit group The Fairness Project, listed under the category of “communication expenditures.”
The Fairness Project is a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit that says it is “dedicated to advancing social and economic justice via ballot measures.”
In Missouri, the group has donated millions to support abortion rights ballot measures, according to the Southeast Missourian. In South Dakota, it backed the successful 2022 campaign to expand Medicaid, a joint federal-state health insurance program for people with disabilities, children and those with low incomes, with a constitutional amendment.
In South Dakota, nonprofit organizations can spend money on political advertising and file reports for their spending as communication expenditures. The only such reports associated with Amendment L so far in 2026 have come from The Fairness Project. 
Funding for L-No comes from what Nistler called a coalition of South Dakota groups, including Dakota Rural Action, the League of Women Voters of South Dakota and South Dakota Farmers Union, among others.
Nistler did not volunteer The Fairness Project as a backer but said the group is part of “the coalition” working against Amendment L.
Both The Fairness Project and the Foundation for Government Accountability — the organization that paid Nelson to lobby on behalf of the Amendment L bill in Pierre in 2025 — are nonprofit organizations required to file 990 forms with the Internal Revenue Service that disclose their funds but not their individual donors. The Fairness Project’s most recent 990, for tax year 2024, lists $33.1 million in contributions.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Vice President Vance to visit Fairbanks on Monday, Trump expected in Alaska later this month
description: Vice President J.D. Vance will hold a campaign event on Monday in Fairbanks to boost Republican candidates in this year’s general election, and President Donald Trump is expected to visit Alaska later this month on a similar mission. The vice-president’s visit was officially announced Friday by the Trump 47 Committee, an operation of the Republican […]
text:
Former President Donald Trump prepares to speak in front of a crowd at the Alaska Airlines Center in Anchorage on Saturday, July 9, 2022. (Photo by James Brooks/Alaska Beacon)Vice President J.D. Vance will hold a campaign event on Monday in Fairbanks to boost Republican candidates in this year’s general election, and President Donald Trump is expected to visit Alaska later this month on a similar mission.
The vice-president’s visit was officially announced Friday by the Trump 47 Committee, an operation of the Republican National Committee and Trump’s Save America PAC.
The President’s visit has not yet been formally announced, but an official with Republican governor candidate Dave Bronson’s campaign said on Friday that they expect Trump to visit Alaska on Oct. 16 at a to-be-announced location and have been filling out paperwork before Bronson meets Trump in person.
Members of other campaigns either declined to confirm that date or said they believed a visit could happen on another date.
Trump and Vance have each been making campaign stops across the country in an attempt to boost Republican candidates ahead of the November election.
Vance visited Florida this week and was in Kansas last month on campaign stops. Trump was in Alabama on Friday and plans to be in Nebraska at the same time Vance is in Fairbanks. He’s also visited Texas and Oklahoma to boost Republican candidates there.
According to a preliminary schedule provided by the Trump 47 Committee, Vance is expected to land Monday afternoon at Fairbanks International Airport, where the rally will take place.
Doors open at 3 p.m., the event begins at 5 p.m. and Vance is expected to begin speaking at 6:20 p.m.
The Fairbanks weather forecast for Monday calls for a 20% chance of snow before 10 a.m., with a high of 43 degrees, dropping to 28 at night. 
Trump has repeatedly said he intends to visit Alaska, particularly to help the campaign of incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, who is in a close race against Democratic challenger Mary Peltola.
The Beacon has asked Sullivan’s campaign whether he will attend the Vance and Trump events but has not yet received a response.
A spokesperson for the campaign of U.S. Rep. Nick Begich III said he will be in Fairbanks on Monday for the Vance event. The spokesperson did not answer a question about the planned Trump event.
Begich’s lead challenger is independent candidate Bill Hill, a former schools superintendent from Bristol Bay. 
The governor’s race includes Democratic candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins and three Republicans — Bernadette Wilson, Bronson and Treg Taylor. Kreiss-Tomkins is currently favored in statewide polling.
Wilson said by text message that she will be in Fairbanks for the Vance event; she did not say whether she would attend the Trump event. Bronson’s campaign confirmed attendance at both.
Taylor’s campaign has not yet responded to questions about his attendance. 
Sullivan, Begich and incumbent Gov. Mike Dunleavy all appeared alongside the President in Washington, D.C. this week at an event about the proposed trans-Alaska natural gas pipeline.
Trump and administration officials said at the event that the nation of Korea was investing in the project, but that was a lie — Korea has only committed to reviews that could lead to an investment of some kind. Korean officials have since protested the administration’s statements at the event.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Milwaukee County votes to remove Flock cameras from parks
description: The Milwaukee County Board voted to remove Flock cameras from its parks Thursday night. Passed unanimously, the resolution also permits the county to replace the controversial cameras with more conventional security cameras. It’s not clear  how the new cameras would be paid for. Supv. Justin Bielinski, who authored the resolution, said he’s excited to remove[...]
text:
A Flock camera outside of Washington Park in Milwaukee, Wisconsin.  (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)The Milwaukee County Board voted to remove Flock cameras from its parks Thursday night. Passed unanimously, the resolution also permits the county to replace the controversial cameras with more conventional security cameras. It’s not clear  how the new cameras would be paid for.
Supv. Justin Bielinski, who authored the resolution, said he’s excited to remove Flock cameras from Milwaukee County parks. The cameras must be removed by the end of the year. 
Flock cameras are equipped with AI-powered automatic license plate reader technology. When a car passes in view, the camera takes a picture of the car and its license plate. The images are then stored in a database which can be searched at will by law enforcement agencies with their own Flock contracts. The searches can be done without a warrant, and allow officers to enter a license plate or vehicle description to determine where a vehicle has been.
Law enforcement agencies say the cameras are invaluable tools for detecting and stopping crime. Numerous law enforcement agencies in Milwaukee County use Flock including the Milwaukee Police Department and the sheriff’s office. In a presentation to a county board committee earlier this week, the sheriff’s office credited the cameras with contributing to a 43% decline in certain crimes around county parks between 2023 and 2026. 
Privacy advocates, concerned citizens and elected officials have increasingly soured on the cameras. Cases of officers using the cameras to surveil protesters, pursue women suspected of seeking out-of-state  abortions and keeping tabs on current or estranged romantic partners have made national news. In Wisconsin, three police officers and one sheriff’s deputy in Milwaukee, Menasha and Kenosha counties have faced charges of misconduct in public office due to their use of Flock to unlawfully monitor people.
Milwaukee County Executive and Democratic candidate for governor David Crowley proposed removing funding for Flock in the 2027 budget.
The sheriff’s office said that without a replacement technology, crime would increase in the 11 parks where the cameras have been installed. It’s estimated that replacing the cameras could cost as much as $140,000. In 2025, the Examiner found that at least 221 Wisconsin law enforcement agencies used Flock during that year. Several communities around the state have removed their Flock cameras since then.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC counties now paying more to help feed hungry people
description: North Carolina counties are now paying more for a federal program that helps some hungry people eat, as a law shifting more of the cost of the nutrition assistance program to states takes effect.  One of the changes in the massive tax cut and social services cut bill Congress passed last year, the One Big […]
text:
The federal mega-bill that cut social welfare programs could leave North Carolina with a big bill for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP. (Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images)North Carolina counties are now paying more for a federal program that helps some hungry people eat, as a law shifting more of the cost of the nutrition assistance program to states takes effect. 
One of the changes in the massive tax cut and social services cut bill Congress passed last year, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, makes states pick up 75% of the administrative costs for SNAP. The federal government had split the cost 50–50 for many years.
NC residents to go hungry, counties to pay more for SNAP under federal changes

North Carolina is one of the few states that has passed most of that expense on to counties, which are responsible for administering the program. 
The N.C. Association of County Commissioners estimated the administrative expenses are expected to cost counties an additional $52 million over nine months starting Oct. 1. The association asked the General Assembly to cover the cost increase. There was a late push among some Democratic legislators and health advocacy groups to have the state pick up the cost. All those efforts failed. 
As of June 2026, 1.2 million North Carolinians received SNAP benefits, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. 
Beginning next year, the state could shoulder even more SNAP costs under a provision of the same federal law. It charges states with high error rates more for SNAP benefits. Counties worry that the state will pass along those charges to them as well.
Starting Oct. 1, 2027, states with SNAP error rates above 6% must begin paying anywhere from 5% to 15% of the cost of benefits. 
According to the agriculture department, North Carolina’s error rate in 2025 was 7.36%. If that law had been in effect for 2025, the state would have had to pay 5% of the benefits cost. 
In its latest budget, the state legislature appropriated about $2.6 million toward reducing the error rate and integrating SNAP eligibility changes into the state’s electronic case management system.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi Medicaid seeks $179M budget increase, less than in 2025
description: Cindy Bradshaw, executive director of the Mississippi Division of Medicaid, listens during a meeting of the Medicaid Advisory Committee at the Sillers Building, Friday, July 25, 2025, in Jackson.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
The Mississippi Division of Medicaid asked lawmakers for a roughly $179 million increase in state spending for the coming fiscal year after receiving a steep increase last year that squeezed other parts of the state’s budget. 
The proposed increase for the fiscal year beginning in July 2027 represents a 15% increase over last year. The agency is also anticipating a $34 million budget shortfall for the current fiscal year.
But Mississippi Medicaid’s $1.3 billion state funding request is expected to change again, Cindy Bradshaw, the state’s executive director for Medicaid, told the Joint Legislative Budget Committee at a Friday hearing.
“The one thing I can guarantee you is that will not be the amount that we need,” she said. “This is a fluid process, and it changes quickly.” 
For example, officials learned Thursday the federal government will increase the share of money it pays towards the state Medicaid program in 2027. Mississippi’s federal matching rate will increase slightly — by .0024% — for the upcoming fiscal year, said Bradshaw. This is expected to reduce the agency’s request by roughly $25 million.
Medicaid is one of the state’s largest budget items, accounting for roughly a 10th of the state’s spending. The agency’s total projected budget for the upcoming fiscal year is $9.4 billion, including federal funds. 
The agency administers health coverage to nearly 700,000 children and low-income pregnant, disabled and elderly Mississippians. The program’s enrollment is at its lowest level in over a decade and decreased by about 7,500 people in the past year. 
Mississippi Medicaid has launched initiatives to lower costs, Bradshaw said. Efforts include audits of contractors and long-term care facilities, reviewing prior authorizations and reducing managed care companies’ profit margins. Managed care companies receive per-member payments to maintain a provider network and implement programs intended to improve health outcomes for enrollees.
The agency’s requested increase is smaller than its ask last year early in the budgeting process of nearly $390 million. Lawmakers were stunned by the request and baffled by Gov. Tate Reeves’ roughly $160-million-lower proposal. Reeves’ office oversees Medicaid. 
Lawmakers ultimately approved a roughly $200 million increase in Medicaid’s budget for the current fiscal year, setting aside $100 million from the state’s capital expense fund. The fund is a reserve intended for one-time expenses, such as repairs and renovations of state-owned properties. State legislators also approved a $35 million deficit appropriation to cover a shortfall for the prior fiscal year.
Medicaid officials said last year’s large funding increase was the result of a a reserve of funds leftover from the COVID-19 pandemic running out, which necessitated a significant boost in state appropriations to maintain services at the same level
After lawmakers balked at the agency’s budget request for the current fiscal year, Bradshaw warned in January that underfunding the agency could force it to cut payments to providers. 
State agencies present budget requests to the Joint Legislative Budget Committee in the fall. The committee makes recommendations in December, and most appropriations bills are passed by lawmakers in the latter months of the legislative session, which ends in April.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Schiltz: ‘I did not violate any ethics rules’
description: U.S. District Judge Patrick Schiltz on Friday publicly recounted the challenges of administering justice during Operation Metro Surge, just two days after the Justice Department filed an ethics complaint against him and other judges for criticizing the federal government’s actions during the immigration crackdown.  University of St. Thomas law professor Mich[...]
text:
U.S. District Judge Patrick Schiltz speaks at a symposium at the University of St. Thomas School of Law on Friday, Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo by Madison McVan/Minnesota Reformer)U.S. District Judge Patrick Schiltz on Friday publicly recounted the challenges of administering justice during Operation Metro Surge, just two days after the Justice Department filed an ethics complaint against him and other judges for criticizing the federal government’s actions during the immigration crackdown. 
University of St. Thomas law professor Michael Paulsen interviewed Schiltz at a symposium on state law remedies for federal lawlessness at the St. Thomas School of Law. Schiltz was until recently the chief judge for the federal bench in Minnesota. 
On Wednesday, the U.S. Department of Justice filed a judicial misconduct complaint to the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals, accusing “all but one” of Minnesota’s federal district judges of unethical conduct, citing a New York Times article featuring interviews with Schiltz and other Minnesota judges.
In the article, Schiltz, who twice clerked for the late conservative icon Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia and was appointed by George W. Bush, said what happened in Minnesota federal court during Operation Metro Surge “created a grave threat to the rule of law.”
The DOJ in its complaint accused Schiltz of making “overtly political” comments and discussing cases pending before him. (The New York Times wrote that Schiltz didn’t comment on specific cases.)
At the St. Thomas law school, Schiltz discussed the federal government’s failure to follow court orders in nearly 200 instances; threats against himself and other judges; unprecedented legal maneuvering by federal prosecutors to secure arrest warrants for journalists; and the filing of more than 1,000 wrongful detention lawsuits, called habeas corpus petitions, and the pressure to rule on them before detainees were shipped out of state.
“I spoke (to the New York Times) repeatedly and explicitly about the threat to the rule of law and the threat to judicial independence, and I have not only the right, but I have the duty to do so,” Schiltz said, citing a judicial code of conduct opinion that affirmed judges’ right to defend the rule of law and their own independence. 
“If I’m going to defend judicial independence, I can only defend against the person who is threatened by judicial independence,” he said. 
Schiltz chose his words carefully, ribbing Paulsen — an old friend — for being a “provocateur” by asking about the federal government’s conduct. 
Paulsen said he once tried to get Schiltz a job at the University of Minnesota, where he was working. “They just couldn’t stomach two conservatives on the same faculty,” Paulsen said.  
Schiltz instead got a job at the law school at the University of Notre Dame, where he taught future Associate Supreme Court Justice Amy Coney Barrett. He joined the federal bench in Minnesota in 2006. 
The attorneys in attendance gave Schiltz a standing ovation at the conclusion of his remarks.

name: WyoFile
title: Lawmakers move to ease financial constraints for nursing home patients on Medicaid
description:
Legislative committee to draft a bill that would bump personal spending and asset allowances for first time in decades.
The post Lawmakers move to ease financial constraints for nursing home patients on Medicaid appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Nursing home residents on Wyoming Medicaid have to limit finances in two key areas to retain coverage. They can’t retain or spend more than $50 monthly on personal needs like eyeglasses or clothes, and their assets cannot exceed $2,000. 
Those limits are too low, critics say, creating unnecessary burdens on many families. 
“This continues to be a big issue for our nursing homes and for the residents that we care for,” Wyoming Hospital Association President Eric Boley told the Legislature’s Joint Labor, Health and Social Services Committee on Friday.
Committee members moved to draft legislation that would change that by bumping the limits to $100 and $5,000, respectively. 
Along with accounting for inflation in the decades since the limits were set, Boley said, the changes would ease administrative burdens of care facilities. “Making this change to keep [patients] from getting kicked off so easily makes great sense to us,” he said.  
The increases, which would cost Wyoming an estimated $1.3 million per year, come amid struggles in access and affordability in elder care across the state. Some 70% of the state’s nursing home residents are Medicaid recipients, Boley said.
Eligibility for care
Medicaid covers nursing home services for people with very low income and assets. Nursing home residents must limit their assets to $2,000 in Wyoming, not including assets like a primary residence or a vehicle. It is common for elderly people to spend down retirement savings on healthcare before they qualify for the assistance.
The state calculates the limit while screening applicants. It’s not as simple as checking a bank balance, said Medicaid Division Administrator Jesse Springer.
“There’s a whole number of things that add up to this $2,000, and it’s actually quite complicated,” Springer said. “So when we talk about resources, it’s not always that each of these individuals has $2,000 cash sitting in a bank account ready to go.”
The current limit was set in 1989.
Once patients qualify, many struggle to keep the total assets under the threshold while juggling incoming streams from pensions or Social Security, Springer said. If they don’t have it within the limit when a new month begins, he said, they are kicked off. 
That creates disruptions including administrative headaches and uncompensated care for facilities, Boley said.
Raising the limit to $5,000 would ease initial eligibility determinations and help patients avoid exceeding their thresholds when they try to save for costs including funeral expenses, according to the Wyoming Department of Health. It could also help patients return to the community after short-term nursing home stays. 
The personal needs allowance, meanwhile, allows patients to retain $50 a month for personal use outside of covered services. Patients use this money for everything from monthly hair appointments to hypoallergenic skincare products, nursing home administrators said. The limit has been in place since 2001.
The purchasing power of $50 has greatly eroded, advocates of the increase said. 
“Over the last five years, and increasing over the last two years, our office has heard troubling stories from residents struggling to afford basic necessities on their current allowance,” said Wyoming Long-Term Care Ombudsman Patricia Hall. That includes essential items like socks, vitamins, prescription glasses and cellphone plans, she said. 
Sen. Lynn Hutchings in the Wyoming Capitol. (Megan Lee Johnson for WyoFile)
Sen. Lynne Hutchings, R-Cheyenne, told the committee that she had to relocate to Denver temporarily in August after her brother was diagnosed with cancer. Having recently faced decisions involving assisted living costs, she said, “I can understand the level of apprehension, the sadness of losing assets … So increasing these limits, I see as something very, very, very, very important.”
The panel will consider the draft when it meets again in November.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Republican Victor Marx fined $58K for campaign finance violations
description: Victor Marx, the Republican nominee for Colorado governor, was assessed a fine of $57,647 on Friday by the Colorado secretary of state’s office for accepting campaign contributions in excess of the legal limit. The fine is believed to be the largest penalty ever assessed by the secretary of state’s Elections Division, which investigated complaints filed […]
text:
Victor Marx, the Republican nominee for Colorado governor, speaks at the 2026 summer conference of the Colorado Water Congress in Steamboat Springs on Aug. 19, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Victor Marx, the Republican nominee for Colorado governor, was assessed a fine of $57,647 on Friday by the Colorado secretary of state’s office for accepting campaign contributions in excess of the legal limit.
The fine is believed to be the largest penalty ever assessed by the secretary of state’s Elections Division, which investigated complaints filed against Marx in May and June by Darcy Schoening, a former state GOP official and a persistent Marx critic.
“The scale of the violations are without precedent,” hearing officer Macon Cowles wrote in a 27-page decision in the case issued Friday.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Colorado’s campaign finance laws limit individual donors to a maximum of $1,450 in contributions to a candidate for governor. But Marx’s own campaign filings showed his campaign had accepted more than 200 prohibited contributions totaling over $83,000, with overages from some individual donors ranging into the multiple thousands of dollars.
Marx’s campaign didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Representatives of the campaign did not dispute the facts of the excess contributions in a multi-day hearing last month, instead asking Cowles for leniency and describing the campaign and its staff as “learn(ing) on the job.”
But Cowles found that the campaign had exhibited “a pattern of knowing indifference to constitutional prohibitions,” which included ignoring automatic warnings of overages generated by TRACER, the state’s campaign finance system, and failing to properly handle instances in which the campaign sought to “reattribute” excess contributions to spouses or other family members who are joint account holders with the excess contributors.
His decision also notes that the campaign kept the excess money throughout an “extremely close” Republican primary for governor. Marx won the GOP nomination in June after defeating his top rival, state Sen. Barbara Kirkmeyer, by fewer than 2,500 votes.
“The volume and duration of the violations, their continuation after notice, the knowing deposit of facially excessive checks, the disregard of TRACER’s warnings, the months-long retention of prohibited funds, the failure to document a single reattribution as the rule requires, and the mass of mistaken and amended reports are each aggravating factors,” wrote Cowles, adding that they “far outweighed” any mitigating factors in the campaign’s favor.
The fine levied against Marx was calculated based on a $100 penalty for each violation, an additional penalty amount equal to 10% of the prohibited activity, and a doubling of the combined total because of the aggravating factors.
Marx, a first-time candidate and ministry leader from Colorado Springs, is considered a heavy underdog in the race against the Democratic nominee for governor, Attorney General Phil Weiser. Colorado has elected only one Republican governor in the last 56 years, and Democrats are widely expected to gain ground in a favorable midterm election year.
He faces additional campaign finance complaints, also filed by Schoening, in relation to his solicitation of unlimited donations through an online merchandise store, a scheme that one campaign finance attorney described as “patently illegal.” Those complaints underwent an initial review by the Elections Division and are still pending.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: What Red Cloud residents said when Dan Osborn returned after shoving them into national spotlight
description: A town of fewer than 1,000 people was shoved into the national spotlight by a bitter Nebraska Senate race between Pete Ricketts and Dan Osborn
text:
A sign of Red Cloud on Oct. 1, 2026 in Red Cloud. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)RED CLOUD —  A small, quiet Nebraska town near the Kansas border was home to the famous 20th-century writer Willa Cather. 
The town has the Willa Cather Center, dedicated to preserving materials related to her life and writing. Red Cloud has several historical landmarks connected to Cather, including her childhood home — the largest collection of historic sites dedicated to one American author in the country. 
It has an opera house, a bowling alley, an art gallery, a winery, a golf course and a pharmacy that serves smoothies and coffee. But this town of fewer than 1,000 people was shoved into the national spotlight by a bitter Nebraska Senate race between incumbent Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts and registered independent candidate Dan Osborn after an audio leak, first reported by the Omaha World-Herald, in which Osborn spoke about a hypothetical Red Cloud resident as a Trump supporter. 
In the recording, Osborn said, “Billy Bob in f—— Red Cloud, Nebraska, who lives next to the f—— Trump store as you pull into town and is waving the flag, all he knows is that he’s on the winning team,” Osborn said. “(Trump has) been so effective at taking Billy Bob and his wife Mary Jane or Mary Jo and telling them … you’re on the winning team. And that’s all they care about, because their lives probably suck so f—— bad.”
The national media parachuted in to cover the leak. The Ricketts campaign and Republicans amplified the audio in an ad. 
Osborn returned Thursday to Red Cloud, prompting several outlets to make the trip to cover the town hall. The former union leader started the roughly 40-minute affair with an apology for the comment.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“I do regret those words. I apologize to the people at Red Cloud.” Osborn said. “They shouldn’t have been said.” 
Dan Osborn waiting to hear from Kathy Stoner during his town hall at Red Cloud Community Center on Oct. 1, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
The Osborn town hall wasn’t fiery. About 50 people attended. Three people raised his leaked comments and asked questions during the Q&A portion of the town hall. People asked Osborn about AI, the Second Amendment, property taxes and Veterans Affairs.
Like much with politics, the reaction to his comments and his return visit was mixed. Near Red Cloud’s Main Street, several Osborn campaign signs stood. 
One woman walking down Main Street, who didn’t wish to be named, said she didn’t care about the comment and she is still voting for Osborn, saying the comment has been blown out of proportion. But she added that others were upset. 
Most business owners and staff didn’t want to talk about the political drama. One bar owner, to an inquiry from the Examiner, said, “Politics and bar business don’t go together. We stay completely out of it.” 
Danny Benge, the owner of Hometown Market, said he wasn’t interested in speaking about it either, but said, “Thanks for thinking of us, though.” 
A server at a local business said some customers would get into heated arguments about the leaked audio. The server added that it has become sort of a joke among the customers. 
Kristen Brooks, who was at the town hall, asked Osborn, why did he “dog on Red Cloud?”
Brooks told NTV that “Red Cloud is a good town to live in and I didn’t appreciate his comments and how he said all the bad things about Red Cloud … that’s not right.” 
Red Cloud City Hall on Red Cloud Main Street on Oct. 1, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
After the town hall, some people who didn’t wish to be named weren’t impressed with Osborn’s apology and questioned why they would vote for someone who spoke like that. 
Also, last week a letter from 45 people, including 20 Republican state lawmakers and 25 county officials, demanded a response from Osborn.
“The people of rural Nebraska do not need our pity. They deserve our respect,” the letter reads. “We are proud of the lives we have built here, proud of the communities we call home, and proud to represent the people who make rural Nebraska what it is.” 
None of the officials who signed the letter were from  Red Cloud or Webster County, where Red Cloud is. State Sen. David Murman, whose legislative district includes Red Cloud, signed the letter. 
Red Cloud’s mayor and council members didn’t respond to a request for comment or interviews. 
Kathy Stoner, a 65-year-old Red Cloud resident, and her husband, Max, were more forgiving of Osborn’s comment. 
“I’m really impressed that he came back, and he took full accountability,” Stoner said. 
Max, who is 74, said he can’t hold the comment against Osborn because he’s sure other people talk like that, but they don’t have people recording them. He added that Osborn seems like a smart and caring person.
Kathy said the reaction to the comments around town has been mixed. She said Red Cloud is a history-filled town with great food and great people.  
Jarrod McCartney, executive director of Discover Red Cloud, told the Examiner in a statement that he “would encourage anyone interested to truly experience what Red Cloud has to offer before making a judgment” — pointing to the roughly $25 million invested in the town over the last two decades. 
“This investment is transforming our downtown and building momentum for additional growth. … They also demonstrate our resiliency and determination to continue to progress as a community by building on our assets and supplementing the economic activity generated by agricultural production. We’re Red Cloud proud and we think life is pretty great here. Book a night at Hotel Garber, and we think you’ll agree,” McCartney said. 
The Ricketts campaign, through deputy campaign manager Max Oberg, said, “Nebraskans already heard what Dan Osborn really thinks of rural communities like Red Cloud. Showing up … doesn’t change that. He looks down on them the same way the coastal billionaires writing his checks do.”
Damion Billing, a 17-year-old turning 18 before Election Day, told the Examiner after the town hall that he laughs at the comment. 
Billing said he doesn’t really like Osborn, but given his stance on marijuana and hemp, he plans to vote for the Navy veteran. 
“Most of the people here … I don’t really think they give a s—,” Billing said when asked about how people in Red Cloud felt about the comments. 
The general election is Nov. 3. Early voting starts  Oct. 5.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas’ third-party secretary of state candidate eager to inspire electoral evolution
description: Scott Schwab, a convert to third-party politics in Kansas, embraces his secretary of state nomination by United Kansas Party as an opportunity for change.
text:
Scott Morgan, the United Kansas Party's nominee for secretary of state in the Nov. 3 election, says the growth of alternative political organizations is central to restoring collaboration and bipartisanship to elective politics at the state and national levels. He says United Kansas is part of a movement to draw the Republican and Democratic parties closer to the center. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA —  Scott Morgan’s third-party candidacy to become Kansas’ top election officer is based on the premise that voters are intensely frustrated by hyper-partisan lawmakers motivated by winner-take-all showdowns instead of good-of-the-whole collaboration.
As the United Kansas Party’s nominee for secretary of state, Morgan said his campaign sought to tap into exasperation among voters who didn’t feel they were being heard by elected representatives in Topeka and Washington, D.C.
He said the campaign was working to change the perception that no third party in Kansas could rattle the Republican and Democratic parties enough for them to embrace, or at least tolerate, bipartisanship.
“It’s trying to do something instead of hitting your head against the wall,” Morgan said during a campaign livestream event with political commentator Bill Kristol. “It’s like a product that the market is crying out for, and nobody’s designed it yet. You don’t know where it’s going to come from, but you know you have to try different things to find the answer for it. And that’s what we are very much a part of.”
United Kansas was recognized in 2024 as an official political party by Secretary of State Scott Schwab, a Republican not seeking reelection. In April, United Kansas merged with Free State Party to work together for moderate candidates and policies. Morgan, an organizer of the Free State Party, assumed the role of executive director at United Kansas.
The Nov. 3 statewide ballot in Kansas features three candidates to replace Schwab. In addition to Morgan, voters  have the option of Democratic nominee Jennifer Day of Lawrence and Republican Pat Proctor of Leavenworth.
Morgan, a Lawrence resident and unsuccessful Republican candidate for secretary of state in 2014, said that if elected he would advocate for making the job of secretary of state an administrative position instead of an elective office. The person with regulatory authority over elections in the state’s 105 counties should be politically agnostic rather than a registered partisan, he said.
“It is an odd thing that we elect the person who runs our elections,” Morgan said. “It really doesn’t make sense that it’s Republican or Democrat. It should be a neutral professional that’s appointed by a board that no one party can fire.”
 
‘Negative partisanship’
Kristol, who worked in the administrations of Presidents Ronald Reagan and George H.W. Bush, is a critic of President Donald Trump. He blames Trump for initiating and exploiting political division in the United States.
He said the U.S. two-party system had become increasingly polarized during the past 15 years. He welcomed Morgan’s bid for political reform in Kansas.
“We once had parties that were pretty functional and pretty partisan at times, where people could work across the aisle,” Kristol said. “Certainly, in most of the country … we had a real two-party system when voters went back and forth and politicians worked together. So, we know we can do it in principle. America has changed a lot. There’s more polarization, more socio-economic sorting, but still it is not something that is beyond our ability to achieve.”
Kristol said during the conversation with Morgan that he was supportive of activists striving to create third parties, promote independent candidates and support insurgents within major parties.
“We need to be experimental in this time. We can’t just sit and say, ‘Well, I guess we’re just consigned to this bitter, negative partisanship.’ It’s really bad for the country,” Kristol said.
He said harm was done to U.S. politics through zealous gerrymandering of political boundaries. The seizure of power by congressional leaders and diminished role of rank-and-file members led to more party-line votes that made politicians distinctly red or blue, he said.
In 1985, he said, 26 states elected one Republican and one Democrat to the U.S. Senate. Currently, only three states fit that mold.
“The key is to realize the system is broken,” Kristol said. “We need people who are willing to go to the state capitals or the national capitol and say, ‘I want to change the system.'”
 
‘They do work’
Morgan, who conceded there was nothing easy about building United Kansas into a political presence, said intense partisanship wasn’t a core value of Kansans. He said Kansans still pulled over to help stranded motorists without quizzing them on their political beliefs.
That’s why he remained convinced a centrist agenda built around a third party could eventually pull the two major parties back to the middle.
He said young voters were so alarmed by the ugly side of modern politics they don’t want their fingerprints on the system. The ability of dark-money donors to drown out the message of individuals discouraged people from taking part in politics, he said.
“That’s a very scary thing. If we lose our next generation … that’s a long-term risk to our republic,” Morgan said. “I call it … the fear and hate industrial complex that has been built to take that money and make us all really mad at something and really afraid of something.”
He said a goal of United Kansas was to earn a measure of legitimacy by netting at least 1% of the vote in November.
“When neither of the two parties are dealing with the issues that we’re all facing, that’s when America actually has changed,” Morgan said. “We need to do that now. The pressure valve is ready.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Attorney: Botched Tennessee execution should ‘force reckoning’ in Florida
description: Gov. Ron DeSantis signed a death warrant Thursday, scheduling James Robertson’s execution for Oct. 13, the same day his administration plans to execute William Lee Thompson. They would be the 17th and 18th executions this year and the second time this year that Florida would execute two inmates on the same day. The governor’s warrant […]
text:
Emergency vehicles at Riverbend Maximum Security Prison in Nashville on Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026. The execution of death row inmate Christa Pike was halted nearly two hours after the state of Tennessee began the lethal injection protocol. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Gov. Ron DeSantis signed a death warrant Thursday, scheduling James Robertson’s execution for Oct. 13, the same day his administration plans to execute William Lee Thompson.
They would be the 17th and 18th executions this year and the second time this year that Florida would execute two inmates on the same day.
The governor’s warrant came just after Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee placed a moratorium executions in his state after Tennessee correctional officials failed to complete an execution for the second time in five months.
Now a capital defense attorney says what happened in Tennessee should “force an urgent reckoning” in Florida, specifically citing the various ailments the 74-year-old Thompson is suffering.
“Thompson’s medical conditions raise serious concerns about what could happen during an attempted lethal injection,” said Maria DeLiberato, legal and policy director for Floridians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty.
In a recent court filing, attorneys for Thompson say he suffers an array of health problems, including sepsis, chronic kidney disease, severe fatty liver disease, and acute systolic congestive heart failure. He has staples in his abdomen from a recent colostomy surgery and staples in his head following a fall. He also suffers from dementia.
Thompson’s poor health compelled more than 100 medical professionals this week to sign a letter calling on DeSantis to withdraw Thompson’s death warrant.
“Doing so would not erase his conviction or require agreement about the death penalty,” they wrote. “It would recognize that executing a gravely ill man with profound cognitive impairment is incompatible with the most basic obligations of medicine, human dignity, and mercy.”
“Mr. Thompson appears to be in the final stages of physical and cognitive decline,” they continued. “He should spend his remaining days receiving appropriate medical treatment and compassionate care — not facing execution while his body and mind are failing.”
Thompson was sentenced to death 50 years ago for the 1976 murder, kidnapping, and rape of 23-year-old woman in Miami-Dade County. His co-defendant, Rocco Surace, also was sentenced to death, but his conviction was overturned on appeal. He was sentenced to life in prison after a retrial and died in prison in the 1990s.
Thompson’s 1976 death sentence was overturned on appeal. In a later resentencing, a jury voted 7-5 to recommend a death sentence. (Existing Florida law requires a minimum of eight jurors for a death sentence).
Robertson pleaded guilty and was convicted of first-degree murder in Charlotte County for murdering his cellmate in Charlotte Correctional Institution in December 2008.
The state executed 80-year-old Dominick Anthony Occhione and James Aren Duckett, 68 on July 28. That was the first time the state executed two people on the same day since 1964.
And the state of Florida executed 77-year-old Curtis Wilkie Beasley by lethal injection earlier this week, marking the state’s 16th execution this year and the seventh prisoner over age 70 executed this year. Beasley was convicted of first-degree murder, robbery, and grand theft auto in the 1995 hammer attack on a woman at her home south of Orlando.
Yet another execution is scheduled in Florida later this month, on Oct. 20. William Reaves Jr. was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death for killing an Indian River County sheriff;s deputy in September 1986.
If that execution takes place, it would be the 19th this year, tying the most executions in Florida in one year set in 2025.
In Tennessee 
Meanwhile, Christa Pike, who was scheduled to be the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than two centuries, remains critically ill and under treatment at a Nashville hospital following her botched execution Wednesday.  She remains intubated, on a ventilator, and is unconscious, according to a court filing Friday by her attorneys in a Tennessee court.
Pike came before that same Tennessee court nine months ago, her attorneys warning that her execution would constitute cruel and unusual punishment in violation of the Tennessee and U.S. constitutions.
They specifically argued her physical characteristics, including thrombocytosis, post-traumatic stress disorder, and small veins “make it sure or very likely that there is a substantial risk that she will experience unnecessary and superadded pain and suffering, terror, and disgrace.” Furthermore, they cited her history of “difficulty with blood draws and needle insertion.”
A Tennessee Department of Corrections team attempted to gain IV access by using at least seven needles.
It was the second time in five months that Tennessee correction officials failed to perform an execution. In May, physicians tried and failed for more than an hour to insert intravenous lines to begin the lethal injection process for Tony Carruthers.
Maria DeLiberato of Floridians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty was Carruthers’ attorney and witnessed his botched execution, as she wrote about in a New York Times op-ed in June.
She says William Thompson’s debilitating state should lead Gov. DeSantis to call off his execution.
“Thompson’s medical conditions raise serious concerns about what could happen during an attempted lethal injection,” she said Thursday in a written statement. “The spectacle we have now seen in Tennessee could repeat in Florida. We have been warned, and there is still time to prevent it.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Brigham and Women’s nurses set October 14 strike date
authors: Alison Kuznitz | State House News Service
description: The nurses overwhelmingly authorized an indefinite strike last week, after their five-day work stoppage in July failed to break the contract negotiation stalemate.
text:
NEARLY 4,000 NURSES at Brigham and Women’s Hospital plan to start their open-ended strike on Wednesday, October 14 unless a contract deal is reached with Mass General Brigham leadership, their union announced.
The Massachusetts Nurses Association said it submitted the required 10-day notice for an Unfair Labor Practice strike to the Brigham on Friday morning. The nurses overwhelmingly authorized an indefinite strike last week, after their five-day work stoppage in July failed to break the contract negotiation stalemate.
“We have repeatedly tried to get MGB to negotiate and avoid a second strike, but the billionaires who run MGB have shut the door on us,” Kelly Morgan, a labor and delivery nurse and chair of the Brigham bargaining committee, said in a statement. “There is still time to reach an agreement that protects patient care and respects nurses. MGB needs to come back to the table and negotiate without preconditions.”
MGB spokesperson Jessica Pastore said the system remains “committed to reaching a fair and responsible agreement” that recognizes nurses’ “essential contributions, maintains market-leading compensation and competitive benefits, and supports Mass General Brigham’s long-term ability to care for the patients and communities who rely on us.”
“We take seriously the union’s decision to issue a strike notice and are fully prepared to continue providing safe, high-quality care for our patients throughout a strike,” Pastore said. “While we had hoped to avoid another strike, our teams have comprehensive plans in place, informed by our experience during the five-day work stoppage in July, to support continuity of care across Brigham and Women’s Hospital.”
Nurses are seeking cost of living increases, affordable health insurance, limits on the use of temporary travel nurses and protections around patient care. MGB says nurses receive annual 5 percent raises as part of a 20-step wage scale, and that the system proposed a new 2.5 percent increase for nurses at the top step.
The MNA claimed Thursday that nurses’ planned picket outside the 10th Annual Mass General Brigham Summit next week prompted hospital executives to postpone the event. Pastore called that claim “inaccurate.”
“Our focus remains on resolving the issues at hand,” Pastore said Thursday. “Through the federal mediator, we’ve attempted to schedule bargaining sessions and have been unsuccessful. We encourage the union to engage with us constructively so that we can all return our full attention to our shared mission of providing high-quality care to our patients.”
The MNA said MGB leadership has “refused to negotiate” following the July strike.
“On August 11, management said it would not continue negotiating,” the MNA said. “Nurses are calling on MGB to resume negotiations immediately and prevent the strike by agreeing to a fair contract.”
The Brigham brought on about 1,300 temporary nurses during the July strike to maintain continuity of care. The teaching hospital is one of the core health care institutions in Boston’s Longwood medical area. 
Boston’s hospital ecosystem could see additional disruptions, after Boston Medical Center nurses also recently authorized a three-day strike. No date has been set yet for that action.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Ag sec candidates debate Iowa’s beef herd, water quality, land ownership, local food
description: Candidates for Iowa’s secretary of agriculture debated over their divergent plans for the role, though the candidates agreed on some issues like growing Iowa’s cattle herd and keeping Iowa land in farmers’ hands.  Current Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig is running for reelection as the Republican candidate against water quality researcher and activist Chr[...]
text:
Iowa secretary of agriculture candidates Chris Jones, right, and Mike Naig debated on an Oct. 2 episode of Iowa Press moderated by Kay Henderson, center, and Donnelle Eller. (Screenshot courtesy of Iowa PBS) Candidates for Iowa’s secretary of agriculture debated over their divergent plans for the role, though the candidates agreed on some issues like growing Iowa’s cattle herd and keeping Iowa land in farmers’ hands. 
Current Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig is running for reelection as the Republican candidate against water quality researcher and activist Chris Jones who has called his bid for the seat a “referendum” on Iowa water quality. 
“I think the condition of our water here is the biggest failure of our state government in the history of the state,” Jones said during the debate on “Iowa Press.” 
Jones has proposed moving away from an ag economy dependent on corn, soybeans and ethanol with taxpayer-funded “off ramps” for farmers. Naig said Jones’ ag policy ideas make him an “outlier” on the Nov. 3 election ticket for state races.
“Both candidates, the Republican and the Democratic candidate for governor are talking about the same things that I am, which is to provide incentives to farmers and work with farmers, not the mandates and taxes that my opponent is talking about,” Naig said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Water quality has become a key issue in the state of Iowa, with Jones’ candidacy as a self-proclaimed referendum to the issue and Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn stating it was a key reason he entered the race. Rob Sand, the Democrat running for governor, has also laid out policies to address water quality, which the majority of Iowa voters say is a top concern, according to a poll from Johns Hopkins Center for a Livable Future. 
Jones pointed out that many of Lahn’s points, like calling to break up dominant agribusiness and diversifying the ag economy, are similar to his own policy proposals. 
Jones said that while it’s not a “foregone conclusion” that Republicans will maintain the majority in the state Legislature, he believes he would be able to work with them on the water quality issues he is passionate about because they are issues felt by the rural Iowans largely represented by Republican lawmakers. 
“Rural people really bear the brunt of a lot of this pollution,” Jones said. “ … So, I think Republican legislators are dialed into this and want to do what’s best for their constituents. I know that they see this as a quality of life issue.” 
Naig said he has already shown his ability to work on a bipartisan basis to advance water quality initiatives, including the Farm to Faucet legislation passed earlier this year to help with conservation practice adoption and water treatment infrastructure.
While the ag secretary candidates have different approaches to improving water quality in the state and improving the farm economy, both candidates shared a desire to grow Iowa’s cattle herd and to push for policies that would keep land in the hands of the people farming rather than absentee owners. 
More cattle, pasture in Iowa 
Jones called the recent move from the Trump administration to temporarily suspend beef tariffs on certain foreign countries in order to import thousands of metric tons of ground beef “one of the stupidest ideas” he’d heard.
President Donald Trump said the decision to import more beef would help lower consumer prices of the protein while the U.S. builds back its beef herd size, which is the smallest it has been since the 1950s. 
Jones argued the decision has hurt Iowa farmers and beef producers. He said with the right policies, Iowa could become the “grass fed state” and market the beef raised in the state as such to “rebuild” the beef industry in Iowa.
Naig also criticized the move to import beef and said if producers are going to invest in growing their cattle herds, or add one to their operations, they need to see that there is profitability in their investments. 
Naig said persistent drought has “put a halt” to expanding the herd in western parts of the country where cattle has historically been raised. 
Meet Iowa’s secretary of agriculture candidates

“If the beef herd is going to expand in this country, it’s going to happen in places east of the Missouri (River)” Naig said. “If it’s going to happen in Iowa, then we need to look at creating more pasture … and then creating certainty in the marketplace that allows somebody to make the investment over a couple of years that it takes to see the payback on that.”
The Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship has been working to help landowners in western Iowa and parts of the Des Moines watershed to transition marginal cropland to pasture with the Cattle and Conservation Working Lands Program. Naig said policies like this are the solution to lowering beef prices, not importing foreign beef. 
Iowa land in Iowa hands
The candidates also talked about the need to keep more of the state’s land owned by the people who are actually farming the land. 
This is an issue that has also come up in the governor’s race with both candidates proposing changes to tax policy to boost in-state ownership. Researchers from Iowa State University say land ownership survey data show that most out-of-state or LLC ownership of Iowa land is connected to succession planning – farmers’ children and grandchildren who own the land but don’t live on it or don’t farm it themselves. 
Naig said Iowa already has the “gold standard” for land ownership regulations that prevent foreign or corporate ownership, but he said the state should “create incentives for more of that to be Iowa owned.” 
“We shouldn’t make any bones about it – we want more Iowa ground being owned by Iowans, and we’d like more farm ground being owned by farmers,” Naig said.
Speaking with reporters after the debate taping Thursday, Naig suggested creating incentives for farmers who own ag land to help change the ownership patterns, especially, he noted, as more and more farmers prepare to retire.  
Outsider farm owners are an issue in the governor’s race. Here’s what experts say.

Jones said the state needs “Iowa farmers to own their own ground, plain and simple.” 
When the people who own the land are the ones farming it, he argued, they are “much more likely to aggressively adopt” conservation practices. Jones said if the state mandated certain conservation practices on rented land specifically, it might “inspire” absentee owners to disinvest, allowing farmers to purchase the land they work.
“We definitely need policy here that’s going to get the land ownership patterns that we want, and what we want is the person farming that land to own it,” Jones said.
Farm economy 
As Iowa farmers enter a harvest season with diesel prices above $6 a gallon and persistently high input prices, Naig suggested a potential tax holiday to cut down on fuel costs and Jones said farmers need a system that is less reliant on fossil fuels and inputs. 
“Talking about the tax on diesel fuel is just scratching at the surface,” Jones said. “Let’s devise some policy here that saves money – saves farmers some real money – by developing a system that’s less reliant on fossil fuels in the first place.” 
Much of Jones’ ag policy proposals center on diversifying Iowa farms, which he argues will help farmers’ bottom lines, improve water quality and provide more locally grown food that Iowans have said they want. Jones has proposed a local food program with an annual budget of $10 million to implement. 
Jones said the “corn and soy and ethanol” system has not brought “prosperity to rural Iowa.” 
“We need to develop a system that’s more diverse, that’s less reliant on the inputs from corporate agriculture, a more diverse assemblage of crops that’s going to be more resilient to climate, more resilient to market forces, more resilient to politics,” Jones said. 
Naig said he believes ethanol is an “upside” to the state as a value-added product that contributes billions to Iowa’s economy. 
He said the pressure on the farm economy is a combination of factors, including input prices that are affected by the war in Iran, the lack of an updated farm bill and “disrupted” efforts to enact nationwide year-round access to E15 fuel. 
“We need to be a state that’s advocating, and we need to be working at the federal level to ensure that we are bringing certainty where we can, that policy is supporting market development,” Naig said.
The secretary of agriculture debate was the first of a series of debates hosted by ‘Iowa Press’ on Iowa PBS. The show will host Senate candidates Ashley Hinson and Josh Turek Oct. 7 for a live debate.
