name: Mississippi Today
title: Fiery crowd caps redistricting hearings. Opponents urge: ‘Leave our maps alone’
description: Participants march to the Capitol after the ACLU of Mississippi’s voting rights rally in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Tempers flared Thursday at a packed redistricting hearing at the Mississippi Capitol, where a large majority of speakers criticized what they said was a power grab aimed at diminishing Black political power and further entrenching Republican dominance over state politics. 
The hearing in Jackson capped off a slate of often fiery public hearings that began in August, and included stops in north Mississippi, the Delta, east Mississippi and the Gulf Coast. A Republican-dominated committee listened to speakers who shared their views on whether Mississippi should redraw its electoral maps, a move that could reshape the state’s political representation for years to come. 
Republicans control the state Legislature and currently hold three out of the state’s four seats in the U.S. House, but they could potentially redraw maps to further strengthen their grip on Mississippi’s political offices.  
Mississippians arrived at the Capitol Thursday wielding placards, megaphones and shirts emblazoned with the phrase “I FIGHT FOR VOTING RIGHTS.” A smattering of pro-redistricting attendees wearing signature red blazers of the Mississippi Federation of Republican Women were sitting in the front row, but opponents of redistricting dominated the crowd. 

Many speakers pointed out the state’s sordid history of racial discrimination, and the committee’s composition reflected the intertwined nature of racial and political polarization in Mississippi. The committee, handpicked by legislative leaders, consists of 16 Republicans, all but one of whom are white, and four Democrats, all of whom are Black. 
Walter Boone, a Jackson resident, urged lawmakers not to further continue a historical pattern of policymaking that harms Black residents, and sign their names to what he called “the Mississippi Plan 2.0.”
Audience members listen as speakers discuss redistricting during a public redistricting hearing at the Capitol in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026.A map of Mississippi Supreme Court Districts is in place during a public redistricting hearing at the Capitol in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026.Rep. Robert Johnson, D-Natchez, joins participants as they march to the Capitol after the ACLU of Mississippi’s voting rights rally in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026.Participants march to the Capitol after the ACLU of Mississippi’s voting rights rally in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026.Participants gather during the ACLU of Mississippi’s voting rights rally at the Supreme Court lawn in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026.Aznii Welchlin, left, and Muarib Abdul-Tawwab hold bullhorns while leading a chant during the ACLU of Mississippi’s voting rights rally at the Supreme Court lawn in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026.Participants gather during the ACLU of Mississippi’s voting rights rally at the Supreme Court lawn in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026.Rep. Robert Johnson, D-Natchez, and State Auditor Shad White exchange words after White’s criticism of U.S. Senator Bennie Thompson during a public redistricting hearing at the Capitol in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026.Audience members react as speakers discuss redistricting during a public redistricting hearing at the Capitol in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026.Participants gather during the ACLU of Mississippi’s voting rights rally at the Supreme Court lawn in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026.People walk past a map of U.S. Congressional Districts before a public redistricting hearing at the Capitol in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026.Aznii Welchlin leads a march inside the Capitol after the ACLU of Mississippi’s voting rights rally in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026.Participants gather during the ACLU of Mississippi’s voting rights rally at the Supreme Court lawn in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026.Participants gather during the ACLU of Mississippi’s voting rights rally at the Supreme Court lawn in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026.Audience members listen as speakers discuss redistricting during a public redistricting hearing at the Capitol in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026.Lawmakers listen as speakers discuss redistricting during a public redistricting hearing at the Capitol in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026.
“The proponents of redistricting talk and stand on a supposed high ground of race neutrality,” Boone said. “But we already know that in Mississippi the most perfectly race neutral laws were used intentionally to disastrous racial effect. Race neutrality in language does not matter if the end result is that Black Mississippians are not fairly represented. And this is where we’re headed.”
A large contingent of Democratic lawmakers sat in the audience, including House Democratic Leader Robert Johnson of Natchez. In an episode that reflects the division sparked by the redistricting push, Johnson sparred with the very first speaker of the evening: Republican State Auditor Shad White. 
White said he had heard lawmakers might not redraw Mississippi’s congressional maps in a special session expected this fall. But he urged the Legislature to do so in the future, specifically to target Rep. Bennie Thompson, the state’s only Black member of Congress and only Democrat.
“The Delta has been at the bottom of far too many rankings for far too long, and the Delta deserves better leadership than Bennie Thompson,” White said. “I’m telling you there’s a silent majority of people who want better representation for the Mississippi Delta.” 
The crowd booed, and Sen. Dean Kirby, the committee chairman, threatened to adjourn the hearing. 
As White began walking toward the exit, Johnson stood up and asked whether it was against the committee’s rules for a speaker to make comments that disparaged another person. Johnson said White told him the Delta needed better leadership. Johnson said he then told White he had “failed us as state auditor” and White responded that he was the “best Auditor Mississippi has ever had.”  
The pair wagged their fingers at each other, and Johnson said he criticized White for prosecuting “poor city clerks” instead of recovering money misspent by state officials. White then “clipclopped away,” Johnson said. 
White, a likely Republican candidate for governor, later said he came to voice an opinion that none of his potential rivals were there to offer. 
“No Republicans thinking of running for governor showed up except me, and I thought it was important for the committee to know that room of activists did not speak for all the people of this state,” White said. “They hurled insults and maybe a couple of four-letter words, but I’m not backing down from standing up for Mississippi, even when it’s a fight.”
The Republican-led effort to redistrict also reignited concerns from opponents that hard-won progress to increase Black representation in Mississippi since the Jim Crow era would be eradicated.
Brooke Floyd, a Jackson resident, said her grandfather was a prominent Black educator and school administrator during the Jim Crow era, and later became a doorman for the state House after integration. She said there was a direct connection between the eradication of Black political power and many of the state’s problems.
“It looks like being one of the poorest states in the union while refusing to raise the minimum wage,” Floyd said. “A state with one of the highest black maternal and infant mortality rates.” 
Those who spoke in favor of redistricting at the hearing said the consideration of race in drawing electoral maps was no longer justified given Mississippi’s efforts to overcome its past, and that the state should instead move toward a “color blind” approach.   
Connie Davis, a resident of Rankin County, said she supported efforts to redraw maps drawn in an effort to meet “racial targets.”
“The government must treat people as individuals and not racial categories,” Davis said. “The scales of justice should not favor anyone unjustly. The laws are applicable to everyone, regardless of their race. All of us here today should want fair representation under the law. That is in our beautifully written, colorblind constitution.”
Down the street from Capitol earlier on Thursday, opponents of the mid-decade redistricting push gathered on the lawn in front of the Mississippi Supreme Court Building for a rally organized by the ACLU. 
Attendees held signs that said “NO JIM CROW MAPS.” 
Amir Badat, the Southern states director for the voting rights organization Fair Fight, said Mississippians across the state showed up at the hearings to voice their opposition, and that lawmakers should act accordingly. 
“This is where all of our voices come together, and we are not going to let any of them be ignored,” Badat said. 
Attendees later streamed into the Capitol, chanting  “Leave our maps alone.” Seconds before a large group filed into the lobby, megaphones in hand, Sen. Kirby, the committee chairman, slipped into a nearby elevator and disappeared until the hearing started. 
The hearing was held in a room at the Capitol that quickly filled, and some attendees were forced to sit in an overflow area outside. Shortly before the hearing got underway, Johnson, the House Minority Leader, hinted at future litigation.
“This is testimony,” Johnson said. “And at some point it may be evidence. So let’s make sure we’re heard.”
The redistricting push in Mississippi and elsewhere was set in motion by the U.S. Supreme Court’s Callais decision, which removed protection for majority minority districts and cleared the way for state legislatures to redraw political lines for partisan advantage. Republican leaders believe the court’s decision ended the practice of allowing race to be considered when drawing political maps.   
Now that the legislative joint committee has finished holding public hearings, the full Legislature is expected to convene in a special session this fall to redraw at least state legislative maps. 
That wouldn’t impact this November’s federal election, but Mississippi lawmakers are likely to target Thompson’s seat with redistricting before he’s up for reelection again in 2028.
In a statement, Nancy Loome, president of the public education advocacy group The Parents’ Campaign, said redrawn maps would elevate the importance of party primaries as general election campaigns become less competitive.   
“In the past, this type of redistricting has yielded gerrymandered districts that heavily favor one party or the other, which tends to make Mississippi’s general elections less meaningful and participation in the primary election of paramount importance,” Loome said in a statement. 
After the nearly three-hour hearing concluded Thursday night, Mississippi Today asked Kirby how the public feedback might influence the imminent redistricting process. 
“I appreciate everyone expressing their opinion. We came to listen, and we did,” Kirby said. “This committee is going to do what the courts tell us to do.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Under a tougher state law, Salt Lake County accuses 3 of recruiting minors to a gang
description: Salt Lake County prosecutors urged lawmakers to toughen penalties for recruiting minors into gangs. Now they say they're putting the new law to work. .
text:
Salt Lake County District Attorney Sim Gill speaks during a criminal justice and mental health symposium on Sep. 24, 2025. (Alixel Cabrera/Utah News Dispatch)Seeking stronger tools to prosecute gang members for recruiting minors, the Salt Lake County District Attorney’s Office made its case to state lawmakers for tougher penalties last year. 
The Utah Legislature listened, raising the severity of the offense from a misdemeanor to a felony punishable by up to five years in prison. Now Salt Lake County District Attorney Sim Gill says his office is putting that new law to use for the first time. 
Gill announced Wednesday that he’s filed formal charges of soliciting, recruiting or intimidating a minor to join a gang against three men. The cases follow a long-running investigation conducted by the Salt Lake County Sheriff’s Office focused on a Utah gang’s efforts to bring in younger members, Gill said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
As the county grows, Gill said they’re seeing gangs operate in more sophisticated ways. 
“They are now trying to recruit younger kids because they know the system holds juveniles accountable to a lesser degree than adults or even older teenage minors,” Gill said in a prepared statement. 
The three men his office charged this week included a “shot caller” and someone who is second-in-command for a Barrio Evil gang, Gill said. Investigators obtained a warrant to look at their social media activity and conversations, finding that one of the suspects urged a young recruit to steal cars and take money and guns from vehicles, but the boy replied that he was almost 17 years old and could be tried as an adult, Gill said. 
The suspect said in response that the charges would be “a slap on the wrist” for a minor who hasn’t already been locked up multiple times, charging documents say. The three men — two of them age 19, and one 20 — were charged Tuesday in Salt Lake County’s 3rd District Court and have not yet appeared in court to face the allegations. 
The 2025 state law makes clear that even if a recruit doesn’t join a gang in the end, it’s still a crime to try to get them to do so. It also stipulates that it’s a misdemeanor for one minor to recruit another. 
Defense attorneys opposed the change, raising concerns that it would do more harm than good. They contend the change allows the criminal justice system to put people behind bars for longer, and as a result, further engrain their involvement in any gangs that have a presence in the state’s jails or  prison system.
“We should focus more on general gang prevention efforts in the community instead of punishing people more harshly for gang activity,” Richard Mauro, executive director of Salt Lake Legal Defender Association, told Utah News Dispatch.  
He and other critics point to research indicating that tougher penalties do not necessarily deter people from committing crimes. But Gill’s office believes the change will go a long way. 
“More and more of the homicides and attempted murders are unfortunately happening for younger and younger people,” Brett Robinson, an attorney in Gill’s office, told lawmakers on a law enforcement committee last year. “And this bill will help us give us the tools to try to counteract that.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan Senate committee considers requirement for state funding in special legislative elections
description: Michigan Sen. Chedrick Greene (D-Saginaw) is no stranger to special state legislative elections — he took office in May as a result of one in the 35th Senate District.  On Thursday, he presented a bill to the state Senate Elections and Ethics Committee that would require Michigan to reimburse county, city and township governments for the […]
text:
Michigan Capitol building. (Photo by Susan J. DemasMichigan Sen. Chedrick Greene (D-Saginaw) is no stranger to special state legislative elections — he took office in May as a result of one in the 35th Senate District. 
On Thursday, he presented a bill to the state Senate Elections and Ethics Committee that would require Michigan to reimburse county, city and township governments for the cost of conducting a special election. 
The legislation, Senate Bill 1186, would cost the state an estimated $4,500 per voting precinct in a given special election based on reimbursements made to local governments for the 2024 presidential primary election, according to a Senate Fiscal Agency analysis of the bill. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Sen. Paul Wojno (D-Warren), expressed his support for the legislation during Thursday’s hearing.
“Being a former municipal clerk, I think every clerk around the state would be supportive of this legislation,” Wojno said.
Sen. Ed McBroom (R-Waucedah Township), however, raised concerns about the wide range of elections that a municipality might have to hold outside of regular election dates.
“There’s some differences in the causes of these special elections. If the locals decide to vote somebody into a different office, I’m not sure why that’s the state’s responsibility then to pay for that local election,” McBroom said. “If the locals decide to initiate a recall election, I’m not sure why that should be the state’s responsibility to pay for that.”
Greene clarified that the bill does not cover any election date where there are already scheduled elections for ballot proposals, bond proposals for schools or any other vote occurring.
“If there’s any local municipality that is having a special election for once again recall of a trustee or something to that effect, they cannot submit to the state for the purpose of a special election reimbursement in this bill,” Greene said. “It is only for single issue state legislative purposes that are in the jurisdiction of the executive branch of the state of Michigan.”
McBroom also noted concerns that such a bill could incentivize the governor to delay calling a special election. The district which Greene now represents sat vacant for 16 months after it became open following the election of U.S. Rep. Kristien McDonald Rivet (D-Bay City). Gov. Gretchen Whitmer was heavily criticized for leaving the seat unfilled.
“Does this then give the governors pressure, actual genuine pressure, not just political pressure, to not call elections? And what if we don’t fund it? What if the legislature won’t fund it? What if we won’t approve that money?” McBroom asked. “Then these people are going to sit without representation for even longer periods of time.”
Saginaw County Clerk Vanessa Guerra testified in support of the bill on behalf of the Michigan Association of County Clerks, explaining that in Saginaw County, the total cost of both the special state Senate primary and the special state Senate general, including costs incurred by local jurisdictions, was $437,543. In Midland County alone, not including local jurisdictions, the elections cost $97,042.
“The special election was called by the governor at the end of August of 2025, so that did not leave a lot of time for local and county clerks to financially prepare for two unscheduled elections. Fortunately, of course, we made the necessary adjustments and we administered very successful elections in all three of our counties, but not without significant cost,” Guerra said. “I also want to be very frank that the burden to finance elections primarily falls on our local clerks, and I want to emphasize that because I think that there is an assumption that counties can easily absorb these unscheduled elections. Obviously, the county budget is much larger.”
Mary Clark, the Delta Township Clerk, urged a change to shorten the amount of available time for the submission of reimbursements, but said that she supported the bill.
Greene’s bill would require each local clerk to submit its verified account of actual costs to the department of treasury not later than 90 days after the date of the special election, though Clark suggested it could be shortened to 45 days. 
“No matter which number you land on, we are in support of the concept because local jurisdictions that did not create the vacancy, and did not create the situation requiring the election, should not be the ones funding the bill,” she added.
On Greene’s legislation, the committee heard testimony only and did not vote on the bill.
In other business, the committee also unanimously passed a package of three bills, House Bills 4793, 4794 and 4795, which would eliminate certain administrative requirements for those elected to school board, intermediate school board or community college board of trustee positions.

name: Washington State Standard
title: As immigrant Medicaid cuts take effect, some in WA can keep their coverage
description: Roughly 10,000 immigrants in Washington are losing their Medicaid health coverage due to federal cuts Republicans in Congress approved last year.  On Thursday, a provision in President Donald Trump’s signature tax cut and spending law stripped Medicaid coverage for refugees, asylees and other lawfully present immigrants, including people who fled the war in[...]
text:
(Photo by Thomas Barwick/Getty Images)Roughly 10,000 immigrants in Washington are losing their Medicaid health coverage due to federal cuts Republicans in Congress approved last year. 
On Thursday, a provision in President Donald Trump’s signature tax cut and spending law stripped Medicaid coverage for refugees, asylees and other lawfully present immigrants, including people who fled the war in Ukraine and trafficking victims, for example. Some of them have disabilities and receive long-term care. 
Advocates say this will lead to many of these individuals getting sicker and putting themselves in danger of dying earlier than they would if they had health insurance. This will further strain hospitals as these patients will fill emergency rooms for treatment. 
“Most of them cannot possibly afford to buy insurance on their own, so will be left with no coverage at all, no access to primary care doctors, no access to prescription drugs, no access to the care that they need,” Service Employees International Union 775 Secretary-Treasurer Adam Glickman told reporters Thursday. 
A federal judge in Seattle on Wednesday provided a temporary reprieve for a segment of those immigrants, saying those who receive Supplemental Security Income, or SSI, are still eligible for Medicaid, despite rules from federal officials trying to flout this longstanding precedent. 
The ruling from U.S. District Court Judge Thomas Zilly allows an estimated 800 migrants to keep their coverage for the time being. The feds can appeal the preliminary order.
Lee Che Leong, senior policy advocate with Northwest Health Law Advocates, called Zilly’s decision a “crucial victory.”
Roughly 3,000 other lawfully present immigrants would have lost their coverage if not for efforts by state officials who updated their immigration information to enable them to keep their Apple Health, the state’s low-income insurance program. Initial projections showed 14,000 noncitizens losing coverage. 
The federal law maintains coverage for lawful permanent residents with green cards and other select categories of migrants.
Come January, it will knock tens of thousands more Washingtonians off Apple Health when new strict work requirements take effect  
Over 1.9 million residents in Washington are enrolled in Apple Health. Of those, at least 200,000 are projected to be stripped of coverage by the end of 2027 as a result of the Republican-backed law, according to state officials. 
Critics of the law fear thousands will lose their healthcare despite meeting the new work requirements because of what they see as cumbersome paperwork barriers to maintaining Medicaid. The state is spending millions of dollars on IT services to verify enrollees meet the forthcoming requirements.
‘Conditions will get worse’
Of the thousands being kicked off Medicaid on Thursday, two in five live in King County, according to county Councilmember Teresa Mosqueda. She argued the cuts will mean less financial reimbursements for healthcare systems. The effects of this will trickle down to patients with insurance, some of whom could wind up paying higher premiums to make up the difference.
“People will be laid off in clinics and hospitals around our county and state,” Mosqueda said in a press conference. “Wait times will soar and care will be delayed. Conditions will get worse and more people will die.”
Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, last month signed an executive order aimed at finding ways to keep Washingtonians insured. It set up a committee of state officials to develop strategies and identify state actions that will help people maintain their coverage. The order also directs a statewide public awareness campaign to let enrollees know about the cuts, and the creation of a database to track coverage losses.
Glickman and other advocates are calling on Ferguson and state lawmakers to fill the gap with state funding so these migrants can regain healthcare. Some are pushing for tax increases to pay for it.
Mosqueda said King County should follow Los Angeles County, which is implementing a new sales tax hike to raise $1 billion per year in response to the Medicaid cuts.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Washington is one of a number of states that provide Medicaid to residents who don’t qualify for the federal program due to immigration status, but capacity is limited. The option is fully state funded. Immigrants without legal status are ineligible for federally funded health insurance.
“While some people may qualify for other Apple Health programs or coverage through Washington Healthplanfinder, understanding those options now is critical to avoiding gaps in care,” said Leanne Berge, the CEO of Community Health Plan of Washington.
The Legislature earmarked nearly $20 million to ensure immigrants here could retain long-term care insurance coverage despite the federal cuts, but the money isn’t expected to go nearly as far as lawmakers expected. Though this week’s court ruling could allow that state funding to cover more enrollees.
Immigrants who remain eligible must be lawful permanent residents, Compact of Free Association islanders or Cuban or Haitian.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Hennepin County sheriff drops undercover classification for some task force deputies
description: The Hennepin County Sheriff’s Office has stopped classifying deputies as “undercover” to shield their body camera footage from the public, following a campaign by public defenders for more than a year and rebukes from at least three judges. As the Reformer first reported earlier this year, the Sheriff’s Office has since around 2022 restricted the […]
text:
Hennepin County detectives Jason Wong and Nick Peterson punched, tased and arrested Allanzo Johnson after stopping him for a broken taillight in north Minneapolis on March 27, 2025. Misdemeanor charges against Johnson were dismissed after prosecutors obtained the officers' body camera footage. (Screenshot from bystander video) The Hennepin County Sheriff’s Office has stopped classifying deputies as “undercover” to shield their body camera footage from the public, following a campaign by public defenders for more than a year and rebukes from at least three judges.
As the Reformer first reported earlier this year, the Sheriff’s Office has since around 2022 restricted the release of body camera footage of members of its Violent Offender Task Force by calling them undercover, even when the deputies were carrying out regular policing duties like traffic stops for broken taillights.
Public defenders argued the practice robbed their clients of public trials and was a blatant attempt to circumvent public transparency, one of the main reasons law enforcement agencies around the country invested millions of dollars equipping officers with body cameras.
Hennepin County public defender Amanda Brodhag said the policy change is a “win” — but one tempered by the Sheriff’s Office increasingly using the classification for deputies in a different task force, the West Metro Drug Task Force.
“Same game plan. Different team,” Brodhag said.
Hennepin County sheriff conceals bodycam footage by calling officers ‘undercover’

Public defenders learned about the policy change in an email from a prosecutor in the Hennepin County Attorney’s Office on Sept. 4, stating they would no longer be seeking protective orders for body camera footage of Violent Offender Task Force members.
The Hennepin County Attorney’s Office confirmed the policy change and said it was made by Hennepin County Sheriff Dawanna Witt.
The Hennepin County Sheriff’s Office did not respond to requests for comment.
Brodhag and her colleagues tallied 78 cases from April 2025 until the policy change last month — about one per week — in which the Hennepin County Sheriff’s Office used protections for undercover officers to restrict body camera footage from being shared with the public.
They’ve counted five requests to restrict body camera footage for deputies with the West Metro Drug Task Force since then.
Body camera footage is already broadly private under Minnesota law but can become public if it’s used as evidence in court, if there’s a public interest in it or if the subject of the footage requests its release.
The Reformer reported on the cases of two men who were stopped by deputies with the Violent Offender Task Force, violently arrested and charged with misdemeanor, “obstructing legal process,” for allegedly not following orders.
In both cases the deputies were wearing vests that said “sheriff” and large body cameras on their chests — hardly an image that the word “undercover” conjures of an officer disguised as a drug dealer or gang member to infiltrate criminal networks.
But the Sheriff’s Office would not turn over the footage until prosecutors secured a judge’s order that it not be shared with the public.
Prosecutors for the city of Minneapolis promptly dropped the two cases after receiving the footage, which highlighted the fact that they had brought criminal charges without reviewing what is often the most important evidence in cases involving abuses against or by law enforcement officers.
The Minneapolis City Attorney’s Office declined to comment on those cases as well as the sheriff’s policy change.
Shawn Gullickson, captain of the Hennepin County Sheriff’s Office Major Crimes Division, said in affidavits to the court that allowing the footage to be public would blow the deputies’ cover and put them in danger.
He also said deputies may “transition between traditional (undercover roles) and other more standard roles such as proactive policing in the community.”
Gullickson has said in court affidavits that all deputies on the Violent Offender Task Force and West Metro Drug Task Force are undercover, but it’s unclear how many deputies serve on them.
For the most part, judges sided with prosecutors and issued protective orders. That’s because under state law, law enforcement agencies have the power to determine which officers are undercover.
At least three judges pushed back in recent months, Brodhag said.
In July, Hennepin County District Judge Andrew Tweeden sided with public defenders in a case brought against a man who was found to have a firearm without a permit after being pulled over for not wearing a seat belt.
Prosecutors sought to redact the videos by blurring the deputies’ faces before showing them in court even though the officers themselves would appear in person in the courtroom.
The officers were all clearly identifiable as law enforcement and wearing body cameras. Tweeden said the fact that they may sometimes engage in undercover work does not justify restricting a defendant’s rights to mount a complete defense and have a public trial.
“This was not a covert operation,” Tweeden said. “It was a public act.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ lawmaker wants to blunt impacts of AI in the workplace
description: Sen. Andrew Zwicker is behind a bill that would retrict when employers can use algorithms, models, computations, and other such tools.
text:
Sen. Andrew Zwicker, who said “nothing has moved at the speed of AI,” is behind a bill aimed at curbing the use of artificial intelligence in the workplace. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)A New Jersey Senate panel unanimously advanced legislation that would require preapproval for a range of automated digital tools in the workplace and limit the use of electronic monitoring inside and outside of the workplace.
The bill is backed widely by New Jersey labor unions and opposed by business groups who cautioned it could ensnare and penalize companies for routine technology decisions or existing tools. It is one lawmaker’s attempt to blunt the job market impacts of artificial intelligence.
“We have never seen a disruptive piece of technology like this before. You can go back to the steam engine, the internet, the light bulb — pick what you want, and nothing has moved at the speed of AI,” said bill sponsor Sen. Andrew Zwicker (D-Middlesex).
NJ data center polluted air for nearly a year before regulators intervened

The bill would bar use of algorithms, models, computations, and other tools employers use to make personnel decisions unless a third-party impact assessment finds they can be used for one of six discrete purposes, like ensuring product quality, administering payroll, or periodically assessing employee performance.
Tools used by public-sector employers, including those that aid the provision of government services, would face the same requirements. There, vendors must pay for impact assessments.
It would ban monitoring employees in nonwork areas like break rooms, wholly bar monitoring outside of the workplace, including through monitoring software on personal devices, and prohibit the use of quotas aided by electronic tools.
Numerous labor unions that testified before the Senate Labor Committee Thursday said new safeguards are needed amid the rapid development of artificial intelligence technologies that are even now being adopted into the workforce.
Kristen Affrime, a staff representative with the Communications Workers of America, said the union’s members are not opposed to new technology.
“The issue is whether workers have basic rights when that technology is used to manage them, monitor them, or make decisions that affect their livelihoods,” Affrime said.
The bill does not define artificial intelligence, and its definitions do not limit its scope to technologies that use AI.
Business groups cautioned the legislation could end up barring the use of a range of payroll, scheduling, and cybersecurity tools as well as technology that has existed for decades.
“Even commonplace tools like Excel spreadsheets can involve statistical analysis or automated processes, but they are fundamentally different from an artificial intelligence system making consequential decisions about hiring, firing, compensation, or promotions,” said Jack Ramirez, a lobbyist for the New Jersey Business and Industry Association.
Zwicker suggested the bill could see changes as it continues to wend its way through the Legislature.
“We’re going to look carefully at definitions and other pieces of this bill as it moves forward, but today we are saying New Jersey is becoming a national leader in how we are going to look at and regulate AI in the workforce,” he said.
The panel discussed, but did not vote on, separate legislation that would create a new fund to pay for workforce retraining, renewable energy projects needed for AI infrastructure, and projects in areas impacted by AI.
The fund would be filled by a 5% tax on gross revenue — not profit — from AI operations and fines on firms that do not annually report water and energy use, enter into community benefits agreements, or conduct environmental impact assessments.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri tightened the rules. The wait still leaves microbusiness owners vulnerable
description: Missouri drew its final round of marijuana microbusiness applicants on Sept. 9. The state received 888 applications and expects to issue approximately 77 licenses beginning in December. I want to write about the months in between, because I work in the trade that operates in them. I am a consultant. I run licensing, compliance and […]
text:
(Getty Images).Missouri drew its final round of marijuana microbusiness applicants on Sept. 9. The state received 888 applications and expects to issue approximately 77 licenses beginning in December.
I want to write about the months in between, because I work in the trade that operates in them.
I am a consultant. I run licensing, compliance and operations work for cannabis operators, and I have sat across the table from first-time licensees more times than I can count. When the state put new microbusiness rules in place in May, I did not read them as an attack on the trade. I read them as rules aimed at the right problem that stop just short of solving it.
The rules are good ones. They spell out what it means to majority-own and operate a license. They let regulators review ownership arrangements before a license issues rather than after, which is the change that should have come first. They require a compliance course before applying and again after the award. And they require eligible owners to serve as the primary point of contact with regulators during the application process, limiting one of the ways consultants can make themselves indispensable.
All of that reaches the contract. None of it reaches the wait.
Consider what a top-drawn applicant actually holds this fall: the prospect of a license coming as soon as December, a facility they may not have secured, capital they may not have raised and no experience operating in a regulated industry. Forty-six licenses from the first two rounds are active but not yet approved to operate. As of Aug. 18, only 21 microbusinesses were operating. Jimi Poe, who won in the first round and became the first to open a microbusiness dispensary, told the division’s own podcast it took him two years rather than the six months he expected.
That is the exposure. Not necessarily a bad clause. It is a long, unfunded, inexperienced wait, during which somebody will offer to carry it for you.
A wait does two things to a person. It drains cash and it makes them feel behind, and both push toward signing. The offer usually arrives sounding like relief: We will fund the build-out. We will handle compliance. We will run it until you are ready. Some of those offers are honest. Others can look just as reassuring on the first read, which is precisely the problem.
Most people who sign a bad agreement are not careless. They are outmatched. The licensee has never done this before and the person across the table may have done it dozens of times.
So let me be useful rather than righteous, and name some things licensees should watch for when dealing with people in my own industry.
Watch for equity that vests on signature rather than on delivery. Ask why an adviser is receiving ownership before the promised work has been completed, and whether that equity could instead be tied to specific milestones.
Watch for a management agreement wearing a consulting label. If the document hands someone else hiring authority, banking authority or control of the seed-to-sale account, that is not simply advice. Under the new rules, those kinds of provisions could also raise questions about whether eligible owners retain the control Missouri now requires.
Watch for fees calculated against gross rather than net. A percentage of revenue does not care whether the operator ever makes money.
Watch for standard operating procedures that do not describe your building. Everyone starts from a template. But if the document refers to rooms you do not have, nobody walked your facility closely enough.
And ask the question that sorts this trade quickly: Which licensees have you taken from award to operation, and may I speak with them? A consultant with a successful track record should be able to provide references.
Lesley Turek, the division’s chief equity officer, has already offered another safeguard. She has advised current and future licensees to run proposed arrangements or agreements past the division so regulators can identify potential compliance problems. That is an open door, offered by the regulator, and in my experience new licensees do not alwayswalk through it because asking feels like admitting you do not know.
That reading is backwards. Running a draft agreement past your own regulator is among the cheapest diligence available in this industry, and it costs nothing.
The state spent this cycle making the paperwork harder to abuse, which was the right move. What regulation cannot eliminate is the vulnerability created during the months when a new licensee has something worth taking and littleexperience defending it.
That is why the most important protection for Missouri’s newest cannabis entrepreneurs may not be another rule. It may be knowing when not to sign.

name: WyoFile
title: A new suicide fatality review sheds light on prevention efforts in Laramie County
description:
Social isolation, intimate partner problems and family relationship stress were the top three risk factors found by the Laramie County Suicide Fatality Review team.
The post A new suicide fatality review sheds light on prevention efforts in Laramie County appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
CHEYENNE—“Persistence, I think, is one of the most important things we have on our side.”
That is Brittany Wardle’s attitude in regard to addressing suicide in Laramie County as she serves as the community prevention project director at Cheyenne Regional Medical Center.
The Wyoming Institute of Population Health released its 2026 Suicide Fatality Review last week. The review analyzed suicide cases in order to provide recommendations that can translate into meaningful community impact. The review was conducted by the Laramie County Suicide Fatality Review team, made up of a multidisciplinary group of professionals who work to address gaps in Wyoming’s system of care.
Wardle gave insight into what information is used to inform the team’s recommendations.
One component is the suicide consolidated risk assessment profile, which is standard information collected on every suicide in Laramie County.
The other component is a review process in which, with the consent of the family or loved ones, a thorough review is conducted of a person’s suicide to understand the context and factors that led to his or her eventual suicide. Wardle expressed gratitude to families who willingly participate and noted how brave that choice is, as they are asking the team to “review the case of my loved one and change the outcome for families in the future,” she said.
“Those two components really give us both a quantitative and qualitative view of what’s happening in our community around suicide,” Wardle said. “And that process is really what drives our recommendations.”
The team then works to either implement its recommendations in the community or pass them onto the Wyoming Department of Health, if the issue is statewide.
Pet care and animal welfare were areas that showed a need for additional resources in the 2026 review due to people experiencing emotional distress over their sick or dying pets, coupled with an inability to afford care.
Wardle emphasized the importance of “physically getting out into the community and making sure that resources are publicly and obviously available in places where we know that risk might be present.”
The review also called attention to the need for improved communication among different branches of the healthcare system to minimize the burden on people struggling. This ensures patients are not solely responsible for their care, especially when they are in the process of transitioning from inpatient to outpatient care.
Wardle gave examples of agencies communicating if a patient missed a referral appointment, and following up to determine whether a patient’s need had been met.
The review also identified the primary risk factors in suicides over the past year. The top three were social isolation at 34%, an intimate partner problem at 34% and family relationship stress at 34%, or an overlap of one or more issues.
Wardle noted that all of these issues involve how humans connect with other humans, but that the actual context of each particular situation could be wildly different. She touted both 988 Lifeline and 211 Wyoming as connectors and support systems to help people who are struggling. The 988 Lifeline is the suicide and crisis hotline that allows people to call or text a crisis intervention specialist to receive support and guidance, whereas 211 Wyoming helps people find solutions to address health and human services needs.
Wardle explained how each program is beneficial in its own way, and that 988 is not only for an absolute crisis because staff are trained for many different situations.
“Our call centers have trained their staff, they’re folks who are caring, they’re folks who will listen, they’re folks who can help walk through, like, ‘Hey, I’m concerned about a friend, what should I do,’” she said.
Wardle then touched on how 211 can address the social needs that tend to accompany suicide — related issues such as job loss, loss of transportation or inability to feed one’s family.
Wardle explained how losing one’s job can compound into a multitude of issues, leading to financial distress and family tension that then lead to conflict and frustration.
The review also found that 69% of individuals experienced a crisis in the two weeks before their death and that the primary factors were a mental health problem at 47%, an intimate partner problem at 37% or an alcohol problem at 34%, or a combination of one or more issues.
Wardle noted the importance of providing appropriate training and resources to the agencies that interact with a person in the midst of a crisis, such as law enforcement.
“Part of it is making sure that our partners interacting with people during a crisis have what they need to provide that support or to be able to refer to that support,” she said.
Another major concern is the role alcohol and firearms play, and how availability and accessibility to firearms is a major risk factor across Wyoming.
The review notes that 3,500 firearm locks have been distributed, and that safe storage of firearms is repeatedly encouraged to mitigate potential risks.
“The discussion is always firearms are not good or bad, but we know firearms are deadly,” Wardle explained.
Overall, Wardle believes this review helps everyone in Laramie County better understand the issue of suicide and how everyone plays a role in making a positive difference.
“I think at the end of the day, our hope really is that people have an understanding of what suicide risk looks like in our community, and they understand what they personally or what their organization professionally can do to support well-being here in Laramie County,” Wardle said.
She concluded by emphasizing the importance of hope and the role this review plays in the larger picture of improving suicide outcomes.

name: Daily Montanan
title: The trap door beneath a 10-year-old
description: I was 10 years old, in the juvenile holding cell of the county jail. I looked down at the floor. There was a perfect square. About four feet by four feet. A deputy stood in front of me.  Badge, handcuffs and gun: He made an impression. Authority? Power? Yes, I was intimidated. He explained to me […]
text:
The hangman's noose. (Photo illustration by Getty Images)I was 10 years old, in the juvenile holding cell of the county jail.
I looked down at the floor. There was a perfect square. About four feet by four feet.
A deputy stood in front of me.  Badge, handcuffs and gun: He made an impression. Authority? Power? Yes, I was intimidated.
He explained to me that I was standing on the trap door.  Of the gallows.
Welcome to Great Falls, Montana.
I wasn’t under arrest.  This was a Cub Scout field trip.  A tour of the Cascade County jail, not a museum. It was an active jail. With prisoners.
It was a different time.  Today, it’s unlikely that Cub Scouts would be allowed to tour an active jail. Then, no one thought twice about it. It was the 1960s.
For the adults, it was ordinary. One month it was the TV station, the next the jail. For me, it was life-changing.  I stood inside the machinery of execution.  I was standing in the space built for the condemned.
No one thought that perhaps it wasn’t a good idea to take 10-year-olds to the place the government built to hang people. To kill them.
I was introduced to capital punishment as a child.
It wasn’t a political issue. It was a place. It was an experience; a memory seared into me.
We had been taught that the police were our protectors. Our government was good. If we were afraid, look for the man with the badge.
And then I learned that our government kills people. The power of the government was beneath my feet. The machinery of death was part of a room for children.
At age 10, I had never attended a funeral. Never.  I didn’t know how to mourn or grieve.  But I had stood on the trap door of the county gallows.
There were no threats, but still I felt threatened by the room. I had a new understanding of government power.
What did I learn?  I learned that government authority could be used to kill people. Power wasn’t just a gun and a badge. It involves the power to decide who lives and who dies. Government violence changes children.
Today, there are roughly 2,000 people on death row in the United States. Capital punishment is the law in 27 states. In Montana, two men are on death row.
One-hundred forty-five countries have eliminated capital punishment by law or practice. Those who haven’t?  Those believed to execute the most: China, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Yemen, and the United States. It isn’t a place of honor.
Yet, since 1973, at least 203 people on death row have been exonerated. Wrongfully convicted, proven innocent. Some of those exonerations have been through DNA evidence. Others because of recanted testimony, new evidence, or proof of official misconduct. And they were on death row probably for many years. How many people have been executed who were innocent?  People who might be exonerated today with DNA evidence.
If only they were still alive.
There were roughly 84 who were lynched in Montana. “Extrajudicial killings” is the term for them.  Many of those executed were taken by the Vigilantes, the citizens-turned-law enforcement mostly during the state’s territorial days. Add to that 74 government executions, the last three by lethal injection. The last one, David Dawson, died in 2006.
Today, we hear about new execution dates and new executions.  Alabama, Texas, and other states.  It’s often in the news.
How do children learn about our government? Not just from books. From what government does. What it protects. What it destroys.
I learned about our government in a juvenile holding cell.  I was 10.  Looking down at a four-foot square beneath my feet.
I still see that trap door, six decades later. It taught me about government and power. And the abuse of power.

name: WyoFile
title: Baseball in a national park? We found 7 ball fields at Grand Teton and Yellowstone.
description:
Turns out, the field of nightmares proposed in Grand Teton National Park wouldn’t be unique.
The post Baseball in a national park? We found 7 ball fields at Grand Teton and Yellowstone. appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
We’ll get the puns about Major League Baseball’s pitch to stage a game in a national park — and the Washington Post’s report the Park Service scouted Grand Teton National Park for a suitable site — out of the way quickly. (Please groan in advance.)
Was it a bush league proposal that came out of left field? Did the Trump administration’s “not a priority” statement mean it won’t play hardball? Was Major League Baseball Commissioner Rob Manfred’s concept a screwball idea, a whiff right off the bat? If it was a Biden idea, please say it ain’t so, Joe.
MLB said Thursday it would not pursue the idea in Grand Teton National Park, even though a ballpark in Grand Teton or Yellowstone would be déjà vu all over again. Research turned up seven ball diamonds in the two federal reserves.






A ball field is visible in an aerial photograph of Grand Teton National Park employee housing in Moose taken in 2007. By 2011 the field was developed as more park housing. (Screengrab/Teton County GIS)






A ball field near the Moran Elementary school in Grand Teton National Park is visible in Google Earth images. (Screengrab/Google Earth)






A ballpark at Old Faithful in Yellowstone National Park as seen in 2017 by Google Earth. (Screengrab/Google Earth)


In Grand Teton, there used to be a ball diamond in the middle of a park staff residential area at Moose. It’s since been developed as staff housing.
Farther north in Grand Teton’s community of Moran, there’s a diamond at the elementary school. And in Yellowstone National Park, Google Earth reveals five other diamonds.
Jackson Hole photographer Brad Boner found perhaps the strangest one near Yellowstone’s West Thumb Geyser Basin. He was researching his book “Yellowstone National Park Through the Lens of Time,” a rephotographing project in which he duplicated the images that pioneer photographer William Henry Jackson took in 1871. Boner was looking for the exact viewpoint of a Jackson image.
Stumbling through the woods south of the West Thumb Geyser Basin, he broke into the outfield of the ball field and saw the looming backstop. (West Thumb Ballpark’s center field tree line is 262 feet from home plate and probably 60 feet high.)
He felt like he was in a movie, he said. “It was like walking out of the cornfield in ‘Field of Dreams.’”
A ball diamond just south of Yellowstone National Park’s West Thumb Geyser Basin is visible in Google Earth images. (Screengrab/Google Earth)
With recent events, he became obsessed and took to Google Earth. He found that there are or were ball fields at the Yellowstone communities of Mammoth, Canyon Village, Old Faithful and Fishing Bridge. The one at Old Faithful can no longer be found in satellite photographs.
Boner and Jackson Hole News&Guide reporter Cory Hatch may have had a hand in the demise of the Moose ball field in Grand Teton. They were touring the housing site before construction began in 2011, working on a story about the planned development.
Park officials were set on building the new housing near the Chapel of Transfiguration, a scenic and storied chapel in the park that features a view of the Grand Teton from the altar. Many thought the park plan intrusive.






A ball field at Mammoth in Yellowstone National Park. (Screengrab/Google Earth)






A ballpark at Canyon Village in Yellowstone National Park as seen on Google Earth. (Screengrab/Google Earth)






A ball field at Fishing Bridge in Yellowstone National Park seen on Google Earth. (Screengrab/Google Earth)


Boner had married his wife Jeannette at the chapel.
The news crew asked why the park didn’t just build housing on the ball field.
“They said that the field was a good place for employees to get outside and recreate,” Boner said. “Cory and I both turned and gestured towards the Tetons at the same time and said something like ‘they have this right here.’”
“I think at that moment they understood that their proposal wouldn’t fly,” Boner said, “and Cory and I take credit for the leveling of that baseball field.”
The post Baseball in a national park? We found 7 ball fields at Grand Teton and Yellowstone. appeared first on WyoFile .

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming should compete for America’s next great base — on our terms
description:
The Pentagon’s call for a new large-scale military base gives Wyoming an opportunity to buck the commodity roller coaster, writes guest columnist David Giralt.
The post Wyoming should compete for America’s next great base — on our terms appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Opinion

Wyoming has an opportunity to compete for one of the most consequential military investments in a generation. On Wednesday, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth invited governors and adjutants general to pitch America’s “Next Great American Base,” an installation for 15,000 to 25,000 troops on hundreds of thousands of acres, with independent power and modern defenses.
Having served as an Army officer and worked on defense policy at the Pentagon and in Congress, I know a serious bid must answer more than whether Wyoming wants the jobs. It must show Wyoming can meet the mission.
This base must be able to keep operating if an adversary disrupts the grid, jams communications, cuts supply lines or targets forces massed near vulnerable coasts. Modern war demands room for drones, long-range missiles, electronic warfare, protected airspace, dispersed training, reliable fuel and dispatchable power.
Wyoming fits that mission unusually well. We have open country and airspace where unmanned systems can train. We sit in the strategic heart of the country, home to F.E. Warren Air Force Base, with interstate and rail connections. We have natural gas, wind, uranium, coal and growing advanced-nuclear potential. The University of Wyoming and our community colleges can help train the technicians, cyber specialists and tradespeople this mission needs.
A fair question some Wyomingites will reasonably ask is whether we should want this here. A base this size could place city-scale demands on a Wyoming community: more pressure on roads, water, housing, schools and hospitals.
One answer is that our budget still rides the commodity roller coaster, while a base offers a different kind of anchor: a durable military mission, years of construction, and lasting demand for Wyoming energy, services and supplies that does not vanish when prices fall. 
Consider Fort Drum, a major Army post in northern New York. Its fiscal year 2024 Army economic-impact statement reported about $1.9 billion in direct economic impact; regional analysis put its broader economic impact at about $2.55 billion and tied it to more than 31,000 jobs. Wyoming’s numbers would differ, but Fort Drum shows what a long-term military mission can mean for a rural region. 
Negotiated correctly, federal investment can build infrastructure that outlasts the construction crews and give more of our kids a reason to stay. Wyoming workers, veterans and contractors should be ready to compete for the work through apprenticeships, veteran hiring and open access to federal contracts. If the base goes elsewhere, Wyoming gets none of the investment and none of the say.
The land question deserves a straight answer, too. Camp Guernsey’s 78,000-acre joint training center is a proven foundation but only a fraction of what the Pentagon described. A real bid must show how it could connect with compatible state land, federal land, and willing sellers to meet that scale. Other Wyoming communities deserve a fair shot at making their case, and a public, merit-based review of sites and costs should come before Wyoming commits any land or money.
No Wyoming family should lose its ranch because the state wants better odds in a federal contest.
Wyoming should compete only on terms we write ourselves. Land should come from willing sellers and public acreage, not annexation. Existing water rights, Wyoming law and interstate compacts must be protected. Hunting and recreation access should be protected where possible and replaced where necessary. Camp Guernsey has partnered with the Wyoming Game and Fish Department since 2003 on the Broom Creek Hunter Management Area, preserving public hunting alongside military training. It can be done.
Before any permanent units arrive, a binding compact should require Washington to cover the foreseeable costs of roads, housing, schools, emergency services, healthcare and water systems. 
Time matters. Gov. Mark Gordon and the adjutant general can start the groundwork now with our congressional delegation, landowners, local governments and the university. Wyoming’s first submission should include a map and a plan for power, water, housing and schools.
Other states will bring land and promises, but Wyoming can bring a plan. We have the energy to run it, the strategic depth to protect it, the training space to prepare the joint force and the people who understand what military service costs and what it is worth.
Wyoming should make its case. 
If the mission fits and the terms hold up, Wyoming should compete to win on Wyoming’s terms.

Boise Democrat tops list of Idaho legislative candidates who have raised the most for 2026 campaign

Incumbent GOP Gov. Brad Little has raised the most campaign money of any statewide candidate in 2026.

Both Stegner and Pickens reported raising a greater percentage of their campaign contributions from people and a smaller percentage from companies.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Grand jury indicted ex-Idaho health official on felony misuse of funds. A judge dropped the case.
description: Two days after a grand jury indicted a former Idaho state government employee on two felony counts of misuse of public funds, a local judge dismissed the case — after a request from the prosecutor.  The case marked the first criminal charges — and a rare public update — to emerge from a yearslong investigation […]
text:
The exterior of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on Jan. 14, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Two days after a grand jury indicted a former Idaho state government employee on two felony counts of misuse of public funds, a local judge dismissed the case — after a request from the prosecutor. 
The case marked the first criminal charges — and a rare public update — to emerge from a yearslong investigation launched by Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador that probed how the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare doled out $72 million in federal child care grants in 2021 and 2022.  
The official who was criminally charged, Ericka Rupp, oversaw the grant program. In the indictment, filed in Canyon County District Court last week, the grand jury charged Rupp with two felony counts of misuse of public funds and securities, for allegedly illegally authorizing, appropriating or otherwise misusing more than $300 of the government’s money. 
Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador speaks at the Idaho Medal of Honor ceremony held Sept. 1, 2026, at the Idaho Statehouse in Boise. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Attorney General’s Office)
Labrador’s special prosecutor, Canyon County Prosecuting Attorney Christopher Boyd, told the Idaho Capital Sun that the amount of money allegedly misused was not specified in the indictment, but that it would’ve been an issue to determine during a potential trial. 
Boyd said he moved to drop the indictment based on feedback from jurors.  
“I, however, asked of them whether they felt the case was one worth pursuing in terms of resources,” Boyd wrote in a text message. “I truly wanted their opinion on this. They had spent several full days taking testimony. The majority of jurors felt my time was better spent focusing on the many other serious crimes they worked on.”
For each count, the penalties could have been up to 14 years imprisonment and up to $10,000 in fines, according to state laws cited in the indictment.
Rupp’s attorney, Scott McKay, declined to comment. 
In a Friday order, Third District Judge Thomas W. Whitney wrote he was dismissing the case upon the state’s request. The court hasn’t released records supporting the judge’s decision to dismiss the case. 
Special prosecutor Christopher Boyd argues in district court that the Idaho Office of the Attorney General should not pay legal fees associated with litigation that set to block the office’s civil subpoena. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)
Pending permission from the court, Boyd said he hopes to release a report with more details in the coming days. 
Asked whether he’d pursue charges against Rupp, or other people linked to the investigation, Boyd said: “The report should conclude my investigation.”
The Idaho attorney general’s office could not immediately be reached for comment.
Department of Health and Welfare spokesperson Greg Stahl directed questions about the case to parties involved.
“(The Department of Health and Welfare) takes seriously its responsibility to be a good steward of taxpayer dollars and remains committed to transparency, accountability, and the appropriate use of public funds,” Stahl said in a statement.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Indictment releases key witness list — including several current government officials

In its first year, news about the investigation and controversies about the grants were public. Powerful lawmakers in the Legislature reported concerns to Labrador that the Department of Health and Welfare’s former director acknowledged that $14 million in funds went to organizations that served some children that weren’t school-aged, against the Legislature’s instructions. 
Labrador, a former Republican congressman, launched the investigation soon into his first term as the state’s top attorney. At first, Health and Welfare leadership refuted a critical state audit. But under new leadership, the audit’s findings spurred reform efforts at the agency. 
Labrador appointed Boyd as a special prosecutor in the investigation after an Idaho judge barred Labrador from pursuing civil subpoenas against public officials who worked for an agency that his office legally represents. 
Months into serving as special prosecutor, Boyd wrote in a civil court filing that he had probable cause that Rupp committed a crime. 
Since then, news about the investigation largely fizzled out as lawsuits challenging the civil subpoenas were resolved.



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



The indictment didn’t detail how the alleged crimes took place, or provide evidence. But it listed the names of six witnesses whose testimony the grand jury relied upon, including Lori Wolff, the governor’s budget chief who received a subpoena to testify to a special inquiry judge at least two years ago; April Renfro, the state’s head auditor who oversaw a critical audit into the state health agency’s grant handling; John Foster, an influential lobbyist who years ago requested government documents related to the grant program; Elizabeth Oppenheimer, the former head of the Idaho Association for the Education for Young Children; and Aubrie Hunt, who works for the Department of Health and Welfare. 
It is not immediately clear whether Boyd used a separate, secretive court process — called a special inquiry judge — that he said he wanted to use for the case. None of the case documents identify the judge as a special inquiry judge. Boyd said he wouldn’t “quite say” the case was pursued as a result of the special inquiry process. “It was a separate additional investigative process,” he said. 
The judge’s dismissal order references a court hearing that occurred Sept. 23. But the state’s official, public-facing court record system doesn’t have any records related to that hearing. Canyon County’s Deputy Trial Court Administrator Sharlene Davis told the Sun that her office doesn’t have more documents in the case. 



 A timeline of Labrador’s investigation into Health and Welfare grants:

Launched months after Labrador became Idaho’s top attorney in 2023, the grants investigation is one of several legal clashes Labrador has had with state government agencies that his office legally represents — including his dropped lawsuit against the State Board of Education related to University of Idaho’s attempted purchase of the University of Phoenix. 

January 2023: Raúl Labrador becomes Idaho’s attorney general.
March 2023: Shortly after the Idaho Legislature orders an audit of Idaho Department of Health and Welfare grants, Labrador serves civil subpoenas, also known as civil investigative demands, to current and former state health officials, and organizations that received the grants. Officials and organizations soon sue over the subpoenas.
August 2023: A state audit finds issues in the grant distribution and spending, despite two legal memos Daphne Huang — who was fired from the Attorney General’s Office — wrote to Health and Welfare, saying the grant funds was legally sound. Labrador’s office later withdrew the legal advice. Labrador calls the advice a “cover your butt” letter, in a December 2023 interview with Idaho Reports. (Huang’s whistleblower lawsuit against the Attorney General’s Office, dismissed by a state district court judge, is on appeal to the Idaho Supreme Court.)
December 2023: Labrador’s appointed special prosecutor, Christopher Boyd, claims in a legal filing that he found probable cause that the agency’s then-grant manager, Ericka Rupp, had committed a crime. But he publishes no specific evidence for the allegation, or says what crime may have been committed. 
January 2024: Months after the critical audit’s release, Health and Welfare announces reform efforts. Initially, agency leadership refuted all of the audit’s findings.
Est. early 2024: Several state government employees — including former Department of Health and Welfare Director Dave Jeppesen, and the governor’s then-director of operations, Lori Wolff, receive subpoenas from Boyd to testify before a special inquiry judge, according to internal emails that the Idaho Capital Sun obtained in a public records request. 
March 2024: Two lawsuits by current and former state health officials that challenged the civil subpoenas conclude — months after Boyd told the officials he’d withdraw the civil subpoenas.
September 2026: A grand jury indicts Rupp of two felony counts of misuse of public funds. Then upon the request of Boyd, a judge drops the case. 

Two state officials linked to the grants investigation — Huang, the fired attorney, and Jeppesen, the former Department of Health and Welfare director — filed complaints against Labrador with the Idaho State Bar, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. 
Boyd told the Sun that he leads the investigation, not the attorney general. 
Boyd said he’s had “sole control over the criminal investigation” since he was first appointed special prosecutor for the Attorney General’s Office in August 2023. 
“I have had sole control of the investigation and the AG removed itself entirely. I did not even consult with them at all about the case, as I treated it as a conflict appointment,” Boyd said.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: After second botched execution this year, Dems call for legislative oversight, GOP for change
description: Republican and Democratic lawmakers are calling for death penalty reform and legislative oversight after the state of Tennessee tried and failed Wednesday to execute a death row inmate for the second time in five months. State Sen. Tom Hatcher, a Maryville Republican, said Thursday he supports Gov. Bill Lee’s order for a hold on executions […]
text:
Tennessee state Republican and Democratic lawmakers are calling for death penalty reform and legislative oversight. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Republican and Democratic lawmakers are calling for death penalty reform and legislative oversight after the state of Tennessee tried and failed Wednesday to execute a death row inmate for the second time in five months.
State Sen. Tom Hatcher, a Maryville Republican, said Thursday he supports Gov. Bill Lee’s order for a hold on executions and third-party review after the state botched Christa Pike’s execution but that lawmakers are going to have to “step forward” during the next legislative session in January to change death penalty laws.
“We may look at several other things instead of just lethal injection,” said Hatcher, a Maryville Republican who chairs a Senate corrections subcommittee. “I think we’ve got to look at alternative ways.”



Quotation







The Department of Correction says it followed every step of its protocol. If that is true, then the protocol itself is a problem.


– Sen. Raumesh Akbari, D-Memphis


​Hatcher was among a group of eight Republican state senators who called for the independent review of death penalty protocol following the failed execution of Tony Carruthers in May.
​State Senate Minority Leader Raumesh Akbari, a Memphis Democrat, and state Rep. John Ray Clemmons, a Nashville Democrat and the party’s House caucus chair, both called the failed execution process “cruel” and “inhumane,” and urged change.
​”The Department of Correction says it followed every step of its protocol,” said Akbari in a statement. “If that is true, then the protocol itself is a problem. The governor’s third-party review is a start, but it is no substitute for oversight. It is time for the General Assembly to exercise its oversight function over the executive branch.”
​Lee stepped to stop Carruthers’ execution when physicians tried and failed for more than an hour to insert intravenous lines to begin the lethal injection process. On Wednesday, Lee stopped the execution of Pike after two failed rounds of the lethal injection protocol.
When Pike’s execution failed, ​Lee put a pause on all executions in Tennessee until the end of 2026 and started a third-party review.
Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike receiving medical care after failed execution

The governor said Thursday it’s his job to carry out the sentence since Tennesseans have determined that the death penalty is the appropriate penalty for the state’s most heinous crimes.
​“It’s exactly why we will have a thorough, comprehensive review of what happened, so that we can know the answers that so many people want,” Lee said. “There are very few answers this morning. It’s very early. There are a lot of questions. The people of our state deserve to have those questions answered. And that’s what this investigation’s for.”
​Lee paused all executions in 2022, after questions arose about the effectiveness of the state’s lethal injection protocol. The state restarted executions in 2025 and executed three death row inmates in 2025 and another in August.
​Pike would have been the first woman put to death by Tennessee in more than two centuries. Her lawyers confirmed Thursday she was in critical condition and receiving life-saving medical care at a hospital.
Sam Stockard contributed to this report.
