name: Virginia Mercury
title: Spanberger’s energy plan keys in on clean energy to meet growing demand and VCEA goals
description: Gov. Abigail Spanberger released the commonwealth’s latest energy plan on Thursday, marking the first long-range blueprint of her term for how Virginia can meet its growing energy demands and achieve the Virginia Clean Economy Act’s decarbonization and energy goals. As she announced the plan in Richmond Thursday morning, Spanberger said it “models four prima[...]
text:
Gov. Abigail Spanberger unveils energy plan that models how the state can meet energy demands while meeting clean energy goals. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)Gov. Abigail Spanberger released the commonwealth’s latest energy plan on Thursday, marking the first long-range blueprint of her term for how Virginia can meet its growing energy demands and achieve the Virginia Clean Economy Act’s decarbonization and energy goals.
As she announced the plan in Richmond Thursday morning, Spanberger said it “models four primary pathways to explore the costs, benefits, and realities of each potential energy mix,” citing a mix of power sources that all keep the state on the path of net-zero carbon emissions by 2050.
State law requires the governor and energy leaders to develop a plan every four years that outlines a 10-year roadmap on how to achieve a net-zero carbon economy. 
In a shift away from the last plan released in 2022 under former Gov. Glenn Youngkin, Spanberger’s plan acknowledges that the state’s growing power demands require a mixed portfolio of energy sources, including natural gas, but prioritizes cleaner energy sources like  community solar and battery storage.
It also suggests demand flexibility strategies for data centers, “whose rapidly growing electricity consumption far exceeds new consumption from the electrification of homes and vehicles,” the plan states. 
Chart showing costs for different policy scenarios under a moderate energy load forecast. (Virginia Energy Plan)
The administration created the plan compiling public comments and feedback from stakeholder meetings that were held across the commonwealth.
Many of the ideas in the varying paths laid out in the plan will need legislative approvals and the cooperation of the utilities and the State Corporation Commission, which oversees many sectors of energy regulation. 
A key point of focus in the document is how to get electrons on the grid in small ways now to ease big strains later. The plan also explores new technologies to bridge the gap of phasing out carbon-emitting generation.
“Understanding the complexity of this moment, we knew that this year’s Energy Plan needed to do more than present a prescriptive path forward, it needed to analyze the options before us,” Spanberger said.
PJM, the regional grid operator for most of the East Coast including Virginia, projects that the load forecast for Dominion Energy and Appalachian Power Company could reach up to 68.8 gigawatts in peak demand. 
Dominion has reported a connection queue of projects requiring 25 gigawatts worth of power that have an electrification date, and noted an additional 75 gigawatts are in the line without a set power up date. 
(Chart courtesy Virginia Energy, the Office of the Chief Energy Officer, and the Secretariat of Commerce & Trade)
That will require a massive amount of energy to be generated for use in Virginia, and the administration’s plan four models lay out a roadmap of how to make it possible. 
One of the modeled options laid out in the plan puts an emphasis on distributed energy resources (DER), such as community and rooftop solar. The state will need to ramp up its deployment of solar energy and battery storage to meet the VCEA goals and bring enough power on the grid to sustain the retirement of fossil fuel power sources.
The state needs about 1.8 gigawatts of solar and roughly 1 gigawatt of battery storage annually over the next two decades to meet demand, according to calculations for all the scenarios that take VCEA benchmarks into account. 
The administration suggests the state focus on more adding solar to brownfields, former minds, parking lots, and rooftops to bring power onto the grid and reform siting and other policies to help localities make decisions on larger solar projects.
Under this version of the plan, the state would implement a demand flexibility for data centers.
This means that utilities would deploy on-site clean energy, local battery storage and other methods to offset power flow to data centers on the hottest and coldest days of the year. 
This would also eliminate the need to build peaker plants that are designed to fire up when the grid requires temporary extra power, the plan suggests.
As part of the governor’s data center framework announced earlier this month, the administration wants to move away from data centers using fossil fuels as their own behind-the-meter power or as a backup power source.
“Instead of having the data center need to have on-site generation, they can contract with this fleet of batteries that they’ll help to finance to have basically the battery fleet doing that same thing on site during those peak hours,” Spanberger said
Additionally, this route recognizes that some gas power generation must serve as a “bridge” between current power generation methods and cleaner energy strategies, to fulfil the VCEA’s mandate that utilities decarbonize by 2045.  
On that front, Spanberger’s plan recommends fuel cell generation and linear generators – gas power sources that release fewer toxic particulates into the air but don’t eliminate carbon emissions.
Fuel cells and linear generators also have a shorter lifespan, putting their retirement much closer to the deadlines of the VCEA compared to traditional combustion gas plants, which usually have multi-decade lifespans.
“So fuel cells have like a five year lifespan, linear generators have a 20 year lifespan.  So even if we’re building them in the next 5 years, by 2030, they’ll basically be reaching the end of their useful life,” Chief Energy Officer Josephus Allmond said.
While these methods are more expensive, Allmond said it would be an example of putting the cost of some energy infrastructure onto the industries that are driving the demand, such as data centers. 
It’s important for Virginia to be a leader in pushing for new technologies, the governor added.
“Virginia is a place where we want this type of in a nation and we want these newer growing technologies, that is part of making them more widely available” Spanberger said.
The governor’s plan not only calculates the cost to build the infrastructure, but also the social and health costs that could be attributed to combustion gas power sources. The SCC typically looks at other factors when determining if a project is in the public’s best interests.  
“I think it is the responsibility of Virginia leadership… to look at the holistic impact because it does have a cost for Virginia. Even if that might not be the central lens (of the) SCC… we’re going to continue to advocate for a holistic view of the cost to Virginia, when we’re talking about balancing impacts and benefits to ratepayers, companies and Virginia citizens,” the governor said. 
Another version of the plan calculated how the state would meet power demands if less solar and battery storage were implemented in the coming years. It explores the impact of more offshore wind, nuclear investments, and less-polluting gas technologies. 
This showed that even if solar infrastructure can’t be built to the extent the administration modeled, the state’s energy demands can be met with cleaner energies.
The plan modeled what the state’s energy profile would look like if the VCEA was repealed and if the state left the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative.
That path would result in a heavy reliance on gas power and although it’s one of the cheaper options, building enough gas plants to meet the current load forecast would stretch into the next decade, leading to potential grid unreliability, according to Allmond.
“Across all net zero aligned modeled scenarios, Virginia will need to more than double its existing generation capacity to meet its projected growth and clean energy goals,” the plan states.
Lawmakers, energy and environmental advocacy organizations and utilities began responding to the Spanberger administration’s plan by Thursday afternoon. The Mercury will provide continuing coverage of those views and the energy plan in the coming days.

title: Colorado commission seeks economists for next phase of racial equity study
description: The Colorado legislative commission tasked with studying the effects of historical racism on Black Coloradans faces a funding gap as it seeks an economic contractor. The Black Coloradan Racial Equity Study Commission could need to raise around $215,000 to pay researchers to analyze a nearly-complete historical study and determine how racist policies and atti[...]
text:
Sen. James Coleman, a Denver Democrat, speaks at the June 4, 2024, signing of a bill to require a racial equity study in Colorado. (Photo by Sara Wilson/Colorado Newsline)The Colorado legislative commission tasked with studying the effects of historical racism on Black Coloradans faces a funding gap as it seeks an economic contractor.
The Black Coloradan Racial Equity Study Commission could need to raise around $215,000 to pay researchers to analyze a nearly-complete historical study and determine how racist policies and attitudes impacted Colorado’s economy.
The group has raised around $1.3 million over the last two years, Jarrod Gibbons, History Colorado’s budget director, told the commission Wednesday. It still needs about $75,000 to finish the historical study, though it has $60,000 in pledged donations.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
There is also $100,000 pledged for the economic analysis, which had a $300,000 estimate in the fiscal note for the bill that created the commission. The commission has not yet picked a group to do that work, however, so the actual cost could be much lower. Legislative staff Thursday published a request for qualifications for the economic analysis, essentially a call for organizations to pitch their plan for the job, and will decide on a contract in January.
Under the 2024 bill that created it, the commission has to pay for its work using donations instead of state money.



Quotation







The notion that we had to fundraise ourselves to look into the harm caused by the state, I think, is quite frankly causing some dissonance.


– State Rep. Jennifer Bacon, member of the racial equity study commission 


“There was a little bit of frustration that we wrestled with when we were bringing the bill forward, of figuring out how we can get this work done and the notion that we would have to support ourselves in doing it rather than asking for support from the state,” Rep. Jennifer Bacon, a Denver Democrat, said. “The research that’s being done, I believe, is critically important to all Coloradans and all of the people who look into our history.”
Historical research for Colorado racial equity study nearly complete

“The notion that we had to fundraise ourselves to look into the harm caused by the state, I think, is quite frankly causing some dissonance,” Bacon added.
Evidence of slave sale
There might be an opportunity, she said, to partner with universities to complete the analysis for below cost or as a donation.
But Sade Cooper, a commissioner and the executive director of the nonprofit Collaborative Healing Initiative within Communities, said she is confident that the money will be raised.
The commission is overseeing a two-part project — the historical research into a range of policies and systems that harmed Black Coloradans and the upcoming analysis into the economic impact of that systemic racism. The final report, due next fall, will have policy recommendations to address the effects of discrimination.
So far, historians have shared research about prominent Coloradans who owned slaves, including Joel Estes, and towns like Fruita that were once “sundown towns” that banned Black people in its boundaries after dark.
On Wednesday, researchers presented evidence of a potential sale of a Black person in the San Luis Valley near Fort Garland. Mill operator Harvey Easterday wrote a letter in 1860 to a business partner and inquired about purchasing a woman. In it, he asked the partner to “buy us a good, strong Negro woman that can do all kinds of housework.” Commission members had an opportunity to look at the letter in person on Wednesday.
“This is a private letter that gives voice to the casual transactions of people,” researcher Melissa Jones said.
“Even though we are not certain that such a woman was ever purchased, it gives evidence to all the other incidents of people we know were either owned or trafficked in the region, and the private ways in which — whether they were publicly referred to as servants — some of these individuals of African descent were talked about,” she said.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: North Carolina cannabis council considers public consumption policy for THC products
description: North Carolina’s Advisory Council on Cannabis faces a December 31st deadline to issue final recommendations for a comprehensive cannabis policy to Gov. Josh Stein. While the legislature would have to agree to enact any changes in existing law, the council gave the public its first glimpse this week of how a public consumption policy might […]
text:
Member of the North Carolina's Advisory Council on Cannabis gave the public its first glimpse this week of how a public consumption policy might be crafted. State legislators would first need to give their approval to any changes to existing law. (Photo by Mario Tama/Getty Images)North Carolina’s Advisory Council on Cannabis faces a December 31st deadline to issue final recommendations for a comprehensive cannabis policy to Gov. Josh Stein. While the legislature would have to agree to enact any changes in existing law, the council gave the public its first glimpse this week of how a public consumption policy might be crafted.
Anne Doyle and Kaycee Deen with the state Division of Public Health told council members that cannabis consumption needs its own framework of policies, because it doesn’t fit neatly within state laws governing alcohol or tobacco use.
To establish a cannabis-specific policy, Doyle said her team has examined how other states have opted to regulate public consumption.
In Virginia, retail sales of recreational cannabis begin July 1, 2027, but it will be illegal to smoke it in public. Lawmakers there are already considering increasing the civil penalty for public use from $25 to $250.
In California, smoking or ingesting cannabis in public is prohibited, but they do allow for its use in designated lounges or cafes.
Colorado likewise bans open products and public consumption but allows for local exceptions in hospitality spaces.
Across all those states, Doyle said the baseline is that legal possession does not mean that you have the right to use or consume cannabis in public.
Defining public spaces 
Deen said after many conversations with policymakers and public safety officials in other states, they drafted five recommendations for THC consumption in North Carolina.
The first recommendation prohibits the consumption of all THC products in any public place. Public spaces could be broadly defined to cover restaurants and bars, beaches, parks, event venues and public buildings.
“The goal is to make the rule very intuitive,” said Deen. “We want the public to understand exactly what this means. We don’t want to have to have law enforcement try to guess at businesses, are they public or are they private?”
The recommendation becomes trickier when it comes to housing. A homeowner would be free to consume cannabis in their private residence, but different rules might apply for renters.
“The landlord who owns the home makes a decision that that home should be smoke-free. You do have to abide by that,” said Deen.
Deen said other states advised North Carolina to avoid relying on “private event” labels that could turn a public business into a consumption site.
“Let’s say a famous pop star decides to rent out the Lenovo Center for her wedding. If we had an exception for a private event, they would be able to allow smoking during that event while it was rented out privately,” Deen explained.
Another policy choice to consider would be a narrow exception for THC beverages, Deen said.
“You could allow licensed restaurants to be able to sell THC beverages for on premises consumption only, not to be taken off the property,” said Deen. “They would be like a menu item similar to mixed drinks or beer wine.”
Deen said restaurants are a very controlled environment, where staff could be trained on THC products, and they would have 21 plus ID verification.
“They have limits on serving sizes and THC per serving,” she said. “Another thing that we’ve learned from the alcohol space is that a way to limit consumption is to raise the price.”
The second draft recommendation would prohibit consumption of THC in a moving vehicle by drivers and passengers. An open THC container in the passenger area would also be prohibited. The vehicle rule would not require impairment to be enforceable.
Narrowing consumption spaces
A third proposed recommendation would be to not allow dedicated consumption lounges.
One of the many decisions the advisory council is considering is where THC products can be safely consumed. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)
“It’s always easier to restrict something at the beginning and then open up those laws later,” Deen advised. “They complicate enforcement.”
A fourth draft recommendation is to preserve authority for private housing to further restrict these cannabis consumption laws.
This would be a safeguard for HOAs or condominium associations. Deen said spelling this out in the initial policy could help prevent a lot of litigation.
Forrest Parker, CEO of Qualla Enterprises and Great Smoky Cannabis Company, said people are looking for safe places to consume cannabis, which is legal for recreational use on  Cherokee land in North Carolina.
While the concept of cannabis lounges may not have worked financially in other states, Parker said they recognize consumer demand.
“We’re actually starting to slightly explore whether it makes sense for us to provide a safe place.” Parker said.
Parker said with a larger portion of their customers being visitors, many are looking for a place they can legally use cannabis when Cherokee hotels, casinos and other public spaces remain off limits.
“We have a lot of campgrounds actually beginning to promote a ‘420 friendly’ vacation model,” Parker said. “They’re closing off certain sections of the campground and building barriers so that children don’t have easy access. Really responsible.”
Recreational cannabis is legal for adults over 21 on tribal land, but upon leaving the Qualla boundary, individuals are subject to North Carolina state laws.
A pushback on civil fines
The final draft recommendation would use civil infractions, or fines, as the default enforcement mechanism for the public consumption rules.
“Just like it was when they enacted the smoke-free restaurants and bars, they got a lot of complaints at the beginning for several years. Then they got less and less,” said Deen. “There was a behavior change.”
Doyle said this is another area where North Carolina can borrow from other states.
“California does not impose infractions or fines on minors. They actually require education,” said Doyle. “That could be a really interesting thing to think about [instead of] punishment.”
Roxboro Police Chief David Hess said the wording on enforcement recommendations needed work.
“If what I’m carrying out of this recommendation is for law enforcement to go around issuing civil fines for public consumption, we’re going to erode public trust,” Hess said.
Hess said in North Carolina municipal law enforcement doesn’t have the statutory authority to enforce civil laws. That’s a function of sheriffs’ departments, he said.
As hemp’s future hangs in the balance, NC policymakers look ahead to regulate cannabis

“You would be entering local law enforcement into a new space that historically has never been permitted in North Carolina. That’s going to come with a significant amount of training,” Hess said.
Col. Freddy Johnson, commander of the North Carolina Highway Patrol, agreed with Hess, but thought many of the state’s open-container laws for alcohol could be adapted to work for cannabis consumption.
Other advisory members indicated they would be agreeable to allowing bars and restaurants to continue to sell THC-infused beverages.
“If we did have legal products, the legislature could limit the amount that you can put in a container, a can, or bottle. Many states have done that,” said Dr. Larry Greenblatt, state health director and co-chair of the advisory council.
Greenblatt said the draft recommendations should be considered a work in progress. Subcommittees will be meeting throughout October and November where the guardrails will be fine-tuned.
Even after the final report is delivered to the governor, the General Assembly would need to agree on the legislation. Attempts to legalize medical marijuana have died in the state House in recent years, despite support from some senior Senate leaders. The Trump administration has called on the U.S. Department of Justice to reclassify marijuana as a Schedule III drug, the same class as Tylenol.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: The government keeps child support owed to poorest Kentuckians. GOP lawmakers seek change.
description: FRANKFORT — Around 14,000 families receiving Kentucky Transitional Assistance Program benefits in 2025 didn’t receive most child support owed to them, experts said Thursday.  During the 2027 legislative session, Sen. Craig Richardson, R-Hopkinsville, plans to renew his 2026 push to reform this process. He presented before Thursday’s Interim Joint Committee J[...]
text:
A Kentucky legislator has proposed legislation to leave more child support in the hands of families. (Getty Images)FRANKFORT — Around 14,000 families receiving Kentucky Transitional Assistance Program benefits in 2025 didn’t receive most child support owed to them, experts said Thursday. 
During the 2027 legislative session, Sen. Craig Richardson, R-Hopkinsville, plans to renew his 2026 push to reform this process. He presented before Thursday’s Interim Joint Committee Judiciary, saying the current process “penalizes the parents that are doing the right thing in paying that child support.” 
“When a Kentucky family is on KTAP and is owed child support, this state currently intercepts it, and it’s sending 72% of those funds to the federal government instead of to the kids that it is meant for,” Richardson said. 
Under his proposed legislation, $100 per child per month — up to $200 per household — would “pass through” to the intended recipient and not be used to recalculate public benefits. 
KTAP, which comes from federal funds from the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) block grant, benefits eligible low-income families for a maximum of 60 months, which do not have to be consecutive, over the course of a lifetime. 
‘Modest but vital’ help for low-income Kentuckians takes a hit 

Dustin Pugel, the policy director at the Kentucky Center for Economic Policy, said the policy of withholding child support funds in these cases can be traced back to the 1970s. 
“The idea at the time was that when parents separate, and one parent falls on hard times and receives what was then Aid to Families with Dependent Children  which is no longer in our program, that the payments that the father was making, the child support payments, should essentially reimburse the government, including the federal government, for the ways that it was taking care of his children,” Pugel explained. “It’s a 50-year-old conception that I think needs to be updated.” 
According to Pugel, in the 2025 fiscal year, Kentucky kept more than $4 million of these payments and sent more than $11 million to the federal government. If Kentucky changed its policy to ensure this money makes it to the families for whom it is intended, it would be the 32nd state to do so, Pugel said. 
“There’s a lot of research that shows that there are benefits beyond that really important social benefit, including that when child support payments are passed through, child support payments are more likely to be made by those dads,” Pugel said. “Dads are more likely to claim paternity. Child support payments increase, and there’s actually a reduction in the likelihood that those children will be involved in the child welfare system later on down the line.” 
Christian Postel, the CEO of Lexington Leadership Foundation, said he grew up with a single mother and now, through one of his organization’s initiatives, tries to strengthen relationships between fathers and their children. 
“Imagine being one of the fathers we serve: You’re in recovery, or you’re just out of incarceration, and you’re doing the right thing,” Postel said. “You’re working, and you’re making child support payments, and your children and their mother receive none of your hard-earned wages. That is a system that degrades the father, disincentivizes family togetherness and deepens the father absence crisis in our commonwealth.” 
If Kentucky were to change this policy in 2027, Postel believes it could also help keep children from entering state custody. 
“Please understand that in Kentucky, the line between poverty and neglect is as thin as a blade of bluegrass,” said Postel. “Any dollars that make it to these children are dollars that keep them further from the system. The surest way to serve a child in state custody is to keep that child from entering custody in the first place. This bill helps do that with money that has already been paid by a working father who already earned it for a child meant to be provided for by it. The bill serves working fathers, the bill serves single mothers and the bill serves vulnerable children.”

description: Flathead County Attorney Travis Ahner is likely to become the next Flathead County District Court judge, after he was the only candidate who submitted an application for the soon-to-be-vacant seat on the bench. Montana Gov. Greg Gianforte put out the call for applications at the start of September. The vacancy on the bench will occur […]
text:
The Flathead County Courthouse, which houses the county's administrative offices, pictured on Dec. 31, 2024. (Micah Drew, Daily Montanan)Flathead County Attorney Travis Ahner is likely to become the next Flathead County District Court judge, after he was the only candidate who submitted an application for the soon-to-be-vacant seat on the bench.
Montana Gov. Greg Gianforte put out the call for applications at the start of September.
The vacancy on the bench will occur following November’s election, where current district court judges — Judge Amy Eddy and Judge Dan Wilson — are facing off in a race for an open Montana Supreme Court seat to replace retiring Justice Beth Baker.
Ahner is a Republican and has twice been elected as the top prosecutor in Flathead County. He is running for re-election again on the November ballot, unopposed.
If Gianforte appoints Ahner to the judgeship, the Flathead County Commissioners will be tasked with appointing a replacement for the county attorney position.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Congress passes bill to make Fulton’s Churchill Museum a National Historic Landmark
description: The U.S. Senate passed legislation Tuesday to make America’s National Churchill Museum a National Historic Landmark, sending the bill to President Donald Trump for his signature. The U.S. House of Representatives passed a corresponding bill in March after the legislation had been stalled in Congress for at least two years. If Trump signs the bill, […]
text:
The Churchill Museum  in Fulton is on track to become a National Historic Landmark. The museum has a collection of material about former U.K Prime Minister Winston Churchill, including pages from his famous 1946 “Iron Curtain" speech (Alex Buchanan/Missourian).The U.S. Senate passed legislation Tuesday to make America’s National Churchill Museum a National Historic Landmark, sending the bill to President Donald Trump for his signature.
The U.S. House of Representatives passed a corresponding bill in March after the legislation had been stalled in Congress for at least two years.
If Trump signs the bill, the museum in Fulton will become one of more than 2,500 National Historic Landmarks in the country. These include the Statue of Liberty, the Liberty Bell, Mount Vernon and the White House, as well as smaller places of historic significance.
According to the National Park Service, the landmarks are “historic properties that illustrate the heritage of the United States.” Each one “represents an outstanding aspect of American history and culture.”
Missouri already has 36 National Historic Landmarks, including Mark Twain’s home in Hannibal, Laura Ingalls Wilder’s home in Mansfield, the village of Arrow Rock and Sanborn Field in Columbia, which played a significant role in the discovery of antibiotics.
Efforts to designate the Churchill Museum as a National Historic Landmark began in 2024 when U.S. Sen. Josh Hawley introduced the legislation. The bill passed in the Senate the same year, but time ran out before it could pass the House.
Earlier this year, Hawley reintroduced the bill in the Senate with U.S. Rep. Bob Onder submitting a corresponding House bill.
Located in Fulton on the Westminster College campus, the National Churchill Museum commemorates Winston Churchill, former U.K. prime minister, who delivered the historic “Iron Curtain” speech in the college gymnasium in 1946.
The centerpiece of the museum is the Church of St. Mary the Virgin, Aldermanbury, a 17th-century building moved stone-by-stone to Fulton from London 60 years ago. Originally constructed in the 12th century and rebuilt in the 17th century in London, the church was brought to the U.S. in 1966 for reconstruction efforts.
“The church is a 17th-century church designed by Christopher Wren, the same architect who did St. Paul’s Cathedral in London,” said Timothy Riley, director and chief curator of America’s National Churchill Museum in Fulton.
“(It) stood proudly in London for hundreds of years but was destroyed, except for the shell of the building, by firebombs in World War II,” he said.
The museum also includes exhibits about Churchill’s personal and political life, with a reading room that houses an extensive research collection about the life of the British statesman. Outside the church is a sculpture called “Breakthrough” that was designed by Churchill’s granddaughter, artist Edwina Sandys, from eight sections of the Berlin Wall.
Churchill’s 1946 speech reminded the world that they couldn’t rest on their laurels, that Soviet communism was a looming threat to Western democracy, Riley said.
“From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the continent,” the prime minister said in his original speech.
Conceived in the 1960s, the museum opened in 1969, and Riley said it could be considered “a presidential library for a British prime minister.”
The church had been heavily bombed during a German air raid in World War II, leaving only the outer walls, columns and bell tower. It remained in ruins until then-Westminster College president Larry Davidson wondered if it could be rebuilt to create a monument to Churchill.
It took four years to secure permission from the British and raise $1.5 million (more than $12 million today) to make the project a reality.
Since then, more efforts to preserve the church have been undertaken. Just recently, the museum completed a $4 million effort to waterproof the exterior of the building — including the original stones.
Fundraising still needs to be done to raise money for internal preservation, Riley said, which could be helped with National Historic Landmark status.
“There’s a section of legislation which instructs the Secretary of Interior to conduct a study to see if there are future partnership opportunities,” Riley said.
There are no guarantees, but Riley said he is hopeful the status alone will lead to improvements.
“From an operational standpoint, nothing will change,” he said. “It’s not going to become part of the federal park system, for instance, and management and control of the museum will remain with Westminster College.”
“But I think the designation will be a great boost for attendance,” he added. “It puts us on par with things like the Arch and Liberty Hall, great monuments around the country.”
And while they’re not celebrating the passage of the bill just yet, Riley said there’s plenty to be excited about. 2026 marked both the 80th anniversary of Churchill’s speech and the 175th anniversary of Westminster College. All of this means it’s a good time to reflect.
“It’s not just looking back at our history, but looking forward to the promise of the next generation,” Riley said. “That’s what excites me, frankly, and that’s what I think is great. For us to be able to say we have an amazing past and a lot of extraordinary history happened here.”
This story originally appeared in the Columbia Missourian. It can be republished in print or online.

title: State lawmakers hear data center concerns from across Kentucky at Frankfort ‘listening session’
description: More than 60 people filled a committee room for the “listening session” on data centers set up by Rep. Adam Moore, D-Lexington, with speakers coming from counties including Barren, Boyle, Boyd, Carroll, Daviess, Breckinridge, Madison, Mercer, Mason, Oldham, Fayette, Franklin, Jefferson, Pike and Woodford. All but one of the speakers voiced concerns or outrig[...]
text:
Constituents from across the state came to the "listening session" on data centers held at the Kentucky Capitol on Oct. 1, 2026. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)More than 60 people filled a committee room for the “listening session” on data centers set up by Rep. Adam Moore, D-Lexington, with speakers coming from counties including Barren, Boyle, Boyd, Carroll, Daviess, Breckinridge, Madison, Mercer, Mason, Oldham, Fayette, Franklin, Jefferson, Pike and Woodford.
All but one of the speakers voiced concerns or outright opposition to the construction of hyperscale data centers, those worries ranging from the loss of farmland, the need for stronger ratepayer protections, a lack of transparency from local government officials reviewing data center proposals, and potential tax breaks that data center developers exploit. 
Some of the speakers came from organized groups in local communities that have formed over the past 12 months that are expressing strong concerns about active data center proposals. 



Quotation







“Protect our farmland, historic sites, horse farms, and the precious water our bourbon industry relies on. Protect ratepayers. Protect open records and open meetings. Strengthen ethics and financial disclosures from government officials and companies alike. Require independent environmental and infrastructure studies and make them public,” Floyd said. “Finally, stop expecting local officials without specialized technical, legal, environmental, or utility expertise to negotiate billion-dollar industrial development deals on equal footing with the wealthiest companies on Earth.”


– Diane Floyd


Diane Floyd, a member of one of those groups, We Are Mercer County, told the state representatives that the state legislature had a responsibility to regulate data centers after lawmakers “recruited” them, referring to statewide tax breaks benefiting data centers passed in 2025. 
“Protect our farmland, historic sites, horse farms, and the precious water our bourbon industry relies on. Protect ratepayers. Protect open records and open meetings. Strengthen ethics and financial disclosures from government officials and companies alike. Require independent environmental and infrastructure studies and make them public,” Floyd said. “Finally, stop expecting local officials without specialized technical, legal, environmental, or utility expertise to negotiate billion-dollar industrial development deals on equal footing with the wealthiest companies on Earth.”
Some speakers were in favor of an outright ban on hyperscale data center construction, others preferred a temporary statewide moratorium. Others called for the repeal of sales tax breaks benefiting data center development. 
At one point, Janet Garrison of Mason County, threw a bunch of letters onto a committee room table; she said the letters were sent from across the country to Mason County residents who have refused to sell their land for a hyperscale data center development in the county. 
“Not only is Kentucky watching, the whole United States and the world is watching how we do this, how we destroy our communities and our land,” Garrison said.
Boyd County resident Suzanne Griffith, a ratepayer of investor-owned electric utility Kentucky Power, said ratepayer protections are needed especially as Kentucky Power ratepayers face high utility bills. 
“There is no more money for people to pay,” Griffith said. “Data centers shall pay for the generation sources needed to power their facilities. The power bills of other customers shall not increase due to data centers.” 
Martin Rivers, a retired software engineer from Fayette County, was the only speaker who explicitly supported the influx of data centers and called the potential of artificial intelligence “amazing.” 
“I want to see it come in faster. To me, data centers are infrastructure, and in this way, I view them no differently than dams on waterways.” 
In regards to regulation, Rivers said he believed there were likely state laws already in place that “cover businesses like this.” 
Janet Garrison of Mason County threw letters on the table that she says were mailed to Mason County from across the country in solidarity with local data center opposition. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)
Toward the end of the gathering, Pete Lynch, an independent candidate for Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District, asked people in the room to raise their hands if they supported an outright ban on data center construction; numerous people in the room raised their hands. 
Lynch told the state lawmakers that both Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear and the “Republican-dominated” state legislature betrayed constituents by passing statewide sales tax breaks for data centers. 
Rep. Vanessa Grossl, R-Georgetown, was the one Republican state lawmaker who sat with Democrats and listened. She said she regretted her vote for House Bill 775, the legislation passed into law providing the state tax breaks. The bill was passed in one of the final working days of the legislative session in 2025.
“I think that it was a little rushed there at the end,” Grossl said. “I don’t think we got it right. I think we need to revisit that.” 
She said she’s heard from “several” fellow GOP state lawmakers that the tax breaks are “something that we’ll likely revisit.” Some Republican state lawmakers have suggested the sales tax breaks could be rolled back with the legislature reconvenes in January.
Moore, the Democratic state representative who organized the listening session, said he wished more Republicans had attended the session. He said he heard from Rep. Kim Holloway, R-Mayfield, and Sen. Matthew Deneen, R-Elizabethtown, about not being able to attend. 
Both he and Rep. Josh Bray, R-Mount Vernon, say they’re working on data center-related legislation for the upcoming legislative session. 
Moore said he believes there’s appetite among lawmakers for ratepayer protections regarding data centers, but he wants the legislature to go further on environmental and local transparency concerns. 
“Don’t know if they would meet us there. I really hope so,” Moore said. “We should find a solution and put it into legislation, and I would oppose any new hyperscale data center developments until we have done that.”

name: VTDigger
title: One vote I’m proud of
description:
Proposal 3 passed the Legislature by rare bipartisan margins. Now it's up to voters.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  One vote I’m proud of.
text:
This commentary is by Conor Casey, who represents Montpelier in the Vermont House and is a co-chair of the Vermont Legislature’s Working Vermonters Caucus. 
You cast a lot of votes in the Vermont House. Some are easy. Some keep you up at night. And, if I’m being truthful, there are plenty I probably won’t remember 10 years from now.
I’ll remember my vote for the Workers’ Rights Amendment.
This November, Vermont voters will have the final say on Proposal 3, which would protect in our state constitution the right of working Vermonters to organize and bargain collectively over their wages, hours, working conditions and workplace safety. I’ve been proud to work on the amendment as a co-chair of the Legislature’s Working Vermonters Caucus. But something else about it has meant a lot to me: This was never just a Democratic proposal.
Republicans supported it, too.
These are colleagues I disagree with on taxes, spending, regulations and plenty else. But we found agreement on one fundamental thing: People who work for a living should have a voice in their workplace and the freedom to join together with their co-workers.
In its final trip through the Legislature, the amendment passed the House 125-15 and the Senate 29-0. If you follow the Vermont Legislature, you know we don’t see numbers like that every day. I think the reason is fairly simple. Most working Vermonters aren’t asking for special treatment. They want to be respected. They want some say in decisions that affect their lives. And if they decide they’re better off standing together with their co-workers, that ought to be their choice.
So why put that right in the constitution?
Because laws can change. Legislatures certainly change. And we’ve seen fights over collective bargaining rights play out in other states when political control changes hands. I’d rather Vermont settle the question. Whatever party controls the Statehouse 10 or 20 years from now, the basic right of working people to organize and bargain collectively should still be there.

READ MORE

That’s one reason the bipartisan support for Proposal 3 has mattered so much to me. Vermont politics can get plenty contentious. But every once in a while, people who disagree about a lot of things decide there are a few things we shouldn’t have to keep fighting about.
This amendment won’t make groceries cheaper. It won’t fix the housing crisis. It won’t make every workplace fair or every disagreement disappear. It does one thing: It protects the right of working people to stand together and speak for themselves.
My time in the Vermont House is coming to an end. I’ve cast hundreds of votes here, and I’m sure I’ll second-guess some of them for years to come.
I won’t second-guess this one.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: How Mainers are weighing the pay-to-play allegation involving Susan Collins
description: Tom McShane of Windham will likely split his ticket in November. He likes a Republican candidate running for his legislative district but plans to vote for Democrat Troy Jackson for Senate, although reluctantly since his first choice dropped out. His choice in the Senate race is irrespective of the recent corruption allegations against incumbent Republican [[...]
text:
Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins of Maine tours the Maine Energy Marketers Association Technical Education Center in Brunswick on Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)Tom McShane of Windham will likely split his ticket in November. He likes a Republican candidate running for his legislative district but plans to vote for Democrat Troy Jackson for Senate, although reluctantly since his first choice dropped out.
His choice in the Senate race is irrespective of the recent corruption allegations against incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins. “That’s pretty common among politicians,” he said.  
As discourse about Collins’ alleged involvement in a pay-for-play scheme ripples across the country, at home in Maine, several voters said they were unsurprised and unmoved, indicative of their dwindling faith that the government is working in their best interest.
The extent to which the accusations first reported by ProPublica will influence voters is unclear. Interviews show that people firmly aligned with one party or the other appear to be dug in, while some swing voters are reconsidering their support of the senior senator — a key bloc in Collins’ 2020 win.
“They’re all doing it,” said Republican Jim Volkernick of New Gloucester. “I’m pretty skeptical about just about anyone.” He is considering leaving the race blank on his ballot, not because of the allegation but because Collins has at times voted against her own party. 
Across the political spectrum, Mainers are collectively disgusted by the influence of Big Money in politics and overwhelmed by the barrage of negative ads blanketing the state, many backed by dark money. Ads supportive of Collins have highlighted Jackon’s son’s past as a lobbyist, and those supportive of Jackson have accused the senator of being in the pocket of special interests. 
Democrats have been trying to nail Collins on corruption for years. Will this time be different?

Amid that landscape, many see the revelation that the FBI was looking into an alleged pay-for-play scheme as “just one more thing,” as several put it. 
“I think all politicians are corrupt,” said Denny Conley of South Portland, who identifies as independent and said he’s probably registered with a party, but “couldn’t tell you what it is.”
Conley doesn’t like Collins or Jackson. “I think you are damned if you do and damned if you don’t,” he said.
Jackson and Maine Democrats have condemned Collins as corrupt and painted the accusation as a turning point that could upend the race, which is viewed as consequential for the balance of power in Congress. 
Meanwhile, Collins’ team has denied any wrongdoing and said the story is a return to claims made during her 2020 campaign. In explaining why the story has no bearing on how they vote, some Collins supporters reiterated the same talking point. 
“It hasn’t swayed my views,” said Shane Hill, a registered Republican who doesn’t always vote party lines. “The way I look at it is, really, you guys are going back to that because that’s all you have. It was never substantiated. Nothing’s ever come out of it. She was never formally charged. There’s nothing but an allegation that anybody can make at any time.” 
One of Collins’ top donors, Martin Kao, the former CEO of defense contractor Navatek, pleaded guilty in 2022 to illegal campaign contributions involving a pro-Collins super PAC. No one in Collins’ orbit was charged as a result of the investigation then.
However, ProPublica revealed that the FBI was looking into the senator, her top aides and a pro-Collins super PAC in recent years — that was until Donald Trump returned to office for a second term and the probe died as part of his purge of the bureau.
As campaign finance experts told the Portland Press Herald, only federal agencies can launch investigations to seek recourse for potential ‘pay-to-play’ schemes and bribery.
Between 2022 through 2024, Kao told the FBI that Collins’ team was aware of the scheme in which he made donations with the understanding that she would award contracts to his company, which ProPublica found to be consistent with FBI records and interviews with dozens of people familiar with Navatek. 
On Thursday, Huff Post reported that Collins’ current reelection campaign is backed by at least $7.4 million in dark money contributions that resemble the shell donations at the center of the alleged pay-for-play scheme. 
Nearly every candidate in a competitive race is buoyed by some dark money. That includes Jackson, who has the backing of WinSenate, funded by a super PAC connected to Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.). There has been little insight into his campaign’s finances so far given his late entry into the race. He replaced former nominee Graham Platner, who dropped out in July after an accusation of sexual assault, which he denies. 
Mainers, and Americans broadly, believe that unlimited super PAC spending leads to government corruption. In 2024, more than 70% of Maine voters passed a law to put a limit on contributions to super PACs, which are political action committees that independently spend money to try to support or defeat candidates. 
But that ran afoul to how campaign finance restrictions have been understood to date. In the 2010 ruling Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission, the high court allowed unlimited spending on the premise that there is a wall of independence between a candidate and outside spending groups. 
Those defending Maine’s law in court do not dispute that. Rather, they argue that such restrictions do not stop the potential for corruption, given that donors and candidates have the opportunity to collaborate even if a PAC is independent. That is what is alleged in ProPublica’s reporting. 
Volkernick and other Maine voters said they do not think how they vote in the upcoming election will make a dent in the enduring political system they decry. 
“You can go in there and try to do something good,” Volkernick said, but “the machine’s too big.”
Lauren McCauley contributed reporting to this story.

name: Daily Montanan
title: The River Runs Through It Act erodes roadless, wildlife protections
description: The River Runs Through It Act, introduced by Montana Rep. Ryan Zinke, would protect just a fraction of public National Forest lands needed for our wildlife and fish to not only persist, but thrive. The act contains new designations for 465,000 acres primarily in the Blackfoot and Clearwater watersheds that are home to bull trout, […]
text:
The Bob Marshall Wilderness (Photo by Victor Albert Grigas | Via Wikimedia Commons | CC-BY-SA 2.0).The River Runs Through It Act, introduced by Montana Rep. Ryan Zinke, would protect just a fraction of public National Forest lands needed for our wildlife and fish to not only persist, but thrive.
The act contains new designations for 465,000 acres primarily in the Blackfoot and Clearwater watersheds that are home to bull trout, cutthroat trout, grizzly bears, lynx, wolverine and a large herd of elk that over-winters on the Blackfoot-Clearwater Wildlife Management Area. 
Commercial logging, new roads and motorized recreation would be allowed on about 330,000 of these acres including a new 70-mile motorized loop trail through sensitive wildlife habitats. The primary elk migration corridor between the Bob Marshall Wilderness complex and winter range would be degraded. 
Wilderness-quality lands that would be opened to development include all of the Lincoln Gulch, Crater Mountain, Specimen Creek and Anaconda Hill roadless areas, half of Nevada Mountain and all of the Lodgepole Creek area in the Monture watershed. It would open to development the Wales Creek and Hoodoo Mountain Wilderness Study areas. More than 36,000 acres would become permanent motorized winter recreation areas.
The roadless lands adjacent to the Scapegoat Wilderness would be split, with the less productive high elevations designated as “wilderness” and the lower elevation, more productive areas committed to logging and motorized use.
New roads create sediment-choking pollution of waterways vital to native trout recovery and corner elk into smaller and more isolated secure areas which would limit successful hunting opportunities.
The River Runs Through It Act would sacrifice both core and connectivity habitat. Habitat connectivity allows wildlife to move through a network of roadless stepping stones, providing sustainability for a multitude of species. According to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, any decrease in conservation threatens the survival and recovery of grizzly bears. This is true for all threatened and sensitive wildlife.
The landscape-level approach embodied in the Northern Rockies Ecosystem Protection Act is a better strategy for protecting remaining roadless areas and habitat connectivity. That act offers a fundamentally different approach from the River Runs Through It Act, prioritizing wildlands and wildlife protection over new roads and motorized recreation. 
Protecting wildlands is essential for safeguarding biodiversity and preserving migration pathways that plants and animals depend on amidst our changing climates, while enhancing the resilience of local communities by ensuring access to clean air, healthy soils and livelihoods rooted in natural systems. 
Looking at the biodiversity account, the Zinke’s act makes more withdrawals than deposits. While the River Runs Through It Act would protect some areas that are deserving of “wilderness” designation, it is not nearly enough, and is short on protection in all the right places. 
At a time when conservation advocates are putting so much collective effort into maintaining the roadless area conservation rule, promoting the opening of large amounts of roadless area for roadbuilding, logging and motorized use undercuts our efforts and credibility. It also sets a bad precedent for other parts of the Northern Rockies.
Another issue is process. The River Runs Through It Act was developed in an exclusionary fashion, with many conservation advocates left out, leading to over-compromise. For Zinke, who is leaving Congress, the only way to pass the bill in the short time left is to short-circuit debate and informed consent. This is the sort of sausage-making despised by the public.
This shrinking resource needs Congress to provide lasting protection. By taking action to preserve these invaluable landscapes, we invest in a sustainable future for all. 
This editorial is submitted by Friends of the Clearwater; WildEarth Guardians; Flathead-Lolo-Bitterroot Citizen Task Force; Alliance for the Wild Rockies; Western Watersheds Project; Wilderness Watch; Wilderness Education School; Bold Visions Conservation; Friends of the Wild Swan; Swan View Coalition; Friends of the Bitterroot; Kootenai Environmental Alliance; Gallatin Wildlife Association; Inland Empire Task Force; Conservation Congress; Gallatin-Yellowstone Wilderness Alliance; Save the Yellowstone Grizzly; Save Our Cabinets; Rock Creek Alliance; Footloose Montana; Our Montana, Inc.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Kentucky agriculture commissioner calls on governor to pause restriction on untaxed diesel
description: Republican Kentucky Agriculture Commissioner Jonathan Shell is asking Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear to temporarily suspend a prohibition on using untaxed diesel on public roads.  A spokesperson for the governor said his office is reviewing the letter.  Shell sent a Thursday letter to Beshear hoping to “draw your attention to the current emergency impacting fa[...]
text:
High diesel prices are hurting farmers during the fall harvest, Agriculture Secretary Jonathan Shell says. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Republican Kentucky Agriculture Commissioner Jonathan Shell is asking Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear to temporarily suspend a prohibition on using untaxed diesel on public roads. 
A spokesperson for the governor said his office is reviewing the letter. 
Shell sent a Thursday letter to Beshear hoping to “draw your attention to the current emergency impacting farmers — the sky-high price of diesel affecting the 2026 fall harvest season.” He added that GOP governors in Texas, Nebraska and Louisiana have taken similar measures to allow red-dyed diesel on roads. The fuel type is commonly used on farmland and is tax-exempt. 
“I urge you to take similar action and allow for the use of untaxed diesel fuel for the remainder of the fall harvest season for the limited purpose of harvesting and transporting agricultural products this year,” Shell wrote to Beshear. 
Shell argued Beshear has the authority to declare an emergency in Kentucky over gas prices under a January 2025 executive order from President Donald Trump regarding energy, but would need approval from Attorney General Russell Coleman, another Republican. 
“Transportation costs are one of many factors that goes into the price of food. Increased transportation costs will result in increased costs of food,” Shell said. “By providing some relief to the cost of transporting agricultural commodities to market, farmers and citizens are both served with lower prices and higher margins.” 
Coleman said on X that he agreed with Shell “and his work to cut costs for our farmers and the Kentucky families who rely on them” before adding that Beshear should sign the order. 
Scottie Ellis, a spokesperson for Beshear, told the Lantern that Trump’s “war of choice and unlawful tariffs have caused prices to skyrocket for hard working Americans – including here in Kentucky” and added that Beshear has already taken some steps to help Kentuckians facing higher gas prices.
“From signing an executive order to lower gas and diesel prices to suspending the gas tax increase and urging Congress to freeze the federal gas tax, the Governor has made it a priority to find relief for Kentuckians and put more money back in their pockets,” Ellis said. “The Governor’s office appreciates that Commissioner Shell now wants to help and is reviewing the letter.”
In June, nearly 40 local governments requested the state continue reducing a gas sales tax after Beshear had signed an executive order in May to lower and temporarily freeze the tax. 
As of Thursday, the average price of diesel in Kentucky was $6.24 a gallon, below the national average of about $6.40 a gallon, according to AAA. 
The price of diesel and gas have gone up in recent months because of global political conflicts, like Trump’s war in Iran over the Strait of Hormuz, where oil supplies are transported.

name: VTDigger
title: Can Vermont afford Proposal 3?
description:
Proposal 3 would bar Vermont lawmakers from adopting a right-to-work law, a tool other states use to compete for jobs.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Can Vermont afford Proposal 3?.
text:
This commentary is by Elizabeth Brown, who is the Vermont state director of the Fiscal Alliance Foundation.
Vermont workers already have the right to bargain. Proposal 3 would lock in a system that costs us jobs, investment and taxes.
According to a new analysis published by our organization, the Fiscal Alliance Foundation, Vermont’s population fell last year by a larger share than that of any other state. From 2015 to 2025, private-sector jobs grew 12.6% nationally. In Vermont, they fell 0.6%. Only two other states went backward. Our cost of living runs 13.5% above average, and after adjusting for it, we rank 42nd in disposable income per person.
What does that have to do with Proposal 3? Unions fight for better benefits and higher wages, but a bigger paycheck only helps if it goes farther. In states without right-to-work laws, living costs run 16.6% above the national average. In right-to-work states, they run 4.3% below. Once you account for what things cost, people in right-to-work states take home about $3,500 more per person each year. Proposal 3 expands union power in ways that will cost Vermonters in jobs, investment and taxes.
Prop 3 is being sold as a way to protect workers’ right to bargain collectively. That right is already protected by state law. Prop 3 does not create collective bargaining. It moves our labor laws out of the Legislature’s hands and into the state constitution.
But it goes beyond that. First, it bars any law that stops unions and employers from making union membership a condition of employment. That takes away employee choice and permanently rules out a right-to-work law. The Vermont AFL-CIO says as much in its own materials.
Second, it sets a new test for every labor law on the books. No law may interfere with, negate or diminish the right to bargain. That puts existing labor statutes in question, including limits on public-employee strikes and on what school boards must bargain over. That could leave judges, rather than the people we elect, to decide which laws survive.
Supporters want to protect a right before anyone threatens it. But no one in Montpelier is threatening collective bargaining. 

READ MORE

Over the past decade, private-sector jobs grew 17.2% in right-to-work states, nearly twice the rate of the rest. Economists comparing neighboring counties across state lines found about 28% more manufacturing jobs on the right-to-work side. States that adopt right-to-work see venture capital investment rise 68% to 82%, according to a study in the Journal of Banking and Finance. That is the money that starts new companies.
Look at dairy. From 2018 to 2025, milk output grew about 15.7% in right-to-work dairy states and about 0.1% in the rest. Vermont’s fell 6%. Prop 3 gives investors one more reason to look elsewhere. Shouldn’t we be doing everything possible to bring opportunity to Vermont?
State and local taxes already take 13.6% of Vermonters’ income. Only New York, Connecticut and Hawaii take more. States with the most unionized public workforces carry tax burdens about 32% higher than the least unionized. Vermont is one of them, with just over 46% of public employees covered by union representation, 10 points above the national average. We also have the second-highest per-pupil spending in the country, behind only New York, according to the National Education Association’s most recent Rankings of the States report, while results decline. Prop 3 would make it almost impossible for future lawmakers to rein in those costs. Vermont property tax payers will be left to foot the bill.
Illinois offers a warning about where this could lead. In 2025, lawmakers added an estimated $11 billion in new liabilities to Chicago’s police and fire pensions with no new revenue to pay for them. Illinois now ranks first in the country for state pension debt per person. According to the Illinois Policy Institute, more than 350 state laws could eventually be overridden by union contracts.
Supporters predicted a dozen states would follow Illinois. None has. Even California let its version die in committee.
Vermont workers would retain the robust protections they have today without Proposal 3. The state would also retain its ability to change course in the future if it becomes necessary. Constitutions are for lasting principles, not for freezing one side of a policy debate in place. Vermont cannot afford to lock in the status quo.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Can Vermont afford Proposal 3?.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming Supreme Court concludes crossover-voting ban is constitutional
description:
The ruling clears the way for November’s general election to proceed with party-affiliation restrictions in place.
The post Wyoming Supreme Court concludes crossover-voting ban is constitutional appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The Wyoming Supreme Court upheld the state’s crossover-voting ban Thursday, ruling that the 96-day period in which voters are prohibited from changing party affiliation ahead of Election Day does not violate their constitutional rights. 
“After balancing the right to vote against the legislature’s duty to ‘secure the purity of elections’ and to ‘guard against abuses of the elective franchise,’… we conclude the party affiliation deadline is not an unconstitutionally onerous burden on Appellants’ right to vote and does not violate equal protection guarantees,” the court stated in its unanimous ruling. 
The decision clears the way for November’s general election to proceed as it has since 2023, when the Wyoming Legislature adopted a law that prohibits what’s known as crossover voting. 
The deadline lines up with the candidate-filing period, requiring voters to affiliate with a party before the slate of candidates has been finalized. Supporters of the law said it was needed to stop registered Democrats, minor party and unaffiliated voters from changing their party affiliation in order to participate as Republicans in the primary election. They’ve blamed farther-right candidates losing to more moderate candidates in primaries on the practice, though those claims were shown to be statistically unfounded.
Prior to the crossover-voting ban, Wyoming voters could change their party affiliation at the polls on Election Day. 

Secretary of State Chuck Gray applauds Gov. Mark Gordon’s State of the State address on Monday, Feb. 9, 2026, at the Wyoming Capitol in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)

“Today’s Supreme Court ruling is a huge win for Wyoming elections, which we have consistently worked to defend,” Secretary of State Chuck Gray said in a press release. The suit named Gray in his official capacity as the defendant.  
Filed in 2024, the lawsuit initially sought to overturn the state’s “sore loser law,” which bars failed primary candidates from appearing on the general election ballot as independents. The plaintiffs, who include voters, former political candidates and a retired state lawmaker, expanded the complaint in 2025 to also challenge the state’s closed primaries and party-affiliation restrictions. After a Laramie County District Court upheld the laws, siding with the state and ruling that the statutes are a “valid exercise of legislative power,” the plaintiffs appealed to the Wyoming Supreme Court. 
The plaintiffs, however, also narrowed the appeal, seeking only to challenge the lower court’s ruling on the 96-day freeze period ahead of the election in which registered voters are prohibited from changing their party affiliation. 
Both parties presented oral arguments in June. At the hearing, the plaintiffs pointed to two sections of the Wyoming Constitution — one that protects the “untrammeled exercise of the right of suffrage” and one that guarantees “equal political rights.” Lawyers with the Wyoming Attorney General’s Office pushed back, arguing that the case is not about voting rights but the state’s constitutional interest in protecting the purity of elections. 
While the Supreme Court disagreed with the state’s argument that primary elections are not elections in the constitutional sense because primaries were not used to select candidates at the time the Wyoming Constitution was adopted, the high court ultimately upheld the lower court’s ruling. 
“The claims at issue here depend on the language of the voting-rights provisions of the Wyoming Constitution, and we begin with those provisions,” the court wrote. 
Those provisions include protecting voters’ interests by providing that “elections shall be open, free and equal, and no power, civil or military, shall at any time interfere to prevent an untrammeled exercise of the right of suffrage.” The constitution also requires the Legislature to “pass laws to secure the purity of elections, and guard against abuses of elective franchise.”
Wyoming Supreme Court justices John Fenn and Kari Gray applaud as Gov. Mark Gordon delivers his State of the State address Monday, Feb. 9, 2026, in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)
The court measures “the 96-day Freeze Period against these provisions,” the ruling states. “Not every restriction on voting is constitutionally forbidden. Article 1, section 27 protects the franchise. Article 6, section 13 directs the legislature to regulate elections to keep them pure. We give effect to both. Election laws will necessarily impose some burden upon voters.” 
The burden of the freeze period “is slight,” the court wrote. 
“The freeze does not lock voters into a party,” the ruling states. “It sets a deadline — affiliation must be declared or changed 96 days before the primary. Electors have fair notice of that deadline, and the statutes provide clear rules for enforcement.”   
Furthermore, the freeze period “applies the same rule to every elector on the same calendar,” the court wrote. “Where the burden is slight and the rule is uniform, article 6, section 13 leaves that line drawing to the legislature. The Freeze Period deters affiliation changes that are not motivated by genuine attachment to the party and the state’s interest in doing so is legitimate and reasonable.” 
Justice Kari Gray authored the decision. Wyoming Seventh District Court Judge Joshua C. Eames filled in on the case after Justice Bridget Hill recused herself because she was attorney general when the lawsuit was filed in 2024. 
This is a breaking news story and may be updated. 
The post Wyoming Supreme Court concludes crossover-voting ban is constitutional appeared first on WyoFile .

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Controversial NJ independent contractor test regulations take effect
description: New regulations codify decades of case law over the state test used to classify employees. They've faced opposition from business groups who say they create uncertainty.
text:
New regulations codify decades of case law over the state test used to classify employees. They've faced opposition from business groups who say they create uncertainty. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)New regulations interpreting a test the state uses to weigh whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor went into effect Thursday over the objections of business groups and New Jersey’s Senate president.
The department has said the new regulations codify decades of case law governing the three-pronged ABC test, while business groups and some lawmakers have worried it would change some workers’ classifications.
“This is a rule that simply puts into place, simply codifies the rules and regulations that are already in place, the court decisions, what we’re acting under. If you are an independent contractor today, you will be an independent contractor tomorrow,” Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D) said on News12 New Jersey Wednesday.
The test was set in statute when New Jersey adopted its Unemployment Compensation Law in 1936 and has remained largely unchanged since.
The new regulations do not alter the test’s three prongs, which measure whether a worker is free from their employer’s control, whether the service they perform lies outside of the employer’s usual course of business, and whether the worker is independently engaged in trade. A worker is an employee unless they meet all three of the prongs.
Some lawmakers had expressed frustration with the regulations as they advanced legislation to exempt certain professions from the test at the urging of industry officials who said the rules make their employment classification uncertain.
Michelle Siekerka, president and CEO of the New Jersey Business and Industry Association, said the new regulations leave an “overly broad” interpretation of the ABC framework in place that represents an unnecessary  hit on New Jersey businesses.
“The result is a system that picks winners and losers. Those with the resources and access to secure a legislative exemption may be protected, while independent contractors and small businesses without a seat at the table are left to pursue their entrepreneurial goals under continued legal and regulatory uncertainty,” Siekerka said.
Senate President Nicholas Scutari (D-Union) had urged Sherrill to further delay the rule’s effective date until July 1, 2027. The rule was adopted in May, but its effective date was already deferred until Oct. 1.
Scutari declined comment through a spokesperson. Sherrill said she is willing to approve legislation exempting some professions from the test.
“If there are areas where it has somehow swept people into its ambit who should not be there, then I am more than happy to work with the Legislature on specific carveouts for those groups,” she said on News12.
