Clemson's Memorial Stadium is seen as the Lot 5 parking renovations continue on Wednesday, June 28, 2023. The project hopes to create an enhanced tailgate experience, an improved visual scenery and a new sidewalk for the football team’s Tiger Walk. (File photo by Jennifer Masters/SIDELINE CAROLINA/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — South Carolina fans have navigated cordoned off areas and construction supplies piled up around the building this season as the university continues its $350 million “reimagining” of Williams-Brice Stadium.
Projects like this remain essential to fans, team personnel, players and prospects, even in an era where sponsorship contracts and court-mandated revenue sharing for players has reshaped the sport.
“I don’t know any fans who want less,” Coastal Carolina athletic director Chance Miller said recently, referring to comfortable seating, easy access to concessions, smooth entry and exit and other amenities that can make the difference between becoming a season-ticket holder and staying at home watching the game on a large-screen TV.
“Gone are the days of opening a facility right now and people want to sit on metal bleachers when it’s 100 degrees outside,” said Miller, who has led the Chanticleers’ sports programs since 2024. “They want something a little better.”
Miller spent 11 years in South Carolina’s athletic department and saw first-hand the race the Gamecocks and just about every other Division I school took part in to have the best, most modern and innovative facilities.
New restrooms, no spiral rampway: Here’s what’s new for Gamecock football fans this season

The push has revamped the state of South Carolina’s three schools who compete in the biggest level of college football, the Football Championship Subdivision.
Clemson, in the Atlantic Coast Conference, and South Carolina of the Southeastern Conference, play in Power 4 conferences. Coastal Carolina, of the Sun Belt Conference, is among schools in the nicknamed “Group of Six” leagues that compete for a spot in the 12-team College Football Playoff that determines a national champion.
For the longest time, facilities were among the main drivers in attracting the best recruits in all sports to play for your favorite college team. Payments to players were against NCAA rules, led to lengthy investigations and, if provable, led to sometimes substantial penalties that could set a program back for years.
But with the NCAA’s $2.8 billion settlement in the House v. NCAA case in 2025, Division I schools distributed as much as $20.5 million to its athletes last academic year.
Allowing players to benefit off their name, image and likeness also means players and their representatives — another new wrinkle in college sports — make money in advertisements.
South Carolina quarterback LaNorris Sellers, receiver Nyck Harbor and Clemson defensive end Will Heldt are among several area college athletes in a TV commercial for a prominent auto muffler company.
Sellers, a junior, earns about $2 million this season, according to NIL evaluations by On3.com, which tracks such deals.
Clemson coach Dabo Swinney believes it’s even more important to have the best facilities to attract players to add to a school’s success.
“”Everybody’s got money,” Swinney said of the power programs.
“The environment they’re going to be in, especially for a young kid who’s going off to college. Locker room, the environment that they’re in, the resources that are there,” said Swinney, who’s won two national titles in his 18 full seasons as Tigers coach.
Swinney was also part of a revitalization of Clemson’s sports facilities, including a $55 million football operations center that had other schools scrambling to match.
The Tigers, under now-retired athletic director Dan Radakovich and current athletic director Graham Neff, upgraded facilities for most of its sports.
It opened a performance and wellness center for $50 million in April 2025. That followed McWhorter Stadium, home to Clemson softball since 2020, a $13 million expense.
Basketball’s Littlejohn Coliseum had a $63.5 million renovation that opened before the 2016-17 season. An additional $40 million upgrade is underway to improve practice gyms, team areas including strength and conditioning, nutrition and sports medicine spaces for men’s and women’s basketball and women’s gymnastics.

A packed Littlejohn Coliseum comes alive as players are introduced before the Duke game in Clemson, S.C. on Saturday, Feb. 8, 2025. (Photo by Travis Bell/SIDELINE CAROLINA/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)

Is it a worthwhile investment?
At Clemson, men’s basketball has made four of the past six NCAA Tournaments while the women’s team reached the Big Dance last season for the first time since 2019.
As for the $55 million football center, Swinney calls it Clemson’s football home for “a hundred years” and was grateful administrators had the vision to take advantage of the moment.
“If we hadn’t built this facility when we built it, it would’ve been a real challenge for Clemson with the timing,” he said.
A similar facility would’ve cost close to $78 million to build today, according to a calculation based on the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Consumer Price Index.
Swinney recalled when the land the center sits on was for practices for many teams or areas of tailgating on Clemson football Saturdays.
He joked how men’s soccer coach Mike Noonan wouldn’t talk to him after losing practice areas. But an $8 million soccer operations center opened in 2020, and the Tigers have since won men’s national soccer titles in 2021 and 2023.
“And Noonan was not happy,” Swinney said. “But now he’s the happiest guy.”
That lesson was also put in place at South Carolina, where second-year athletic director Jeremiah Donati has led the building renovation that will be fully completed in time for the 2028 season.
Phase one created a Cockaboose Club near the iconic, tailgating train cars along the stadium, removed one of the spiral walkways, created a new visitors locker room and improved restrooms and concession areas throughout the building.
Phase two, ready before the 2027 season, will concentrate on club level seating, increasing luxury suites from 18 to 43 and adding escalators.
Phase three, the school says, focuses on player areas like improved locker rooms, team rooms and recruiting space for future Gamecocks.
“You’ve got to make sure that your investment, as best as you can, is future proof,” Donati said the construction expenses.
“All these projects are expensive and getting more expensive, so you’ve got to be careful” with plans, he said.
South Carolina, Clemson and Coastal Carolina all must go through multiple oversight approvals from school and state fiscal oversight panels before undergoing major projects.
South Carolina has spent more than $200 million over the past two decades to transform its athletic footprint. It spent about $20 million on the Rice Athletic Center as sports administration’s headquarters and the Dodie Anderson Academic Enrichment Center.
There’s been a new baseball and softball facilities, and upgrades to the Stone Soccer Field that helped the women’s team win SEC titles in 2019 and 2021l and the men’s team reach No. 1 in the country this year.
Improvements to the basketball’s Colonial Life Arena and the old Carolina Coliseum have been essential in the women’s program keeping coach Dawn Staley, landing centerpiece players like WNBA stars A’ja Wilson and Aliyah Boston and winning three national titles (2017, 2022, 2024).
‘It could be the edger’: USC’s Dawn Staley launches leadership program for students

The school has spent between $5 million and $6 million on Coliseum updates to set up men’s and women’s basketball offices and practice courts.
Like Clemson, South Carolina’s biggest expenses go to football. The Long Operations Center across from Williams-Brice opened in 2019 with a price of $50 million.
The adjacent Indoor Practice facility, named for ex-Gamecocks coach Steve Spurrier and wife Jerri, cost close to $15 million.
South Carolina coach Shane Beamer believes you can’t compete for the best players without modern, updated facilities.
Beamer tells his players the adage, “Even if you’re on the right track, you’re going to get run over if you just sit there.”
He says the school is on the right track in investing in athletics. But schools like Auburn and Florida have opened improved buildings since the Gamecocks’ center came on line seven years ago.
Beamer said fresh paint and carpet, improvements in training rooms and the players’ lounge show current Gamecocks, “We’re going to continue to do these things for you.”
Improvements, though, need money and the best way to ensure the financial flow is win.
“Every coach here at Carolina certainly has a wish list of what they want,” he said. “And I know the importance of us back in that stadium and winning football games to help everybody here at Carolina.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Trump nominates Jackson-based lawyer Todd Butler to federal appeals court
description: President Donald Trump speaks during the National Prayer Breakfast, Thursday, Feb. 5, 2026, in Washington.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
President Donald Trump on Thursday said he plans to nominate Jackson-based labor and employment lawyer Todd Butler to a Mississippi-based opening on the U.S. 5th Circuit Court of Appeals. 
“The wonderful people of the Great State of Mississippi (one of my favorites!), and the rest of the Fifth Circuit, can count on Todd to protect the Constitution and the Rule of Law,” Trump said on social media. 
Butler has spent the last 17 years practicing with the Jackson-based law firm Phelps Dunbar, according to his LinkedIn profile, and he previously clerked for Judge Leslie Southwick, the judge whose seat he would fill if confirmed. Southwick recently took senior status. 
Todd Butler
Butler graduated from Mississippi State University and Mississippi Christian University School of Law, and both Mississippi’s Republican U.S. senators, Roger Wicker and Cindy Hyde-Smith, support him. 
“Todd Butler is an excellent pick for the federal bench,” the two senators said in a joint statement. “He believes in interpreting the law as it is written, pursuant to the text and original meaning of the Constitution — exactly the quality that should characterize a jurist.”  
The Senate Judiciary Committee will likely schedule a confirmation hearing for Butler in the coming months. The court hears federal appeals from Mississippi, Louisiana and Texas.

name: Delaware
title: Stray Cats to headline The Grand’s 50th annual gala
description: Wilmington institution will celebrate a half-century of its signature fundraiser Dec. 5, honoring longtime leader Skip Pennella and raising money for community arts programs WILMINGTON, Del. — The Grand will mark a major milestone in Wilmington’s arts and social scene this December, celebrating the 50th anniversary of its annual Grand Gala with a performance[...]
text:
Wilmington institution will celebrate a half-century of its signature fundraiser Dec. 5, honoring longtime leader Skip Pennella and raising money for community arts programs
WILMINGTON, Del. — The Grand will mark a major milestone in Wilmington’s arts and social scene this December, celebrating the 50th anniversary of its annual Grand Gala with a performance by the Stray Cats, an elaborate after-party at the Hotel DuPont and a tribute to longtime Grand leader Skip Pennella.
The 50th annual Grand Gala is scheduled for Saturday, Dec. 5, with the Stray Cats taking the stage at The Grand Opera House’s Copeland Hall before guests move to the Hotel DuPont for what organizers bill as the “Ultimate After Party.”
The gala has grown into one of Wilmington’s signature annual fundraising and social events. Proceeds support The Grand’s Community Engagement and Outreach programs, which provide arts experiences for more than 20,000 students and residents. The Grand says gala support helps provide music and dance instruction, theater performances and other arts programming.
Rockabilly icons come to Wilmington
The Stray Cats — Brian Setzer, Lee Rocker and Slim Jim Phantom — helped bring rockabilly back into mainstream popular music in the early 1980s, combining a 1950s-inspired look and sound with the energy of contemporary rock.
Formed in 1979 on Long Island, the trio initially struggled to gain traction in the United States before heading to London in 1980, where a growing rockabilly revival helped launch the band’s career.
The group ultimately found major success on both sides of the Atlantic, becoming known for songs including “Rock This Town,” “Stray Cat Strut” and “(She’s) Sexy + 17.”
Following the concert, gala guests will head a few blocks up Market Street to the Hotel DuPont, where the celebration will continue with themed rooms, live music, gourmet food and signature cocktails.
Pennella to receive Grand Medal
The evening will also recognize Francis “Skip” Pennella with the 2026 Grand Medal for Excellence in the Performing Arts.
Pennella recently retired as executive director and transitioned to a senior advisory role. His relationship with The Grand, however, stretches well beyond his tenure as its top executive. He previously spent 11 years as chairman of The Grand’s board, helping lead the organization through a period of change and an expanded emphasis on community service.
“Skip answered the call when The Grand needed him most,” Board Chair Roger Kirtley said. “Through his steady leadership, unwavering commitment and deep care for this organization, he helped guide The Grand through an important period in its history and positioned us well for the future.”
Pennella called serving as executive director “one of the greatest privileges of my career.”
“I am incredibly proud of what our Board, staff, volunteers, donors, and community partners have accomplished together,” Pennella said. “We have a unique opportunity to build upon a proud history while ensuring The Grand continues to serve and inspire our community for generations to come.”
Leadership transition underway
The gala comes as The Grand moves through a leadership transition.
The Board of Directors has appointed Mike Woodin as interim executive director while conducting a national search for Pennella’s permanent successor. Woodin has served in senior leadership at The Grand and has worked on the organization’s finances and strategic planning.
“It is an honor to serve an organization that means so much to our community,” Woodin said. “Every day, our talented staff creates experiences that inspire audiences, educate young people, and strengthen Delaware through the performing arts.”
The Grand’s 50th gala also continues a tradition of bringing prominent performers to Wilmington for the fundraiser. Recent galas have featured Kool & the Gang in 2024 and Bruce Hornsby with the Delaware Symphony Orchestra in 2025.
More than a night out
While the gala has long been part of Wilmington’s social calendar, its primary purpose is fundraising.
The Grand says proceeds help make arts programming available to thousands of Delaware children and community members who might otherwise have limited opportunities to experience live theater, dance and music. The organization has described the gala as a major source of support for its community engagement, Stage of Discovery and arts education programs.
That gives this year’s celebration two milestones: 50 years of gala nights in downtown Wilmington and a changing of the guard for one of Delaware’s best-known performing arts organizations.
TO GO

When: Saturday, Dec. 5, 2026
Where: Concert and presentation at The Grand Opera House, 818 N. Market St., Wilmington; Ultimate After Party at the Hotel DuPont
Tickets: $250 to $550. A $1,600 package includes two tickets, a hotel stay and additional benefits.
Benefits: The Grand’s Community Engagement and Outreach programs serving students and Wilmington residents
Information and tickets: The Grand Gala
Box office: 302-652-5577

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Family of Renee Good sues federal government, Trump officials over killing
description: The family of Renee Good filed a pair of lawsuits against the federal government and top Trump administration officials Thursday morning, seeking compensation and a trial to determine the liability of several federal officials in Good’s killing. Good was shot and killed by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent Jonathan Ross on Jan. 7 as she […]
text:
Becca Good, widow of Renee Good, speaks at a press conference on Oct. 1, 2026, announcing lawsuits against the federal government over Good's killing by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent. (Photo by Madison McVan/Minnesota Reformer)The family of Renee Good filed a pair of lawsuits against the federal government and top Trump administration officials Thursday morning, seeking compensation and a trial to determine the liability of several federal officials in Good’s killing.
Good was shot and killed by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent Jonathan Ross on Jan. 7 as she and her wife, Becca Good, protested the agents’ presence in their south Minneapolis neighborhood. 
Ross has not been charged with a crime in Good’s killing, though local and federal law enforcement officials say they are still investigating the shooting. 
Attorneys for Good’s family called the lawsuits “historic” and framed it as an opportunity to hold the Trump administration accountable for abuses committed during Operation Metro Surge and beyond. 
“Our government is killing our citizens without any legal justification,” said Antonio Romanucci of the Chicago-based law firm Romanucci & Blandin, which is representing Good’s family alongside Minnesota attorney Kevin Riach. Romanucci was co-counsel for the estate of George Floyd. 
Good’s brother, Brent Ganger, and Becca Good are the lead plaintiffs in the two lawsuits. One was filed under the Federal Tort Claims Act, which provides for the compensation of people abused by federal employees, and names the U.S. government as the sole defendant. 
The second complaint relies on a novel legal theory based on the Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871, which outlaws conspiracies to deprive people of their constitutional rights. Good’s family argues that Operation Metro Surge was one such conspiracy targeted at Somali and Hispanic people. The lawsuit names several individual defendants, including Ross, White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, former Border Patrol Commander Gregory Bovino and more.
Becca Good made her first public appearance Thursday morning at a press conference announcing the lawsuits. 
“Renee and I believed in something simple: that being good can change the world,” Becca Good said. “And she believed every person deserves love and compassion, care and dignity.”
Becca Good appeared alongside Ganger, Renee Good’s parents and other members of their family, who held each other and wiped away tears as Becca Good spoke.
Activists and immigrants have filed similar claims under the FTCA.
The FTCA provides the “clearest path to accountability” for federal agents, said Sarah Raisch, an attorney with Romanucci & Blandin, though Romanucci said federal law doesn’t provide adequate paths to justice for people abused by federal agents.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Mail-in ballots heading out as Pennsylvania voter registration deadline approaches
description: Interested Pennsylvanian voters must apply for mail-in ballots by Oct. 17. The voter registration deadline is Oct. 19.
text:
Interested Pennsylvanian voters must apply for mail-in ballots by Oct. 17. The voter registration deadline is Oct. 19. (Photo by Simone Hogan/Getty Images)More than one million Pennsylvanian voters have requested a mail-in ballot ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm election, with counties reporting nearly 64,000 returned ballots at the end of September.
At a press conference Wednesday, Secretary of the Commonwealth Al Schmidt saidthat the percentage of returned ballots this year outpaced the 2022 midterm election, noting that the deadline to apply is Oct. 27.
“Voting by mail is a convenient, safe and secure option for eligible Pennsylvanians,” he said. “And even though the deadline is several weeks away, those who prefer to vote by mail should apply today to ensure they have time to receive, mark and return their ballot by Election Day.”
Secretary of the Commonwealth Al Schmidt speaks to the media about primary elections at a 9 p.m. press conference on May 19, 2026. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
Ballots must be received by the county board of elections by 9 p.m. on Election Day to be counted. More than 30 counties have started mailing out ballots, according to Schmidt. 
He added that voting systems are tested daily to ensure ballots are marked correctly, and never connected to the internet. 
“Every vote is cast on a voter-verifiable paper ballot that is subject to two audits after every election,” he said.
Schmidt emphasized that law enforcement officers are prohibited from polling places unless they are voting — with the exception for someone serving a warrant or preventing a disturbance. Trump administration officials have floated the possibility.
“State and federal laws strictly limit military and law enforcement presence at polling places, and they also prohibit voter intimidation,” he continued. “We encourage anyone involved in the electoral process — whether they’re an election direction, a candidate, a poll worker or a registered voter — to immediately report threats of violence to appropriate law enforcement partners.”
Additionally, reports can be made to the Pennsylvania Department of State online or at 1-877-VOTESPA. Oct. 19 is the last day to register to vote.

name: National
title: District attorney elections linked to more prison admissions during ‘tough on crime’ era
description: County and local district attorneys oversaw higher state prison admissions during election years than in other years during the height of the nation’s “tough on crime” era, according to a new study from Northwestern University’s Pritzker School of Law. State prison admissions were about 3% higher in years when district attorneys were up for election […]
text:
Clouds float above the Gallatin County Court House in Bozeman, Mont. A study on prison admissions during district attorneys’ election years found the increase in incarcerations was concentrated primarily in less serious, nonviolent cases rather than violent crimes. (Keila Szpaller/The Daily Montanan)County and local district attorneys oversaw higher state prison admissions during election years than in other years during the height of the nation’s “tough on crime” era, according to a new study from Northwestern University’s Pritzker School of Law.
State prison admissions were about 3% higher in years when district attorneys were up for election compared with non-election years, the study’s author found. From 1986 to 2006, that amounted to roughly 63,000 additional prison admissions.
The findings suggest that electoral politics may have influenced prosecutors’ decisions about who enters the criminal legal system and how long people are sentenced to serve. But the study does not show that elections caused the broader rise in incarceration during that 20-year period, and its findings are limited to state prison admissions and sentencing during an era when incarceration was rising sharply nationwide.
The study, led by Chika Okafor, an economist and assistant law professor at Northwestern, examined more than 4,200 district attorneys and prison admissions in nearly 40 states. The study was published in the October edition of the Journal of Public Economics. 
States put criminal justice, marijuana policies before voters in 2026

Prosecutors represent the government and have broad discretion in criminal investigations over whether to bring charges, what charges to pursue, whether to offer plea deals and what sentences to recommend. 
In his research, Okafor found that prison admissions were about 4.3% higher in election years than in the previous year. Months sentenced to state prison also increased by about 3% in election years, or about 4% compared with the preceding year, according to the study.
The increase was concentrated primarily in less serious, nonviolent cases rather than violent crimes.
“For high-profile murders, the behavior is going to be kind of agnostic to where you are in the election cycle,” Okafor said in a news release, in part because voters may be more likely to remember such cases.
Okafor also found that the election-year effects were strongest in parts of the South and in Republican-leaning counties. The effects declined as national support for harsher punishment softened after the mid-1990s, according to the study.
During the 1980s and 1990s, politicians frequently campaigned on being “tough on crime,” amid the war on drugs and passage of the 1994 federal crime bill under President Bill Clinton. Prison populations grew dramatically during those decades.
Okafor’s research suggests that prosecutors at the time may have responded not only to laws and formal criminal justice policies, but also to what they perceived voters wanted.
“The study provides evidence consistent with prosecutors having responded to perceived voter preferences,” Okafor said in the news release. “That is why efforts to change public attitudes toward punishment deserve as much attention as efforts to change policies or officeholders.”
But there are limits to what the research can establish.
The study compares election years with non-election years. It does not measure every form of political pressure a prosecutor may experience throughout a term, nor does it establish that an election itself caused the broader increase in incarceration during the period.
The broader “tough on crime” political climate could have influenced prosecutors outside election years as well, according to Okafor. Because of that, the 63,000 additional admissions associated with election years should not be interpreted as the total amount of incarceration attributable to electoral politics.
The research also focuses on 1986 to 2006, a period that predates many of the major criminal justice policy changes adopted by states in the years since.
“District attorneys are critical in promoting justice within the criminal legal system,” he said in the news release. “One responsibility is consistency: an office should charge and make plea offers the same way in an election year as in any other year.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Underground utility damage topped $515M in Louisiana last year
description: Damage to underground utility lines cost Louisiana ratepayers an estimated $515.5 million every year to fix, according to a new report.
text:
Louisiana had a total of 5,054 incidents of reported underground utility damage in 2025 out nearly 214,000 across the country. The Common Ground Alliance stressed that damage to underground infrastructure can result in service outages, business interruptions, property damage, injuries and even deaths. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)Damage to underground utility lines cost Louisiana ratepayers an estimated $515.5 million every year to fix, according to a new report. 
The new findings from Common Ground Alliance, a nonprofit trade association dedicated to protecting utility infrastructure, show damage to utility infrastructure across the United States surpassed $83.2 billion in 2025. In Louisiana, the impact on buried power, water, natural gas and internet lines cost ratepayers an estimated $515.5 million in repairs, or more than $1.4 million a day. 
The highest dollar amount of damage in the state by far is for phone, internet and cable lines, according to the report, amounting to almost $500 million. Next were natural gas lines, totaling just over $7 million in reported damages across Louisiana. 
The report’s methodology combined 2025 data from the alliance’s online damage information reporting tool, interviews with its members and industry executives, publicly reported incidents and government data on utility damage to compile its results. 
Louisiana had a total of 5,054 incidents of reported underground utility damage in 2025 out nearly 214,000 across the country. The Common Ground Alliance stressed that damage to underground infrastructure can result in service outages, business interruptions, property damage, injuries and even deaths.
“An annual cost of $515.5 million in Louisiana makes clear that this is an economic problem, a public safety problem and an infrastructure challenge,” CGA president and CEO Sarah Magruder Lyle said in a news release.  
Louisiana law requires excavators and demolition teams to call before digging to avoid hitting and damaging utility lines. It also requires utility owners and operators to mark underground utility locations and make information available on their location before construction work or demolition begins. 
Louisiana’s 811 program provides free information on utility line locations to any individual or company to help them avoid underground damage. The service is available at 1-800-272-3020 and online.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Remember the ‘us’ in the prayer to ‘give us this day our daily bread’
description: During last year’s interruption in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits, commonly known as food stamps, I was given the names of more than 100 people who would go without food if we didn’t act. We mobilized funds, packed grocery bags, baked casseroles, and started making deliveries. One evening, I drove to a mobile home park […]
text:
Breads are sorted in the donation center at Feed More, a central-Virginia-anchored food bank. (File photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)During last year’s interruption in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits, commonly known as food stamps, I was given the names of more than 100 people who would go without food if we didn’t act.

Empty shelves in the warehouse of Harvest Hope Food Bank pictured Monday, Oct. 27, 2025, in Columbia, S.C., during the federal government shutdown. The warehouse would typically be filled to the ceiling. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)

We mobilized funds, packed grocery bags, baked casseroles, and started making deliveries.
One evening, I drove to a mobile home park to deliver a box of nonperishable food and a few casseroles. The road was little more than rutted dirt. It was dark, and I couldn’t find the numbers on the buildings.
I found a man standing outside and asked if he was the person I had been looking for. He said “yes,” so I handed him the food and drove away.
Before I reached the end of the road, my phone rang.
It was the woman who I had been trying to reach. She was crying, angry, and desperate. Her children were hungry. It turned out I had delivered food to the wrong person.


To read more commentaries in this series, click here.


I went back with more.
What stayed with me was not the mistake, but the panic in her voice, the sound of someone living so close to the edge that one wrong delivery could leave her children without nourishment.
This is not simply a story about one family. It is a story about how many of our neighbors are living without margin for error.
On mornings when I drive into Columbia, cars are already idling outside Harvest Hope long before the pantry opens. Across Sumter, children discreetly receive backpacks filled with food on Fridays because there may be nothing in the refrigerator or pantry over the weekend.
And families living in motels often have no kitchen, stove, or oven, which means that even when we bring groceries, we have to consider what can be prepared with nothing more than a microwave.
In Sumter County, more than one in five children experiences food insecurity.
Statewide, more than 590,000 South Carolinians rely on SNAP, nearly half of them children. Yet South Carolina has declined to participate in SUN Bucks, which would provide families an additional $120 per child to buy groceries during the summer, supplementing programs that provide free prepared meals when school’s not in session.
Every SC student to get free breakfast with state funding

A 12-year national study from 2004 to 2016 linked greater SNAP participation to fewer child protective services and foster care cases, evidence that food assistance can help keep families safely together.
The idea that access to food strengthens entire communities is not new.
Thousands of years ago, the Old Testament offered a striking vision of what people with abundance owed to those without it.
In Leviticus, landowners were commanded not to harvest their fields to the edges but to leave part of what they grew for the poor and the stranger. Deuteronomy extended that protection to widows and orphans. Provision for people in need was not treated as an afterthought; it was built into the harvest itself.
It was called gleaning.
Dignity was built into the system. Hungry people did not have to prove their destitution before they were allowed to eat; those with abundance were simply required to leave something at the
edges for those who needed it.
Today, we ask people to document every facet of their financial lives to prove they are poor enough for help. But people rarely ask strangers for food casually. When someone says they are hungry, perhaps we should begin by believing them.
The ancient command is simple: do not take everything for yourself; leave something at the edges for your neighbors.
When Jesus taught his disciples to pray, he did not say, “Give me this day my daily bread.” He said, “Give us this day our daily bread.” In that framing, bread belongs to “us.”
Life’s necessities are not individual concerns. The well-being of our neighbors is inextricably woven into our own.
Food pantries, canned food drives, grocery deliveries and casseroles are incredibly important.
I’ve witnessed them sustain families through impossible seasons. But compassion cannot become an excuse for accepting conditions that should never have become normalized.
Daily bread should not be extraordinary in a country that wastes an estimated 30% to 40% of its food supply every year.
The question is not simply whether we will feed someone when they are hungry; it is whether we will leave enough room at the edges so fewer of our neighbors face hunger at all.
We have enough food. What we have not built is a reliable way to ensure that everyone shares in it.
Because if we pray, “Give us this day our daily bread,” then “us” has to mean all of us.

title: New Mexico U.S. Sen. Heinrich and colleagues announce bipartisan regulatory reform bill
description: U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), ranking member of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, on Wednesday helped introduce the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which sponsors say will help bolster cheaper energy, and more jobs by reforming the federal government's regulatory process for energy projects.
text:
U.S. Senators Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) center, with (l-r) Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Mike Lee (R-Utah) and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), on Sept. 30, 2026, held a news conference at the U.S. Capitol to introduce bipartisan permitting reform legislation. (Screenshot)U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), ranking member of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, on Wednesday helped introduce the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which sponsors say will help bolster cheaper energy and create more jobs by reforming the federal government’s regulatory process for energy and infrastructure projects.
The bipartisan agreement was announced shortly before the Senate left for the break by Heinrich, along with West Virginia Republican Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, chairwoman of the Environment and Public Works Committee; Rhode Island Democratic Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, ranking member on that committee; and Utah Republican Sen. Mike Lee, chairman of the Energy and Natural Resources Committee.
A fact-sheet on the legislation lists some of its key provisions as: providing the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission more authority to approve major interstate power line; requiring regional and interregional transmission planning to account for new transmission and future transmission needs; and forcing data centers to “pay their fair share.”
The bill also proposes introducing a two-year deadline for Environmental Impact Statement reviews and a one-year deadline for Environmental Assessment reviews; along with “securing a statutory role for Tribes in determining how projects affect historic and cultural resources and protecting Tribes’ rights to formally consult during the processes.”
In a virtual news conference with New Mexico reporters, Heinrich cited the SunZia wind and transmission project in the state, which took 17 years to permit and build. “Mostly to permit,” he noted. “My experiences with permitting Sunzia led me to fully appreciate how slow and sometimes broken our permitting system can be. That’s a real problem right now because if we have any hope of cutting energy costs for families, America needs to be able to build things in years, not in decades.”
Heinrich, who said he spent the “better part of this entire Congress” negotiating the bill, said it will “deliver cheaper energy to New Mexico homes, create more jobs for New Mexico workers, and make sure that our growth is responsible, not by permitting every project, but by getting our permitting decisions to a yes; or if it’s a bad project, to a no, faster than in the past.”
During a Wednesday news conference on Capitol Hill in Washington D.C., Capito said the goal is for the package to be the first vote when the Senate returns in mid-November, to start the sometimes long and complicated floor process.
Whitehouse said negotiators had to go down several “dead-end avenues” before they were able to reach the final agreement they unveiled Wednesday, though that’s not the end of the process.
“This is a hugely important milestone but there are two big pieces of work in front of us,” he said, noting that their Senate colleagues now get to review the bill and offer amendments.
Jennifer Shutt contributed reporting to this story.

title: Judge blocks federal prosecutors from refiling charges in Reflecting Pool case
text: WASHINGTON — A D.C. Superior Court judge ruled Thursday that prosecutors cannot, for a second time, charge former Olympic canoeist David Hearn with damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.Judge Todd E. Edelman wrote in his ruling that “the observed damage to the Reflecting Pool was due to a contractor's ‘rushed and botched’ installation of the lining while conducting renovations, and Mr. Hearn's actions had no effect on the value of the Pool.”U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro sought to drop the charges against Hearn, of Maryland, in August, writing in a brief to the court that she wouldn’t have filed a case against him had she had more information from the Interior Department, which manages the Reflecting Pool. “Specifically, the newly released documents reveal that work on installing the lining almost immediately fell behind, due to a combination of very rainy and windy weather, repeated failures of testing on the sealing of the expansion joints, and delays in obtaining sealing product at the worksite,” Pirro wrote. “The rush to complete the project led to hasty and botched work that was not remediated before the project was finished and the fencing removed.”But Edelman had to hold a hearing on the future of the case in early September after federal prosecutors signaled they may try to refile the charges. The judge’s 26-page ruling blocks that from happening. “The Court respects the authority of the Office of the United States Attorney to decide which cases to prosecute and which to dismiss,” Edelman wrote. “However, in the exceptional circumstances posed by this case, the government has no right to retain the ability to compound the errors it has already made, or even to threaten to do so, at Mr. Hearn's expense.”
