name: Alabama Reflector
title: National ACA disenrollments could impact trust in programs, overall Alabama state health
description: As enrollment in the Affordable Care Act in Alabama drops, recent threatened disenrollments could impact the state’s health as a whole, experts say. Enrollment in the program, also known as Obamacare, rose steadily from 2020 to 2025 due to enhanced premium tax credits that lowered insurance costs and made those making more than 400% of […]
text:
As enrollment in the Affordable Care Act in Alabama drops, recent threatened disenrollments could impact the state’s health as a whole, experts say. Enrollment in the program rose steadily from 2020 to 2025 due to enhanced premium tax credits, but those credits expired last year leading to a 23% drop in enrollment. (krisanapong detraphiphat/Getty Images)As enrollment in the Affordable Care Act in Alabama drops, recent threatened disenrollments could impact the state’s health as a whole, experts say.
Enrollment in the program, also known as Obamacare, rose steadily from 2020 to 2025 due to enhanced premium tax credits that lowered insurance costs and made those making more than 400% of the federal poverty level – $132,000 per year for a family of four or $86,500 per year for a family of two – eligible for tax credits through the marketplace. By 2025, more than 427,000 Alabamians were enrolled in ACA plans, up from 143,000 five years previous. 
Those tax credits expired at the end of 2025, leading to 95,000 Alabamians – about 23% of the state’s enrollees – to exit the marketplace. 

The Trump administration last week announced the planned disenrollment of 760,000 more enrollees over claims of fraud. 
Although state-level data of the disenrollments are not available yet, experts say that a combination of not understanding what fraud looks like within the marketplace and healthy people being disenrolled because they have not filed a claim undercuts trust in the program as a whole. 
“If there’s this continuing idea of fraud in the marketplace, we might not see people sign up as much if they distrust the type of insurance that they’re getting,” said KFF Policy Analyst Matt McGough in an interview Tuesday. 
A request seeking the state-level data and any additional information about the disenrollments was sent to U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) on Friday. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
While fraud and misuse of ACA does exist, Debbie Smith, director of Alabama Arise’s initiative Cover Alabama, said in an interview Tuesday that broad disenrollment is not good for the broader society. 
“I think it’s really important that we root out fraud, and that if there is indeed fraud that is definitely something that we want to take care of,” Smith said. “But it’s never good when a bunch of people get disenrolled from health coverage, whether it’s from the announcement last week or people just losing their health insurance and coverage in general because of the prices going up dramatically last year because of the enhanced subsidies expiring.”
Roughly 19.2 million Americans are actively enrolled in ACA marketplace health plans as of early 2026, according to the Department of Health and Human Services website.
According to the CMS, most of the disenrollments are unauthorized enrollments by “bad actors” in insurance brokerage. An estimated 80% of enrollments are supported by brokers. 
McGough said that many people are used to using brokers for other types of insurance, so they gravitate towards the service for health insurance as well. 
“I think time is going to tell to truly understand how successful this action was in combating the fraud that’s out there,” McGough said. “Potentially the only people that know who was fraudulently enrolled or not are the brokers who were acting illegally to enroll these people.”
McGough said that it is hard to determine the collateral damage of the disenrollment because the public does not have access to the personal data that CMS does.
“It’s really not clear at this point if there is going to be any collateral in trying to fight this fraud, so to speak. Potentially there are going to be people who are legitimately enrolled who go to the marketplaces every year, or go to their broker, and they are enrolled and they think they have health insurance coverage, and now they don’t,” McGough said. 
The administration also claimed that some enrollees had not filed an insurance claim within a year of being insured, which CMS attributes to individuals being enrolled without their knowledge by brokers. 
“While zero utilization is not, on its face, indicative of an unauthorized enrollment (healthy individuals may go an extended period without filing a claim, for example), onExchange plans purchased through the Federal platform were more likely than unsubsidized, off-Exchange plans to have zero utilization in Plan Year 2024,” a CMS interim final rule from last week reads. “This 11 percentage point differential between on-Exchange and off-Exchange zero utilization is notable and may be indicative of unauthorized enrollment (since consumers enrolled in plans without their knowledge or consent would not be expected to utilize those plans).” 
The interim final rule is what CMS will use to disenroll individuals. 
Smith said that healthy people are crucial to the healthcare system’s foundation, recalling that she rarely used her health insurance when she was in her 20s.
“The whole point is to spread the risk among the thousands of people who are enrolled in coverage. If you don’t have healthy people to balance it out, then premiums just continue to go up and up and up because there’s only sick people using the coverage, and it’s not a very good balance,” she said. 
According to a March study by KFF, Americans under 34 make up 44% of the insured population, but only 21% of total healthcare spending. 
“People who pay more into the risk pool than they are getting out in a given year, like through claims, are integral to keeping health insurance affordable,” McGough said. 
Smith said that the federal navigator program, a service that helps individuals shop for health plans with no “skin in the game,” would help prevent some of the back actor brokers that have led to the mass disenrollment. However, the program’s funding was cut last year because they “are not enrolling nearly enough people to justify the substantial amount of federal dollars previously spent on the program.”
“If we really care about making sure that people aren’t fraudulently enrolled, then we need to be investing in programs like that that don’t have skin in the game,” Smith said.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Nursing Nashville mom reunited with kids 3 months after ICE arrest
description: By the time she was released from a Louisiana immigrant detention center, a Nashville mother of two could no longer breastfeed her young daughters. Her milk had dried up.  An asylum seeker from Guatemala, she had not seen or spoken with her children since being detained by immigration agents at her home on May 19 […]
text:
A nursing mother and asylum seeker living in Nashville was separated from her infant and toddler for three months after being detained by ICE, despite agency rules that bar the detention of nursing, pregnant and postpartum mothers with few exceptions. She was reunited with her infant and toddler with Down syndrome last month. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)By the time she was released from a Louisiana immigrant detention center, a Nashville mother of two could no longer breastfeed her young daughters. Her milk had dried up. 
An asylum seeker from Guatemala, she had not seen or spoken with her children since being detained by immigration agents at her home on May 19 as she was packing them into the car to head to an early morning doctor’s appointment. 
They reunited nearly three months later at the home of a neighbor who had volunteered to care for the kids. Her 2-year-old-daughter was “very angry,” she said in an interview with the Tennessee Lookout. She asked that her name be withheld due to fear of retaliation.
“She thought her mom left her behind, that I abandoned them,” the woman said of her eldest daughter, who has Down syndrome and a history of chronic medical conditions.
“The baby,” she said, breaking into tears when referring to her 1-year-old daughter, “The baby, I think … I felt … she knew I was her mom.”

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
Seeing her daughters again was all she thought about during her nearly three months of detention. Seeing them again almost didn’t feel real, she said.
“I was thinking it was a dream, that I wasn’t here,” she said. “My mind was foggy, blurry, but every time I was holding them and crying and touching them and kissing, I was still thinking it was a dream and I wasn’t there, that it wasn’t true.”
ICE policy bars detention of nursing mothers
The woman was released from the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center on Aug. 14 after a group of human rights organizations intervened. The woman’s partner remains detained at an immigration facility in Oklahoma.
In a complaint filed with the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of Inspector General, the organizations alleged that Immigration and Customs Enforcement violated its own policy against detaining pregnant, postpartum and nursing parents, and facilitating visits with children.
The policy says ICE must make an effort to arrange, upon written requests, visits with a minor child within the first 30 days of detention. It also states that the agency may only detain nursing, pregnant and postpartum parents under narrow “exceptional circumstances” such as risks to national security or an imminent threat to others.
ICE separated nursing mom from infant, toddler in Nashville, against its own rules, advocates say

The complaint demands that federal officials confirm in writing whether they contend any exceptional circumstances apply to the woman, who has no criminal record and was arrested as immigration agents were serving a federal warrant to her partner. The Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition, Southern Poverty Law Center, Sanctuary of the South, Amnesty International, the Kennedy Human Rights Center and ACLU of Louisiana signed the complaint.
A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security on Wednesday did not directly respond to a question about the status of the complaint. Instead, the spokesperson provided an identical statement it released when the woman’s detention was first made public in May.
“Pregnant and nursing women in ICE detention are exceedingly rare. When this occurs, the women receive regular prenatal visits, mental health services, nutritional support, and accommodations aligned with community standards of care,” the statement said.
“This includes medical, dental, and mental health intake screening within 12 hours of arriving at each detention facility, a full health assessment within 14 days of entering ICE custody or arrival at a facility, and access to necessary medical appointments and 24-hour emergency care.”
‘I feel like too many doors — they are closing’
Immigrant and reproductive rights advocates nationwide have accused the agency of routinely flouting its own policies against detaining pregnant, postpartum and nursing mothers. The rules were repealed in 2017 during the first Trump administration before being reinstated by the Biden administration in 2021 and remain in place today. 
ICE has declined to release data on the number of pregnant, postpartum and nursing mothers in its custody, according to Anthony Enriquez, vice president of U.S. advocacy and litigation for the Kennedy Human Rights Center, which represents two individuals challenging their detention under the rules.
In response to a demand for data earlier this year by U.S. Sen. Patty Murray, a Democrat from Washington State, ICE provided snapshot data in February that showed there were 86 pregnant women, 35 postpartum women and 15 nursing women in ICE detention as of Feb. 16.



Quotation







The harm inflicted on this family was pointless, unlawful, and has created wounds they will carry for years to come.


– Katie Blankenship, Sanctuary of the South


The data includes women in 23 detention centers served by the ICE Health Services Corps, a medical provider. It does not include pregnant, postpartum and nursing detainees at more than 200 other immigration detention centers whose medical care is provided by private contractors, including at the Louisiana detention center where the mother of two was detained.
Attorneys for the woman greeted her release with relief, but criticized her confinement — and that of other pregnant, postpartum and nursing women — as “unlawful.”
“The harm inflicted on this family was pointless, unlawful, and has created wounds they will carry for years to come,” said Katie Blankenship, managing attorney for Sanctuary of the South, in a statement.
“The cruelty of the Trump Administration is unforgivable … there are thousands of mothers and children suffering the same fate,” the statement said.
Last week, the woman said while she is relieved to be with her children, day-to-day life is “very, very difficult right now.”
“I don’t have my partner and he was the provider because I was taking care of my kids,” she said. “My friend is supporting me with everything right now.”
Her 2 year old has missed medical and therapy appointments because she does not drive and she worries about how much longer she will be able to remain a burden on her friend, she said.
“I feel like too many doors — they are closing. I feel trapped that I cannot find the light,” she said. “But I believe in God and truly think he can help. I’m working hard. We came to this country to work hard, to provide our kids a better life. We didn’t come here to suffer more than we suffered in our countries.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC Housing Coalition joins lawsuit against HUD over housing counseling cuts
description: A North Carolina housing advocacy group and nine other nonprofits have asked a federal court to issue a temporary restraining order to block the Trump administration from withholding funds for housing counseling programs. The request for a temporary restraining order was filed Wednesday in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. It comes […]
text:
A Habitat for Humanity Home in Durham. (Photo: Greg Childress/NC Newsline)A North Carolina housing advocacy group and nine other nonprofits have asked a federal court to issue a temporary restraining order to block the Trump administration from withholding funds for housing counseling programs.
The request for a temporary restraining order was filed Wednesday in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. It comes a day after the organizations sued the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development over the agency’s “abrupt cancellation” of $56 million in housing counseling grants it and other longtime recipients expected to receive.
Trump administration revokes $810M approved by Congress for refugee aid and more

The lawsuit was filed by Democracy Defenders Fund and Jacobson Lawyers Group on behalf of the housing coalition and nine other nonprofit organizations across the nation that provide housing support services.
The plaintiffs contend the Trump administration’s “pocket rescission” jeopardizes housing security for thousands of families facing foreclosure or eviction, adding that the cuts come as “households face severe affordability pressures and a rising cost of living, making housing guidance essential.”
In a statement to the court, Samuel Gunter, executive director at the North Carolina Housing Coalition, said delays in receiving the grants have already created financial hardships for his organization and others that rely on them. The organizations often borrow from reserves to pay for counseling programs, then submit invoices for reimbursement, he said.   
“For over thirty years, agencies have provided services to clients with the expectation that they would be reimbursed by the grant on a quarterly basis,” Gunter said. 
Gunter said the counseling services are critical for families.
Samuel Gunter (Photo: N.C. Housing Coalition)
“Local housing counseling agencies are on the front lines keeping families in their homes in the midst of financial crisis and preparing first-time homebuyers for homeownership,” said “Their work preserves and builds wealth for communities across the state.”
North Carolina will lose $1 million in federal money, the housing coalition said, if the cuts stand. Funding delays have already resulted in the loss of invaluable housing counseling services, Stephanie Watkins-Cruz, the housing coalition’s director of housing policy, said on the group’s weekly housing call.
“North Carolina families will lose access to a vital financial education resource at a time when housing costs are at an all time high,”  Watkins-Cruz said. 
Stephanie Watkins-Cruz (Photo: N.C. Housing Coalition)
She urged housing organizations to contact Republican Senators Thom Tillis and Ted Budd and other members of congress to let them know how the cuts will impact their communities. 
The loss of funding for housing counseling is part of a Trump administration clawback of nearly $1 billion in congressionally approved funding that the plaintiffs say is illegal. 
The plaintiffs argue the administration violated the First Amendment because the clawback of federal dollars was targeted to “penalize recipients for disfavored viewpoints and protected speech outside the program.” 
Marc Morial (Photo: National Urban League)
“The White House effectively has admitted that this rescission was motivated, at least in part, by criticism of the administration’s policies.” Marc H. Morial, National Urban League president and CEO, said in a statement. “That’s not how our Constitution works.”
Morial is referring to the Trump administration’s efforts to rid the federal government of diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) initiatives.
When the Trump administration announced the cuts last week, it accused grant recipients of peddling “DEI and discrimination based on race.” 
“This HUD program funds NGOs [non-governmental organizations] that ostensibly provide housing counseling, but the program has not shown reduced delinquencies for counseled homebuyers and instead focuses on grantees with DEI-centric discriminatory agendas,” the administration said in a statement posted on the White House website.
Tianna Mays (Photo: Democracy Defenders Action)
Tianna Mays, legal director at Democracy Defenders Fund, said the Trump administration’s decision is as “iIllegal as it is heartless.”
“The president cannot unilaterally slash congressionally appropriated housing funds, putting thousands of vulnerable families at risk,” Mays said. “We will fight this in court on behalf of every household in America that depends on these support services as the cost of living continues to rise.”
The lawsuit also claims that HUD’s actions violate federal law, ignore established regulations and arbitrarily reverse three decades of policy. Under the Administrative Procedure Act, the complaint asserts that HUD acted arbitrarily and capriciously by failing to explain its abrupt policy shift, disregarding reliance interests, and withholding congressionally mandated funds.
In addition to the NC Housing Coalition, The National Urban League, Housing Action Illinois, New Jersey Citizen Action,  Housing & Community Development Network of NJ,  National CAPACD, Fair Housing Resource Center, Southwest Fresno Community Development Corporation, Somerville Community Corporation and the National Foundation for Debt Management are all plaintiffs in the lawsuit.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV pays $4.4M in historic child abuse case after CPS didn’t rescue kids from slave-like conditions
description: Child victims in a gruesome abuse case have been awarded $4.4 million in a settlement with the state Department of Human Services due to Child Protective Services failures in the case.   A white couple living in Sissonville, West Virginia, had kept their adopted Black children in deplorable conditions, treating them as slaves. Some of the […]
text:
On Oct. 2, Kanawha County Sheriff deputies responded to a 911 call about children locked in a shed in Sissonville, West Virginia. 
(Photo by Rafael Barker/ West Virginia Watch)Child victims in a gruesome abuse case have been awarded $4.4 million in a settlement with the state Department of Human Services due to Child Protective Services failures in the case.  
A white couple living in Sissonville, West Virginia, had kept their adopted Black children in deplorable conditions, treating them as slaves. Some of the children were forced to live in a shed without running water or a bathroom.
Neighbors notified CPS about the abuse, but said they didn’t hear back about their ongoing referrals. Law enforcement discovered the children in October 2023.
Jeanne Kay Whitefeather, 63, and her husband, Donald Lantz, 64, received the maximum sentences of decades in prison for abusing the adopted children.
On Tuesday, Kanawha County Circuit Judge Maryclaire Akers approved a $4.4 million settlement with the state of West Virginia for the five children who were abused.
Dante’ diTrapano
“It means that these kids will have an opportunity to be children,” said attorney Dante’ diTrapano, who represented the children. “They were robbed of their innocence and robbed of their youth by the monsters that were their former parents.” 
The money, which will be split between the children, will be used by the victims to recover and move forward. Several of the children have high-level needs due to trauma stemming from the abuse. 
The payout is the maximum each child could receive under the state’s limitations within the Board of Risk Management, which paid out the settlement amount. BRIM did not respond to an email for this story. 
DiTrapano brought the suit against the West Virginia Department of Human Services, explaining CPS’ missteps in the case.
West Virginia Watch reported in 2023 that DoHS did not produce documentation showing CPS made contact with the children while the agency had a referral in its system about slave-like conditions. 
The adopted parents’ trial later revealed that CPS left a card at the families’ door. 
“There were a ton of calls that came in from neighbors, and I think only one visit out there. There should have been many more,” diTrapano said.

DiTrapano said CPS later conducted an interview with the children within earshot of their adopted parents.
Lars Dalseide, spokesperson for Gov. Patrick Morrisey, said that DoHS does not comment on specific legal settlements or ongoing litigation.
The abuse case predates the Morrisey administration.
“The employee involved was terminated by that administration,” Dalseide said.
“We cannot speak to what additional policy or operational changes the previous administration may have made specifically in response to this case. Since taking office, however, the Morrisey administration has made substantial changes to strengthen West Virginia’s child welfare system,” he added.
Dalsiede listed changes like restructuring leadership with clearer expectations across regions and stronger training for frontline workers. The administration is now using the “SAFE Model” to assess child welfare cases with the goal of providing a more consistent approach to decisions.
“The safety and well-being of West Virginia’s children remain our highest priorities,” Dalseide said. “DoHS will continue evaluating its policies, oversight and operations and making changes where needed to better protect children and support families.”
DiTrapano maintains that the “whole system is broken.”
“There’s all kinds of things that need to be changed,” he said. “The quality of the employees that they’re having to go out here and look after the welfare of these children, some of the manner in which they do these interviews and document things, they have to take these calls seriously.” 
The children in the Sissonville case were placed with new adopted families, diTrapano said. Two of the new adoptive mothers spoke in court about the children’s lives now, which included details about a trip to the beach.
“It means everything to us to be able to help these kids,” diTrapano said. 
DiTrapano and the Salango Law Firm plan to bring charges against Washington’s Human Services Department because the agency approved Whitefeather and Lantz transferring children from Washington to West Virginia. There were prior reports of child abuse against the couple in Washington, DiTrapano said. 
There is no monetary damage cap in Washington on what the children could receive in that payout if the attorneys are successful in their challenge. 
Del. Hollis Lewis, D-Kanawha, speaks on the House of Delegates floor in Charleston, West Virginia on March 3, 2026. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Kanawha delegate will push anti-abuse legislation related to case
In response to the historic child abuse case, Del. Hollis Lewis, D-Kanawha, will reintroduce legislation — called the Child Captivity Prevention Act — that would require families moving to West Virginia who intend to homeschool to notify the Department of Human Services. 
Whitefeather and Lanz had homeschooled the children prior to police’s discovery of the abuse.
“This is an attack on abusers because we don’t want our relaxed homeschool and school choice policies to be a conduit for abusers,” Lewis said in a phone interview. “I do not believe they landed on West Virginia because of our beauty or our economy. I believe they came specifically because they knew they could operate in a manner and have little oversight.”
Lewis introduced the measure earlier this year in the legislative session, but it didn’t move forward before lawmakers adjourned in March. Republicans control the House and Senate, giving them the power to decide what bills will be vetted in committees before floor votes. 
Hollis said he’ll push for the legislation again in 2027.
“We’re for parents having options about how they wish to educate their children, but we are also for sensible, common sense guidelines and provisions to ensure that you know those educational choices don’t lead to abuse,” Lewis said. 
Lewis noted that Sissonville residents who lived near Whitefeather and Lantz should be thanked for their continued calls to CPS and police about the horrific conditions at the couple’s home. 
“The community was the one that actually blew the whistle on this, and not for the community’s effort … those kids could possibly still be enslaved now and getting abused now, or even worse,” Lewis said.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Corey Hill, Ron Sparks face off in race for commissioner of Agriculture and Industries
description: In next month’s election for commissioner of Agriculture and Industries, Alabama voters will choose between a mayor and a former state agriculture commissioner. Republican nominee Corey Hill, the mayor of Douglas in Marshall County, and Democratic nominee Ron Sparks, who served in the office from 2003 to 2011 will face each other in the Nov. […]
text:
Republican nominee Corey Hill (left) and Democratic Ron Sparks (right) will face each other in the November general election for commissioner of agriculture and industries. (Corey Hill by Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector; Ron Sparks courtesy of Sparks2026; Graphic by Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)In next month’s election for commissioner of Agriculture and Industries, Alabama voters will choose between a mayor and a former state agriculture commissioner.
Republican nominee Corey Hill, the mayor of Douglas in Marshall County, and Democratic nominee Ron Sparks, who served in the office from 2003 to 2011 will face each other in the Nov. 3 general election.
Hill became the Republican nominee after winning the June 16 runoff election against Christina Woerner Mcinnis. Sparks did not have a Democratic opponent.
Sparks said in an interview Wednesday that he was running for the seat because “farmers and people are struggling right now.”
“We’re probably going through some of the toughest times in the history of the state with the prices of diesel fuel, farmers going broke, the prices of fertilizer, they’ve basically destroyed the Department of Agriculture in the last few years,” Sparks said.
Sparks previously served as the commissioner from 2003 until 2011. He cited his efforts in the wake of Hurricane Katrina in 2005 to crack down on price gouging at gas pumps, and said during the interview he wants to get the department back to how it was when he was in office.
“I don’t think there’s ever been anyone that worked any harder at the Department of Agriculture than I did, and built as good a department as we had,” Sparks said.
Sparks’ priorities include removing the 1.5% sales tax on farm equipment and reinstating state employees as gas inspectors. 
Al.com reported last week that former Alabama Attorney General Troy King, a Republican, endorsed Sparks. Sparks said he wasn’t shocked by the endorsement.
“I have a lot of respect for Troy King, and I certainly appreciate his endorsement. He feels the same way that I feel. I think it’s time for this tribalism and running to our corners and not talking to each other and division to stop.” Sparks said.
Hill said in an interview Wednesday the department can’t be run the same way it was when Sparks was in office.
“My opponent was a Democrat 15 years ago, and that’s a totally different Democratic Party than we have now,” he said. “Totally different mindset, different challenges. The administration’s different. We’ve had COVID since then. The whole department’s different. The economy’s different. It’s got to be a different mindset to run that department than it was. You can’t run it the same way today you did 15 or 20 years ago.”
Hill said he would also work to eliminate the tax on farm equipment. Another one of his priorities is putting Alabama produced food in schools.
“We’re gonna make it to where it’s gonna be easier for us to buy food from Alabama farmers for our schools to feed Alabama kids in our Alabama schools,” Hill said.
Sparks said voters should choose him because of his time in the department.
“When I served as commissioner of agriculture before, I received awards from every ag organization in the state, whether it be ALFA (Alabama Farmers Association), cattlemen, catfish folks, the veterinarian folks,” he said. “The last time I ran for commissioner of agriculture, we won 62 out of 67 counties, and I feel the momentum in this race. And I can assure you, won’t nobody work for farmers and consumers in Alabama any harder than Ron Sparks.”
Hill said he should be elected because of his experience as a farmer.
“Our family has been in the grocery store business for many years, many generations, actually, and so food safety and knowing about the recalls and how to handle food to keep that from happening is very important to us because as a retailer, when those things happen, even if they’re no fault of your own, it affects your business,” Hill said. “So nobody wants that. So handling the food and keeping it safe is something we know a lot about.”
According to campaign finance reports, Hill has raised $581,400 and spent $553,500 and Sparks has raised $153,100 and spent $57,700 as of Wednesday afternoon.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: The promise of a free education is fundamental to our democracy
description: The American Civil Liberties Union of West Virginia announced a lawsuit last week over the unconstitutional underfunding of public schools. I’m not exaggerating when I say this may be the most important case we have filed in my 10 years with this organization. The promise of a free education is fundamental to our democracy itself. […]
text:
During the 2022-23 school year, West Virginia’s average per-pupil expenditure was $14,909 — a total that includes state, local and federal money. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)The American Civil Liberties Union of West Virginia announced a lawsuit last week over the unconstitutional underfunding of public schools. I’m not exaggerating when I say this may be the most important case we have filed in my 10 years with this organization.
The promise of a free education is fundamental to our democracy itself. It’s so vital that it was enshrined as a right in our 1863 state Constitution, and courts have interpreted that right to mean that schools must not only be adequately funded, but also fairly funded from county to county.
And yet, West Virginia sits at or near the bottom of most national rankings. Politicians have blamed schools, teachers and parents for poor educational outcomes, when the true cause is in black and white on the balance sheets.
During the 2022-23 school year, West Virginia’s average per-pupil expenditure was $14,909 — a total that includes state, local and federal money.  While $14,909 was the reported average, the actual amount per student spent by counties ranged from a low of $12,158 in Barbour County to a high of $22,500 in Doddridge.
That gap gets even wider when you look at only the funding within the state’s control. Combined state and local education funding per pupil ranged from $10,542 in Barbour County to $24,924 in Tyler. In a system that requires that education funding be allocated fairly, some counties receive double the funding of others — not only presenting constitutional concerns, but driving averages up in a way that hides how significantly underfunded many West Virginia counties are.
Across the country, states spend more on education in counties with high rates of students with disabilities and students experiencing poverty because providing quality education to those students is often more expensive. In West Virginia, we do just the opposite: we spend less in counties with the greatest need, and more in counties with higher property wealth. 
Chief among the many flaws in West Virginia’s school funding system is the failure to account for special education services. West Virginia’s special education funding is worse than it was decades ago. Because these services are required by law, failure to provide sufficient funding means that school districts need to dip into funding that would otherwise be used for general education services, or to cover the costs of keeping schools operational.
Looking beyond the funding formula, and including all state grants and special education funding, West Virginia provided an average of $8,057 per student. When the state doesn’t pay enough, counties are left to foot the bill. And a county like Lincoln will never be able to generate enough local wealth to operate the school system that students deserve. Counties generate local revenue for schools primarily through the general school levy, with statewide rates established by the Legislature, and optional excess levies meant to supplement basic school spending. Because these funding sources are tied to property tax, the amount of revenue available to counties — and the amount that gets spent on students — varies not based on need, but on whether students are being educated in counties with high property wealth.
The last time the courts took up this issue the case became so influential it still bears the name of the judge who decided it: the Recht Decision set the standard for school funding in West Virginia and changed the nationwide conversation about it. Despite these clear legal requirements set by our courts, the current funding system leads to outcomes that are worse than what was declared unconstitutional almost 50 years ago.
The current staffing formula provides Lincoln County with fewer staff than the formula at the time the system was declared unconstitutional. The gap between what counties receive, and what they spend, has widened instead of narrowed. School closures are increasing rapidly, as schools struggle to stay afloat with the meager funding provided by the state.
The law believes — as do I — that every West Virginia child is capable of great things that make our communities stronger, healthier and happier. A thorough and efficient system of free schools is what permits those futures to come to fruition.
After years of neglect by the Legislature, it has become clear that children’s constitutional right to education will be left to erode if the courts don’t demand action and declare that the current system isn’t just immoral — it’s also unconstitutional.

name: Michigan Advance
title: As anti-trans attacks escalate, Michigan-based Stand With Trans empowers by building community
description: Oct. 1 marks the start of Transgender Empowerment Month — a series of events launched by Michigan nonprofit Stand With Trans that has grown to a national and even global audience of transgender people, their families and allies.  Stand With Trans executive director Roz Gould Keith says that this year’s theme, “Stronger Together,” reflects the fact […]
text:
Stand With Trans, a Michigan-based transgender rights organization, marches in the Motor City Pride parade in downtown Detroit. June 7, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. Oct. 1 marks the start of Transgender Empowerment Month — a series of events launched by Michigan nonprofit Stand With Trans that has grown to a national and even global audience of transgender people, their families and allies. 
Stand With Trans executive director Roz Gould Keith says that this year’s theme, “Stronger Together,” reflects the fact that “we really feel that we have to be on the same team, and we are so much stronger together. We want young people and their families to feel like they have a community, and that they don’t have to be isolated and alone.”
Trans Empowerment Month began in 2015 as a one-day workshop for trans youth, Keith explained, to celebrate young trans people and to give them an opportunity to be in community with one another. During the pandemic, the programming switched to a month-long conference-style format to meet the need for a virtual setting. 
“We started out local, Southeast Michigan, and then once we went virtual, we were tracking this national and then international audience, so that’s the plus side of being virtual,” Keith explained. “There’s the recognition that people don’t always live in places where they have access to local resources. There might not be a community center. There might not be a support group they can attend.”
Aidel Hawkins, the program manager for Stand With Trans, noted 2026 programming will include speakers from Berlin and Abu Dhabi, and the programs are drawing participants from an international audience, including Brazil, Canada, Colombia, Germany, the Philippines, the United Kingdom and Thailand.
Stand with Trans tent at Motor City Pride on June 9, 2024. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)
The transgender community has increasingly become the target of political and legal attacks, with the Trans Legislation Tracker showing 835 anti-trans bills introduced across 43 states in 2026, including 32 in Michigan. 
“I think any opportunity that we have to break that up and show stories of resistance, of helping each other within the community, of celebrating each other, the ways that our efforts to support trans people help the community at large, even beyond just trans and queer people, are really important for people to hear,” Hawkins said.
She added that, in spite of attacks on the LGBTQ+ community and transgender people specifically, Trans Empowerment Month proves the strength of the community. 
“It feels like some of the trans and queer communities that I’m part of are feeling stronger than ever,” she said. “Although there’s a lot happening, there are many points to highlight the ways that we are stronger together, and we’re building deeper methods of community, like organizing and supporting each other.”
“With everything going on in our state, in our country, in the world, we really want to reinforce that,” Keith added. 
In 2025, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer officially recognized Transgender Empowerment Month and National Coming Out Day, which is observed annually on Oct. 11.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Kiggans faces questions over financial industry money and consumer protection votes
description: U.S. Rep. Jen Kiggans is facing renewed scrutiny over her votes to roll back consumer financial oversight after receiving tens of thousands of dollars from political committees tied to the financial services industry, including a Republican group that has received substantial funding from payday and title lenders.  The Virginia Beach Republican supported rep[...]
text:
U.S. Rep. Jen Kiggans, R-Virginia Beach, speaks at a rally for then-presidential candidate Donald Trump in Chesapeake on June 28, 2024. Kiggans faces scrutiny over financial industry PAC contributions and her votes to roll back consumer protections. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)U.S. Rep. Jen Kiggans is facing renewed scrutiny over her votes to roll back consumer financial oversight after receiving tens of thousands of dollars from political committees tied to the financial services industry, including a Republican group that has received substantial funding from payday and title lenders. 
The Virginia Beach Republican supported repealing federal rules governing major payment apps and bank overdraft fees in 2025, five years after opposing Virginia’s overhaul of payday and car title lending. 
The record is drawing attention as Kiggans seeks reelection in a district with Virginia’s largest veteran population, according to U.S. Census Bureau data, and a substantial active-duty military community. 
“Jen Kiggans is a pay-to-play politician who cashes checks from predatory corporations that target veterans and service members, and then does their bidding in Washington. That’s corruption in plain sight,” a spokesman for her Democratic challenger, former U.S. Rep. Elaine Luria, said Wednesday.  
The Cook Political Report rates the Kiggans-Luria rematch a toss-up race. 
Kiggans campaign spokesman Calvin Moore did not answer a list of questions from The Mercury about the congresswoman’s votes and contributions, instead providing a statement defending her record. 
“Democrats have tried pushing these debunked attacks for years, and Virginia voters have rejected them every single time,” Moore said in an email. 
He pointed to Kiggans’ experience as a former U.S. Navy helicopter pilot, military spouse and mother. 
“Jen knows firsthand the sacrifices military families make and the challenges they face,” Moore said. “Which is why her top priorities in Congress have been standing up for our service members, lowering costs for military families, and making sure they have the pay, housing, healthcare, and support they’ve earned.”
The federal votes did not eliminate the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s authority over payday or “buy now, pay later” lenders. Instead, Kiggans voted to repeal two specific Biden-era rules involving large digital payment companies and overdraft fees. 
The CFPB separately deprioritized enforcement based on its buy now, pay later rule under the Trump administration. 
Alex Keena, an associate professor of political science at Virginia Commonwealth University, said an incumbent’s voting record can become a liability when opponents are able to connect it to voters’ everyday concerns. 
Keena said Kiggans’ support for Republican priorities, including rolling back consumer protections, gives Democrats an opportunity to make that connection to household finances.
“This is a bad look, and it will be very easy to show that her voting record has directly affected the economic interests of voters in the district,” he said.  
 What the federal votes changed

On April 9, 2025, Kiggans voted to overturn a CFPB rule that subjected the largest nonbank digital payment companies to routine federal examinations. The resolution passed 219-211, with every voting House Republican supporting it and every voting Democrat opposing it. 
The rule applied to companies processing at least 50 million transactions annually, including major payment wallets and money-transfer apps. Repealing it removed that basis for routine CFPB supervision but did not exempt the companies from federal consumer protection laws. 
Nor was the rule aimed specifically at buy now, pay later lending. The CFPB explicitly distinguished payment services from lending and declined to extend that rule to that market. 
The Trump administration took separate action on buy now, pay later products the following month, when the CFPB announced it would deprioritize enforcement of an earlier interpretation that extended credit card-style protections to those loans. 
Buy now, pay later services commonly allow consumers to split purchases into four interest-free payments. They differ from traditional payday loans, although missed payments and multiple overlapping loans can pose financial risks. 
Kiggans cast another vote on April 9 to overturn the CFPB’s overdraft rule, which would have required banks and credit unions with more than $10 billion in assets to cap overdraft fees at $5, limit them to costs and losses, or comply with additional credit protections and disclosure requirements. 
Republicans argued the rule would make banks less willing to offer overdraft services. But consumer advocates said it would curb excessive fees that can disadvantage consumers living paycheck to paycheck, including military families. 
Moore, however, pointed to other parts of Kiggans’ record that he said show her commitment to service members. 
In September 2025, she introduced the Pay Our Troops Act of 2026 to maintain military pay during government shutdowns and worked on legislation aimed at reducing barriers to VA-backed home loans. 
Another bipartisan measure Kiggans sponsored would broaden mortgage eligibility for some National Guard and Reserve members. 
 Contributions and an earlier lending dispute

The campaign money at issue came from several types of political committees, and not all of it can accurately be described as coming from payday lenders. 
State campaign filings show Kiggans received $17,500 from GOPAC in 2019, when Kiggans ran for the Virginia Senate in the 7th District. Federal filings list another $10,000 from the GOPAC Election Fund for her congressional campaign in 2021 and 2022. 
GOPAC is a Republican political organization, not a lending company. But a 2018 Louisville Courier Journal review of the organization’s finances found substantial contributions from payday and title lending businesses. 
Kiggans also received a combined $22,000 from PACs associated with Ally Financial, American Express, Capital One, Regions Financial and Experian. 
Those companies operate in different parts of the financial industry. Experian, for example, is a credit reporting company rather than a lender, while some installment-payment products offered by the companies operate through traditional credit cards. 
Combined, the two categories account for $49,500 in contributions. Some of the money arrived long before Kiggans’ federal votes, and some afterward, including a November 2025 contribution to her leadership PAC. 
The contributions do not establish that donors influenced Kiggans’ votes. 
However, questions about Kiggans’ relationship with the lending industry date to her time in the Virginia Senate. 
During her 2022 congressional campaign, WAVY questioned her about her opposition to the Virginia Fairness in Lending Act and contributions she had received from GOPAC. Kiggans repeatedly declined to explain her vote before ending the interview. 
“I would never vote for anything that I thought would be considered to be hurtful or harmful to veterans,” Kiggans told the network. 
The 2020 law overhauled Virginia’s rules for payday, title and other small-dollar loans. Among other changes, it capped certain costs, imposed repayment requirements and closed regulatory loopholes that had allowed some lenders to avoid existing restrictions. 
VCU’s Keena said bringing the issue back before voters could matter even if it does not persuade many people in the 2nd District to change their minds. 
“I think it is a useful line of attack, but it may not necessarily change voters’ views,” Keena said. “Rather, it may undermine Kiggans’ ability to mobilize the constituency that put her into office in 2022.” 
The criticism could also mobilize Democrats and left-leaning independents to support Luria, Keena said. Many voters are unfamiliar with their representatives’ congressional votes, he said,  giving campaigns an opportunity to connect an incumbent’s record to broader concerns about the economy. 
“In the context of an economic downturn, voters have a tendency to blame the party in power, so campaigns use mass marketing to draw contrasts between a challenger’s positions and an incumbent’s record on these issues,” Keena said.

name: Maryland Matters
title: New laws: No Kings, no trying youths as adults, no ‘dynamic pricing’ — and a prehistoric shark
authors: William J. Ford, Danielle J. Brown
description: The more than 370 bills that became law Thursday are the usual grab bag of serious and silly, of technical tweaks, of answers to sweeping national issues and personal responses to situations that took young lives in Maryland. Many were years in the making.
text:
Gov. Wes Moore signing legislation into law in this file photo. The governor, who is ambidextrous, alternates between his right and left hands as hundreds of bills are signed. (Photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)Police will no longer be able to wear masks, hospitals will not be able to deny emergency abortions in life-threatening situations and retailers will prohibited from setting different prices for the same item based on shoppers’ personal data, under new laws that took effect Thursday.
Motorists, meanwhile, will be required to clear snow and ice off their cars before driving, businesses will be required to accept cash for essential goods like food and medicine at certain times — and the state is getting another official symbol, this time a prehistoric shark that has not swum in state waters for 3.6 million years.
The more than 370 bills that became law Thursday are the usual grab bag of serious and silly, of technical tweaks, of proposed answers to sweeping national issues and personal responses to situations that took young lives in Maryland. Some passed on their first try, but many were years in the making.
Youth auto charging
One of those was the  youth auto charging bill by Sen. William C. Smith Jr. (D-Montgomery), which took more than a decade to get approved. Maryland’s system of automatically charging youth as adults in some cases was an outlier among states, with only Alabama sending more 14- to 17-year-olds to adult court.
The law will raise the age from 14 to 16 when a youth could be tried as an adult for most crimes. It would still send 14- and 15-year-olds to adult court for first-degree murder or rape charges, but specifies that 16-year-olds charged with offenses such as first-degree assault and some firearms offenses would start in juvenile court.
The bill also prohibits youth charged as adults from being “detained or confined” in an adult prison, except when no “secure juvenile detention area” is immediately available, in which case a youth could be processed in an adult jail, but not be held for more than six hours.
Crackdown on out-of-state vehicle registrations to start in October

The measure also requires annual reports, beginning Oct. 1, 2027, by the Governor’s Office of Crime Prevention and Policy to the General Assembly and the Commission on Juvenile Justice and Emerging and Best Practices. The reports will include the number of youths charges as adults, the charges they faced, and the number of federal violations that prohibit youth “from having sight and sound contact with adult offenders.”
No Kings
Spurred by the immigration confrontations across the country that led to arrests and shootings — and the deaths of Alex Pretti and Renée Good, who were shot by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in Minneapolis — lawmakers pushed back with the No Kings Act.
Senate Bill 346 and House Bill 351, sponsored by Montgomery County Democrats Sen. Jeff Waldstreicher and House Majority Leader David Moon, let Marylanders or the attorney general’s office pursue civil litigation against a federal official who violated another’s constitutional rights under color of law.
The “color of law” language came from a bill previously sponsored by Del. Lorig Charkoudian (D-Montgomery), who has said the act creates a pathway against “federal lawlessness.” The law will not apply to a person acting under the authority of a joint task force “that primarily enforces the United States Code.”
Opponents argued that the measures were an overreach that will negatively affect the work of law enforcement, but the measures passed the House and Senate by comfortable margins.
Lawmakers also approved SB 1, a bill sponsored by Sen. Malcolm Augustine (D-Prince George’s) that will prohibit the wearing of face coverings by law enforcement officers while on duty, including those with ICE. Officers would also have to identify themselves in most circumstances.
The law calls on the Maryland Police Training and Standards Commission to develop guidelines on masks that will be used statewide. Any officer violating the law would be subject to a civil citation and a fine of up to $1,500.
Face coverings will include balaclavas, ski masks or neck gaiters. Exceptions would be made for officers “actively engaged in an undercover operation,” someone wearing a motorcycle helmet, a garment worn for religious purposes or for health-related reasons.
Say their names
A number of measures are named in honor of state residents whose deaths or endangerment sparked legislation that aims to prevent a repeat of their circumstances.
A series of new laws increasing oversight of the state’s foster kids took effect Thursday, including one named in honor of Kanaiyah Ward, a 16-year-old who died in a Baltimore hotel while in state custody from an apparent overdose of diphenhydramine, an over-the-counter allergy medicine.
Kanaiyah’s Law creates a new State Foster Youth Ombudsman in Human Services to serve as a neutral voice for youth in out-of-home placements. The new ombudsman will also investigate complaints made by foster kids and otherwise ensure that children in the state’s care are in safe and healthy locations.
Thousands of immigrants in Maryland to lose Medicaid coverage under H.R. 1

After Kanaiyah’s death, the Department of Human Services instituted a new policy prohibiting the placement of foster children in unauthorized settings, like hotels and hospitals, overflow solutions that had been used by the state when it could not immediately find a foster placement. House Bill 1559 codifies that policy starting Thursday.
The Jillian and Lindsay Wiener Short-Term Rental Safety Act, HB 1221 and SB 624, were named for the Montgomery County sisters who died in a 2022 fire at a New York short-term rental without working smoke detectors. The law requires that short-term rentals like Airbnb and Vrbo have functioning fire extinguishers, smoke detectors and carbon monoxide alarms.
It also requires that evacuation routes and emergency response numbers be posted in such rentals to help ensure that, whether on vacation or a work trip, Marylanders can sleep safely in short-term rental units.
Mason’s Law will require that municipalities inventory all open drainage inlets, public and private, in their jurisdictions by next July and have a plan by April 1, 2028, for safety improvements of those drains. The law, sponsored by Sen. Karen Lewis-Young (D-Frederick) and backed by Lt. Gov. Aruna Miller (D), is named in honor of Mason Kearns, a Mount Airy 13-year-old who was  swept into an open storm drain and drowned during a July 2025 storm.
Shari Bailey pushed for a package of bills collectively known as the LEAD Act, for Laila’s Elopement Awareness and Dissemination Act.  It is named for Bailey’s daughter Laila who is autistic and nonverbal and who one day “eloped” — or wandered off from her caregiver, a situation familiar to many families with autistic kids or those caring for someone with dementia.
Laila was later found unharmed, but the fright spurred Bailey to act. That led to the passage of companion bills, House Bill 634 and Senate Bill 745, sponsored by Del. Aaron Kaufman (D-Montgomery) and Sen. Mike McKay (R-Western Maryland). The bills will require training for police on how to respond to a case of elopement.
One other bill in the package of five survived to become law today: HB 1434, sponsored by Del. Aletheia McCaskill (D-Baltimore County), requires the Maryland Department of Health to create a webpage of resources for family caregivers, including information on safety planning for wandering and elopement.
Protections for emergency abortions
Thursday also marks the start of statewide protection for emergency abortion access in cases where terminating a pregnancy is necessary to stabilize a pregnant patient.
The enactment of Senate Bill 169, whose lead sponsor was Sen. Clarence Lam (D-Anne Arundel and Howard), and House Bill 372, which was sponsored by Del. Lesley Lopez (D-Montgomery), enshrines Biden-era federal guidance that permitted emergency abortions to save the lives of pregnant patients under Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act (EMTALA).
In 2025, the Trump administration rescinded that guidance, muddying the waters of what is required under EMTALA, particularly regarding abortion services at faith-based institutions or in states with strict abortion bans.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Medical facilities in Maryland will now be required by state law to operate under the Biden-era guidance, regardless of federal policy, ensuring pregnant patients facing a medical crisis can receive an emergency abortion or be transferred to a medical facility that will perform that procedure so long as the patient’s situation does not worsen during the transfer.
Dynamic pricing prohibited
As of Thursday, grocery stores and delivery services in the state are prohibited from using surveillance data to tweak the price of items from shopper to shopper, also referred to as “dynamic pricing.” House Bill 895, the Protection from Predatory Pricing Act, aims to ensure that Marylanders are not charged extra for groceries on the assumption that certain shoppers may be willing to pay more for certain items.
It’s not clear how many food retailers in Maryland are engaging in “dynamic pricing” but Gov. Wes Moore (D), along with presiding officers in the House and Senate, pushed to prohibit the practice in the state at a time when household budgets are stretched thin.
Sharks, rappers, religious heritage and more
After it appeared to be as dead as its namesake, a bill making the megalodon the official state shark managed to pass on the last day of the session, after it was cobbled together in SB 35 with bills to make the Natural History Society of Maryland the state’s official natural history museum and to have the governor proclaim Oct. 1 “Purple Lights Night,” to honor survivors of domestic violence.
The megalodon is a prehistoric shark with huge jaws that lives in Maryland today mainly in the form of teeth found on Chesapeake Bay beaches. It joins a long list of other state symbols, including an official state bird, dog, gem, dessert, sport, folk dance, spirit — rye whiskey, not anything to do with ghosts — and more.
Other bills that became law on Oct. 1 include:

House Bill 661, sponsored by Montgomery County Democratic Dels. Sarah Wolek and Jared Solomon, proclaims January as Muslim American Heritage Month and May as Jewish American Heritage Month; the bill briefly ran into trouble in the Senate over a failed push to add a Christian American Heritage Month to the list.
Lam and Sen. Katie Fry Hester (D-Howard and Montgomery) sponsored SB 627 to make Jan. 13 “Korean American Day,” to mark the day in 1903 when the first Korean immigrants arrived in the United States.
The Protecting Artists Creative Expression, or PACE Act, would make it harder for prosecutors to admit the “creative expression” of an artist as evidence against the artist at trial, unless specific criteria are met. The bill, which took several years to pass, came after trials of rappers whose words were used against them at trial.
HB 497 extends the duration of temporary protective orders in domestic abuse cases from a week after the order is served to two weeks after it is issued, and it requires a hearing on a final order within that two weeks.
HB 191, sponsored by Del. Greg Wims (D-Montgomery), requires that businesses accept cash for in-person purchases of “essential goods” like food, fuel, health and hygiene products. The bill only applies between 6 a.m. and 10 p.m. on purchased less than $300, and it prohibits businesses from charging more for cash purchases.
The Clear Before You Drive Act, HB 474 and SB 698, requires motorists to clear snow and ice off their vehicles before they hit the road, or face steadily escalating fines.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Here’s how incumbents in Virginia’s 1st, 2nd and 5th Congressional Districts have voted on abortion
description: Abortion is on the ballot this fall, with Virginia voters slated to select their next slate of congressional representatives after federal protections for the procedure ended in 2022.  Voters will also decide on Election Day whether a reproductive rights amendment should be cemented into the state’s constitution, reflecting the weight abortion and reproducti[...]
text:
A sign outside a clinic that provides abortions in Richmond, Va. (Photo by Sarah Vogelsong/Virginia Mercury) Abortion is on the ballot this fall, with Virginia voters slated to select their next slate of congressional representatives after federal protections for the procedure ended in 2022. 
Voters will also decide on Election Day whether a reproductive rights amendment should be cemented into the state’s constitution, reflecting the weight abortion and reproductive healthcare access are levying in both state and federal elections this year. 
A Pew Research Center survey conducted earlier this year found that 60% of Americans believe abortion should be legal in all or most cases.
More than 12% of Virginia respondents in The Mercury’s ongoing reader survey name shrinking healthcare access — including reproductive healthcare — as a top motivator for them to cast their ballot for any candidate.
Republican incumbents in three of Virginia’s congressional districts that could help determine partisan control of the U.S. House of Representatives — the 1st, 2nd and 5th — have all voted for abortion bans or restrictions. 
 1st Congressional District’s Wittman supported a six-week limit

U.S. Rep. Rob Wittman, R-Westmoreland, is facing Democratic challenger Shannon Taylor in the 1st District. With a large voter population centered in Henrico, Chesterfield, Hanover and James City counties, the district stretches from Westmoreland to Newport News and wraps around Richmond’s west side. 
Historically a safe GOP seat, the district has grown more politically purple in recent years. In late September, veteran analyst Larry Sabato’s nonpartisan political analysis newsletter changed the district’s rating from “leans Republican” to “toss up.” 
In 2017, Wittman co-sponsored the Heartbeat Protection Act. 
Reproductive rights advocates have said the bill and similar ones from other members of Congress effectively propose a six-week abortion ban, as some embryonic cardiac activity can be detected as early as six weeks into a pregnancy. 
When Texas enacted a state-level version of the law in 2021, physicians called it “misleading” to refer to activity detected in ultrasounds during that phase of pregnancy as a heartbeat, because fetuses have not yet developed heart chambers. 
“What pregnant people may hear is the ultrasound machine translating electronic impulses that signify fetal cardiac activity into the sound that we recognize as a heartbeat,” an American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists online guide stated. 
More recently Wittman has voted against the Women’s Health Protection Act. That bill would have codified federal abortion protections and has been reintroduced numerous times since the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade.  
H.R. 1, the reconciliation bill Congress passed last summer which is slated to put 300,000 Virginians at risk of losing Medicaid, also excluded Planned Parenthood from Medicaid reimbursement for one year. 
The organization provides reproductive healthcare, including abortions.
If Va.’s reproductive rights amendment passes, challengers say they’ll fight to overturn it in court

Wittman’s campaign team didn’t reply to The Mercury’s interview requests.
Meanwhile, Taylor has no track record of reproductive votes because she has not served as a lawmaker. 
On the anniversary of the Supreme Court overturning federal protections in June, Taylor vowed to work to restore them if she joins the nation’s legislature and to ensure patients and doctors are not criminalized for the procedure. 
Emily’s List, a national organization that backs pro-reproductive rights candidates, has endorsed her. 
 Jen Kiggans voted to block veterans’ abortions

Kiggans is seeking reelection in Virginia’s 2nd Congressional District, one of the most contested political battlegrounds in the country.
The district, which has oscillated between partisan control over the years, stretches from the Eastern Shore through Virginia Beach and down to Chesapeake and Suffolk. It also includes the state’s highest concentration of military constituents. 
During 2023’s annual defense spending appropriations, Kiggans voted for a provision to block military personnel from being able to receive abortions, regardless of where they are stationed. 
She also voted to block abortions at Veterans Administration medical centers and to block the Defense Department from paying for expenses related to abortions. 
“Taxpayers should not be funding elective procedures,” Kiggans told WAVY, a Hampton Roads NBC affiliate, in 2023. “If I wanted to get a Hollywood nose job in California, I do not expect the Navy to pay for my travel expenses to get there.”
Kiggans’ challenger, Democrat Elaine Luria, also previously represented the district for two terms before Kiggans ousted her in 2022. 
Luria’s reproductive voting record includes supporting the Ensuring Women’s Reproductive Right to Freedom Act and the Women’s Health Protection Act. Both bills cleared the House but did not advance further. 
Though Kiggans didn’t clarify if she would have voted for a national 15-week limit, which former South Carolina Rep. Lindsey Graham proposed in a failed 2022 bill, she called the idea “common sense.” 
Kiggans’ campaign did not respond to interview requests for this story.
Virginia’s reproductive rights amendment reflects years of similar debates between state legislators’ over gestational limits for abortions. 
In 2023, as Republicans lost their majority in Virginia’s House of Delegates, many GOP candidates coalesced under a 15-week proposal that lacked exceptions for severe fetal anomalies — which are often not diagnosed until around or after 15 weeks. 
 John McGuire carried a life-at-conception bill

In the 5th District, U.S. Rep. John McGuire, R-Goochland, is seeking a second term against Democrat Tom Perriello, who previously represented the district for one term from 2009 to 2011. 
The 5th is the state’s largest district, sprawling from just north of Charlottesville down to Danville at the North Carolina border. 
It has long been a stronghold for Republicans, but Perriello represents a formidable challenger for McGuire, as the lone Democrat to hold the seat in the past 20 years. The Cook Political Report shifted the district’s rating from “Solid R” to “Likely R” in late September.
Republicans nationwide are also fending off criticism over inflation, the Iran war, and healthcare affordability concerns. 
More than abortion: What Va. patients and providers want you to know about reproductive health laws

McGuire, a military veteran and former state lawmaker, co-sponsored a “life at conception” bill in 2025.
The bill  would have confirmed that “the right to life guaranteed by the Constitution is vested in each human being at all stages of life, including the moment of fertilization, cloning, or other moment at which an individual comes into being.”
The measure didn’t include exceptions for rape, incest or danger to the life of a pregnant person. It did include a disclaimer noting the bill didn’t “authorize the prosecution of any woman for the death of her unborn child.”
On social media McGuire called abortion “American genocide” and while still a state lawmaker, he carried a bill to block public funding for abortions. His campaign did not respond to requests for comment on this story.
 Democrat Perriello once voted in favor of a ban

In contrast to Perriello’s current campaign pillars that include protecting reproductive rights, he once voted for an abortion restriction during his term in Congress. 
In 2009, as Congress was creating the Affordable Care Act — a health insurance marketplace for people without employer-provided healthcare — an unsuccessful provision emerged to block federal funding from covering abortions except for rape, incest or to save the life of the pregnant person. 
Though the bipartisan amendment ultimately didn’t make it into the ACA’s final version, Perriello was among Democrats to vote with Republicans to advance  the amendment. 
Perriello did not answer directly when asked to explain his reasoning for the vote at that time, but his spokesperson Brytan Mendes said that Perriello would try to  recodify federal abortion protections, if he is elected.
“Tom would join efforts to codify access to contraception, abortion, and fertility care nationwide, so no family’s rights depend on their ZIP code,” Mendes wrote in an email, adding that Perriello also supports all three of Virginia’s constitutional amendments. 
Early voting in Virginia began on Sep. 18 and runs through Oct. 31. Election Day is Nov. 3. Visit The Mercury’s Voter Guide to learn more.

name: VTDigger
title: 1 in 5 Vermonters say they have struggled to keep up with rent and mortgage payments
description:
Vermont’s cost of living was top of mind for poll respondents, and 20% said they had been late or come up short on housing payments in the past year.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  1 in 5 Vermonters say they have struggled to keep up with rent and mortgage payments.
text:
Homes in Williston on Sept. 29. The median sale price of a primary home in Vermont has nearly doubled over the last decade. Photo by April McCullum/Vermont Public

Carly Berlin covers housing and infrastructure for Vermont Public, in partnership with VTDigger. 
One in five Vermonters report that they have struggled to keep up with housing payments in the last year.
That’s according to the Vermont Public 2026 Poll. Twenty percent of people surveyed in September said they have been late or come up short on rent or mortgage payments because of other financial burdens in the past year. Another 12% indicated that they almost fell behind on those payments.
The poll results underscore just how many Vermonters live with some degree of housing precarity. Lapsed payments make people vulnerable to eviction or foreclosure. Housing costs have spiked in Vermont amid a historic housing shortage in recent years, and mortgage rates have remained stubbornly high, too. Wages have not kept up.
The median sale price of a primary home last year reached $379,000, a more than 91% increase from 10 years prior, according to state property transfer tax data. In 2021, nearly a third of all Vermont renters had the income needed to buy a median-priced home, but that number plunged to 6% just two years later, according to the state’s most recent Housing Needs Assessment. 
Vermont’s cost of living was top of mind for poll respondents, as was housing — typically a person’s single greatest expense. Thirty-one percent of people surveyed said the most important problem facing the state is affordability or the economy. Another 13% named housing and homelessness as their top issue. 
Young people are more likely to have fallen behind on rent or mortgage payments than older Vermonters, according to the poll results. Twenty-seven percent of respondents between the ages of 18 and 44 indicated they struggled to keep up with housing expenses, compared to 22% of people between 45 and 64 and 9% of people over the age of 65.
Liz Courtney, 46, lives in an intergenerational home in Wolcott. She and her husband bought the house with Courtney’s parents a few years ago, expecting to share expenses. But then the marketing and communications firm where Courtney works cut back her hours. She and her husband recently launched a music recording studio, but have yet to turn a profit as they pay off their start-up expenses.
Courtney’s mother, who’s on a fixed income, has taken on more of the mortgage payments — something that has left Courtney feeling stress and guilt, she said. Meanwhile, she has been accumulating credit card debt, and her family dropped their health insurance after pandemic-era premium subsidies ended, she said.
“We’re putting off repairs on our septic system and our deck,” Courtney said. “The kids are at an age where we’d love to take them to Disney World, and I’m like, well, I don’t know how that’s going to happen in the next couple of years.” 
Jennifer Beane-Edgar, 43, works as an administrative assistant in a dentist’s office and lives with her children in a small subsidized apartment in Hartford, she said. She’d like to move into a bigger unit, but affordable options are limited nearby, and she needs to stay local to keep her kids with disabilities close to services. 
Beane-Edgar has been able to keep up with her rent. But it hasn’t always been easy. 
“Sometimes it’s choosing between, you know, medical necessities for my kids, or gas in the car, or food,” Beane-Edgar said. 
Over 30% of all Vermont households were considered cost-burdened as of 2024, meaning they pay more than a third of their monthly income toward housing expenses — making it difficult to afford other basic necessities, like food, transportation and healthcare. That roughly lines up with the national average. 
One recent national study found that a growing number of middle-income renters have fallen behind on rent payments due in part to the rising costs of everyday essentials.
