title: DOE announces $29.5 M to national labs to advance critical mineral supply chain
description: AMES —  Researchers at the Ames National Laboratory are part of a U.S. Department of Energy initiative, called Mine of the Future Initiative, aimed at boosting the nation’s supply chain for critical minerals which are currently held almost entirely by China.  Audrey Robertson, assistant secretary of energy for the Office of Critical Mineral and Energy Innova[...]
text:
Audrey Robertson, assistant secretary of energy for the Office of Critical Mineral and Energy Innovation at the DOE announced funding for critical mineral mining research in Ames, Iowa Sept. 30, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)AMES —  Researchers at the Ames National Laboratory are part of a U.S. Department of Energy initiative, called Mine of the Future Initiative, aimed at boosting the nation’s supply chain for critical minerals which are currently held almost entirely by China. 
Audrey Robertson, assistant secretary of energy for the Office of Critical Mineral and Energy Innovation, announced Wednesday at the Ames National Laboratory the DOE was awarding $29.5 million toward Mine of the Future Initiative projects. 
Robertson, speaking with reporters after the announcement, said the U.S. is “very far behind” China in terms of critical mineral supply, and said in “some cases we are 100% dependent or 90% dependent on China specifically for those materials.” 
“But that doesn’t have to be the case,” Robertson said. “The innovation we talked about today, that can help liberate critical minerals from ore bodies that are here in the United States; they can help with recycling technologies and using what we already have in this country, and the ability to reprocess it into usable form.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Critical minerals include the rare earth materials used in electric vehicles, minerals like lithium or cobalt that are necessary for batteries and electronics. Robertson said these minerals are not necessarily “rare” but rather “uneconomic” because they are “very difficult and very expensive to process.”
Access to critical minerals has been a key element of U.S. trade negotiations with China in recent years as the country is currently a key supplier of the materials. 
Updated mapping from the U.S. Geological Survey found the U.S. has more critical mineral deposits across the nation than the agency had previously thought. According to USGS, the U.S. has deposits of nine of the 10 criticial minerals “at greatest risk for supply chain disruption.” 
Robertson said the U.S. sits at a point, similar to when the Ames National Laboratory was initiated under the Manhattan Project, where researchers don’t “have time to sit back and think about problems for 10 years” but have to “act immediately.” 
“I think we’re in that period where the creativity and the innovation that happens in this lab will have, and does have, some of the most important and strategic applications in the real world as it relates to our national security and our economic security,” Robertson said. 
The Ames National Laboratory is operated by Iowa State University as one of more than a dozen DOE national labs across the country to carryout long-term government research.
Robertson said the Mine of the Future Initiative is about “applying American ingenuity to every stage of mineral production” to create more precise mining, improve mineral recovery, use less energy and create less waste materials through the process. Robertson said the goal is also to move technologies quickly from the lab and “into the real world.” 
Iowa company recycles rare earth materials from wind turbines, electronics

“If we don’t control our supply chains, every part of our modern way of life is in jeopardy, and so the time to act is now from the standpoint of innovation in that supply chain,” Robertson said. “To secure the supply chain is the only way we’re going to do it – it’s just more critical now than it’s ever been.”
Better crushing
Projects in the Mine of the Future Initiative aim to support the domestic critical mineral supply chain by prioritizing technologies that advance discovery, recovery, processing and management of critical materials and reduce the energy use, waste and environmental impacts associated with making the materials usable. 
The Ames Lab project, titled Magnetoacoustic-Induced Conditioning of Rare-earth Ores Guided by Computer Vision or MICRO-Vison, will use acoustic and magnetic fields to more intentionally crush rocks in the mineral extraction process. Robertson said by doing so, the critical minerals can be extracted with less energy, as compared to a traditional crushing system that pulverizes all of the rock to get to the minerals. 
“The goal is to free more of the valuable minerals we need while using less energy, generating less waste, and that’s exactly the kind of innovation we need in the United States,” Robertson said. 
Research at the Ames National Laboratory will also make use of computer vision and machine learning to figure out the best places to break the rocks apart, according to the lab. The project will be led by lab scientist and ISU associate professor of mechanical engineering Shan Hu. Hu will be joined by three colleagues, Ikenna Nlebedim, Yuderka Trinidad and Mark Mba-Wright.
Role of artificial or “super” intelligence in critical minerals
While critical minerals are essential for the expansion of artificial intelligence and data center build outs, Robertson said AI, or “super intelligence” as President Donald Trump renamed the technology Tuesday, will also help researchers “tackle” the challenge of onshoring critical mineral supplies. 
‘Dumbfounds us all’: Congress struggles with policies rippling from AI development

“It’s not just in mining; it’s all of those steps along the way that we can iterate more quickly, we can find solutions more quickly,” Robertson said. 
The Trump administration has launched a number of AI focused initiatives, including the Genesis Mission to accelerate government scientific research, and the recently launched America.gov site designed to help folks navigate government information. 
Trump met with technology industry leaders Tuesday, to sign an accord for voluntary controls on artificial intelligence programs amid increased fears about the technology’s rapid development. This coincided with the “super intelligence” or SI executive order, which said the new term would “recognize the continuously advancing technological frontier and the limitless promise it offers the American people.” 
Robertson said “super intelligence” can help researchers better understand where critical materials exist, and how to more efficiently extract them from the ground. She also referenced a recent article from the Ames lab that outlined how AI tools were helping to advance research on a critical-mineral-free magnet. 
Karl Mueller, the director of the lab, said as researchers, they always want to do things “more efficiently” and quickly and that AI is one of the tools that allows that. 
“The advanced artificial intelligence and machine learning tools that have been pioneered here at Iowa State and at Ames Lab as well will allow us to more quickly and more efficiently understand these materials and what processes work best for unlocking these minerals,” Mueller said.
The Ames National Laboratory was one of 12 national laboratories selected for award negotiations with the DOE for Mine of the Future initiative projects. According to the lab, it was selected for a $1.5 million project award.
“We’re not going to compete by doing what we did 100 years ago,” Robertson said. “ … We’re going to compete in the next century by taking new technology and innovation, by changing the way that we’re doing things.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Blake Miguez’s primary residence is in New Iberia, outside 6th District, AG says
description: State Sen. Blake Miguez’s official domicile is in New Iberia, according to an opinion released by Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill’s office Wednesday. In practical terms, her staff determined Miguez’s primary residence is located outside the 6th Congressional District, where he is currently running for office.
text:
State Sen. Blake Miguez, R-New Iberia, is running for Congress in Louisiana's 6th District, even though his primary residence is outside of its boundaries. (Photo by Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)State Sen. Blake Miguez’s official domicile is in New Iberia, according to an opinion released by Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill’s office Wednesday. In practical terms, her staff determined Miguez’s primary residence is located outside the 6th Congressional District, where he is currently running for office. 

“[B]ased upon a review of the relevant facts, it is the opinion of this office that Senator Miguez’s domicile is still in Senate District 22 even though he has a residence in East Baton Rouge Parish,” assistant Attorney General Jennifer Byrd wrote. The AG’s office provided a copy of the opinion to the Illuminator.  

The writeup from the attorney general’s office won’t have a legal impact on the congressional race, as candidates or officeholders are not required to live in the U.S. House districts where they are running.

But the opinion could have affected his ability to stay in his state Senate seat representing part of Acadiana. Unlike members of Congress, state legislators are legally obligated to reside in the district they represent. If the attorney general had determined Miguez’s primary residence was in Baton Rouge instead of New Iberia, he could have been vulnerable to removal from his current elected position. 
“[A] person may have more than one residence but only one domicile,” Byrd wrote.
David Levy of New Iberia, a former Democratic candidate for the state House of Representatives, asked the attorney general’s office to weigh in on Miguez’s residency, according to the document from Murrill’s office. 
Miguez campaign spokesman Chris Pack characterized Levy’s inquiry as a publicity stunt done to benefit state Sen. Rick Edmonds, R-Baton Rouge, who is Miguez’s most high-profile opponent in the 6th Congressional District race. 

“Rick now owes Louisiana voters an explanation for why he pushed this nonsense when he had every reason to know it was baseless and whether he thinks it’s appropriate for taxpayers to foot the bill for his desperate political stunt,” Miguez spokesman Chris Pack said in a written statement Wednesday. 
Miguez bought a house in Baton Rouge on March 16 after announcing he would run for Congress in the 6th District, which includes most of the capital city.
In April, online records for the East Baton Rouge assessor showed Miguez claimed a homestead exemption at the address that would indicate it was his primary residence. In mid-September, Miguez no longer claimed the exemption. Murrill said at a news conference Wednesday there are no public records that verify that Miguez had listed his Baton Rouge residence as his homestead.    
Since jumping in the race, Miguez has played up his connections to the Baton Rouge community, suggesting he has lived there on and off for decades. 

Miguez attended LSU and Southern University Law Center, both in Baton Rouge, but it’s unclear whether he has lived in the 6th District full-time outside of his time as a student. 
In one of his campaign videos, Miguez’s daughter tells the camera that he “moved to Baton Rouge in 1999,” around the time he would have started at LSU. 
Yet multiple documents identify the Republican’s New Iberia home as his primary residence, according to the attorney general office’s written opinion. Miguez’s homestead exemption designation, which can only apply to a primary residence, is registered to that property. His voter registration, bank information and vehicle registration also identify his New Iberia home as his domicile. 
Edmonds has sought to make Miguez’s residency a campaign issue. He called a news conference earlier this month to draw attention to Levy’s inquiry about Miguez’s primary residency. 
Miguez responded by highlighting an overdue state income tax bill Edmonds owed in Mississippi, where Edmonds works as a senior pastor at the First Baptist Church of McComb. 
Even though Edmonds works in Mississippi, the state senator said he has lived in Baton Rouge and the 6th Congressional District for several years. The Edmonds campaign said the state senator has paid the outstanding taxes. 
“I know the people of Senate District 22 have been as surprised as we are that Blake
continues to say he has lived in Baton Rouge for many years when that is not true,” Edmonds said a written statement Wednesday. “He will have to explain himself to the voters of Senate District 22 when he tries to represent them in the State Legislature next year.”

Patrick Morrisey announced Wednesday. Another $4 million in Rural Health Funds will benefit[...]
text:
Gov. Patrick  Morrisey announces a $2.4 million award for Ascend WV to recruit and retain healthcare professionals in rural communities across the state on Sept. 9, 2026 in Hurricane, West Virginia. (Photo courtesy of the West Virginia Office of Gov. Patrick Morrisey)The state of West Virginia will allocate $1.1 million of its federal Rural Health Transformation program funds to Community Care of West Virginia, a federally qualified health center, and another $3.2 million for other investments to rural hospitals in the state, Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced Wednesday.
Another $4 million in Rural Health Funds will benefit the Minnie Hamilton Health Center in Grantsville, Morrisey announced. The funding will support the hospital’s new mobile healthcare unit, help the hospital deploy an autonomous drone delivery for supplies and will implement artificial intelligence-supported clinical documentation technology.
The funds for Community Care will be used to expand access to healthcare in rural communities, Morrisey’s office said.
Of the $1.1 million, the money will be divided between four efforts:

$92,736 to upgrade telehealth technology and infrastructure supporting behavioral health, addiction medicine, maternal health, school-based health and medical weight management services
$574,082 for a mobile healthcare unit providing primary care, preventive services, behavioral health, addiction medicine and care coordination in Braxton, Clay and Pocahontas counties 
$82,432 to help current healthcare employees advance their careers through certifications, licensure programs, specialized training, and educational opportunities. 
$354,364 to establish a statewide rural healthcare apprenticeship program combining paid employment with classroom instruction and hands-on clinical training. 

Morrisey announced the $3.3 million investment in healthcare innovation, provider productivity, workforce development, and care coordination initiatives during an event at Stonewall Jackson Memorial Hospital Wednesday. The investments will include: 

Funding to deploy artificial intelligence-powered ambient clinical listening technology at five hospitals: Stonewall Jackson Memorial Hospital, Mon Health Marion Neighborhood Hospital, Preston Memorial Hospital, Plateau Medical Center and Webster Memorial Hospital. The technology can reduce documentation burden and allow providers to spend more time with patients, Morrisey’s office said
Broaddus Hospital in Phillippi received funding to establish the Mansfield Place TeleHub Pilot, expanding access to specialty care, behavioral health services and urgent clinical consultation for rural skilled nursing residents through telemedicine technology.
Vandalia Health received an additional award to help rural hospitals and clinics fill critical staffing shortages, support more than 100 healthcare staffing placements, and strengthen long-term recruitment and retention of healthcare professionals across West Virginia.

West Virginia received $199 million in federal dollars from the Rural Health Transformation Program for 2026. The five-year program from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid was part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which made historic cuts to healthcare and food assistance spending. 
The program aims to “empower states to transform the existing rural healthcare infrastructure and build sustainable healthcare systems that expand access, enhance quality of care and improve outcomes for patients,” according to CMS. 
Last week, Morrisey announced a $500,000 award from the Rural Health Transformation program to CHANGE, Inc, a Federally Qualified Health Center and Community Action Agency in Weirton, to implement provider productivity, care management, and artificial intelligence tools designed to improve patient care while reducing administrative demands on healthcare professionals. 
Morrisey has previously announced allocations of the funding will go toward the WVU Medicine Center for Nursing Education, the Ascend program and to support employer-based healthcare programs throughout the state, among other initiatives.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: U.S. Conference of Mayors moves 2027 meeting from Providence to Atlanta after Smiley loss
description: Providence Mayor Brett Smiley lost the Democratic Primary for the city’s mayorship earlier this month to challenger and state Rep. David Morales. And now the capital city has lost its status as the host of the U.S. Conference of Mayors 2027 annual meeting. Providence’s hosting of the conference, first announced in 2024, would have run […]
text:
The Providence skyline is seen across the Providence River. The U.S. Conference of Mayors is moving its 2027 annual meeting from Providence to Atlanta after a change in mayoral leadership. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)Providence Mayor Brett Smiley lost the Democratic Primary for the city’s mayorship earlier this month to challenger and state Rep. David Morales. And now the capital city has lost its status as the host of the U.S. Conference of Mayors 2027 annual meeting.
Providence’s hosting of the conference, first announced in 2024, would have run June 24 through 27 next year. But the conference has pulled out and is moving the annual meeting to Atlanta, the group’s CEO and Executive Director Tom Cochran told Rhode Island Current Wednesday. 
It’s the organization’s tradition, Cochran explained, to reconsider the host city when a change in the mayorship happens in the year before its annual meeting.
“We believe the mayor serving in the year leading up to the meeting should be closely involved in both the bid and the planning that follows,” Cochran wrote.
The move took the Providence Warwick Convention and Visitors Bureau, also known as GoProvidence, by surprise. 
Kristen Adamo, the bureau’s president and CEO, said Wednesday in an email that she was unaware a change in the mayorship could prompt relocation of the conference. Adamo added the Conference of Mayors hadn’t contacted the bureau directly about the canceled plans.
Adamo expressed concern at the loss of expected economic impact from the approximately 200 mayors and their staffs, who would have descended upon the city to attend the conference but also to wine, dine and shop at local businesses. 
“It is extremely disappointing to lose an event that has a direct spend impact of more than $2 million for Rhode Island,” Adamo said.
There were also logistical headaches attached to the change in plans. Convention center dates are usually booked more than a year in advance, Adamo said.
“In the meetings and conventions world, this is extremely last minute,” Adamo wrote, “but we have a top-notch team that is reaching out [to] meeting planners as we speak. Our industry typically books events out 18 months or more. To fill these dates will be extremely challenging.”
Smiley’s Sept. 9 loss in Democratic mayoral primary saw him secure 46.43% of the vote, compared to Morales’ 53.57%.
Providence itself has not incurred any costs related to either hosting the meeting or its cancellation, mayoral spokesperson Carl Austin Miller Grondin told Rhode Island Current.
A decisive victory and a potential new chapter for Rhode Island’s capital city

Miller Grondin said the city was notified Saturday.
GoProvidence also has no contract with the Conference of Mayors, Adamo said, and added that any contracts would instead be between the organization and individual hotels.
Conference CEO Cochran added that hosting the annual get-together is a big commitment for host cities, and that “a new mayor’s first months in office are already full.” 
“We know Providence’s new mayor will want to devote that time to hitting the ground running for residents, and we look forward to working with them,” Cochran added.
Providence last hosted the annual mayors’ meeting in 2009.
Morales will face Republican Dave Talan in the Nov. 3 general election.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Judge finds probable cause in Tasia Fortune case
description: Christy Spivey, mother of Tasia Fortune, heads to Jackson Municipal Court on Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026, for the preliminary hearing of Jarques Ratliff, who is charged with murder in the death of her daughter.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
A Jackson municipal judge ruled Wednesday that probable cause exists to send to the grand jury the case against Jarques Ratliff in the killing of Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old mother who was found hanging in west Jackson.
Media organizations, including the Clarion Ledger, successfully argued to keep the preliminary hearing open to the public. Judge Lilli Evans Bass had considered closing the hearing in the ongoing investigation.
Wednesday’s proceeding was a continuation of an earlier hearing in which Detective Samuel Dukes of the Jackson Police Department testified that Fortune’s hanging was staged, and she was killed over stolen drugs. 
The discovery of Fortune hanging from a tree on Aug. 3 received national attention because of Mississippi’s history of racist violence. She was Black, as are Ratliff and two other men charged with murder in her killing.
At Wednesday’s hearing, Dukes referred to a witness by the pseudonym Jane Doe to protect her identity during the investigation. He said Doe saw Fortune leave with Ratliff and two other men in a car. When the group returned, Fortune was not with them.
Dukes said the witness also told police that Ratliff said Fortune “fought hard.”
The detective testified that when Fortune’s body was found, she was wearing men’s shoes. The shoes are being tested to determine whether they belonged to Ratliff, 51. 
Dukes also revealed that documents with Fortune’s name on them were found in Ratliff’s closet, and video footage exists of Fortune before her death.
The judge’s Wednesday ruling means a Hinds County grand jury will determine whether there is enough evidence for Ratliff to be placed on trial on a murder charge.
Fortune’s mother, Christy Spivey, traveled from Kentucky to Mississippi with her husband to attend court proceedings. 
Speaking to reporters after the hearing, she said she is grateful the proceeding remained open. She also does not believe Fortune stole any drugs.
“Everyone knows that she did not steal,” Spivey said, “that she would hustle and do whatever she needed to do to get money for food, clothes, whatever she needed, or she would call and ask for money.”
Toney Baldwin, Ratliff’s attorney, also spoke to the media.
“We all want to get to the truth, and I think once we get to the truth, my client will be exonerated,” he said.
Ratliff is the first person arrested and charged with murder in Fortune’s death. Earnest Lloyd Jr., 25, and Eric Derrell Clark, 45 have also been charged, and more arrests are expected, police officials have said.
Clark’s bond was set at $5 million. Lloyd and Ratliff were denied bond.
JPD Police Chief RaShall Brackney said Monday that all three suspects had a “known association” with Fortune. 
At Clark’s initial appearance, Jackson Municipal Court Judge Jeffery Reynolds called the staged hanging “an extremely heinous act” that “invoked the terrible history of our state.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Hegseth taps LSU cadet corps for new generation of military officers
description: U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced Wednesday he is elevating LSU’s corps of cadets program and granting the university a new military designation.  LSU will be made a Distinguished Military College, a newly revived federal designation that offers graduates of its Reserve Officer Training Corps program priority in becoming a commissioned militar[...]
text:
LSU’s Memorial Tower displays the time on Monday, March 20, 2023, on Tower Drive in Baton Rouge, La. (Matthew Perschall for Louisiana Illuminator) U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced Wednesday he is elevating LSU’s corps of cadets program and granting the university a new military designation. 
LSU will be made a Distinguished Military College, a newly revived federal designation that offers graduates of its Reserve Officer Training Corps program priority in becoming a commissioned military officer, Hegseth announced at his State of the Force address at the U.S. Marine Corps base in Quantico, Virginia. 
Other schools given the designation are Mississippi State University, Tuskegee University, Hillsdale College and Liberty University, though Hegseth said more will be named soon. 
The distinction also puts LSU on the path to becoming a Senior Military College, a prestigious designation that is essentially a step between a normal ROTC program, like what LSU currently offers, and one of the U.S. service academies, such as West Point or the Naval Academy in Annapolis. 
The existing Senior Military Colleges, designated in federal law, are Texas A&M, Norwich University, the Virginia Military Institute, The Citadel, Virginia Tech and the University of North Georgia. 
LSU, sometimes referred to as the “Ole War Skule,” was founded  in 1860 as the Louisiana State Seminary of Learning & Military Academy. It has maintained a close connection to military service, including sending more officers into World War II than any other university except the service academies and Texas A&M. 
“LSU’s history has long been tied to service, leadership and preparing graduates to meet the needs of our state and nation,” LSU Chancellor Jim Dalton said in a statement. “This designation recognizes that long-standing commitment, and positions LSU to build on that legacy for the next generation of military and civilian leaders.”

title: Utah’s court system lacks ‘accountability’ and needs change, legislative audits say
description: Legislative auditors on Thursday released a slate of four reports that found a lack of “accountability” across the governing structures that make up Utah’s judiciary.  The audits — which come during a time of ongoing tension between the GOP-controlled Utah Legislature and the courts in the wake of rulings that have frustrated Republican lawmakers — […]
text:
The Utah Supreme Court inside the Scott M. Matheson Courthouse in Salt Lake City is pictured on Wednesday, June 10, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Legislative auditors on Thursday released a slate of four reports that found a lack of “accountability” across the governing structures that make up Utah’s judiciary. 
The audits — which come during a time of ongoing tension between the GOP-controlled Utah Legislature and the courts in the wake of rulings that have frustrated Republican lawmakers — recommended a long slate of changes to improve Utah’s court system, including when it comes to investigating judges and ensuring voters are equipped to hold them accountable.
In recent years — despite cries of court packing and the concerns of encroaching on the judiciary’s independence — the Utah Legislature has already expanded Utah Supreme Court from five to seven seats and given the governor and Senate say over who the high court’s next chief justice will be. 
The new slate of audits may lay the foundation for lawmakers to make more changes to the judiciary that could come as soon as the upcoming legislative session that begins in January. 
While reviewing the audits in the Legislative Audit Subcommittee on Thursday afternoon, House Speaker Mike Schultz applauded auditors for their work while thanking judiciary leaders for their “willingness to work together” on the audit’s recommendations. He also acknowledged the ongoing tension between the branches. 
Utah State Bar ‘deeply alarmed’ by bills it says would ‘weaken’ the judiciary’s independence

“I know we’ve been in some challenging times,” said the Republican lawmaker, who has been one of the leading voices calling for more transparency and accountability in the courts in recent years. 
Schultz added that he “fully supports” independence of the judicial branch. At the same time, he said Utah’s three branches of government “all have the responsibility, and it’s set up this way … to hold the other branch of government accountable.” 
In their reports, auditors zeroed in on the Judicial Conduct Commission and the Judicial Performance Evaluation Commission, the bodies tasked with investigating judges for misconduct and evaluating their job performances. 
Notably, it’s the first time in 20 years legislative auditors have evaluated the Judicial Conduct Commission.
In the JCC, they found “governance gaps” that “limit confidence in investigations and decisions,” and “weak data practices” that “limit accountability and transparency,” according to the audit report. Auditors also determined that JPEC’s judge evaluations have “significant weaknesses, and the process falls short of providing complete and accurate information to voters.” 
In another report, auditors also critiqued the performance of the state court system as a whole, calling out “inconsistent leadership” that have led to “sentencing disparities,” and a question mark around whether Utah’s sentencing guidelines “are achieving their intended purpose.”
JCC audit calls out recusal, disqualification issues related to Hagen resignation
The audit of the JCC also comes after a controversy that led to the recent resignation of Utah Supreme Court Justice Diana Hagen. 
Hagen resigned after the Utah House, in response to a public records request from KSL, released a complaint that was previously dismissed by the JCC. That complaint alleged Hagen had an extramarital affair with an attorney involved in the state’s high-profile redistricting case. 
The Judicial Conduct Commission had dismissed the complaint as lacking evidence and credibility, but Gov. Spencer Cox and Utah’s top Republican legislative leaders called for an independent investigation into the claims after the story was reported. Hagen denied the allegations, but to avoid dragging her family into the independent investigation, she resigned. 
Amid affair allegations, Utah Supreme Court Justice Diana Hagen resigns

The audit did not name Hagen specifically, but alluded to a “recent case before the JCC involving a member of the Utah State Supreme Court” as an example of why the commission should write clearer rules for when a JCC member should be disqualified.
As previously reported, the JCC’s Cheylynn Hayman — whom Hagen has named as a friend and included on her recusal list — recused herself from the JCC vote to dismiss the allegations against Hagen. 
Auditors, however, noted in their report that “a commissioner commented on the character of the complainant before recusing from further participation.” 
“Disclosing personal relationships with individuals involved in the matter is common and expected,” auditors wrote. “However, this example was unusual because the commissioner used the disclosure to also raise questions about the credibility of the complaint. This example illustrates the risks to impartiality that can arise when policies do not clearly define the scope and purpose of disclosures made before recusal.”
In a written response to the audit, JCC Executive Director Alex Peterson agreed with the auditors’ recommendations and included details on their plans to implement the changes. 
Utah Supreme Court says affair allegations against justice were ‘inappropriately’ released

“As your audit acknowledges, we are an extremely small agency that has not been audited by your office in over 20 years,” Peterson wrote. “While the Judicial Conduct Commission has been successfully meeting its statutory and constitutional obligations, we understand there is always room for improving our processes. Accordingly, we sincerely appreciate the personnel time, energy, and effort put into this audit.”
Shortly after Hagen resigned in May, Utah’s top Republican leaders including Gov. Spencer Cox, Senate President Stuart Adam and House Speaker Mike Schultz  — along with former Utah Supreme Court Justice Matthew Durrant, before he retired — all issued a  joint statement presenting a united front to strengthen “accountability” in the Judicial Conduct Commission. 
“The judicial, executive, and legislative branches are committed to working together on potential reforms to the Judicial Conduct Commission — ensuring it upholds the highest standards of accountability and earns the confidence of the people of Utah,” the joint statement said without elaborating on what those potential reforms could be. 
Legislative auditors’ recommendations are likely to inform many of those coming changes. 
Auditors recommend considering changing Judicial Council membership
 In a fourth report taking a broader look at the judiciary’s independence and accountability, auditors said that “although judicial independence is needed, stronger accountability can improve judicial governance and strengthen public confidence in the court system.” 
“The issues in the judiciary share a common cause: an approach that has traditionally placed greater emphasis on judicial independence than accountability,” auditors wrote. 
As part of a long list of recommendations to improve Utah’s court system — many of which were operational and that judiciary leaders generally agreed with — one stuck out as controversial. 
Utah State Bar warns against lawmakers’ ‘aggressive’ moves to change courts

Auditors recommended that the Legislature “consider reviewing statute” to determine whether to add representation from the executive and legislative branches to the Judicial Council, the policy-making body for the judiciary that has constitutional authority to adopt rules for court administration. The council also sets standards for judicial performance, court facilities, and other operations across all levels of the state’s court system.
“This could help promote broader accountability in judicial governance,” auditors wrote. 
Schultz, during Thursday’s committee meeting, said he had some “concerns in regards to the makeup of the Judicial Council” based on the audit, but also because of its size, calling it “problematic.” 
The Judicial Council, according to the judiciary’s website, currently has 16 members. The Utah Supreme Court’s chief justice serves as the chair, while other members include one other Supreme Court justice, one Court of Appeals Judge, six District Court judges, three Juvenile Court judges, three Justice Court judges, and a state bar representative. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
One of the committee’s Democrats, House Minority Leader Angela Romero, D-Salt Lake City, urged lawmakers to be “careful” when considering changes to the Judicial Council. 
“We want to make sure that we, as the Legislature, are respecting that independence, and we’re also not putting together a board or a commission that are people that are group thinkers or people that want to appease us as legislators.” 
Senate Minority Leader Luz Escamilla, D-Salt Lake City, also questioned whether the Utah Constitution would allow legislative appointments on that board, and if so, whether they could ensure those appointments are “bipartisan.” 
While the Utah Constitution creates the Judicial Council, its makeup and membership is determined under state law, auditors said. 
The Utah Constitution says the Judicial Council “shall consist of the chief justice of the Supreme Court, as presiding officer, and other justices, judges, and other persons as provided by statute. There shall be at least one representative on the Judicial Council from each court established by the Constitution or by statute.”
State Court Administrator Ron Gordon told the committee’s lawmakers that the judiciary has “no argument that the Legislature is authorized by the Constitution to establish that membership” of the Judicial Council. 
“We would just want to avoid anything that could have the effect, or even the appearance, of infusing partisan politics in the governance of the judiciary,” Gordon said. 
Jay Jorgensen (left) greets Utah Supreme Court Associate Chief Justice Jill Pohlman after a news conference announcing Cox’s appointment of Jorgensen and Stephen Dent to the Utah Supreme Court at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on June 2, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
 Associate chief justice raises concerns of keeping judiciary ‘free of political influence’
In a written response to that recommendation, Judicial Council leaders — including the current chair of that council, Utah Supreme Court Associate Chief Justice Jill Pohlman — pushed back, warning it could upset the balance of powers between the three branches of government.
“The Judicial Council acknowledges and respects the authority of the Legislature to supplement the constitutional membership requirements,” the judiciary’s response said. “The Judicial Council believes that representation or membership from the executive or legislative branches may violate principles of separation of powers and may undermine the ability of the Judiciary to accomplish its work free of political influence.”
However, Pohlman, in a letter responding to the audit’s recommendations, agreed with most of the auditor’s other recommendations.
“We agree that there are opportunities to strengthen the Judiciary’s governance processes, use of data and performance measures, judicial education, and organizational accountability,” Pohlman wrote. 
She noted that the judiciary’s written responses to the recommendations “identify the work already underway, and the steps we intend to take moving forward.” 
“We believe administration and organizational accountability can be strengthened while we continue to respect the organizational structure of the judicial branch and preserve the independence of judges in deciding individual cases based on the law and facts presented,” Pohlman wrote.

name: WyoFile
title: Billionaire Joe Ricketts resurrects plans for luxury Bondurant resort after ‘Saving Yellowstone’ accolades
description:
New effort to develop “The Confluence" is one of several recent business moves by the TD Ameritrade founder, who also bought the Rim Station and Timberline Ranch near Merna. 
The post Billionaire Joe Ricketts resurrects plans for luxury Bondurant resort after ‘Saving Yellowstone’ accolades appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Fresh off a spate of positive publicity for his conservation-oriented work under the banner Saving Yellowstone, billionaire Joe Ricketts has renewed his efforts to develop a luxury resort on ranchland that runs along the rural, remote Upper Hoback River. 
In 2024, the TD Ameritrade founder and patriarch of the family that owns the Chicago Cubs halted an underway upscale resort after Sublette County commissioners declined to waive stipulations that prohibited construction from Nov. 15 to April 30 to protect wintering elk and moose. Ricketts contended the abridged building season would add $60 million in construction costs when he pulled the project.  
Two years later, the 85-year-old financier is trying again. In July, his agents submitted a permit application to the Sublette County Planning and Zoning Department for a resort called The Confluence. The effort escaped media attention until Tuesday, when it was reported by the Cowboy State Daily. 
The modified project proposal calls for a recreational lodge, restaurant and bar, a wellness/spa center and 20 guest suites. But that’s just the first phase. More phases are expected, according to the application, and will be pursued with future applications. Construction is anticipated to begin this fall and wrap up by 2031. 




Click to enlarge: A detail of the main 20-room guest lodge from a landscape plan submitted July 20, 2026, to Sublette County Planning and Zoning for a new development on Joe Ricketts’ property along the Upper Hoback River Road in Bondurant. (Courtesy)
Ricketts has repeatedly espoused the idea that developing resorts and getting wealthy tourists to understand conservation are needed to protect the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem. He made that case to a Pinedale audience in 2023, pitching his own luxury resort as a form of conservation, and echoed those views in August at a conference he hosted at his ranch under his new nonprofit, Saving Yellowstone.
“We need to accommodate growth in a way that [protects] the places that you see,” Ricketts told conference attendees in his opening remarks.
Ricketts’ earlier attempt at a resort, which had been dubbed the Homestead, went over very poorly in the small Bondurant community. The ranchland being developed by the billionaire Nebraskan is crossed by the longest known mule deer migration route in the world, which connects the Red Desert to Hoback Basin and beyond. It also contains crucial winter ranges for elk and moose. 
The first attempt in 2020 to rezone the ranchland from its former agricultural status failed, but he tried again the next fall and was given the OK by county commissioners in December 2021.
TD Ameritrade founder Joe Ricketts welcomes guests at the August 2026 Saving Yellowstone conference hosted at his ranch. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
At public meetings about the resort plans, oftentimes the only person speaking in support of Ricketts was Morgan Fischer, his former agent, who Ricketts is now suing alleging he was defrauded. 
In written responses to WyoFile’s questions on Wednesday, spokesperson Jessica Jaubert said that Ricketts is committed to being a good neighbor.
“[That] includes keeping people informed, answering questions directly, following County requirements and paying attention to how construction affects those who live and work nearby,” she said. 
A resolution appended to the resort application shows that Ricketts has agreed to not build from Nov. 15 through April 30 this time around.
Jaubert highlighted other wildlife-friendly measures in the plans. He’s committing to wildlife-friendly fencing, bear-resistant trashcans and dark sky-friendly lighting, she said. Guests will be given “toolkits” with instructions on being a good ecosystem tourists.  
“Mr. Ricketts is committed to these added measures to help wildlife move safely through the property, reduce conflicts between people and animals, and help guests understand their responsibility to care for the place they’ve come to enjoy,” Jaubert said. 
Some neighbors aren’t buying it, like Upper Hoback Road residents Lisi Krall.
“I am more skeptical than I’ve ever been,” Krall said. 
Krall, who’s a retired environmental economics professor, is especially critical of Ricketts’ theory that conservation and development are intertwined. 
“He frames it like this is an eco lodge, where he’s going to teach people about the Hoback region, blah blah blah,” Krall said. “This is not conservation. Building eco lodges for the very wealthy that have huge footprints up small river valleys is not conservation, and it negates his good conservation work.” 






Earth-moving equipment shaped out this construction site along Upper Hoback Road in 2024 in anticipation of a later-canceled luxury resort sought by billionaire Joe Ricketts. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)






Construction crew barracks and stockpiles are leftover from a luxury resort that billionaire Joe Ricketts began building but canceled in July 2024. This photograph was taken from a public Bridger-Teton National Forest road. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)


In Krall’s judgement, the nonprofits Saving Yellowstone and Ricketts Conservation Foundation are little more than public relations tools — and effective ones. 
“Based on the number of conservationists that he’s brought into his fold,” she said, “I’d say he’s doing a pretty good job of making conservationists believe this is the way to conservation.” 
Jaubert disavowed any connection between Ricketts’ resort and environmental initiatives. The Confluence application and Saving Yellowstone conference happening within a month of each other was “entirely coincidental,” she said. 
Fellow Upper Hoback Road resident Pat Burroughs attended the conference, and has tried to give Ricketts the benefit of the doubt. But she’s simultaneously skeptical.
“At the summit, Joe said that the thing that causes the most problems for the ecology of the ecosystem is Starlink,” she said. “Baloney. It’s commercialism.”
The on-again, off-again resort is “making me crazy,” Burroughs said. “I want to believe that our little valley is going to be safe,” she said. 
In the two years since Ricketts halted construction, he’s stayed busy with land dealings in Sublette and Teton counties. He purchased a Bridger-Teton National Forest inholding up Granite Creek, northwest of Bondurant, and this summer construction crews have been working to renovate and expand a guest ranch he’s dubbed The Hawken.
Ricketts also bought the Rim Station, a small market and RV Park located along U.S. Highway 191 at the divide between the Hoback and Green rivers. It’s now registered to Rim Station LLC, an entity that was organized in June by Ricketts agent Steve Christensen. 
And the billionaire also purchased the Timberline Ranch near Merna, formerly occupied by hunting influencers brought down for poaching. That property is now owned by Moose Lake Acquisition LLC, which was organized in March by Christensen. 
Some debate remains on whether Ricketts is on sound legal footing to develop The Confluence resort without again having to rezone the property. Neighbors are pointing to Sublette County zoning regulations, which stipulate that property rezoned to accommodate resorts must see “substantial development” within two years or the zoning change “shall” revert.
Ricketts’ ranchland was rezoned nearly five years ago. 
Sublette County Attorney Clayton Melinkovich declined to comment on the matter, citing the potential for litigation.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas lawmakers told helping inmates return to society will ease prison overcrowding
description: Arkansas lawmakers and criminal justice reform advocates agreed Wednesday that improving the systems that help inmates return to society after incarceration will alleviate the state’s prison overcrowding problem. State correctional facilities have 15,362 beds and 16,804 inmates as of Sept. 1, and county jails are often tasked with holding inmates waiting for[...]
text:
Former Arkansas lawmaker Jeremy Hutchinson, who served two years in prison on federal bribery and tax charges, presents the House and Senate Judiciary committees with suggestions to reduce prison overcrowding on Sept. 30, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)Arkansas lawmakers and criminal justice reform advocates agreed Wednesday that improving the systems that help inmates return to society after incarceration will alleviate the state’s prison overcrowding problem.
State correctional facilities have 15,362 beds and 16,804 inmates as of Sept. 1, and county jails are often tasked with holding inmates waiting for state prison beds. 
“We also need to examine what happens before someone reaches those prison beds,” said Marybeth Hill, event coordinator with the ARCHway Institute, a Florida-based substance use treatment organization. “We cannot incarcerate ourselves out of a public health crisis.”
Hill, one of 19 advocates who testified during a daylong hearing on prisons before the House and Senate judiciary committees, said a combination of support, accountability and substance use treatment helped her move on after serving time for drug charges.
Arkansas’ 3,000-bed prison site is on hold. What are the other options?

One obstacle to reentry to society is the presence of drugs in prison, said Jarad Harper, executive director of the faith-based Shackle Free Ministries, based in Clarksville. Committee members said this needs to be addressed legislatively, especially if corrections employees are supplying inmates with drugs.
“I’m asking if we should be throwing the book not at the first-time criminals…but maybe throw the book at people who are government employees making a very good living and eventually getting a huge pension for being part of the problem,” Ferndale Republican Sen. Mark Johnson said.
Wednesday’s hearing was the latest in series of meetings the panel is holding on prisons and overcrowding. The meetings are being held as the state is looking at alternatives after Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders’ plan to build a 3,000-bed prison in Franklin County was put on hold because of legislative resistance. 
Former Republican lawmaker Jeremy Hutchinson, son of former U.S. Sen. Tim Hutchinson and nephew of former Gov. Asa Hutchinson, also shared his criminal justice reform ideas with the committee.
Jeremy Hutchinson resigned from the Legislature in 2018 after he was indicted in federal courts in Missouri and Arkansas on federal bribery and tax charges. The corruption scandal involved several other lawmakers, as well as lobbyists and healthcare executives.
Hutchinson served two years of an eight-year prison sentence before President Donald Trump pardoned him last year. He then became director of strategic initiatives for Unify.US, a Washington D.C.-based criminal justice reform organization that works primarily with Republican-led states.

Overcrowded: Protect Arkansas Act to drive continued prison population growth for at least a decade


Sanders and the majority-GOP Legislature passed the Protect Arkansas Act into law in 2023. The law is expected to increase the demand for prison beds, likely adding 2,902 offenders by 2040, because it requires longer criminal sentences and reduces parole eligibility.
One policy change Hutchinson suggested was to allow nonviolent offenders over 60 years of age to serve their sentences in home confinement instead of in prison. This would save the Department of Corrections “a fortune” in inmates’ healthcare costs, since those individuals could be eligible for Medicaid, Hutchinson said.
“Their sentence isn’t being relieved, and if they screw up, they can be hauled right back into the prison environment, but they’re still in custody,” he said.
Hutchinson also suggested that Arkansas’ court system automatically expunge nonviolent crimes after inmates complete their sentences, since having a criminal record makes it difficult to obtain housing and employment and increases the likelihood of reoffending.
One of the contributors to Arkansas’ rising prison population is recidivism, a term applied when inmates violate the terms of their release or are convicted of new crimes within three years of leaving prison. Corrections staff turnover and high caseloads can reinforce the problem, according to experts.
Another policy change that could reduce recidivism and strengthen inmates’ reintegration into society would be to hold inmates financially responsible for it, said Sharon Garrett, executive director of Safe Haven Ministries, a Clarksville-based nonprofit that assists formerly incarcerated women.
Overcrowded: Arkansas’ prison system costs inmates, taxpayers

If the state paid reentry programs only $50 per day for 45 days, it would save $1,870 per inmate that uses the program, Garrett said. She added that many reentry programs are only 90 days, but many inmates need at least a year to make the changes that prevent them from reoffending.
“I propose that we treat them with dignity, we make them stay longer, we inspire their vision and we let them share in the cost of their journey,” Garrett said.
Arkansans can already rack up a variety of expenses while incarcerated, such as payments for court proceedings and commissary products, and they often continue to owe the corrections system after being released.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Crackdown on out-of-state vehicle registrations to start this month
description: Under a law that takes effect Thursday, Marylanders who register their cars in other states will have 60 days to register them in Maryland or face fines and other possible penalties, although state officials said they hope drivers will take advantage of the grace period.
text:
Maryland residents with vehicles registered in other states will have 60 days to register in Maryland or face fines and other penalties. Notices are expected to go out later this month. (File photo by Bruce DePuyt/Maryland Matters)State officials say they are ready to crack down on Maryland residents who register their vehicles in other states.
Under a law that takes effect Thursday, Marylanders who register their cars in other states will have 60 days to register them in Maryland. Those who do not could face fines and other penalties, but Maryland Motor Vehicle Administrator Chrissy Nizer said her agency hopes most will make use of the grace period.
“That’s the end goal of this. It really is not to fine people,” Nizer said. “We don’t want to have to do that. We want people to come in compliance prior to that.”
The number of vehicles registered in Virginia to Maryland drivers is a growing problem.
In November 2023, more than 101,000 vehicles registered in Virginia were associated with Maryland addresses. That number jumped to more than 111,000 by the following June, according to an analysis presented to lawmakers in January.
Motor Vehicle Administration Administrator Christine Nizer. (File photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
In Baltimore City, 10% of fatal accidents from 2023 to 2024 involved vehicles registered in Virginia. Over 7,000 nonfatal crashes — about 47% of all non-fatal accidents during that same period — involved vehicles registered in Virginia.
Baltimore City Police Lt. Col. Derek Loeffler told lawmakers in January that out-of-state registrations account for 11% of all unpaid parking, speed camera and other citations.
In July, the Office of Program Evaluation and Government Accountability reported that 25% of all speed camera citations issued over a three-year period were issued to vehicles registered out of state. Topping the list were vehicles registered in Virginia.
Of primary concern is safety, Nizer said.
“It really all starts with safety, and we know what the requirements are in Maryland,” she said. “You have to have that safety inspection when you title and register a new vehicle. You have to comply with insurance requirements.”
Virginia has different insurance requirements. Additionally, Nizer said data shows that Maryland vehicles registered in Virginia are not in compliance with Virginia inspection requirements.
“Over 90% of them either were not completed or were not in compliance,” Nizer said. “That’s a real concern because if those vehicles are out there driving on the roads but don’t meet basic safety standards, and they are in a crash — obviously, that means that the risk of injury or even death is much higher.”
There are also budgetary concerns.
Registering in Virginia allows the vehicle to avoid Maryland registration fees. Those fees, based on weight class, make up 17% of the state’s Transportation Trust Fund, which pays for highway and transit projects. Some of the registration fees also help pay for emergency medical services and Shock Trauma.
Additionally, those vehicles avoid Maryland vehicle emissions testing.
A recent audit found that out-of-state vehicles owed more than $818 million in unpaid tolls and fees. Vehicles registered in Virginia owe nearly $235 million — more than any other state
Over the summer, officials started promoting the “Plate where you live” program. The goal was to give owners as much notice as possible.
The MVA and its counterpart in Virginia identified nearly 80,000 individuals who live in Maryland but register vehicles in Virginia. Seventy percent of the notices went to drivers in three jurisdictions — Prince George’s County, Baltimore City and Baltimore County. More than a third went to residents in Prince George’s County, according to the MVA.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
In July, those owners received “courtesy letters” announcing the new law. About 3,400 registered their vehicles in Maryland, Nizer said.
The agency expects an updated file from Virginia in October. The new data will be used to send official compliance notices.
“Most of our compliance periods start when we send that first notice out,” Nizer said.
Motorists who get their vehicle titled in Maryland within that 60-day window will face no fines or penalties. After that, owners of vehicles face a fine of $7 per day for the next 60 days. The maximum fine is $420.
After that first 120-day period, owners of vehicles not registered in the state are subject to other penalties that could include seizing license or immobilizing those vehicles.
For now, most of the discussion about enforcement has centered around vehicles registered in Virginia, but supporters of the program insist that the out-of-state tag bill is not meant to focus on one state.
“We try to call it the out of state tag enforcement bill,” Nizer said. “To be clear that it’s not about Virginia specifically.
Virginia law — unlike Maryland — allows non-residents to title their vehicles in the state.
“There are some other states who also have that kind of law,” Nizer said, adding that her agency is looking at other states with similar laws. Her agency also takes “complaints from individuals,” a process that has been “in place for many years.”

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota to use ‘anchor partners’ to manage Rural Health grants
description: North Dakota’s Health and Human Services Department is turning to outside “anchor partners” to manage a federal grant program for millions of dollars meant to boost rural health care initiatives. Lawmakers wondered what an “anchor partner” actually is, how they are chosen and how the change will affect the timing to get more than $160 […]
text:
North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services Chief Financial Officer Donna Aukland addresses a legislative panel on Sept. 30, 2026. (Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota’s Health and Human Services Department is turning to outside “anchor partners” to manage a federal grant program for millions of dollars meant to boost rural health care initiatives.
Lawmakers wondered what an “anchor partner” actually is, how they are chosen and how the change will affect the timing to get more than $160 million of awarded funding out the door by a looming deadline.
Earlier this year, the Republican-led Legislature accepted $199 million in federal Rural Health Transformation Program funding. The money is meant to improve technology, increase health care access in rural areas, boost workforce and promote healthy lifestyles.
All 50 states received a portion of the money under the five-year, $50 billion program.
North Dakota rural health plan approved, ‘now we’ve got to implement it’

North Dakota is the only state managing every single grant included in the Rural Health Transformation Program, estimated at 500 to 700 grants, HHS Chief Financial Officer Donna Aukland told a panel of House and Senate budget writers on Wednesday. The other states have “anchor partners,” she said.
“Anchor partners” are in-state organizations that directly handle grant applications and funding opportunities and individually manage the grants, Aukland said. HHS would still manage the grants but “from a higher level to ensure that the work was getting done,” she said. 
HHS will use three anchor partners, including the University of North Dakota Center for Rural Health. The two others are not finalized.
HHS chose partners it was already working closely with, but plans to work with more in the future four years of funding and figure out whether there will be an application process for anchor partners, Aukland said. 
Rep. Eric Murphy, R-Grand Forks, said details are lacking on the department’s change, a move Aukland called a “slight pivot.”
Rep. Jon Nelson, R-Rugby, said he doesn’t see the change helping the timeline for dispersing funds and wondered about a decision-making lag. More than $161 million remains to be awarded to grantees, awaiting final reviews, Aukland said. The deadline to do so is Oct. 30.
“There’s a lot of angst out there that the awards haven’t been granted yet,” Nelson said. 
More than $50 million available in new rural health grants

In the next week, HHS will look at all of the awards going out to anchor partners and will notify grant recipients that money is coming, “but we don’t know the total amount yet” because HHS needs to verify the amount in their grant application is allowable, Aukland said.
So far, HHS has obligated about $37.3 million of the funding.
HHS still has to have staff for the program to ensure the money is used according to plan, Aukland said. The change to anchor partners allows the department to focus on strategy and more follow-up “to ensure that we are actually getting the things out of the plan that we wanted to get.”
Earlier, she told another panel of lawmakers that HHS has had to hire about 20 positions to administer the Rural Health Transformation Program. Even with anchor partners, the department will still have administrative costs as it monitors the work for compliance with federal rules, Aukland said.
Anchor partners are allowed up to 10% of grants for administrative costs, she said. HHS requires information on administrative costs, she said.
The U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services will announce North Dakota’s second-year funding amount in October. HHS has estimated it will be around $200 million.
Evaluations for the next four years of Rural Health funding will be under HHS guidance with the anchor partners, Aukland said.
Deputy Editor Jeff Beach contributed to this report.
Reach North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: VTDigger
title: Texas company presents ideas for future Vermont Yankee property use
description:
PowerTransitions seeks community reactions and ideas about potential battery storage at the longtime nuclear reactor site. The company says it decided not to pursue solar or data center projects there, based on earlier feedback.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Texas company presents ideas for future Vermont Yankee property use.
text:
A worker cuts apart a beam during the deconstruction of the former Vermont Yankee nuclear power plant in Vernon in October 2023. The salvaged metal from the plant, which is not radioactive, is being recycled. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

This story by Olga Peters was first published in The Commons on Sept. 29, 2026. 
VERNON — PowerTransitions officials who held another community meeting on Sept. 23 faced community members who filled a meeting room, expressing skepticism and concern that Vernon could become home to an expensive, potentially hazardous energy installation.
Employees at the Texas-based company, which recently signed an option lease agreement with NorthStar to install an energy project on the 140-acre site of the former Vermont Yankee nuclear plant, arrived at the Governor Hunt House prepared to take feedback on a potential battery storage project.
PowerTransitions is considering using the Vermont Yankee property for a 110 MW to 440 MW battery energy storage system.
The company would negotiate an annual payment to the town, in addition to local and state taxes.
It operates multiple projects, including natural gas, and has redeveloped former energy facilities, such as the Quindaro Power Station in Kansas City, Kansas.
NorthStar is decommissioning the Vermont Yankee nuclear plant and preparing the property for redevelopment. Fifty-eight canisters of nuclear waste will remain on site.
“You have a very unique site here,” said PowerTransitions’ head of external affairs, Carrie Hitt. “It is electrically very interesting to people.”
“It housed one of the only large nuclear facilities in New England until very not too long ago, right?” she continued. “It’s very complicated. It’s very complex. It’s very interesting. I’m just going to say it’s very challenging.”

Zon Eastes and Laura Sibilia (standing behind those seated, from left), both state representatives, were among the attendees at a community meeting called by PowerTransitions to discuss uses for the former Vermont Yankee property. Eastes represents Vernon, while Sibilia, from Dover, is the Brattleboro Development Credit Corporation’s director of regional economic development strategies and programs. Photo by Olga Peters/The Commons

At times, the audience and PowerTransitions staff seemed as disconnected as the computer presentation that refused to open.
Several attendees expected to learn details about a specific project, but Hitt said that, with the company still exploring options for the site, nothing has been finalized.
Hitt said the company wants community support for any energy project it pursues before beginning the state permitting process that requires energy projects to earn a certificate of public good from the Vermont Public Utility Commission under Section 248 of the state’s statutes.
“We do want to work closely with the town and community before filing anything official,” she said.
“We view community engagement as essential and want to be fully engaged with the town long before we file for 248 — because we’re not going to file for 248, which is the statewide regulations for siting, if the town’s not in agreement with what we’re doing,” Hitt added.
Audience members raised concerns about the project’s potential use of river water for cooling, the risk of airborne toxins during a fire, and possible costs to the town if increased staffing, such as for the fire department, would become necessary.
Engineer and consultant Derek Porter explained that the battery energy storage system cooling uses a closed-loop system and therefore would not require water from the nearby Connecticut River.
Fire and battery safety expert Rocky Edwards told the audience that battery storage and fire-suppression technology have improved and that they have more safety features than current facilities do.
Recent fires at battery storage installations include two facilities in California: Moss Landing in 2025, a three-day blaze that caused $400 million of damage, and this year in La Verne, where a lithium-ion battery fire caused more than 500 residents to evacuate their homes, schools and businesses for days.
Community gives more feedback
Hitt said PowerTransitions decided not to pursue solar or data center projects after evaluating feedback from town officials and from those who attended an August community meeting.
Several audience members said they would prefer solar over a battery installation.
Hitt said the company is still investigating and will continue to seek community input before deciding the nature of the project and finalizing a design.
If a project moves forward, construction would begin in three to five years, she said.
The battery project would likely serve as an initial phase while the company develops a larger energy generation project for the site, Hitt said.
Hitt told the audience that PowerTransitions plans to hold additional community meetings. She emphasized that Vernon residents know the area best and understand what they want to protect — such as the Connecticut River.
“We’re just here sharing information because we’re trying to move through the process and see what the questions are, where the concerns are,” she said. “We’re trying to get that feedback from all of you so that we can put a plan together.”

name: WyoFile
title: Fremont County avoids EMT strike after extending contract
description:
The new two-year deal buys time to shift first-responder services under local government control while addressing employee needs, parties say.
The post Fremont County avoids EMT strike after extending contract appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The union representing 30 emergency medical technicians and paramedics serving Fremont County cancelled plans to strike later this week after the county extended its contract with their employer as a stop-gap measure.
Organized under United Steel Workers Local 9012, the first-responders originally planned to walk out Monday and then postponed the strike to Thursday. The union officially stood down Wednesday, however, a day after Fremont County commissioners inked a new two-year contract with the bargaining group’s employer, Tennessee-based Priority Ambulance, which operates as Frontier Ambulance in the county.
Although the new contract includes a series of raises for the workers and an increase to their health savings account, “It was never about money,” United Steel Workers Staff Representative William Wilkinson told WyoFile. “It was about the safety of this community.”
Fremont County was paying Priority $1.9 million annually. Under the new contract, the county will pay about $2.3 million the first year and $2.4 million the second year, according to Fremont County Commissioner Mike Jones, who helped negotiate the contract. Those totals include a 5% salary increase for EMTs the first year and 4% the second year.
Nobody is 100% satisfied with the deal, Jones told WyoFile, “But at the end of the day, I think you hold to the faith that everybody wants ambulance service to continue on Oct. 1.” 
Messy negotiations
Normally, the union negotiates directly with the employer, Priority, and the county negotiates separately with Priority on its contract. But those independent negotiations became complicated because the county and the first responders share a common goal to eventually end their relationships with Priority and move the service under local government control.
The commission earlier this year signed a memorandum of understanding with towns in the county to shift EMT services under the Fremont County Association of Governments — a move that would better serve everyone, including tribal governments and the first responders, according to both county and union representatives who spoke with WyoFile. To help pay for it, Fremont County voters passed a ¾-cent sales tax in August.
Revenue from the new tax won’t begin arriving until the spring, however, and the county’s contract with Priority was set to expire Oct. 1. The separate negotiations both went sideways. The county wanted a short-term contract with Priority to fill the gap until the association can take over, and the union workers, Wilkinson said, found it difficult to gain traction on their interests.
A paramedic loads a gurney into an ambulance at Cody Regional Health. (Madelyn Beck/WyoFile) 
In the maw of fraught bargaining and positioning, commissioners flirted with an offer from Cody Regional Health to fill the gap. That angered first responders because, among other things, the proposed arrangement would not allow them to continue with union representation. Local 9012 promised to strike. 
But with the contract set to expire and the threat of a strike looming, all three parties found themselves at the negotiating table.
“Since it was down to the wire, it was really a three-party deal,” Wilkinson said.
The union is generally pleased with the outcome, he added, because it’s a nod from the county that the EMTs can maintain union bargaining power — a necessity given that first responders in Fremont County have continuously had to work long hours due to insufficient staffing. Plus, both Wilkinson and Jones agreed, the new two-year contract buys time for the Fremont County Association of Governments to prepare to take on the service. Doing so requires obtaining multiple certifications, as well as training and infrastructure for the nuts-and-bolts of managing the business side of EMT services — from scheduling shifts to bidding for equipment and supplies.
“You need administration — you need all kinds of stuff that you just can’t do overnight,” Wilkinson said.
The higher dollar figures under the new Priority contract have already raised some eyebrows, Jones said. Some of it can be chalked up to folding in some costs that were already coming back to the county and other entities under the old contract, he said. Other factors are simply the rising cost of providing the service.
“Yes, it’s an increase,” Jones said. “But, you know, fuel costs have gone up. Everything’s gone up. It’s inflationary.”
