name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: 6 takeaways from the 5th Congressional District candidates’ forum
description: Candidates running for Congress in Louisiana’s crowded 5th District race had the sharpest disagreements over artificial intelligence regulation and economic development at a forum held Tuesday night at the University of Louisiana-Monroe.
text:
The U.S. Capitol building in Washington, D.C., amid fog on Tuesday, Dec. 10, 2024. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)Candidates running for Congress in Louisiana’s crowded 5th District race had the sharpest disagreements over artificial intelligence regulation and economic development at a forum held Tuesday night at the University of Louisiana-Monroe.
Seven of the nine candidates on the ballot for the Nov. 3 primary election participated in the event sponsored by several Northeast Louisiana broadcasters, Monroe-area business groups and the university.
They are running to replace U.S. Rep. Julia Letlow of Baton Rouge, the Republican nominee for U.S. Senate who is not running for reelection. The 5th District covers all or part of 24 parishes.
Here are six takeaways from the event:
1. Most candidates back AI rules but offer few specifics.
Six of the seven candidates said they think it’s appropriate for Congress to have some oversight of the burgeoning yet already powerful artificial intelligence industry. But most weren’t very specific about what restrictions they would like to see.
Democrat Dan McKay, an attorney from Bunkie, was the most precise of the group, calling for a moratorium on data center construction. Austin Magee, a Franklinton Republican who owns a welding business, also shared a similar skepticism about data centers, several of which are already under construction in the 5th District.
“I don’t necessarily like these data centers, solar farms, things like that, that really don’t create, in the end, very many jobs,” Magee said. “Maybe a lot of initial construction jobs, but at the end of the day, they don’t really improve our way of life.”
State Rep. Michael Echols, R-Monroe, said he would be in favor of some AI regulation, though he mentioned restrictions on which there is typically some agreement already. There should be laws passed to protect children from AI and to regulate “deepfakes,” which are AI content generated to mimic real people, he said.
State Rep. Gabe Firment, R-Pollock, said he was opposed to the government taking private property in order to facilitate powering the data centers that support the AI industry.
“We do not need to be seizing property to benefit private businesses,” Firment said.
State Sen. Stewart Cathey, R-Monroe, stood out as the candidate most wary of placing restrictions on AI. He said he worried that too many restrictions could push AI developers to other countries and create a national security crisis.
“I’d rather them be here in America than in China,” Cathey said.
2. Nuclear power could meet growing energy needs.
Cathey, Echols and Louisiana Board of Regents chair Misti Cordell, a Republican from Monroe, all mentioned nuclear power as a solution for meeting the AI industry’s enormous power needs.
“Nuclear is something that’s very effective, and it’s also clean,” Cordell said.
Echols and Cathey said they favor development of small nuclear reactors, which President Donald Trump has also pushed during his second term in office. As a legislator, Echols even sponsored a resolution in 2025 to study small nuclear reactors at the state level.
3. Prohibit farm sales to foreign countries.
All of the participants, seven Republicans and two Democrats, said they would support a ban on foreign countries owning U.S. farmland. This issue is particularly pertinent in the 5th District, where agriculture is a major industry.
4. Restrict members of Congress from trading stocks.
The candidates agreed there should be more restrictions on members of Congress trading stocks.
“All of our elected officials, from the top to the bottom, we should not be profiting from information that we receive,” state Rep. Pat Moore, D-Monroe, said.
Cathey and McKay said there could be some narrow allowances for mutual funds, blind trusts and other investing mechanisms where members of Congress don’t directly manage their trades. Magee said a “complete ban” on stock trading by lawmakers would be appropriate.
The topic is particularly relevant because Letlow has been criticized for trading Meta and AI-related stock after she signed a nondisclosure agreement related to the expansive data center project in Richland Parish. Letlow has said she was unaware the stocks were being traded on her behalf at the time.
5. Privatize Social Security for younger workers.
Every candidate at the forum said Congress needs to protect Social Security benefits for seniors when asked at the forum, while Echols and Firment said it would be appropriate to look at “private alternatives” for workers in their 20s and 30s.
Echols mentioned conservative mutual funds as an option.
“There needs to be … a bifurcated effort to make sure that we have some market-driven solutions, but then protect those that are receiving the benefit today,” Echols said.
6. Candidates mostly avoid Trump as a topic.
The candidates mostly avoided mentioning the president during the 75-minute forum.
The only Republican who said Trump’s name was Echols, who briefly said he had been in Washington, D.C., when the president signed a ratepayer protection pledge meant to protect consumers from paying for data center power usage. But he didn’t dwell on the president’s role in the issue.
Only McKay made a direct reference to Trump, saying he influenced his decision to seek the 5th District seat.
“One of my main goals in running, and one of my main goals in Congress, will be to get control of Donald Trump. He is the worst thing that has happened to this country, and I will fight him,” McKay said in his closing remarks.
The four Republicans who gave their closing remarks after McKay — Cathey, Cordell, Echols and Magee — did not respond to his attack on the president.
– Antonio Wilson, a Democrat from Tallulah, and Omar Dantzler, a Republican from Hammond, did not take part in the forum.

name: National
title: States OK solar panels for balconies. Safety guidelines haven’t caught up.
description: Over the past year and a half, a dozen states have embraced a new vision for solar power: small, cheap panels that can be hung from a balcony or porch, be plugged into a standard wall outlet and take a dent out of residents’ utility bills.  These systems, known as balcony solar or plug-in solar, […]
text:
Solar energy panels hang from a residential apartment balcony in Erfurt, Germany. Balcony solar systems have become popular in Germany, and some state lawmakers believe the technology has huge potential in the United States. (Photo by Sean Gallup/Getty Images)Over the past year and a half, a dozen states have embraced a new vision for solar power: small, cheap panels that can be hung from a balcony or porch, be plugged into a standard wall outlet and take a dent out of residents’ utility bills. 
These systems, known as balcony solar or plug-in solar, are attractive because they can be installed without permits, contractors or large investments. They can allow renters to tap into clean electricity. 
Lawmakers say the systems can help at a time when residents’ power bills are skyrocketing and utilities are struggling to keep pace with demand. They also can be paired with a battery, which can provide backup power during area outages. 
Backers see a future in which solar panels deployed across millions of balconies, porches and yards could ease strain on the electrical grid and save residents hundreds of dollars each year on their power bills. 
Twelve states — Republican and Democratic alike — have recently passed bills authorizing residents to install such systems. Nine have been signed into law, while three are awaiting signatures from a governor. 
But for most Americans, even some in states that have passed laws, the systems still sit in a legal gray area. That’s because the “plug and play” simplicity that creates balcony solar’s appeal might not yet work safely with most household electrical systems, experts and utilities say. Work is underway to develop industry standards for such products, and advocates agree that such guidelines are necessary to draw manufacturers to the U.S. market. 
Backers say that plug-in solar systems have a long track record of operating safely in Germany and other countries, and argue that it’s imperative for the standards to allow for products that do not require a permit, home upgrades or a certified electrician to install. 
Meanwhile, power utilities haven’t strongly opposed the bills, though some have expressed concerns that unregistered systems could affect power flows or endanger line workers. 
For all the legislative action to boost balcony solar, advocates say the market won’t take off until safety groups give the all-clear for systems that don’t require red tape or electrical upgrades. 
Solar bills
The recent burst of balcony solar bills kicked off in Utah. Republican state Rep. Ray Ward read an article about the balcony solar boom in Germany, where the devices have surged in popularity and are widely available in stores such as IKEA. 
In Germany, more than 1 million balcony solar systems have been installed across the country, providing more than 2 gigawatts of power — the equivalent of a large power plant. 
“I thought, ‘How come I cannot do that in Utah and in the U.S.?’” Ward said. 
In Utah, as in many states, putting any amount of power onto the grid requires a contract with a utility, an impossible barrier for the average homeowner. Ward’s bill removes that requirement for solar panels up to 1,200 watts, roughly the amount of power used by a hair dryer. 
The bill passed unanimously through both houses of the Utah legislature last year, and Ward has balcony solar at his home. But the law also requires systems to meet National Electrical Code and Underwriters Laboratories certification standards, guidelines that are still in development.
“The safety standards don’t exist, even though the products are plainly safe,” Ward said. “There is a way to make it safe, as Germany has shown, and we’ve just got to get safety standards in place here.”
Since Utah’s bill became law, state lawmakers across the country have drafted similar bills. 
Many of the bills also prevent landlords and homeowners associations from restricting balcony solar. And many also seek to establish safety guidelines for the technology. 
“These things are just easy, simple, affordable, permitless ways to generate your own electricity — in whatever your living arrangement is — that enables everyone to contribute to reducing energy consumption in our country,” said Virginia state Sen. Scott Surovell, a Democrat. 
His bill drew bipartisan support and was signed into law in April. 
In New York, a bill passed in May awaits action by Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul.
Relief from energy bills unlikely as utilities request billions in rate hikes

“These solar panels could help you save 10% of your electricity bill each month, which is significant considering how much costs are going up,” said New York state Sen. Liz Krueger, a Democrat who sponsored the balcony solar bill. “In New York city, a huge percentage of us are renters, and up until now there’s been no way for us to participate in green energy or energy lowering projects.”
Krueger said Hochul may ask for some small technical changes, which lawmakers are prepared to adopt.
Colorado enacted a new law in May. 
“With power prices going up, people are wanting to find a way to be able to participate and have some control over their own energy,” said Colorado state Sen. Cathy Kipp, a Democrat who sponsored the measure. “As more states adopt it, it will drive down costs, which will further increase adoption.” 
Connecticut, Maine, Maryland, New Hampshire, New Jersey and Vermont have also enacted balcony solar laws since 2025. Bills in California and Massachusetts have passed and sit on the governor’s desk. 
The state measures have been supported by Bright Saver, a nonprofit advocacy group that envisions 60 million balcony solar panels deployed across the country by 2035. Cora Stryker, the group’s co-founder, said several lawmakers told her they’d never seen a measure go from an idea to a law so quickly. 
But the success of those new laws, she said, hinges on the development of safety standards that allow balcony solar systems to be simple “plug and play” devices. 
“The widespread adoption we’re talking about will only happen when we get out of this legal gray area and every American can feel confident that they can plug it in without contacting their utility,” she said. 
Bright Saver sells balcony solar systems at cost, offering 180-watt panels for $285 and 360-watt panels for $414. But it cannot sell to customers in some states that have passed solar legislation, because products don’t yet exist that can meet their safety certifications. 
Other companies sell kits online, but experts say it’s hard for customers to know if those devices meet safety thresholds. While backers do not have estimates for nationwide adoption totals, they say the numbers will remain low until balcony solar systems are widely available at popular retailers. 
Safety standards
Underwriters Laboratories, a global safety science company, recently issued certification standards that would require residents to modify circuits before plugging in devices — a hurdle that advocates fear could slow the adoption of balcony solar. 
The main concern, experts say, is that power outlets in U.S. homes are not designed to carry power in two directions. Sending electricity back into the system could bypass circuit protection devices, overloading wires and creating fire or shock hazards. 
“Some of these (bills and laws) are a little ahead of their time,” said Nadav Enbar, program manager at the nonprofit Electric Power Research Institute. “There isn’t yet a product that can meet the letter of the law.”
Some of the state laws call for products to achieve certification from Underwriters Laboratories. The company issued its certification program, known as an outline of investigation, in January.
States fast-track wind, solar permits and contracts to beat Trump’s deadline

While those guidelines are still working through a committee process — which could take a year or more — to be finalized as a permanent standard, the company says they still count as official certification for manufacturers seeking to comply with state laws. 
The current certification requires residents to modify circuits in their home to safely receive electricity. Electrical experts said it’s possible that manufacturers will eventually be able to develop balcony solar systems that address the circuit overload concerns with onboard technology.
“Could there in the future be another way to address these problems? Sure,” said Joe Bablo, principal engineering manager with UL Solutions, one of the three organizations that makes up Underwriters Laboratories. “Will the standard adapt to that? Of course.”
The certification also requires the use of a proprietary connector that ensures the blades will not continue carrying electricity after being unplugged from the wall. 
The National Electric Code offers another possibility for a widely accepted standard that manufacturers could follow, but new revisions to the code will not be issued until 2029.
Some utilities have also raised concerns about large-scale adoption affecting local power flows, or solar systems feeding power into the grid during blackouts and putting line workers at risk. Utility leaders have called for a program that requires balcony solar users to register or notify utilities when installing their devices. 
“We just need people to let us know what they’re plugging in, so we can track anything that feeds back into the grid and can be a danger to line workers,” said David Eisenhauer, spokesperson for the California power utility Southern California Edison.
The utility initially opposed the California bill, but adopted a neutral position after language was added to allow utilities to require registration of balcony solar units. 
Stateline reporter Alex Brown can be reached at abrown@stateline.org.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Education advocates to legislature: No cuts to Blueprint education plan
description: They acknowledged the looming budget shortfall, and said there have been challenges implementing the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, but the main theme of a meeting Tuesday on the state's sweeping education reform plan was plain: Don't cut it.
text:
Attendees raise their hands after Kenzie Funk, standing, a policy advocate for Strong Schools Maryland, asked a question about education during a community meeting at Elkridge Branch Library in Howard County. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)They acknowledged the looming budget shortfall, and said there have been challenges implementing the Blueprint for Maryland’s Future, the state’s sweeping education reform plan, but those weren’t the main themes at a meeting on the plan Tuesday.
“They better not cut it,” said Cheryl McLeod of Howard County after a two-hour meeting Tuesday night.
McLeod, a member of a nonprofit organization called World Class Grads, was among two dozen parents, educators, community leaders and others gathered at the Elkridge Branch Library to talk about education, with a specific focus on the Blueprint.
It was the latest in a series of meetings by the Blueprint Coalition, a collection of nonprofit organizations, community leaders and education advocates who support implementation of the 10-year, multibillion-dollar plan. Five years in, the costly plan is increasingly seen as a target for lawmakers grappling with budget issues in the 2027 legislative session.
The coalition has already held community sessions in Montgomery and Prince George’s counties. Another meeting is scheduled in Baltimore City and at least one more virtually in the next two months. The General Assembly convenes for the 2027 session Jan. 13.
“The main point of this conversation is that we stay connected and continue talking about it, especially as we lead up to the legislative session,” said Kenzie Funk, policy advocate for Strong Schools Maryland.
In respect to the Blueprint, some people said Tuesday that challenges in their communities include hiring and retaining staff, teacher preparation programs in higher education and larger class sizes.
Kali Schumitz representing as a member of the Fair Share Maryland coalition. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
A summary at the meeting outlined the five pillars, or priorities, of the plan: early childhood education; high-quality and diverse teachers and leaders; college and career readiness; more resources for students to be successful; and governance and accountability.
Those at the meeting acknowledged the state faces a projected $3 billion budget gap for the upcoming fiscal year, about $1.8 billion of which is tied to education under the Blueprint, according to the Maryland Associations of Counties (MACo).
The projected budget shortfall for fiscal 2028 also comes in the first year in which Blueprint costs will exceed dedicated revenues. To cover the balance, the state will have to dip into the general fund, as a first-in-the-nation digital ad tax that was supposed to help pay for the Blueprint remains in legal limbo.
At least one group will offer the General Assembly a solution to bring in revenue to help close the gap.
Fair Share Maryland, a coalition of 75 organizations, will renew its call for the passage of a tax package known as the Fair Share Act. The 2024 proposal included changes to corporate income tax reporting, increased taxes on the state’s wealthiest residents, more auditors and increased capital gains surcharges. Supporters claimed it could raise $1.6 billion when fully implemented.
“Those are the kinds of things that we’re trying to fix that could raise revenue,” said Kali Schumitz, director of communication with the Maryland Center on Economic Policy, part of the Fair Share Maryland coalition. “We’ve already been through several cycles of state budget cuts that are affecting a lot of different things already,”
Some changes, even if they’re minor, are already under review.
The Blueprint for Maryland’s Future Accountability and Implementation Board that oversees the 10-year plan is scheduled to meet Oct. 15 to discuss and possibly vote on recommended changes.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
One proposal in the 15-page document released this month includes increasing the annual appropriation for the prekindergarten expansion grant program. The General Assembly approved $10 million toward the program in this year’s fiscal budget.
Another proposal would be to allow health assistants lead after-school coverage under the supervision of a registered nurse. But the AIB document notes the Maryland Board of Nursing dictates whether a health assistant can lead an after-school program, even under a registered nurse’s supervision.
The Blueprint Coalition wants to partner and work with legislators, but members said Tuesday that any cuts to the Blueprint are not part of its agenda.
“Yes, it’s not perfect, but we need that funding to move forward, and then we can build upon it,” said Riya Gupta, executive director with Strong Schools Maryland. “But without that base, we’re not going anywhere. We’re going to take a step back because someone’s kid is losing out.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: What do braids, cornrows and Bantu knots have to do with the news?
description: Black journalists on TV have had to think about their appearance on air in ways that other journalists do not. In August 2020, broadcast journalist Jalea Brooks knew she needed to have an uncomfortable conversation with her news director about her hair. She had been working in Montgomery, Ala. for nearly four years and wanted […]
text:
WTHR anchor Jalea Brooks had to get permission to change her hairstyle for her on-air look early on in her career while working in a different market. (Courtesy WTHR)
Black journalists on TV have had to think about their appearance on air in ways that other journalists do not. In August 2020, broadcast journalist Jalea Brooks knew she needed to have an uncomfortable conversation with her news director about her hair. She had been working in Montgomery, Ala. for nearly four years and wanted to wear a new style on air: braids.
Previously, a white manager in Montgomery pulled Brooks aside and told her that if she wanted to continue anchoring, she would need a consistent look. She could choose her hairstyle, they said, but would need to stick with it. At the time, she was between looks and had her natural Black hair pulled back into a bun. 
“I could read between the lines, and I understood what he meant by that,” she said. “And I definitely knew that sticking to the status quo felt like the safest option.” Straight hair, she felt, was that safe option and it was stated in her contract that she would need to get permission to change her look in the future. 
Because of that conversation early in her career, years later Brooks said she was hesitant to approach her news director in Montgomery about her desire to wear braids on air. However, she felt empowered by other Black journalists who were choosing to do the same. After talking to her news director and showing pictures of the style she would like to wear, she was given approval to wear braids and started doing so in August 2020.
She accepted a new job as anchor at WTHR here in Indy in December 2020, and she knew she wanted to have an upfront conversation about on-air appearance, specifically her hair and her desire to wear different styles. She was assured by her new boss that the way she wanted to wear her hair was her choice. Since then, every subsequent news director at the station has also supported her right to wear her hair how she chooses.
This issue is about much more than individual journalists’ personal choices. How Brooks and other Black journalists wear their hair has wider implications for Indy news consumers. The reason we watch local TV news is to hear the truth about our community from journalists who are members of our community. Newsrooms strive to reflect the people they serve. If the journalists sharing those stories conform to only white standards of beauty and professionalism, that comes at a cost. Viewers are less equipped to understand and relate to all of the people they encounter in their communities. 
Also, representation matters. Presenting only straight, shoulder-length hair and thin body types as the standard is a distortion of our community and a disservice to it.
A risk worth taking: Indiana does not have a CROWN Act
Any time you see a Black TV journalist with braids, locs, or other natural hairstyles, know that they are taking a risk. This state does not protect them by law from discrimination because of their hair texture.
(Courtesy banner)
State Rep. Vanessa Summers (D-Indianapolis) tried to get such a law through the legislature in 2023. It was Indiana’s version of the CROWN Act, short for “Creating a Respectful and Open World for Natural Hair.” It prevents employers from discriminating against workers because of their hair texture, including Black hairstyles. It also protects people seeking housing and students in school settings. Thirty states have passed similar laws since California first adopted the policy in 2019.

When Summers introduced the bill, her fellow representatives in the Indiana General Assembly did not support it. She could not get a hearing for HB1284. It did not make it out of the education committee. Committee chair Rep. Robert Behning (R-Indianapolis) responded with a flat “no” when he was asked to consider it. As a Black woman, Summers could relate to the legislation and said she wanted to help women statewide and her constituents in District 99, where 52% are female and 37% are Black.

“I’ve had every hairstyle and every color that you can have, and I understood some of the discrimination you can get from having your hair a certain way,” Summers told me.

With today’s political climate, she said the measure is probably a nonstarter, but she will resurrect it in the next legislative session. Summers said it will take bipartisan support and a white female ally to at least give it a hearing and allow it to gain publicity, which she would count as “moving the needle a little bit.” Further success would be an “uphill battle,” she said, with the state legislature currently split 70 to 30, Republicans to Democrats.

Research documents that bias against Black journalists’ natural hairstyles is real. A 2023 CROWN Workplace Research Study, co-commissioned by Dove and LinkedIn, found that Black women’s hair is twice as likely to be perceived as unprofessional as non-Black hair. Studies in 2024, by a researcher at Indiana University-Purdue University Indiana, found that Black women did not want to work for companies with dress codes that restrict their hair choices. These dress codes sent a message that they could not be authentically themselves in the workplace, along with acting as a signal that Black women would overall not be valued in that workplace.
Even as the formal rules governing the hair styles of women in TV news have receded, Black journalists say they remain wary. 

“Culture’s obviously going to be much harder to change than a piece of paperwork, but it is the most important step at the same time, right?” said Jasmine Beecham, who penned her PhD thesis, “Dress to Repress: Exploring How Dress Codes and Norms Harm Black Women in the Workplace.” By showing up to work with an array of hairstyles, Black journalists can help reshape cultural norms, making Indianapolis employers and residents more accepting of everyone in the community, she told me.
For better or worse, looks matter on TV news 
WTHR’s Brooks said that Hoosiers’ perception of her professional abilities matters. As a TV journalist she believes appearance is a big component of how she is perceived. 

“I would love to say that no, it shouldn’t matter, the journalism should matter, the story, the communities that we cover matter, but, no, it absolutely does,” she said. Being in a highly visible occupation leaves her open to public comments about her choices in clothes, makeup and hairstyles. Since coming to Indy, she’s received overwhelmingly positive feedback from viewers. She changes hairstyles often. For Brooks, straight hair has been the anomaly.

I want to hear from you. Please write to me at indypubliceditor@poynter.org.

“So much so, that when I did actually wear my hair straight—after months, maybe even a full year on the job—I would often get questions of concern on whether my station ‘made me’ change my hair, to which I would tell them, no, the choice was my own,” Brooks said. “But, I absolutely understood why that would be a concern, as that has been a reality for other TV journalists.”
Former WRTV anchor and multimedia journalist Naja Woods embraced her natural hair long before launching her broadcasting career in South Bend, Ind. She started as a producer and transitioned to an on-air role. Woods, who wore her natural hair curly, was nervous about reporting the news in braids when she decided to change up her look.
“I didn’t know, it’s like, ‘are braids unprofessional on air?’” she asked herself at the time. “So all that went through my mind. I looked up examples of other Black women wearing their hair in braids, and I just went for it and never turned back.”
The positive reception she received from viewers of all ages was confirmation that she made the right choice.
“If I did anything with kids, in particular kids of color, little Black girls, they would say, ‘oh, I really love your hair,’ and, ‘that’s so cool that you wear your hair like that, if I get on TV, I want to wear my hair like that,’” Woods said. “Even parents or grandparents will come up to me and be like, ‘you’re really an inspiration’ because not only do I wear my hair naturally primarily, I’m a dark-skinned woman as well. They would say that was really inspiring to their grandkids or kids, stuff like that, so that was cool.”
Woods said she’s never had an issue with station management anywhere she’s worked. 

“I’m not going to straighten my hair, put constant heat on my hair just to please somebody else,” she said. Woods said she would change stations if it came to an ultimatum, but she would stay in the industry because she does believe natural hair has become more accepted.
Representation in newsrooms is a window into communities
You’re seeing more journalists with Black natural hairstyles. It’s a movement that was slowly gaining ground, starting with hashtags like #FreeTheCurls in 2019. After the protests and movement that was sparked following the murder of George Floyd in 2020, the hashtag #BlackHairOnAir went viral. Black female on-air journalists and meteorologists started posting photos of themselves reporting the news in braids, afros, cornrows, Bantu knots and other natural hairstyles.

In 2026, with Black women of all occupations losing jobs due to the political climate, and the backlash against diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives, we don’t want our journalists to feel pressured to censor how they show up on air. 

Telling diverse stories and presenting the many faces of a community is a tool for helping Hoosiers understand and relate to the people around us. When the storytellers can express their own style and show their authentic selves, the stories resonate.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: New Hampshire’s sluggish housing growth is leading to longer commutes, report suggests
description: There is a growing gap in New Hampshire between how much it costs for housing and how much residents are earning — and nowhere is it clearer than in the cities. In Lebanon, the hourly wage needed for one person to afford median rent in the city in 2026 is $47.06. But the statewide average […]
text:
The cost of housing in New Hampshire has continued to climb — and the gap between housing costs and what residents are earning keeps getting wider. Here, affordable housing is under construction in Hanover in July 2021. (Bulletin file photo by Amanda Gokee/New Hampshire Bulletin)There is a growing gap in New Hampshire between how much it costs for housing and how much residents are earning — and nowhere is it clearer than in the cities.
In Lebanon, the hourly wage needed for one person to afford median rent in the city in 2026 is $47.06. But the statewide average median hourly wage, as of June 2025, was $25.29.
And $47.06 per hour is more than the average in New Hampshire for many essential workers: Registered nurses make an average of $45.49 per hour; electricians make $30.50; and childcare workers make $16.26.
The numbers, included in a new report by New Hampshire Housing, underscore a trend. As median home prices continue to hit record highs, workers in the Granite State are increasingly being priced out of the cities they serve.
Lebanon presents the starkest example of the high cost of rent, but other cities are not far behind, the report found. In Portsmouth, the hourly wage required to afford the median rent is $46.23 an hour; in Nashua it is $41.12; and in Dover it is $40.71 — each far above the $25.29 state median.
In 11 of New Hampshire’s 13 cities, the median rent in that city exceeds the state’s median wage, the report found. Just Franklin and Berlin defied that trend. The needed wages were determined by limiting spending on rent to 30% of income, the maximum level experts advise.
The report, titled “Housing is New Hampshire’s Future,” presents a number of data points indicating that New Hampshire’s housing scarcity is having measurable effects on employees, businesses and the broader economy. 
As workers increasingly face higher rents in cities, more and more are forced to commute to their jobs, leading to burnout and thoughts of moving. Those living in apartments whose rents have not drastically increased are unwilling to leave them, reducing opportunities for new employees to move in. And the overall shortage has stymied businesses’ ability to attract talent and thinned the ranks of workers essential to thriving cities, like home health aides and nurses, the report warns. 
“The effects of inadequate housing supply and housing choices are all around us,” said Rob Dapice, executive director and CEO of New Hampshire Housing, the quasi-public agency that conducts research and helps distribute federal housing grants, in an interview. 
Affordability gap has widened since the pandemic
For decades, New Hampshire’s median income has steadily increased year after year, and housing prices have kept pace.
But the New Hampshire Housing analysis shows a dramatic shift after the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, in 2020. As wealthier out-of-state homebuyers sent New Hampshire housing prices skyrocketing, the amount of income needed to afford a home in the Granite State suddenly increased at a faster rate than the median income. That trend has persisted for six years, creating a yawning chasm between median incomes and home prices in New Hampshire that has begun to slow, but is not yet shrinking.
In 2026, the gap between the median annual income needed to buy a home — $160,885 — and the actual median income in the state — $103,983 — is $56,902.
Meanwhile, with median housing prices nearing $600,000, the percentage of New Hampshire homeowners who can afford that median price tag is 26%. Just 6% of renters, who don’t have homes to sell to help with down payments, can afford that median currently.
Some counties, like Strafford and Carroll, have worse ratios of home prices to incomes than others, like Coös. But median home prices in all counties currently exceed median incomes.
“Your businesses, your economic tax base needs employees, and to have employees, you need housing,” Dapice said. 
In cities, housing stock not keeping up with jobs
In many of New Hampshire’s biggest population centers, it is not just the price of available homes keeping people out. It is also the number.
In Portsmouth, the report found, there are 3.37 jobs for every one nonseasonal house. In Lebanon there are 2.82 jobs per home, in Bedford 2.45 and in Concord 2.21.
It is normal for job centers to have slightly more employees than housing units. But one urban planner, Reid Ewing, a professor at the University of Utah, has said the ideal ratio is between 1.3 and 1.7 jobs per home. Some New Hampshire cities, like Keene, Manchester and Nashua, are in that range, the New Hampshire Housing report found, but many exceed it.
The ratios suggest that larger than ideal numbers of workers are commuting into places like Lebanon and Portsmouth, the report notes.
That “commute tax,” in turn, drives up transportation costs for workers, delays for employers and burnout. And it prevents potential economic cohesion, known as agglomeration, that allows certain areas to thrive, experts warn.
“It enriches the life of the community when you have people who serve the community who can also live there,” Dapice said. 
No quick fixes
Facing those structural barriers, some New Hampshire employers are turning to remote work, the report notes. But New Hampshire Housing said the proportion of remote work jobs in New Hampshire was just 16% in 2024, and remote flexibility is not feasible in many professions.
“Remote work cannot staff an operating room,” the report states. 
Nor, the report argues, can employers solve the problem on their own by financing housing. Through a series of interviews with state businesses, New Hampshire Housing highlighted some examples: the CEO of Monadnock Community Hospital, Richard Scheinblum, said he bought a condo to lease it to a physician. “I don’t want to be in the property management business,” Scheinblum said, according to the report. And such approaches “reach only a small share of the workforce,” the report notes. 
There are some reasons for optimism in the housing market, Dapice said, such as a rise in the number of housing permits in New Hampshire that suggests an uptick in construction, and the eventual effect of a series of pro-housing zoning overhaul laws from 2025. 
New Hampshire Housing has projected for years that the state needs more than 90,000 housing units by 2040 to keep up with its population. Its report noted that the state is making progress: Between 2020 and 2025, developers built 39% of the housing units needed by 2030, and 25% of those needed by 2040.
Some counties have made a bigger dent than others: Between 2020 and 2025, Coös had already built 72.9% of its proportionate share of the statewide units needed by 2040, while Rockingham had built 25% and Hillsborough — which requires the largest number of new housing units as the most populous county — had built 22.9%, according to the report. 
But Dapice said the economic argument for housing from businesses is still fighting to be heard. And more and more, businesses should sound the alarm themselves, he said. 
“I think there is tons of opportunity there,” he said. “If we can go from like 1% of employers talking about it to their local select board and city council to 3%, I think that will really move the needle.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: No fines against Indiana retailers so far for SNAP violations
description: No Indiana retailers have been fined since the state banned the purchase of candy or soda using Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits. A spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Food and Nutrition Administration said the agency has taken action 61 times this year against Indiana retailers for either criminal or administrative violat[...]
text:
The federal government hasn't issued any enforcement actions related to its pop and candy ban against Indian retailers (Photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)No Indiana retailers have been fined since the state banned the purchase of candy or soda using Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits.
A spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Food and Nutrition Administration said the agency has taken action 61 times this year against Indiana retailers for either criminal or administrative violations, but none have been related to the state’s SNAP restrictions pop and junk food.
Gov. Mike Braun issued an executive order last year directing the Indiana Family and Social Services Administration, which administers SNAP benefits, to apply for a federal waiver allowing the state to restrict the use of SNAP electronic benefits transfer cards to purchase candy or soft drinks.
The order states that “despite the program’s purpose of providing a more nutritious diet to low-income households, soda is the number one commodity purchased with SNAP benefits, and purchases of sweetened beverages, desserts, and candy exceed the combined sales of fruits and vegetables with SNAP benefits.”
It further claims children enrolled in SNAP consume 43% more sugary drinks than similarly situated peers, putting them at risk of obesity, heart disease, type 2 diabetes and hypertension.
Indiana is one of 18 states approved by the USDA to test restrictions on the use of SNAP benefits to purchase unhealthy foods as part of President Donald Trump’s “Make America Healthy Again” campaign.
‘A pain’: SNAP retailers, shoppers pan Indiana sugary drinks, candy ban

 
Each state sets its own rules for which foods are no longer SNAP eligible — a source of confusion for retailers with stores in multiple states where SNAP restrictions differ.
Even within a state the definitions are something confusing, including Indiana.
The state defines soft drinks as non-alcoholic beverages made with natural or artificial sweeteners, unless those drinks contain milk, milk substitutes or were sweetened exclusively with juice.
Candy products prepared with sugar, honey or other sweeteners mixed with chocolate, nuts, fruit or flavorings are no longer SNAP eligible, unless the products require refrigeration.
Federal law already prohibits the sale of hot meals, alcoholic beverages or tobacco products paid for with SNAP benefits.
Retailers were given a 90-day grace period after Indiana’s waiver took effect in January to update product codes and verify which foods met the state’s definition of “candy” or “soft drinks.”
Months after the grace period ended, a federal judge blocked SNAP waivers in Colorado, Iowa, Nebraska, Tennessee and West Virginia, finding the waivers unlawful because the USDA did not have authority to redefine “food” or eliminate entire categories of food already authorized by Congress as SNAP eligible.
Joe Lackey, president of the Indiana Grocery and Convenience Store Association, said the USDA may be wary to enforce waivers in other states as a result.
“The courts could come back and force Indiana to stop doing what they did,” he said.
A spokesperson for the USDA said the agency continues to monitor each state where it has approved a SNAP waiver, excluding the five states affected by the federal court ruling.
Failure to comply with Indiana’s waiver could result in the USDA withdrawing a retailer’s authorization to accept SNAP benefits in Indiana, though the agency will first issue a warning.
The waiver will remain in effect through 2027 unless state officials apply for a renewal. The Food and Nutrition Administration division of the USDA will monitor results from waiver states in the meantime.
Lackey said some retailers confided in him that it’s become impractical to continue participating in SNAP, between state waivers and a new rule adopted by the USDA in May doubling minimum stocking requirements for basic food groups.
“In a smaller store like a convenience store or a neighborhood guide market, that in some cases makes it just not feasible to be in the program anymore,” he said, adding: “Our clerks and our stores are the ones who have to do all the education (for SNAP recipients), because they come in the store, they have their card and they say, ‘Well, what do you mean I can’t buy this? What do you mean I can’t buy chocolate chips? That’s not candy.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Could MLK Corridor title help revitalize Bridgeport’s East End?
description: The East End is one of seven CT areas designated as a Martin Luther King, Jr. Corridor, a program intended to stimulate economic development.
text:
In the 1970s, Stratford Avenue, one of the main arteries running through Bridgeport’s East End, was designated as Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Boulevard.
The name has honored King’s legacy, but a state designation could now give the neighborhood an opportunity to put that name to work in a more tangible way — bringing attention to economic development, investment and opportunities for the people who live and work along it.
The East End is one of seven areas in the state designated as a Martin Luther King, Jr. Corridor under a program intended to promote secured and unsecured lending and stimulate economic development. Other municipalities with these corridors include Middletown, New Britain and Norwalk. 
“The designation gives the East End an opportunity to focus attention and resources on the neighborhood,” said Kelvin Ayala, an urban planner and economic development strategist with LBU & Associates, which is serving as the lead local organization for the Bridgeport effort.
The designation can also give applicants additional weight when seeking future state grants and funding, according to the Connecticut Department of Banking.
A separate East End streets study is examining issues on Stratford and Connecticut avenues like pedestrian safety, transit, bicycle access and improvements that could also support future economic development.
Councilman Ernie Newton, who represents the East End, said he is open to development that strengthens the neighborhood. “If there’s a way to generate more revenue, improve on what we’re doing, I’m all in,” Newton said.
For Newton, part of that vision is bringing back the kind of neighborhood he remembers growing up in, where residents could find many of the services and businesses they needed close to home.

Businesses and vacant storefronts are seen on Stratford Avenue in the East End of Bridgeport on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

The neighborhood has long sought basic services, including a grocery store and bank. Honey Locust Square, a long-delayed project on Stratford Avenue, now has an M&T Bank branch, while a Gala Foods supermarket and other businesses remain part of the planned development. The project has received nearly $4.5 million in city, state and federal support, but has faced years of delays and financial challenges.
Opportunities for growth
The stretch of Stratford Avenue that runs through the center of the East End is only open to eastbound traffic, while Connecticut Avenue to the north provides only westbound traffic access. Some residents and business owners have in the past complained about the one-way designation and the limits it places on access to the local businesses that make up the commercial corridor.
Bill Coleman, deputy director of Bridgeport’s Office of Planning & Economic Development, said the city’s work on Stratford Avenue is intended to complement the MLK Corridor effort. The city has been working with East End leaders and state lawmakers on a plan to convert Stratford Avenue to two-way traffic and redesign Connecticut Avenue to include a two-way protected bicycle track.
“The thought is to really try to recreate, particularly on Stratford Avenue, the MLK Boulevard, a neighborhood street that is supportive of a higher quality of life for residents and of a higher degree of neighborhood-based commerce,” Coleman said.
The avenue also connects the neighborhood to downtown Bridgeport on the west and continues east into the town of Stratford, where it opens to two-way traffic. Local planners and community leaders see the designation as an opportunity to build on what is already there and bring more investment, jobs and opportunities to the area.
For some East End business owners, the neighborhood already has something that can’t be created through a development plan: a strong sense of community. Syed Imran, who has operated ELA Discount on Stratford Avenue for 21 years, said neighbors regularly look out for one another.
“If you treat them better… they help you. They will look after you. Like I look after them,” Imran said. Despite what he sees as negative perceptions of the area, Imran said he remains invested in the neighborhood. “I love this neighborhood. I have no problem,” he said. “Just people got a wrong conception about this area.”
Ayala said the designation creates an opportunity to build on the East End’s existing strengths.
“The broader objective is to create a stronger local economy,” Ayala said.
Ayala said the goal is to support existing businesses and create opportunities for residents to build wealth. LBU has divided the Bridgeport effort into three areas: public art and beautification, small business and workforce development, and real estate investment and economic development.
Keith Williams, head of the East End Neighborhood Revitalization Zone, said they need investment in several areas, particularly housing and infrastructure. “We need more for housing… and more businesses in the neighborhood,” Williams said.

East End resident Cherie Oeea, left, and a friend talk outside a vacant building on Stratford Avenue in Bridgeport on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

He said improvements to Stratford Avenue, including the proposal to convert part of the corridor to two-way traffic, could help bring more activity to the area and support local businesses. Unlike other more high-density neighborhoods in the city, there is also some vacant land along the avenue that can provide opportunities for further development.
Coleman said the city views the MLK Corridor as complementary to its existing work, including efforts to improve infrastructure and complete projects such as Honey Locust Square. He said the goal is for Stratford Avenue to become a place where people spend time and do business.
“You don’t want to see Stratford Avenue and the MLK Corridor as a place you go through, but rather see it as a place you go to or that you live alongside,” Coleman said.
LBU is exploring ideas that could include helping entrepreneurs start and expand businesses, identifying opportunities for vacant properties, connecting residents with jobs and creating new public spaces along the corridor.
The designation itself does not guarantee those projects will happen. Instead, Bridgeport will have to use the designation to pursue investment and funding from other sources. Ayala said the goal is to bring together state and local officials, community organizations, businesses and residents around a common economic development strategy while building on what residents have already said they want.
Pastor Carl McCluster, senior pastor at Shiloh Baptist Church and managing director of the Freedom Faith Collaborative, which helped establish Connecticut’s MLK Corridor program, said Bridgeport’s success will depend on making the process broad and collaborative.
“It shouldn’t be a political prize, and should be an adventure in collaborative work in the community instead,” McCluster said.
Norwalk’s efforts
The state created the MLK Corridor designation in 2016, but expanded it in 2024 to increase the number of corridors the banking commissioner could designate from three to seven. 

A sign marking local streets in the East End of Bridgeport on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Matt Smith, the banking department’s director of government affairs and public policy, said the department only adds the designation and other agencies and organizations can consider it when awarding grants or other funding.
“There is no money associated with it,” Smith said. “We do not administer any money.”
Smith said the Department of Banking does not track whether other agencies use the designation when making funding decisions, so the department does not have data showing how often the designation has helped communities secure additional funding.
Rep. Kadeem Roberts, D-Norwalk, who has been involved in that city’s MLK Corridor work, said the designation became part of a broader local planning and investment effort that included public art, trees, walkways and bike infrastructure. Roberts said artists were brought into the process to create murals and other artwork reflecting Black history and culture in the neighborhood.
Norwalk’s corridor includes about two miles of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Drive and surrounding streets near the South Norwalk train station.

A sign marking welcomes visitors and residents to the East End of Bridgeport on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Roberts also pointed to a $14 million federal RAISE grant that Norwalk received in 2024 for improvements along MLK Drive and six surrounding roadways near the South Norwalk train station. 
McCluster said the designation was created to bring residents together on economic development efforts and help leverage additional resources.
“I think you have to learn how to really bring the community together and to leverage a small amount that you have,” McCluster said. He pointed to Norwalk, where about $3 million in state funding helped leverage roughly $30 million for improvements, including facade work for longtime homeowners along the corridor.
Norwalk has used the broader MLK Corridor initiative to support other investments as well. Since 2019, the city says it has identified more than $7.6 million in priority investments in economic and community development, education, housing and safety, with funding from local, state and federal sources. Those efforts have included residential facade improvements, low-interest home improvement loans, streetscape projects and support for minority- and women-owned businesses.
Bridgeport’s vision
In Bridgeport, Ayala sees several ways the corridor could help the area grow and build on existing plans.
One idea being explored through the local effort is creating a pocket park near Stratford Avenue and Sixth Street on city-owned property. Ayala described it as a concept, not a project that has been approved by the city. The idea could create a small public gathering space while improving pedestrian safety. He also sees opportunities to connect East End residents with jobs and provide technical assistance to people interested in starting or expanding businesses.
A view of the East End of Bridgeport on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
Housing is another piece. Vacant and blighted properties could potentially be redeveloped, while existing housing and property-improvement programs could be pursued as part of broader investment efforts in the neighborhood.
“I’m hoping that we get more home ownership,” Newton said. “Because you need a middle class … in order to sustain any community.”

A cat inside the ELA Discount Store on Stratford Avenue in Bridgeport on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Longtime East End resident Cherie O’Dea said new investment alone will not be enough. She said residents also need better access to education, job opportunities and basic resources that can help them take advantage of that investment.
“I think it goes farther than just the East End,” she said. “It comes from putting systems in place that actually help people — more education systems, more systems to help people get their licenses. Because a lot of us, we didn’t have a chance from starting out.”
Ayala said the designation is one tool that can help bring people and potential resources to the same table, but the outcome will depend on whether the ideas developed locally can attract funding and move into implementation.
Ayala believes the opportunity is there for the neighborhood many residents have argued has been ignored by economic development officials and developers for years. 
“We still have time to salvage it,” he said.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Gargantuan feedlot telegraphs woes for cattle and the environment
description: I was just reading about a feedlot in Nebraska, near where that state meets Kansas and Colorado. It is set to become the largest in the country, holding in one square mile up to 150,000 head — as many cattle as were driven here in 1886 during the peak of the great drives. After reading […]
text:
Cattle crowd a Kansas feedlot in 2022. Plans call for an enormous new operation in the region. (Jill Hummels for Kansas Reflector)I was just reading about a feedlot in Nebraska, near where that state meets Kansas and Colorado. It is set to become the largest in the country, holding in one square mile up to 150,000 head — as many cattle as were driven here in 1886 during the peak of the great drives.
After reading that I did some math. One cow slaughtered yields about 550 pounds of beef, or about a quarter of a metric ton. According to a recent social media post from President Donald Trump, he will allow 300,000 metric tons of beef imported tariff-free from countries not mentioned (mostly not even shown on the JBS website, the mega packing firm controlled by Brazilian billionaire and Trump donor Joesley Batista).
Afterward, the August Feeder Board dropped several dollars per head. I figured that much beef would come from 1.2 million cows. (Likely more than that. Those Brazilian cows don’t look as heavy in spite of being raised on tropical grasses all year long, maybe due to the parasites.)
Instead of riding in boxcars to slaughterhouses in Omaha, Chicago or Kansas City, these cattle ride in aluminum double-decker semi-trucks called “cattle pots” for, you know, where the waste collects. Maybe they’re roomier than boxcars, but who can say, watching those faces through the slots as you pass one on the highway.
Before the feedlots, these cattle have only known rolling pastures, or the welcome sound of the rancher’s truck bringing hay or breaking ice on the water tank. One day comes the confusion of being rounded up and trucked to pens with crushed concrete floors and robotic waterers and feeders, packed alongside other terrified animals.
There isn’t even natural darkness there, as intense lights flood the area and can be seen from the next county. Residents of the nearby town of Haigler don’t get to see the night sky either.
The swill they are fed is mostly corn and distiller’s waste from ethanol plants — an industrial system. No selective grazing among native plants, no exercise, no respite from the flies and other tormenters. Their weight swells as their veins clog. The hormones reboot their physiology, the antibiotics disrupt their gut flora and they belch methane, the gas that disproportionately heats the planet.
Excuse me if I mentioned antibiotics. Or is it the growth hormone we like to say isn’t used in beef production (wink, wink, nudge, nudge).
Backers in Canada promise jobs and prosperity (wink, wink, nudge, nudge). But as the trucks roll in and out, damaging road surfaces and raising dust, few stop at local businesses. Few locals find employment.
Talk at the Country Café in Haigler is often about water woes of the region, where the Ogallala Aquifer has dropped out of reach and the nearby Republican River is reduced to a trickle of bathtub warmth, devoid of dissolved oxygen. It’s not just the drought (although recent summers have rivaled the Dust Bowl). Most of those planted windbreaks are gone. So is the Rockies snowpack.
The Bluestem Bison Ranch near Glade and pasture-finished cattle operations farther east offer sustainable alternatives, if only granted a level playing field with the big boys, those multinational conglomerates with deep pockets but shallow concern for local enterprises.
Wendell Berry passed from this earth in August. He was an eloquent voice in the 1970s warning against the corporatization of agriculture and emptying of small towns, which he called the “Unsettling of America.” He lived to watch it happen. His talks at the Land Institute in Salina were inspiring and hopeful, and his poetry warms the soul like the Chinook winds.
The company says it will compensate for the massive water use of the feedlot and its waste management system by buying irrigated crop fields that will be retired (as they would have been anyway). Supposedly they will be replanted to prairie.
Anyone who believes this is possible knows nothing of a prairie. True prairie develops over centuries or longer where soils are deep. They take much longer on the high plains, where competition with cheat grass and other invasives requires intensive management.
Once the banks of the Republican were home to vast herds of bison, although at least they moved about over an area stretching from Dakotas to the Pesos. The Pawnee called it the river of “much manure,” and how prescient they were!
Bill Beachly was a biology professor at Hastings College in Nebraska for 27 years before semi-retiring near Concordia, Kansas (where he still works at Cloud County Community College).
